name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Increases in farm building assessments fuel calls to revisit Indiana’s property valuation system
text:
A wind turbine near a rural Indiana farm in September 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana farmers facing steep increases in building assessments are calling for changes to the state’s property valuation system, warning lawmakers Wednesday that similar structures are being assessed differently across county lines.
Indiana Farm Bureau representatives told the Interim Study Committee on Fiscal Policy that updated state cost tables have pushed up the assessed values of barns, grain bins and livestock facilities ahead of next year’s tax bills.
They urged lawmakers to address those discrepancies rather than leave individual property owners to challenge their assessments.
State officials acknowledged the concerns but cautioned that assessment changes alone would not resolve complaints about rising tax bills. They instead recommended preserving annual adjustments while improving assessment data and testing automated valuation tools.
Lawmakers also raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments climb as new or renovated houses change the surrounding market, and questioned whether new technology could help catch errors before taxpayers have to appeal.
The committee additionally heard an update on Indiana’s childcare voucher programs and proposals to finance expanded access ahead of the 2027 budget session. Discussions focused on sustaining the state’s recent voucher expansion and drawing more investment from employers, philanthropy and local governments.
Farm building increases draw concerns
Katrina Hall, Indiana Farm Bureau’s senior director of policy strategy and advocacy, said the organization commissioned Policy Analytics to examine agricultural building assessments after members began reporting large increases earlier this year.
The analysis initially showed a statewide increase of about 44% in assessed value for the agricultural buildings studied, she said. Later data, reflecting appeals and discussions with assessors, reduced that increase to 29% — still about $2 billion in additional assessed value for taxes payable in 2027.
More than half of the parcels in the later analysis had increases of at least 15%, Hall said. The figures show how much assessed values increased, not how much farmers’ tax bills will rise.
Story continues below.
attachment_6377
 
Hall said the discrepancies suggest a problem with statewide consistency. Some assessors made adjustments to the cost tables, she said, while others appeared to use them without similar changes. Identical buildings of the same age can consequently receive different values in neighboring counties.
She argued that appeals cannot substitute for correcting the underlying assessment process.
“Appeals are like a parcel at a time,” Hall said. “They are not fixing problems with assessing in the tax base.”
Farm Bureau wants the state to consider a nationally recognized valuation system, like Marshall & Swift, and examine outdated depreciation schedules. Hall said taxpayers seeking to challenge assessments often get appraisals using that system, creating a mismatch with the state’s tools.
The organization also proposed moving agricultural improvements from the 3% property tax cap category to the 2% category. Hall said its analysis estimated about $44 million in savings across agricultural properties.
That would be a tax relief change separate from revisions to assessment methods.
The proposals follow Indiana’s 2025 property tax overhaul, which changed homeowner deductions and credits, business personal property taxation and local government revenue rules.
A subsequent Indiana Fiscal Policy Institute analysis found that most homeowners would likely receive relief, but owners of low-value homes could face increases while more expensive homes received larger breaks.
State defends annual adjustments
Tim Rushenberg, general counsel for the Department of Local Government Finance, said Indiana can change its assessment tools, but the results must still meet constitutional requirements for uniform, equal and just valuations.
The department’s report explains that assessed value is only one part of a property tax bill, which also depends on local budgets, tax levies, deductions, credits and caps.
“An individual parcel can see a higher bill even when the district rate falls, or a lower bill despite increasing gross assessed value,” Rushenberg said. “There’s a lot of moving parts, so there is no reliable shortcut from gross assessed value to taxpayer impact.”
Annual adjustments, commonly called trending, help keep assessments aligned with market evidence between physical reassessments, he said.
Story continues below.
attachment_6376
 
Less frequent updates could reduce annual changes but allow inequities to accumulate and produce larger increases when properties are eventually reassessed. Limits tied to purchase prices or annual assessment growth could also raise constitutional questions if comparable properties receive different treatment.
Cost tables provide a common starting point for estimating property values, Rushenberg continued, but their results must remain open to challenge using credible evidence.
Barry Wood, the department’s assessment division director, said the state previously updated cost schedules once every four years. It’s moving toward annual review of the schedules or a related adjustment factor to help limit large fluctuations.
Rushenberg said the department wants construction costs, appraisals and other evidence to evaluate whether particular agricultural building schedules need correction. Public comments on readoption of the state’s real property assessment rule close Oct. 23.
“We want to look at the data,” Rushenberg said. “We’ve asked for data to see where, maybe in the cost schedule, something isn’t adding up there. But we certainly don’t want to make a general assumption that an entire schedule is is incorrect.”
Homeowners face hurdles, too
Rep. Cherrish Pryor, D-Indianapolis, raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments rise as new or renovated houses elevate housing prices, even when they have made no improvements themselves.
She urged officials to make the process easier to understand and reduce the need for homeowners to challenge inaccurate values.
“We live it, and so it’s easy for us, but it’s not easy for the average person, particularly if you’re an older individual,” Pryor said.
Wood said assessors can distinguish between different types and ages of homes within a neighborhood when applying adjustments.



Quotation







Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences.


– Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis


Automated valuation models could help identify inconsistencies requiring closer review, said Hamilton County Assessor Kevin Poore. An assessor-led pilot is underway in Hendricks, Clark, Lake, Vanderburgh, LaPorte and Allen counties.
The department recommended beginning with an advisory or quality-control pilot, retaining local assessor judgment and taxpayers’ notice and appeal rights.
Still, Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis, pressed for clear error measures and analysis of who would pay more or less before broader implementation.
“Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences,” Qaddoura said.
Childcare funding debate continues
Also Wednesday, Adam Alson, director of the Office of Early Childhood and Out-of-School Learning, said Gov. Mike Braun intends to continue the voucher expansion supported by a one-time $200 million infusion announced this spring.
“The additional 14,000 CCDF vouchers are funded solely with state dollars and for one fiscal year,” Alson said. “The governor is committed to continuing this increase in enrollment, and as such, this additional investment and allocation will be reflected in its upcoming budget.”
September figures presented to the committee showed 46,579 children enrolled across the Child Care and Development Fund and On My Way Pre-K programs, with 17,732 on their combined waitlists.
Story continues below.
attachment_6393
 
Regulated childcare capacity nevertheless fell about 3.3% from a year earlier, to 156,151 seats.
Alson said the administration is pursuing regulatory changes and additional ways for employers, philanthropy and local governments to invest.
Whitney Coake, a Taft public affairs director speaking on her own behalf, proposed a “QuadShare” framework combining employer, taxpayer, state and philanthropic contributions. It would fund expanded childcare assistance, 12 weeks of paid parental leave and an early care trust fund.
Her model estimated about $1.74 billion in annual operating expenses, separate from proposed trust fund deposits. Financing would include a 0.3% employer payroll contribution and a 0.15 percentage-point increase in the individual income tax rate. Philanthropic contributions and investment returns remain proposed or illustrative.
Alson emphasized that communities need flexibility to develop approaches suited to their families and employers.
“There are places throughout the state that are saying this is important,” he said. “How do we figure out how we do it?”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawsuit alleges MDOC staff filmed incarcerated woman while giving birth, violating privacy statute
text:
Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA new lawsuit filed Oct. 8 in federal court against eight employees of the Michigan Department of Corrections, alleges that the right to privacy of Natalie Forrest, who was incarcerated at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility at the time, when officers recorded her on their body cameras while she was giving birth to her son. 
“It was hard to be able to even try to connect with my newborn son, just for the simple fact that they were sitting there recording everything,” Forrest said in an interview. “I can’t even put into words how uncomfortable I felt. I felt degraded. I just felt like I couldn’t even actually enjoy the moment of my son being born.”
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Michigan, argues that filming Forrest while giving birth on March 8, 2025, violated Michigan’s criminal voyeurism statute — and that the Department of Corrections was notified on Feb. 17, 2025, nearly a month before Forrest delivered her baby that the policy in place allowing that filming to happen was illegal. Changes to the policy, which had also allowed correctional officers to record on their body cameras during strip searches, did not go into effect until March 24, 2025.
A spokesperson for the Department of Corrections did not respond to multiple requests for comment by Michigan Advance on the lawsuit. This story will be updated when a response is received.
Forrest described the practice of recording, up until she gave birth, as a pattern, adding that “There were multiple times where I was strip searched due to the simple fact that I had to leave the prison to go to doctor’s appointments for the baby, seeing that I was high risk. Every time that I had to leave the prison to go to a doctor’s appointment, they would strip search me, pregnant at all.”
Complaint ECF 1
According to the complaint, two correctional officers, one of them male, remained inside the delivery room with Forrest through cervical exams, labor and delivery, not outside the door or behind the privacy curtain, with chest-mounted cameras facing her bed. 
Maura Battersby, an attorney with Flood Law representing Forrest along with her minor son and her mother, who was present at the time of Forrest giving birth, described the situation in the lawsuit as “treating these women like they’re subhuman.”
Battersby emphasized that, even though incarcerated individuals have a lower expectation of privacy than non-incarcerated individuals, and some recording is necessary for the safety of guards and others in custody, she does not believe that there is a justification for recording during strip searches or similar nude settings.
“When you are incarcerated, you have a much lesser expectation of privacy than a citizen out in the world, not in custody,” she explained. “But as far as the standards go, and where it is more important, nude is top of the list as far as your expectation of privacy, even as an incarcerated individual.”
Recording during strip searches at Women’s Huron Valley was the subject of an earlier lawsuit from Flood Law against department leadership — and though a state circuit court dismissed that lawsuit, an appeal remains open according to online court records. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“You’re not supposed to follow an illegal order if you know that to be wrong. You are not supposed to do that. So I don’t think that absolves even just the corrections officers from doing that,” Battersby said of the recording policy. “From the top all the way down, there’s blame to be had all around there. They knew for a very long time this is what was happening. They were told by lawmakers … Part of our complaint in the exhibits shows the emails with the lawmakers saying this is illegal. You have to stop doing this immediately.”
Forrest emphasized that having officers who she did not know made her feel uncomfortable communicating with both her mother, who was present as her support person while giving birth, and her doctors. She also said that it made it harder for her to connect with her newborn son — something that was already difficult for her because she was incarcerated for the first months of his life. 
“I got less than 48 hours with him. They took my baby. My mom had to take my baby. I didn’t get to actually physically hold him, connect with him, see him,” she said. “And the simple fact that I’m sitting here thinking about the moment I gave birth to my son. It’s all recorded. Who knows where those recordings are? Who knows who has access to those recordings? Who knows what they could do with them?”
Forrest said that the whole experience continues to take a toll on her mental health, saying, “I still think about it every single day.”
The lawsuit alleges that after Forrest’s son was born, a corrections officer told her mother, who is also a plaintiff, that two years would be added to Forrest’s sentence if she took a picture of her newborn grandson in the hospital. 
Battersby said she was unaware of any mechanism for an individual officer to do that, adding, “What’s important is that it was meant to intimidate and meant to control, whether true or not. I would be interested to see what that complaint was or what any additional charge was for that.”
On March 14, 2025, eight days after her son’s birth, Forrest filed an internal grievance with the department, describing her experience which, the lawsuit claims, “described conduct constituting
sexual abuse as defined by the Prison Rape Elimination Act and MDOC’s own policy directives governing sexual abuse and the mandatory referral of such allegations to the facility’s PREA Coordinator rather than the ordinary grievance process.” 
Instead of referring the grievance to the Prison Rape Elimination Act coordinator, the lawsuit says that it was thrown out for being “Untimely,” despite Forrest’s arguments that, in her recovery from pregnancy, she submitted the grievance as quickly as was reasonable. An appeal of the grievance was also denied.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: A plan to introduce competitive bidding for these medical products will hurt patients
text:
Scheduled to take effect no later than Jan. 1, 2028, The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) says competitive bidding for ostomy supplies will lower costs for beneficiaries and reduce fraud, waste and abuse. But patients worry their choices will be limited in an effort to save money that could cause them harm. (Getty Images Creative)Do you know someone with an ostomy? I bet you do, but you might not know it.
The public often refers to an ostomy as a “colostomy bag.” But that’s an oversimplification.  An ostomy is a surgery that creates a new opening (stoma) on the abdomen for an individual to eliminate waste.
When the fit is right, most people get on with their lives. When it is wrong, the consequences can be immediate and deeply disruptive. It is this precise reason why Medicare’s decision to bring ostomy supplies into competitive bidding is bad policy.
Scheduled to take effect no later than Jan. 1, 2028, The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) says competitive bidding will lower costs for beneficiaries and reduce fraud, waste and abuse. These are both worthy goals. But saving money on an ostomy product is not necessarily saving money on healthcare—and fighting bad actors at the expense of patients’ access and choice is the wrong strategy.
As a patient, I know where the real cost can show up.
It shows up when my pouch leaks and effluent damages my skin.
It shows up when I cannot leave the house because I am worried about an accident, or when I lose sleep because I fear missing work.
And, in more serious cases, it shows up as a trip to the emergency room.
The fundamental problem with competitive bidding is that it treats products as though they are interchangeable, like a walker or knee brace. Ostomy supplies are not one-size-fits-all. They are prescribed to meet each person’s unique needs — stoma type and size, skin condition, body shape and lifestyle. I went through three different brands of skin barriers and bags before I found a combination that fit my body, and provided me with a sense of security.
Consider eyeglasses. A prescription that works for one person would not work for everyone. Ostomy supplies are no different.
Two products may look similar while behaving completely differently on an individual’s body. One person may need a particular adhesive because of their skin type. Someone else may require a specific pouching configuration for their body or lifestyle.
The federal government points to safeguards, saying that when a physician specifically prescribes a particular brand to avoid an adverse medical outcome, contract suppliers must provide it or help the beneficiary find a supplier that can. This all sounds reassuring on paper. But patients should not have to become medical advocates, insurance experts and supply negotiators every time they reorder the products that allow them to function normally. Nor should they have to wait until a problem becomes a documented “adverse medical outcome” before getting access to what works. Preventing complications is the whole point of good ostomy care.
I am not opposed to controlling Medicare spending. I want to eliminate unnecessary costs just like any taxpayer. But there is a difference between eliminating waste and creating incentives to substitute products that are cheaper but less appropriate for a particular patient. 
If a lower-priced product works perfectly for me, great. But the determination should be based on whether it works for me — not simply whether it won a bidding process.
An ostomy is already a profound adjustment. Many of us have had this life-saving surgery because of birth defects, cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, trauma or other serious medical conditions. We have learned to care for a part of our body in a way we never expected. We have adapted our routines and our sense of self. The least our healthcare system can do is recognize that the products we depend on are not interchangeable widgets.
The question should never be, “How cheaply can Medicare buy this pouch?” but rather, “What does this patient need to stay healthy, independent and out of the hospital?
I am reminded daily that when it comes to something as essential as managing my own body safely and with dignity, the lowest bid should never be more important than the right fit.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio early vote way up compared to 2022 but absentee ballot requests are down
text:
Early voters leave after casting their ballots. (Photo by Daniella Heminghaus/States Newsroom)Last week, Ohioans began casting ballots in this November’s midterm election. Voters will choose a brand-new slate of state-level leaders from governor to treasurer, a U.S. Senator, and representatives for Congress and the Ohio General Assembly.
With three weeks until election day, there’s still a lot of voting to come. So far, data from the Ohio Secretary of State indicate early in-person voting is up — by a lot — while absentee voting has slipped compared to the last midterm election in 2022. Taken together, early voting in the current cycle is running behind that election.
Voters have been moving away from mail-in voting for several cycles, but growing suspicion of the process among Republicans can hardly have helped.
Despite voting by mail himself, President Donald Trump has spent years attacking it. In just one of many examples, last year he asserted without evidence that “ELECTIONS CAN NEVER BE HONEST WITH MAIL IN BALLOTS/VOTING.”
In Ohio, state lawmakers have eliminated the grace period for late-arriving absentee ballots and proposed — but not yet enacted — onerous new requirements like including a photocopy of your ID when voting absentee.
Trump plan to limit mail voting hinders Democrats more than GOP, analysis finds

League of Women Voters of Ohio Executive Director Jen Miller said, “Absentee voting is secure and the most accessible method for many Ohio seniors, people with disabilities, military families, college students, and those who live far from their county Early Vote Center.”
“Absentee ballots are stored in rooms that require both Republican and Democratic keys to open,” she added. “Bipartisan teams of election workers work in concert to verify a voter’s identity before a ballot is mailed out and again when it is returned; otherwise, it won’t be counted.”
In the last few weeks, President Trump has changed his tune about absentee voting — a rhetorical reversal he’s made before.
Ohio 2022 early voting totals as reported by the Ohio Secretary of State on Oct. 18, 2022. (Photo by Ohio Secretary of State’s office)
The figures
In 2022, after a week of early voting, Ohioans had cast 50,368 ballots in person and requested 871,041 absentee ballots.
This year, 194,841 Ohioans have cast a ballot in person during the first week of early voting, or nearly four times as many as the previous cycle.
Statewide, counties have so far tallied about a third of the early in-person vote they saw in the entire 2022 election.
Franklin County, the strongest early vote performer that year, lags that statewide average slightly, but several other large counties are outperforming it.
Cuyahoga, Lucas, Lorain, and Summit counties — accounting for the Cleveland, Toledo, and Akron metro areas — have all already cleared 40% of their 2022 early vote totals.
At the same time, the number of absentee ballot requests has dropped by almost a quarter million.
So far, just 631,079 Ohio voters have asked for a mail ballot.
“I think it’s pretty easily explainable,” University of Akron Political Scientist David Cohen said. “The President of the United States for the last 20 months has been claiming that voting by mail is not secure.”
Trump’s last minute bid to boost absentee voting gets overshadowed by his past statements and actions, Cohen said.
He pointed to the president’s attempt to commandeer the U.S. Postal Service to impose new voting restrictions as one example.
The U.S. Supreme Court chose not to intervene in that case after a lower court barred the administration from going forward.
Cohen also brought up state lawmakers nixing Ohio’s grace period.
Trump drops longtime aversion to mail-in voting with GOP trailing in polls

“I think there are a lot of people on both sides of the aisle now that don’t actually trust (voting by mail),” he said, “and would prefer to just do it in person to ensure that their votes count.”
In terms of demographics, older voters make up the biggest share of the total so far. Seniors, for instance, have accounted for more than half of the ballots cast through Monday.
Democrats and unaffiliated voters lead Republican voters to this point. Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, and unaffiliated voters account for a little more than 67,000. GOP voters have cast nearly 64,000.
Although a lot can happen between now and Election Day, Cohen thinks those figures offer a warning for Republicans.
“If we believe the public opinion polling that we’ve seen,” Cohen said, “about two-thirds to maybe even three-fourths of those independent voters are voting Democrat this year.”
“There’s a reason that Donald Trump keeps coming back to Ohio,” he added, “and it’s not to vacation and it’s not to play golf.”
Follow Ohio Capital Journal Reporter Nick Evans on X or on Bluesky.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bookman: Ossoff’s presidential ambitions are undeniable
text:
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff at an Atlanta rally Aug. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderThe late Harry Reid saw a lot of people come and go during his 30 years in the U.S. Senate. In an oral history with Columbia University, he recalled the first time he saw a newcomer from Illinois, a man named Barack Obama, deliver a speech on the Senate floor.
“I walked over to him. He’s sitting at his desk. I look down at him and I said, ‘Senator, that was really a good speech. That was good.’ He looked at me so seriously, and so intently, without a hint of braggadocio, and said, ‘I have a gift.’”
Jon Ossoff also has a gift, and like Obama, he knows it.
How could he not?
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He’s running up 10-point poll margins in his Senate re-election campaign, in a state that Donald Trump carried two years ago. Brian Kemp, Georgia’s popular but term-limited Republican governor, decided that discretion was the better part of valor and declined to run against Ossoff. The national press sees him as a telegenic star. And in his debates with his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, Ossoff has had Collins wriggling at the podium like a worm impaled on a fish hook, just as he did with David Perdue in his first Senate campaign six years ago.
So people have noticed. People are talking. People are talking about the White House. Democrats love him. Republicans fear him. Donors flock to him. And like another white Southern Democrat, Bill Clinton, Ossoff has earned enough faith and confidence from Black voters to take him a long way in Democratic primaries, should he choose to run.
Yet Ossoff insists he’s not running and will not run. He gets asked the question in interviews and debates, and he has been steadfast in his rejection of a 2028 presidential campaign. As recently as his debate this week in Atlanta, he said he had “zero interest” in running and pledged to Georgia voters that if he is re-elected, he would serve his full six-year term in the Senate. 
Of course, they all say that. Obama said the same thing when he was running for the Senate in 2004, claiming to have no interest in the White House. Like Ossoff, he had two young daughters, ages 6 and 3 at the time, and a wife and partner who was skeptical of politics. He dismissed the idea of a presidential run as silly.
But party leaders, including Reid and Ted Kennedy, saw Obama’s talent and twisted his arm, reminding him that you don’t get to pick your time to run for president, the times pick you. 
And as we know, by the end of 2008, Obama was president-elect.
I have no doubt that Ossoff intends to be president. He’s been a man in a rush, elected to the Senate at the age of 33, the youngest senator in 40 years. The politician that we now see before us is the product of a lot of hard work and preparation for seeking the ultimate goal.
However, I also think Ossoff is being honest when he says he has no intention of running in 2028. He comes across as a man who sets his own timetable, who makes his own decisions and sticks by them. His self-discipline is part of his gift.
He is also 39. It will be another eight years before he turns 47, which happens to be the same age Obama was when first elected president. In 14 years – another three presidential cycles from now – Ossoff will still be just 53, and entering what for most people is their political prime. He has time to pick his time.
But the main reason I doubt Ossoff will run in 2028 is that his seatmate in the Senate, Raphael Warnock, is himself taking all the steps that a wannabe presidential candidate would be taking at this stage. He is visiting early primary states, raising his national profile, refusing to rule out a campaign.
Ossoff and Warnock are close friends and political allies. They campaign together, strategize together, spend time together. Given that relationship, it seems inconceivable that the two men haven’t discussed the 2028 presidential cycle. If Warnock is as serious about a presidential run, as he seems to be, then I take Ossoff at his word that he is serious about his refusal to run. They would draw from the same voter base and donor base, making both weaker, and it’s hard to imagine them as opponents.
So, if there’s a Georgia Democrat running for president in 2028, it will probably be Warnock. If there are two Georgians running for president in 2028, it will be Warnock and Kemp. 
There won’t be – probably won’t be – three Georgians seeking that office.

title: Cleveland State University latest Ohio college to offer free tuition for qualified in-state students
text:
Cleveland State University in July 2026. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal)Cleveland State University will be offering free tuition for qualified first-year students starting next year. 
Cleveland State University Board of Trustees recently approved the Cleveland State Commitment, which is for incoming first-year students with at least a 3.0 GPA who are Ohio residents whose families have an adjusted gross income of $125,000 or less. 
Qualifying students will not pay tuition for up to eight consecutive semesters.  
“For too long now, the dream of a college education has not been possible for many Ohio families simply due to the cost,” Cleveland State President Laura Bloomberg said in a statement. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We firmly believe that access and excellence are fundamentally linked. The Cleveland State Commitment rewards hard work by opening doors and providing a financial boost for those who need it most.” 
Cleveland State will cover any tuition remaining after federal and state grants and scholarships are applied. 
Students will need to complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid every year to determine eligibility. Students will remain eligible by maintaining a 2.0 GPA, full-time enrollment and the family income requirement. 
The Cleveland State Commitment only covers tuition. It does not cover housing, meals, books, transportation, or program-specific fees. 
“Cleveland State University is providing the certainty Ohio students and families want from higher education,” Ohio Department of Higher Education Chancellor Mike Duffey said in a statement. 
“If you make the grade and have demonstrated need, Cleveland State will pick up the full cost of tuition for four years. This is a great initiative and I strongly support it.” 
Cleveland State undergraduate tuition for a full-time, in-state student is $6,828.00. 
Cleveland State’s enrollment has been on the decline, according to the Ohio Department of Higher Education.  

12,872 students enrolled during fall semester 2025
13,999 students — fall semester 2024 
14,160 students — fall semester 2023  
14,500 students — fall semester 2022  
15,413 students — fall semester 2021  
15,331 students — fall semester 2020  
15,630 students — fall semester 2019 

Other Ohio universities also offer free tuition to qualifying students. 
The University of Akron offers free tuition for new, transfer and continuing students whose family income is $85,000 or less and are residents of Summit, Stark, Medina, Portage, Cuyahoga or Wayne counties.
Shawnee State University’s Free Tuition Guarantee covers full tuition for first-time, full-time freshman who qualify for a Pell Grant and live in Scioto, Lawrence, Adams, Pike, Jackson, Ross, Gallia, Brown, Highland, and Vinton counties, or Greenup, Boyd or Lewis Counties in Kentucky.  
Columbus State Community College students can finish their bachelor’s degree at Ohio State University tuition-free starting this semester through a new initiative called the Buckeye Bridge. 
It’s good universities are looking at the affordability issue, said Jennifer Tisone Price, executive director of the Ohio Conference of the American Association of University Professors. 
“We believe that college needs to be affordable and accessible to all,” Price said. “But the next question is, how are they paying for this? And that follow-up issue is making sure that they’re not doing so on the backs of faculty.” 
About 1.78 million student borrowers live in Ohio and the average student loan debt is $35,072, according to the Education Data Initiative.
Nearly half of Ohio’s borrowers are younger than 35 and 15% of Ohio residents have student loan debt, according to the data. About a fifth of Ohio borrowers owe between $20,000 to $40,000, according to the data.

title: Trump slashed healthcare for Ohio families and spiked premiums. Now he’s offering small checks.
text:
(Getty Images)Do you celebrate an arsonist who brings a cup of water to a fire they started? Is the president a hero for cutting small, health care relief checks to people struggling under his destructive policies that include the largest rollback of federal support for health care in American history? 
Will Ohioans being wiped out by spiking premiums, out-of-pocket costs, and less medical coverage be wowed by what Ohio AFL-CIO chief Tim Burga called Trump’s attempt to “buy votes” weeks before the midterms? 
Or will voters view the legally questionable windfall from a convicted felon the way Burga does — as a lame PR stunt that does little to move the pre-election needle and “reeks of desperation”? 
You decide why a president, facing historic lows in approval ratings, rushed ACA and Medicare checks to millions of Americans with campaign-like letters boasting about his greatness and signed in Sharpie Marker. 
You weigh why the Affordable Care Act money was only doled out to a subset of enrollees — most Obamacare enrollees will not receive any — who also (by pure coincidence) live in many states with tightly contested U.S. Senate races. 
Scrutinize, too, the propaganda notes attached to Trump’s $500 Obamacare “refund” checks. 
The missives sent to households in prime political battlegrounds (falsely) accused the Biden administration of “overcharging” Americans for their health care and touted Trump’s commitment to “put America first, restore affordability, protect your hard-earned money, and lower the cost of healthcare.” 
Put a pin in those easily debunked claims. 
Trump also offered electioneering cash (attempted bribes?) to 20 million traditional Medicare Part B enrollees to offset monthly premiums of about $200 for a program that covers outpatient care, doctor visits, preventable care, etc. 
Like the narrow scope of insured who received ACA checks, Trump’s one-time payments of $90 for eligible seniors  excludes roughly 35 million Medicare Advantage enrollees, (who make up over half of Medicare beneficiaries) plus other people with disabilities and low-income Medicare recipients. 
This midterm sweetener will cost the government $2 billion and come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, created by Congress to improve program management and conduct oversight of contracts and contractors. 
The funding has been diverted before to expand healthcare coverage through the ACA, but it has never been used to directly pay recipients. 
Is any of this legal? Trump writing Medicare and ACA checks without Congress? He has thrown another frontal assault on Congress’ constitutional power of the purse, but no court has blocked either payment yet.
Putting the rule of law aside, (as Trump does on the daily) the political impact of his money giveaway in the waning days of the 2026 midterm campaign is negligible in Ohio. 
Don’t get me wrong. The estimated 70,000 Ohioans who got $500 ACA checks, out of the roughly 336,000 Ohio residents who still get their health insurance from the ACA marketplace, cashed them. 
So did the 748,000 seniors in Ohio — less than a third of the total 2.5 million Medicare recipients in the state — who received Trump’s legally dubious $90 checks. 
But the Trump pay-outs to seduce voters clobbered economically by Medicare Part B monthly premiums (that went up nearly 10% in 2026 and will climb again in 2027), or ACA premiums (set to jump 14.7% next year by the 11 remaining insurance companies on Ohio’s federal marketplace) probably won’t cause Ohioans priced out of medical care to swoon. 
They know the truth. They crunch the numbers over strained budgets. Trump, and every Republican in Congress, gutted their health care funding to finance a trillion-dollar tax break for billionaires and corporations.
Last year GOP lawmakers on Capitol Hill also blocked healthcare subsidies that lowered health insurance costs for over 20 million Americans. 
Monthly ACA premiums more than doubled for many enrollees. Some 160,000 Ohioans, (a third of those enrolled in the state) who simply could not make those monthly premium payments, lost their healthcare coverage. 
Ohio led the nation in the highest percentage of ACA enrollment decline with a staggering 32.4% drop-off between February 2025 and February 2026. 
Now the state faces more than $33 billion in lost Medicaid funding over the next decade, thanks again to Trump and his compliant congressional Republicans, including Ohio U.S. Sens. Jon Husted and Bernie Moreno, who voted for the ridiculously named One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
More than 3 million Ohioans, nearly 1 in 4 residents, depend on Medicaid, including 40% of all children in the state. 
Trump’s signature healthcare package, which slashed federal Medicaid funding by $911 billion over a ten-year period, could soon end government-sponsored health insurance for hundreds of thousands Medicaid users in Ohio just trying to get by. 
When new OBBB Medicaid work rules kick in January 1, researchers estimate millions of working Americans could lose their coverage. 
The federal changes — which create heavy administrative and procedural burdens that often strip eligible low-income adults of health insurance — are expected to purge up to 356,000 Ohioans from Medicaid. 
As coverage falls access to health care across Ohio disappears. 
Eleven rural and safety-net hospitals in Ohio face risk of closure because of Trump’s 2025 spending law cuts to Medicaid. 
Hospitals across the country have already begun cutting services and jobs in response to the devastating measure heralded by the president and his Republican puppets on the stump as their chief legislative accomplishment.
But go ahead, mail out checks to mitigate the damages wrought by the sender. Just don’t expect voters to be dazzled by a drop in the bucket that does nothing to put out the fire.

title: History: When Ohioans came to watch the synagogues rise
text:
This historic Isaac M. Wise Temple in Cincinnati (Getty Images file photo)In 1836, Cincinnati’s small Jewish community dedicated a synagogue.
It was reported to be the first building erected as a synagogue in the western United States. The congregation behind it, B’nai Israel, had been organized twelve years earlier. When it received a charter from Ohio in 1830, it counted 32 adult men and 20 adult women.
The synagogue did not rise through the congregation’s efforts alone.
According to an account published several years later in “The Occident and American Jewish Advocate,” 52 Christians had each given $25 toward its construction. When the building was dedicated, so many Christian neighbors came that not everyone could be admitted. The congregation gave preference to local clergy and to the families of those who had contributed to the building.
Ohio’s Jewish population would grow considerably in the decades that followed. Congregations formed and new synagogues rose in Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus and elsewhere. Again and again, their construction became a public occasion.
In Cleveland, the Jewish community was still new enough in 1845 that a synagogue cornerstone laying attracted significant attention.
A “large number of citizens” gathered as members of Anshe Chesed laid the cornerstone for a new building on Eagle Street. “The Cleveland Herald” predicted that the synagogue, when completed, would be “an ornament to our flourishing city.”
When the congregation opened the following year, it had about 70 members, and a newspaper noted that its members had “received some aid from other citizens.” Hanging on a wall inside was a framed inscription:
“A testimonial of gratitude to J. M. Woolsey, Esq., and Lady for their liberal assistance in erecting this edifice.”
Jewish worship also required some explanation.
A reporter at the dedication described the women’s gallery, hats being worn during worship, the ark and the Torah scrolls kept inside it. A tallit became a “light shawl.” The bimah was described as an “Altar.”
“As the consecration of a synagogue is somewhat new in this quarter,” the newspaper explained, “we will briefly describe the ceremonies.”
Members of the congregation formed a procession at their former place of worship and carried five Torah scrolls to the new synagogue. Reaching its doors, they chanted in Hebrew:
“Open unto us the gates of righteousness.
“O, let us enter and praise the Lord.”
Not every observer regarded Judaism generously. “The Cleveland Plain Dealer,” writing about the dedication, called the worshippers “deluded people” who had resisted Christianity for 1,800 years.
Public welcome and religious prejudice occupied the same city at the same time.
Twenty-two years later, another synagogue cornerstone was laid in Cincinnati.
Protestant ministers attended. Beneath the cornerstone went copies of the Declaration of Independence, the United States Constitution, the Articles of Confederation and George Washington’s Farewell Address.
Rabbi Max Lilienthal, a speaker at the occasion, declared, “America is our Palestine; here is our Zion and Jerusalem!”
Lilienthal rejected the expectation of a restored Jewish kingdom governed by an earthly Messiah. Instead, he spoke of Washington and the signers of the Declaration of Independence and looked toward a time when people would live together in “brotherly love, peace, justice and mutual benevolence.”
One newspaper ended its account with another detail about the rabbi.
“This is the same Rabbi who preached some time ago in a Christian church.”
Two years later, thousands gathered in Columbus.
It was May 1870, and the city’s Jewish community was laying the cornerstone for what would become its first purpose-built synagogue, at Friend and Third streets. Bands played as fraternal organizations and public officials joined the procession, while people crowded around the foundation to watch.
Rabbi Isaac Mayer Wise of Cincinnati spoke for more than an hour on what he called human dignity.
“God hath made man upright,” Wise told the crowd, drawing from Ecclesiastes.
The new synagogue, he said, would proclaim not only the unity of God but the dignity of human beings. Wise rejected the idea of inherited depravity and original sin. Human beings were free moral agents, he argued, responsible for what they did.
“God is just, and you are free,” he said.
“God is love supreme, and man is His image.”
The synagogue would stand, Wise said, as “the fortress of defense to the holiest and highest treasure of the human family, the divine acknowledgment of human dignity.”
When the building was dedicated later that year, “The Israelite” reported that Christians took pride in its construction. Members of the congregation remembered assistance from “the liberal and pious of all sects.” Jews and Christians gathered together for the first Friday evening service.
The relationship continued outside the sanctuary.
In 1872, municipal officials allowed the congregation to use City Hall for a fair that helped pay the remaining debt on its synagogue. Among the attractions were contests to elect the fair’s “mayor” and “marshal.” The winning mayor received a gold-tipped cane.
The winning marshal received a revolver.
When the congregation promoted a concert at the Opera House later that year, it publicly thanked Columbus residents for their “liberality in assisting them in the erection of their house of worship.”
Similar scenes continued as Ohio’s Jewish communities grew.
In Cleveland in 1886, Anshe Chesed began another synagogue, this time at Scovill Avenue and Henry Street. The cornerstone ceremony became what one newspaper called “the most extensive festival in the history of local Judaism.” About 4,000 people gathered.
Members of the Masons took part in the ceremony, which included remarks from former Cleveland mayor George W. Gardner and closed with a prayer from a Unitarian minister. Sunday school children and members of several Jewish congregations joined a procession through the streets to the new temple.
“Every square foot of standing room on the temple floor was occupied,” a reporter observed, while late arrivals stood outside in the street.
The synagogue was dedicated the following year. Again, Jewish and non-Jewish Clevelanders came. City officials and Christian ministers were among those present. An American flag hung outside. Two more stood on either side of the ark.
In the yard was a sign bearing a single word:
“Welcome.”
By the beginning of the twentieth century, Columbus’ first synagogue was no longer large enough for its congregation. A new building rose on Bryden Road.
More than 1,000 people witnessed its cornerstone ceremony in 1903. The Ohio Grand Lodge of Masons participated. The mayor spoke.
Rabbi David Klein thanked the congregation’s “neighbors and friends.”
“Judaism is a faith pure and simple and sublime,” he said.
If Judaism required a creed, Klein continued, it might be this: “One God over us all, and in Him all his children must form one brotherhood sustained and animated by the spirit of the Father.”
Above the entrance would appear words from Isaiah:
“For my house is a house of prayer unto all nations.”
When the synagogue was dedicated in 1904, one of its three dedicatory services was devoted to “good fellowship.” Ministers from Congregational, Universalist and Methodist churches participated. The president of Ohio State University spoke of Jews as “the teachers of the nations.”
Klein told those gathered that the new temple was open to people of all creeds.
More than six decades had passed since Cincinnati’s first synagogue opened its doors to a crowd of Christian neighbors. None of these stories erases the reality of religious prejudice or disagreement. But the crowds are difficult to miss.
For decades, Ohioans gathered as synagogues rose in their cities. Some helped build them. Others simply came to watch.
Inside, Ohio’s Jewish communities spoke for themselves.

 Catching Our Eye

• AI-driven white-collar job layoffs have arrived in Ohio. The Associated Press reports, “Kroger to lay off 3,000 corporate employees over 3 years as it leans into artificial intelligence.”
Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.
“Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.”
• Bernie Moreno apparently wants to weaponize the government to go after the press for reporting on possible corruption. Cleveland.com’s Sabrina Eaton reports, “Bernie Moreno seeks federal probe into ABC News story on Trump sons’ Anduril investment.”
U.S. Sen. Bernie Moreno wants the Federal Communications Commission to investigate ABC News over a story about President Donald Trump’s sons and defense contractor Anduril Industries that the network pulled from its website, then republished with corrections.
In a Saturday letter to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, the Avon Republican described the story’s “flagrant lies” as “personal” to Ohio because Anduril is building a factory worth more than $900 million in Pickaway County.
• FBI using Flock in Ohio. The Dayton Daily News’ Eileen McClory reports, “FBI accessed Dayton Public Schools Flock data for ‘immigration,’ records show.”
Outside agencies accessed Dayton Public Schools Flock camera records thousands of times, including multiple times where the outside agency listed the reason as “immigration,” and thousands more where the reason is unclear, according to records obtained by the Dayton Daily News.
• Obama coming to Ohio. The Columbus Dispatch’s Haley BeMiller reports, “Obama to stump for Sherrod Brown, Amy Acton in Ohio.”
Former President Barack Obama will return to Ohio this month as Democrats fight to reclaim the governor’s mansion and a key U.S. Senate seat.
Obama will join gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton and former Sen. Sherrod Brown at a Cleveland rally on Oct. 24. The event marks Obama’s first visit to the Buckeye State since 2018, when he campaigned for Rich Cordray amid a hotly contested race for governor.
• MAGA Pac supporting Ohio socialist candidate? The Associated Press reports, “Mailers promoting a socialist candidate in Ohio Senate race have links to MAGA super PAC vendor.”
Campaign mailers urging Ohio voters to support a socialist U.S. Senate candidate over Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown are being underwritten by a newly incorporated PAC with ties to President Donald Trump’s MAGA Inc., public filings show.
The mailers are sponsored by Enough Promises Ohio PAC and began arriving in voters’ mailboxes in recent days. They promote independent candidate Greg Levy over Brown with messages such as “Join the Revolution” and “Send a Worker to the Senate.” Levy describes himself as “Socialist running for the U.S. Senate to represent Ohio in 2026” on his X account.

title: Powell and Harding duel it out in Nebraska 2nd District debate
text:
Republican nominee Brinker Harding, left, and Democratic nominee Denise Powell before the 2nd Congressional District debate in Lincoln on Oct. 14, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Democratic nominee Denise Powell and Republican nominee Brinker Harding dueled it out Wednesday in the second Nebraska 2nd Congressional District debate, hosted by Nebraska Public Media. 
Powell and Harding are competing to replace Rep. Don Bacon, who decided not to seek another term in Congress, in Nebraska’s most politically divided and diverse congressional district. The two also had a debate on ABC’s affiliate KETV last week. 
On Wednesday, the pair were asked questions on topics including the Iran war, affordability, bipartisanship, Social Security and immigration.
Throughout the debate, each tried to paint the other as extreme, as they’ve been doing throughout the campaign.
In opening remarks, Powell said she is running because she loves Nebraska and wants to address affordability. Harding said he also would address affordability and make Washington more accountable, while dismissing Powell as an outsider in Nebraska. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Harding said the Iran war needs to “be settled as quickly as possible,” emphasizing that Nebraskans are feeling the “pain in the pump.” He added that Iran can’t be allowed to have a nuclear weapon.  
“We need to be energy independent, and we got lost under the Biden administration with the Green New Deal. That was something,” Harding said. “Now we have to rely on foreign despots and their energy, and so we need to get a quick resolution to that and bring the price of gasoline and fuel down.” 
Powell said she had been opposed to the war since the beginning, saying the Trump administration didn’t have a “good plan.” 
Democratic nominee Denise Powell, right, and Republican nominee Brinker Harding are seen through a viewfinder before the 2nd Congressional District debate  in Lincoln on Oct, 14, 2026. (Juan Salinas II)
“This is not popular. We need to get a handle on this. … While I absolutely agree that Iran should never have a nuclear weapon, nothing about this conflict or the way this administration is handling it is making America any safer,” Powell said, “On the contrary, I think it is putting us at great risk.” 
The two were asked what issues they would be willing to work on with the other party — as the slightly red-leaning 2nd District is known as a swing district. Powell said she would work across party lines on “everything.” Harding said his city council record shows he can be bipartisan. But Powell contended that his record doesn’t show him doing that. 
Harding said that in the primary, Powell was fighting for the “blue dot” and not for everyone else in the district. Powell pointed to Harding’s endorsement by President Donald Trump.
After a question about federal tax breaks to benefit private schools, Harding claimed that Powell supports “sex education” for kindergartners and “transgender surgeries” for minors. 
Powell said that is not true, saying she does “support comprehensive health education that is age-appropriate for kids in schools, and I support a parent’s right to decide whether or not that’s right for their kid.” 
“Of course I don’t support children having risky surgeries; I do believe that parents, their physicians and their children deserve to have the right to access information while navigating their difficult conversations,” Powell said. “That’s not why I’m running. I’m running because there are kids in this state that can’t go to a doctor anymore because their parents lost their health insurance.” 
Nationally, Republicans have used transgender rights as a wedge issue against Democrats, specifically whether trans athletes should be allowed to participate in girls’ sports. Some Democrats running have tried to distance themselves from the issue or called it a distraction. 
Libertarian Eric Michael Foreman is also running for the 2nd District seat. He wasn’t a part of the debate; he held a live conversation on X Space. 
There is one more debate between Harding and Powell later this week. The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already begun.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: New Florida stormwater rules don’t fix our pollution problem
text:
A typical stormwater retention pond in a Florida community is both a visual amenity and a poorly functioning pollution control device. New standards were supposed to make the stormwater system more effective, but the Florida DEP removed their teeth. (Photo via Southwest Florida Water Management DIstrict)Do you have a favorite movie? Mine is “Singin’ in the Rain.” Maybe because I grew up in the rainiest city in Florida, Pensacola. I could identify with Gene Kelly splashing around in all those puddles.
You know what you never see in “Singin’ in the Rain”? Where all that rainwater goes. It swirls around the pavement, but you never see it slosh into a stormwater drain. It’s one clue Gene’s dancing on a Hollywood set, not a real street.
Gil Smart via Vote Water
We Floridians know that stormwater never simply disappears. We try to drain it away as fast as possible, and it then flows into our canals, creeks, rivers, bays, estuaries, and oceans. Often, it’s carrying a load of pollution from fertilizer, cars, and leaking sewer plants.
The stormwater system originally set up under state law — drains, ditches, and retention ponds galore — has generally failed to clean up that flow. Instead, it’s fueled serious toxic algae blooms that have wiped out seagrass beds, starved manatees, and killed fish.
The Florida Legislature, to its credit (and my great surprise), took steps to clean up our stormwater runoff.
“But since then,” the Tampa Bay Times reported last week, “the state’s environmental agency has quietly taken the teeth out of another new program meant to help local governments and developers meet these stricter stormwater rules. It has raised concerns from environmentalists who say meaningful efforts against Florida’s water pollution are being undercut.”
You may read that and think, “Oh, those tree-huggers! They’re never satisfied.”
Wait until you see the very next paragraph.
“Even the companies working with developers are unhappy with the changes. Three businesses have formally challenged the rule, saying the environmental agency’s actions went beyond its authority.”
You know Florida’s pollution regulations are messed up when even the companies working with developers think the Florida Department of Environmental Protection isn’t actually, you know, protecting the environment.
“Clean water takes a back seat to the ‘need’ for Florida to keep growing at all costs,” said Gil Smart, executive director of Vote Water. “And with moves like this, the state is ensuring that cost will be high.”
Fort Lauderdale airport after rain-bomb, via screen grab
 A major source
We call ourselves the Sunshine State, but that’s just a lie we tell the tourists so they’ll come on down and spend their money.
The truth is, most of our cities get more annual rainfall than famously drizzly Seattle. Four show up on this list of the rainiest cities in America: Pensacola, Jacksonville, Miami, and Tallahassee.
Sen. Gayle Harrell (Photo via the Florida Senate)
We need the rain to refill our aquifer, where we get most of our drinking water as well as the wet stuff we sprinkle on our lawns, crops, and golf courses. (Don’t get me started about the water bottlers who pay the state a pittance to suck a lot of the public’s water out of the ground and sell it all over the world.)
Thanks to climate change, the storms are becoming heavier. Three years ago, Fort Lauderdale got hit by what some people called “a rain-bomb” — 26 inches in 24 hours. That’s a level of precipitation that would make Noah n-n-nervous.
When you’re drenched by such a deluge, your stormwater infrastructure better be built to handle the load. A lot of Florida stormwater infrastructure is not, because it was built before we started seeing these larger quantities of liquid sunshine.
The first Florida rules for handling stormwater came out in the 1980s, but they ignored a lot of the pollutants we now know are important. Worse, they were based on rainfall data from the prior decade.
Yet regulators assumed that if you built everything the way they required, you’d clean up the pollution.
Those rules “did not sufficiently address water quality, and therefore, water quality continued to deteriorate,” a Florida Bar analysis says. “Additionally, there were no real maintenance requirements, so systems that were effective when permitted degraded over time.”
When the Times did a special report last year on water pollution, here’s what it found regarding stormwater runoff: “In 2007, regulators discovered the methods were a bust. Far more chemicals fouled the environment than officials originally believed. Florida leaders didn’t fix the problem. They let matters get worse.”
In 2010, state regulators drew up tougher new standards for storm runoff. But they never got beyond the draft stage. Their progress was stymied by opposition from big-money developers. It was like watching your favorite football team’s drive for a winning goal get stymied at the 5-yard line.
The results are about what you’d expect.
Take, for instance, the Miami River Canal, which WLRN-FM reported on in May. The canal, which the radio station described as “one of the backbones for South Florida’s drainage system,” begins at Lake Okeechobee and cuts 60 miles across three counties to deposit its tainted load into Biscayne Bay.
“It has repeatedly failed to meet limits for fecal coliform, the bacteria found in human and animal waste,” the radio station noted. “It contains nutrients, heavy metals and microplastics. Fish are loaded with mercury. The canal is also not unique. Canals across South Florida carry stormwater loaded with chemicals.”
Far be it from me to accuse the Legislature of dragging its feet about remedying this problem, but I’ve seen gopher tortoises that moved faster. Nevertheless, two years ago, our fine lawmakers passed a bill pushing for tighter rules.
“Stormwater is a major, major source of nutrient pollution in our waterways,” said Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Republican who runs a Stuart health strategies company and sponsored the 2024 bill, “These rules are in place to make sure that we are going to improve our natural waterways.”
But those good intentions didn’t go far enough.
 Loosey-goosey
This year the Legislature passed a different stormwater bill, one sponsored by Sen. Keith Truenow, a sod grower from Mount Dora.
This bill allows the state to do something unusual. Rather than force every new development to cut pollution in its own stormwater runoff, the bill says the DEP can instead use a system similar to its wetland protection rules. The rules had to be in place by this month.
State Rep. Keith Truenow via Florida House
This is a system that I think you could best describe as “loosey-goosey.” It allows developers in one place to buy “credits” from people who are cleaning up pollution in another place.
Officially, this system is called “mitigation banking,” but I think of it as the Wimpy Evasion, based on what that character used to tell Popeye: “I will gladly pay you Tuesday for a hamburger today.”
You’ll have to excuse my skepticism about any mitigation banking scheme. In the early 2000s, I teamed up with another reporter to investigate Florida’s lucrative and growing wetland mitigation banking industry.
We found lots of problems. There were banks that counted dry land as if it were wet and banks that considered preserved wetlands as if they had been newly created. They employed the kind of creative accounting you’d see at a CPA firm called “Dewey, Cheatem & Howe.”
Which leads us to the Water Quality Enhancement Areas, or WQEAs for short.
Here’s how the Times explained WQEAs: These areas allow landowners “to earn credits for cleaning up pollutants — mainly nitrogen and phosphorus — on their property. Landowners can then sell credits to developers that need to curb stormwater pollution generated from projects like condominiums and commercial developments.”
Haley Moody via Linkedin
This allows the developer to still pollute the nearest waterway while writing a check to someone who is cleaning up pollution on a different parcel.
These mitigation banking systems CAN work. But the key to making them effective is setting up checks and balances that would keep everyone honest.
“If you’re going to mitigate off-site, then you need to know if it’s working,” said Haley Moody, executive director of the Florida Springs Institute in High Springs.
But the DEP isn’t interested in making sure the system works.
The agency only cares about making it look good on paper.
 Loopholes in the diet
Picture the new stormwater regulations as a way of putting all the developers on a really strict diet. The goal would be to trim the excess stuff they’re putting into the runoff.
Now picture the developers holding their big tummies, moaning and complaining that the diet is just too haaaaaaaaarrrrrrrrrrrrrrd! Oh, they’ll never be able to meet these requirements! Have mercy!
So, the DEP gave them some ways to get around the restrictions — like dieting but not dieting. Every day is Cheat Day!
“It’s just providing them an easy out,” Smart told me.
The DEP initially issued draft regulations that could have worked. But then the agency changed them to accommodate the whiners — er, excuse me, developers.
“Some of the really important language was removed,” Moody said.
And the agency did it in such a way that anyone who might object didn’t have much time to complain.
Kim Dinkins via 1000 Friends of Florida
“The changes were made fairly late in the process,” said Kim Dinkins, policy and planning director of the smart-growth group 1000 Friends of Florida.
One change the DEP made eliminated any chance of ensuring the companies selling credits are actually reducing the pollution, she explained.
The agency decided it doesn’t need to measure the pollution that’s supposedly being eliminated between the inflow and outflow of the stormwater system, Dinkins said. There’s just a computer model for the system that may or may not prove accurate.
Given that this is the same agency that came up with a computer model for issuing water supply permits that’s got more holes than a Swiss cheese factory, I’m not holding my breath for the accuracy of this one.
Even worse, the DEP decided it would be OK to issue the “credits” for sale before checking whether the clean-up work has actually cleaned up anything, Dinkins told me. They’re giving credit before any such credit is earned.
Audubon Florida managed to get its objections to these provisions on the record before the DEP adopted them. The DEP’s response to these objections was … well, let’s just say it wasn’t warm and sunny.
“They essentially told us to pound sand,” an Audubon Florida representative told the Times. “Those companies got DEP to make changes, but after years of work on the rule, DEP really should explain why it added these provisions so late and did not give the public a fair chance to review them.”
I asked the DEP about this, and a spokeswoman replied: “The department reviewed and considered all comments that were received timely throughout each rulemaking step, and changes to draft rule language were made when deemed appropriate or necessary.”
There’s another big problem with the new DEP rules, Moody told me. They focus only on what’s happening above ground.
“There’s no mention of what happens under the surface,” she said.
All that pollution occurring on the surface can infiltrate the caverns deep underground where our aquifer flows, she explained. That’s a problem for our water supply.
It can also harm Florida’s spectacular springs, many of which are owned by us taxpayers as part of the state park system. But I’m not sure the people in charge care.
 Tap-dancing as fast as they can
Recently, there have been some journalistic efforts at assessing Gov. Ron DeSantis’ environmental legacy once his eight years in office conclude. It’s not a pretty picture, considering this is the guy who built a tent city prison in the Everglades and tried to put golf courses in the state parks.
It’s especially icky when the topic is water quality.
As a candidate in 2018, DeSantis promised to fix our toxic algae bloom problem, but then disregarded what a panel of scientists told him to do.
Instead, he cut a deal with an Israeli company to dump a hydrogen peroxide mixture in waterways afflicted by the blooms. That’s only a temporary solution, like treating a broken arm with a Band-aid.
Given how much the guv hates rainbows, I guess it makes sense that he doesn’t care much about stormwater either. As a result, his DEP has been trying hard not to put its foot down in a way that would hurt the politically powerful development industry.
Instead, the agency has been desperately dodging accountability, tap-dancing faster than Gene Kelly in a flooded street scene.
I don’t know which candidate will take over from DeSantis next January, or what the top priorities will be. But in the interest of sheer honesty, we should consider changing the DEP’s name to something that more accurately reflects its performance. I’d propose “the Department of Enabling Polluters.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Flock cameras: public safety and privacy can coexist
text:
Recently West Hartford police have been involved in two high-profile cases where automated license plate readers helped officers locate vehicles they were looking for.
So, what exactly is an automated license plate reader?
Simply put, these cameras read license plates and can alert police when a vehicle connected to a stolen car, wanted person or criminal investigation passes one of them. Here in West Hartford, we know many of these devices as Flock cameras because they are made by Flock Safety.
I think we need to have an honest conversation about them, especially as we approach another election season.
I understand the concerns about Flock cameras. People have legitimate questions about privacy, how long information is stored, who can access it and which agencies can receive it. Those questions deserve answers.
At the same time, we shouldn’t ignore what has happened right here in our community.
On September 29, Middletown police were searching for a suspect in a homicide. Information about the vehicle connected to that investigation was shared with other law enforcement agencies. A Flock camera in West Hartford alerted police to the vehicle. Officers located it, and after a pursuit that continued into Hartford, the suspect was eventually taken into custody.
Just a few days later, West Hartford police received another automated license plate reader alert, this time for a stolen BMW M6 in the New Park Avenue area. Detectives located the BMW and another vehicle that had been traveling with it. Two men were arrested. Police said one was driving the stolen BMW and the other was found carrying an illegal firearm.
These aren’t the only examples.
In August, an officer in Saratoga Springs, New York, received a license plate reader alert for a vehicle wanted by Rocky Hill police in connection with a homicide. The officer located the vehicle and the suspect was taken into custody.
Think about that. A police department in Connecticut was looking for a vehicle connected to a homicide, and an officer in another state was able to receive that information while on patrol.
That is what this technology can do. So where does the controversy come from?
For me, the concern isn’t whether the technology exists. The concern should be how we make sure it isn’t abused.
Put policies in place. Limit how long information can be kept. Make sure officers have a legitimate law enforcement reason to search the system. Keep records of who accesses it. Audit those searches. Establish consequences when someone misuses the information.
Connecticut has already taken steps in that direction with new rules governing how automated license plate reader information can be accessed, retained and shared.
Law enforcement agencies have shared information with each other for decades. That isn’t new. What has changed is how quickly information can now get from one department to another.
When police are looking for someone accused of a serious violent crime, minutes matter.
Could police have eventually located the individuals involved in these three cases without license plate readers? Maybe. We will never know. What we do know is that in each case, this technology provided officers with information that helped them locate a vehicle they were actively searching for.
I believe Flock cameras, when used properly, can be a valuable public safety tool.
That doesn’t mean giving law enforcement unlimited access to people’s information. It doesn’t mean ignoring privacy concerns. And it certainly doesn’t mean operating these systems without oversight.
It means recognizing the value of the technology while putting strong protections around its use.
We can protect people’s privacy while also giving police tools that can help locate stolen vehicles and people accused of serious crimes. Those two things don’t have to be in conflict.
We should demand both.
Alberto Cortes lives in West Hartford.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Key takeaways from Maine’s fourth and final gubernatorial debate
text:
Maine's three candidates for governor, (left to right) Republican Bobby Charles, Democrat Hannah Pingree, and independent Rick Bennett, met on October. 14 for their fourth and final debate. (Screenshot courtesy of WMTW)The three candidates running to be the next governor of Maine — Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles, and independent Rick Bennett — met for the fourth and final time on the debate stage Thursday evening. 
In the hour-long debate, hosted by WMTW, the candidates touched upon familiar topics, including housing, education, immigration enforcement, healthcare, and the state budget. 
The event also highlighted several key dynamics that have emerged in the race, with Charles frequently attacking Pingree, seen as the frontrunner, often repeating falsehoods about her record serving in the administration of Gov. Janet Mills and as former speaker of the Maine House of Representatives. 
Charles also accused Pingree of corruption, saying without evidence that she used her position in the Mills administration to secure a loan from MaineHousing for a nonprofit now run by her husband, Jason Mann. According to the Bangor Daily News, North Haven Sustainable Housing received an $840,000 forgivable loan from MaineHousing for rental units. Pingree said she was not involved in the award.
At one point, he also said these facts “are on ProPublica,” an apparent reference to the investigative outlet’s recent report on allegations of corruption surrounding Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins — not Pingree.
Bennett, who left the Republican Party to run as an independent, used those moments of finger-pointing to highlight what he described as the toxicity of the two-party system. Meanwhile, Charles rebuffed accusations that he has moderated his positions since the GOP primary. Maine Democrats have accused him of trying to mislead voters, an allegation he disputes.
At one point, Pingree brought up an audio clip leaked to the Bangor Daily News in which Charles said he would ask Trump administration border czar Tom Homan to send U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. marshals “to be at our voting booths.”
Charles denied that he said that. “I never invited them into the polls,” he said.
Here are some other take-aways from Thursday’s debate:
On affordability, who’s to blame?
A key issue across the state is the rising cost of living, something moderator Jon Chrisos touched on repeatedly. But the candidates’ responses showed that when it comes to the reasons behind the state’s current economic challenges, some are looking at Augusta while others have their eyes on Washington, D.C. 
In response to a question about energy prices, Pingree noted that the rising cost of natural gas and storm recovery expenses “are the primary driver of Maine’s electricity rates,” and said she would rein in utility profits, invest in clean electricity and efficiency to help make energy more affordable. But she quickly pivoted to the war in Iran and the need to become less reliant on imported fossil fuels. 
“I will just say that my opponent Bobby Charles has supported Donald Trump’s war in Iran, his tariffs that have raised energy prices,” Pingree said.
In response, Charles was quick to pin energy prices on Pingree, who served several years as director of Mills’ Office of Policy, Innovation and the Future focusing on climate, workforce development, housing, issues facing youth and older Maine people, the opioid crisis, and Maine’s long-term economic prosperity — not energy.
“Hannah Pingree was in charge with Janet Mills for the last six and a half years and beyond…She owns this issue,” Charles said. Pointing to rate increases in recent years, he added, “That is not Trump’s fault. Now, a reminder that Maine is spelled M-A-I-N-E, not T-R-U-M-P.” 
Later, in response to a question about what the candidates would do to address the closure of healthcare facilities, Pingree repeated her support for a public insurance option, increasing investments in primary and maternity care, and making a plan to keep birthing clinics open. But then again she pivoted to Trump. 
“I will say that Donald Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill is going to make it much much worse,” Pingree said. “Cuts to Medicaid, Medicare, cuts to our prescription drug programs. We’ve already lost (Affordable Care Act) coverage for thousands of Maine people, so the job is not going to be easy.” 
Charles said the Mills administration expanded MaineCare but did not fund it, even though 90% of Medicaid expansion is paid for by the federal government. He said if elected he would raise the state’s reimbursement rate for healthcare providers and incentivize doctors to practice in areas of need.
Bennett said “both Hannah and Bobby are correct” that the healthcare system is “under assault by the Trump administration.They’ve also been under assault by inaction by the Mills administration.” He said the closure of 12 birth centers “were lost while (Pingree) was in office working with the governor on healthcare.”
Chrisos clarified that Pingree did not work for the state health department or on issues related to healthcare. 
Not party people
Each candidate also made a point to distance themselves from the establishment parties, which polls have shown to be consistently underwater in terms of favorability.
Pointing to Washington Post reporting that after the GOP primary, Charles’ campaign website “removed references to MAGA for Bobby Charles and other Trump-related material,” Chrisos asked the Republican about his relationship to Trump and the MAGA movement.
“At the end of the day, there are things that Trump’s done right, and there are things that he’s done wrong,” Charles said. 
Reiterating his opposition to tariffs and the war in Iran, he continued, “I’ve never met the guy. I have no pictures with him, but I’ll interact with him, and I’ll have a good relationship, because we need a relationship with the federal government that will help Mainers.” 
When Vice President JD Vance came to Bangor in August, Charles did not attend, though Vance said he’d “been an amazing fighter for the state of Maine,” and would “make a more amazing governor.”
And despite Pingree’s high profile role in the Mills administration, she outlined the ways she disagreed with the governor, including Mills’ opposition to tribal sovereignty, the data center moratorium, the red flag law and some labor bills. She also said she would tackle challenges with healthcare and housing in a “much more accelerated way.”
“We don’t all agree in the Democratic Party, and I think that’s how it should be,” she said.
Bennett, who formerly chaired the Maine GOP and served for years as a Republican in the Maine Legislature, was put on the defensive when asked why he left the party. He said, “in recent years, I’ve come to the conclusion that the parties are actually a large part of the problem of our democracy.”
Describing partisan bickering as “toxic and off-putting,” he said, “The fight goes on and on and on, and people’s needs aren’t met. We need to get back to a politics of compromise and collaboration. The party candidates can’t do that.”
But Pingree pushed back. Acknowledging that Bennett was always “independent minded,” she said he’s a lifelong Republican who only left the party when he decided to run for governor, “because he knew he couldn’t beat Bobby Charles because the party has gone MAGA.”
“You could have left the Republican Party on Jan. 6,” she said.
