title: Democrats aiming for control of Congress vow action on healthcare, cost of living, Iran war
authors: Shauneen Miranda, Ariana Figueroa, Ashley Murray, Jonathan Shorman
text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats are touting an ambitious legislative agenda centered on affordability and accountability if they take back the U.S. House or Senate — or both — in November. A slew of pressing policy debates are on tap for Democrats, including healthcare, immigration, voting rights, the war in Iran, oversight, education and beyond, as they aim to reverse many of President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans’ actions since January 2025. Some issues, while surging to the forefront, likely will provoke internal divisions, such as “Medicare for All,” a movement popular among progressives to extend single-payer national health care to all Americans. “Healthcare costs have consistently been at or above other concerns on the public's affordability worries,” said Liz Hamel, a senior vice president and director of public opinion and survey research at KFF who oversees the nonpartisan health organization’s polling program.Democrats also are poised to conduct tougher oversight of the Trump administration.

 






(Photo by Getty Images)

Any legislation from Democrats faces the threat of Trump’s veto, making any legislation without broad bipartisan support almost certain to fail. In addition, Democrats would need a filibuster-proof majority of 60 votes to advance most measures in the Senate.Democrats remain heavily favored to regain the majority in the House, while Senate races continue to move in the party’s favor, amid Trump’s plummeting popularity, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, an elections forecaster. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats, including two independents who generally vote with the party.“House Democrats are committed to fighting for an affordable America, lowering the high cost of living, lowering the cost of groceries, lowering the cost of gas, lowering the cost of housing and fighting to make healthcare affordable for every single American,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters in September. The New York Democrat is in line to become the next speaker — the first Black person to hold that office — if the party clinches control of the lower chamber. Jeffries announced five working groups on affordability — housing, healthcare, gas and utilities, groceries and goods, and caregiving — which House Democrats will concentrate on at the beginning of the new Congress. The Democratic Party’s campaign apparatus for House races echoed an agenda centered on affordability. “House Democrats are going to win the majority because voters know we’re focused on lowering costs, and that’s exactly what we’re going to do when we’re in charge,” Nebeyatt Betre, a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson, said in a statement shared with States Newsroom.“From ending the war in Iran to lower gas prices, restoring (Affordable Care Act) tax credits to lower health care prices, to rolling back reckless tariffs to lower prices on everything in between, House Democrats’ number one priority will be making life more affordable for working families,” Betre said. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the corresponding campaign arm for Senate races, cited healthcare access and affordability as a top priority in a Democratic-led upper chamber. “I think the most important issues that I’ve heard from voters is restoring their healthcare, making sure that those cuts to Medicaid get restored, making sure that people can afford healthcare and get access to good, high-quality healthcare,” Gillibrand said in a September interview with States Newsroom and other members of the Regional Reporters Association. 

 







Dozens of Kentuckians with disabilities and their loved ones and advocates came to Frankfort and pleaded with elected officials to find a way to protect the services they receive through Medicaid waivers, on July 17, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)

The New York Democrat, who leads the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said other major priorities include “trying to fix the problems Trump has created, end the war in Iran” as well as getting “costs of groceries, housing, and healthcare and other everyday costs down.” While not a major part of the party’s messaging in the general election, House Democrats are poised to take a harder line with Israel amid the country’s war in Gaza. Jeffries said a measure meant to discourage violence in the West Bank, where Israeli settlements have inflamed tensions, “should be considered” next year, according to The Hill. With less than three weeks to go until Election Day on Nov. 3, here’s a closer look at what Democrats want to accomplish in both chambers: Anti-corruption, impeachments Democrats are all but certain to open investigations into the Trump administration if they gain power over congressional subpoena decisions.“Our promise to the country in the new Congress is that beginning on Day One, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable,” Jeffries vowed at an Oct. 8 press conference. High-ranking Democratic House members say multiple probes are on the table, including Trump’s IRS settlement, brokered by his administration’s Justice Department, which delivered retroactive tax audit immunity for him and two of his sons as well as the creation of an “anti-weaponization” fund.A federal judge slammed the settlement in a July order prohibiting Trump, his sons Eric and Donald Trump Jr., and the Trump Organization from claiming they reached a “settlement,” and referred Trump’s personal attorneys to the bar for investigations. Democrats are also weighing whether the party would attempt to impeach Trump if they take back control of the House. The president was impeached twice in the House and acquitted twice in the Senate during prior sessions of Congress. Jeffries told PBS Newshour in September “we certainly haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out,” when asked about any impeachment proceedings against the president if Democrats regain the majority in the lower chamber. 

 







President Donald Trump headlines a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)

Democrats could also try to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth if they clinch control of the House. Outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September for the secretary’s handling of the war in Iran.But House GOP leadership sent the lower chamber home early for its weeks-long campaign break, punting any vote until after the midterms. House Democrats will also likely dog the administration’s legally mandated release of files related to the 2019 federal sex trafficking investigation of deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, who kept the company of powerful and wealthy individuals, including Trump.Trump denies any knowledge of Epstein’s involvement in trafficking girls and young women for sex.Democrats and Republicans on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform opened a months-long probe, subpoenaing documents from the Epstein estate and compelling closed-door testimony from Epstein associates and former Attorney General Pam Bondi. Healthcare On the healthcare front, House Democrats want to undo the healthcare provisions tucked into a mega tax and spending cut law signed by Trump in July 2025, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”  “Undoing (that law) is the floor, but not the ceiling,” according to a September memo obtained by Politico from Democrats’ affordability working group on healthcare. The 84-page memo proposes myriad healthcare policy priorities in the first 100 hours, first 100 days and first year of the next session of Congress, broken down into eight wide-ranging categories. “There is broad consensus in the Democratic caucus that the Democratic agenda must both reverse the immediate harms of the administration while also taking bold action to rein in corporate monopolies, invest in a durable healthcare system, and pursue an ambitious path towards universal coverage,” per the memo.  

 







Hundreds of public workers rallied outside the Statehouse in Trenton, New Jersey, on June 18, 2026, to demand lawmakers rein in rising healthcare costs. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)

Part of Democrats’ healthcare agenda includes reversing the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law’s sweeping Medicaid cuts, which axe roughly $1 trillion in program spending over 10 years and impose new work requirements.The party is also looking to “permanently restore” the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, which expired in December 2025 and were used by individuals who buy their own health insurance through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace. The expiration of those credits has “sharply increased” individuals’ out-of-pocket costs toward premiums, according to KFF. The memo also underscores a commitment to “achieving universal coverage” in the first year of the next session of Congress, and mentions the “Medicare for All Act” as one avenue to examine in achieving this ambition. The bill would establish a national health insurance program administered under the Department of Health and Human Services. Iran warThe costly war in Iran that has caused prices at the gas pump to soar for Americans is a major reason for Trump’s sagging poll numbers, and Democrats, if the House and Senate flip, would likely pass a measure to try to end any further conflict without congressional approval.The war has cost $40 billion and counting, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, and will continue to cost American taxpayers $2 billion to $3 billion per month as the conflict drags on.The national average price of diesel remains above $6 per gallon in the U.S., according to AAA, as Iranian officials continue to block petroleum products from reaching the global market. The national motor club, which monitors daily fuel prices, reported that Americans were paying a national average of $4.33 for a gallon of gasoline as of Oct. 14.

 






Gas and diesel prices at a station in Silver Spring, Maryland, on Oct. 12, 2026. (States Newsroom photo)

Meanwhile, Democrats’ attempts to rein in Trump’s military campaign in Iran have slowly picked up some Republican support over multiple votes in both chambers.Senate Democrats have forced 14 War Powers Resolution votes to curb Trump’s unilateral military decisions without input from Congress. The votes are privileged, meaning they can be brought to the floor without the blessing of majority leadership.The measure has advanced twice in the upper chamber, but the latest attempt to advance a House-passed War Powers Resolution narrowly failed, 49-50. House Democrats picked up seven Republicans on Sept. 15 to approve the War Powers Resolution. Administration officials contend the War Powers Resolution, established by Congress during the Vietnam War era, is unconstitutional, so it’s unclear what might happen if a resolution were approved. Immigration To help the president carry out his mass deportation campaign, congressional Republicans used a legislative tool to skirt Democratic support and allocate more than $200 billion for immigration enforcement through two measures. With the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” more than $170 billion was given to the Department of Homeland Security to hire more immigration agents, expand detention centers and carry out deportations. The “Secure America Act” funded Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement until late September 2029, at nearly $70 billion, after Democrats refused to approve funding for DHS following two deadly shootings of American citizens by immigration officials in Minneapolis. Though it’s unlikely Democrats will be able to claw any of that funding back even if they take both chambers, there are several avenues they are likely to pursue amid the president’s immigration crackdown. The first avenue is oversight and the ability to subpoena Trump officials. Democrats are likely to hold oversight hearings into the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were shot and killed by federal immigration officials in Minneapolis in January. Members of both parties on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee reached rare bipartisan agreement at a grilling of top Trump immigration officials after the killings. Democrats will also likely hold hearings on the scores of U.S. citizens detained by ICE and also shot by federal immigration officers, such as Marimar Martinez, who has already appeared several times before lawmakers as the minority witness for Democrats. She was shot in her car five times by Border Patrol agents during the aggressive immigration deportation campaign in Chicago in October 2025 and was labeled a domestic terrorist by DHS. The DOJ dropped charges against Martinez after the Trump administration accused her of using her car as a weapon.

 







Bypassers stop by a memorial to Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the Biddeford, Maine resident and father who was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)

Democrats are also likely to continue with oversight at federal facilities that detain immigrants, including the high death toll of immigrants at those detention centers. So far, 61 immigrants have died in ICE detention, which has doubled under the second Trump administration. Democrats have demanded answers from the administration about the deaths, along with concerns about medical neglect at the facilities. And even though former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem stepped down earlier this year, Democrats still plan to question some of her decisions while leading DHS, such as a $220 million ad campaign that prominently featured her and the practice of no-bid contracts awarded to her close allies. Apart from oversight, Democrats are likely to introduce and pass legislation related to immigration reform, such as creating a pathway to citizenship for immigrants who were stripped of their Temporary Protected Status and for children brought into the country without legal authorization under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA. The Trump administration has stripped more than 1 million immigrants of their legal status, and House Democrats, with a handful of Republicans, in April moved to extend TPS for more than 500,000 immigrants hailing from Haiti. TPS is granted to nationals who hail from a country deemed too dangerous to return to due to violence, disasters or other destabilizing forces.In the Senate, Democrats have tried to pass legislation through unanimous consent to grant a pathway to citizenship for TPS recipients, but were blocked by Republicans. If Democrats regain the Senate, they will need a 60-vote majority for that legislation to move ahead. Some Democrats in Congress also likely will advocate an end to funding for ICE, but it’s unclear whether that would have enough support to advance.Voting rights and democracyVoting rights and democracy are likely to be high priorities for Democrats if they retake one or both chambers of Congress. A gerrymandering war egged on by Trump and a U.S. Supreme Court decision this spring that severely weakened the federal Voting Rights Act left Democrats and their base deeply angry and eager for action.Democrats are likely to again turn to the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, named after the late civil rights activist and Georgia Democratic Rep. John Lewis. Though the U.S. House last passed the measure in 2021, the bill did not advance through the Senate. The legislation would seek to restore preclearance, a major provision of the Voting Rights Act that was previously blocked by the Supreme Court in 2013. Preclearance required states and local governments with a history of discrimination to obtain federal permission before making voting changes, and it applied to most Southern states and a handful of others.

 







A woman raises a fist as protesters march on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama as part of the All Roads Lead to the South rally on May 16, 2026. The two rallies, protests against redistricting efforts by southern Republicans, drew over 5,000 people. (Photo by Andi Rice/Alabama Reflector)

“We fight to pass the John Robert Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act so we can end the era of voter suppression in the United States of America once and for all,” Jeffries said in an August speech.The renewed focus on the voting rights legislation comes after the Supreme Court in a 6-3 decision in April sharply weakened Section 2 of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. The section prohibits voting practices or procedures that discriminate on the basis of race and other characteristics. In 1982, Congress expanded Section 2 to ban voting practices that have a discriminatory effect, whether or not the law was intended to discriminate.Louisiana had redrawn its congressional map in response to a court order to include a second majority-minority district where a majority of residents are Black. The Supreme Court ruled the new map was an unconstitutional gerrymander.In response, several Southern states quickly redrew their congressional maps to eliminate majority-minority districts — part of a larger wave of gerrymandering that swept the country over the past two years after Trump initially urged Texas to enact a more GOP-friendly map.In response, some Democrats are also pushing for gerrymandering reform. At a minimum, some lawmakers want to require states to return to a once-a-decade redrawing process. That was the norm before 2025, and followed the census every 10 years.Over the summer, the bipartisan House Problem Solvers Caucus unveiled a framework for changes to the redistricting process. The proposal calls for restricting new maps to once a decade, requiring “clear, objective” criteria to draw lines and supporting steps to reduce partisan influence, such as turning to independent commissions to develop district lines.Education Congressional Democrats also want to halt and undo the administration’s ongoing efforts to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education and repeal major education provisions in the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law.The department has entered into a series of interagency agreements with other departments that transfer several of its responsibilities to those agencies, including Health and Human Services, Labor, Interior, State, Justice and Treasury. If Democrats take back the Senate, Virginia Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine told States Newsroom his first goal in education is to “stop the handoff of critical components of (the Education Department) to other agencies that don’t want them.”In the most-far reaching of the interagency agreements yet, the department said in June that HHS would administer programs under Education’s Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, while civil rights enforcement under Education’s Office for Civil Rights would be transferred to the DOJ. 

 







From left, Olivia Sawyer and Jeremy Bauer-Wolf protest the U.S. Education Department’s mass layoffs during a "honk-a-thon" and rally March 14, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)

Kaine sponsored a bill, with GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska as original co-sponsors, that would block interagency agreements that transfer programs regarding special education, elementary and secondary education, postsecondary education and Native American education. That measure advanced out of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions in July. Sen. Mazie Hirono told States Newsroom “we need to restore federal support for education and how it’s going to look, I mean, clearly we need to support IDEA and support it to a greater extent than we have normally,” pointing to the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which guarantees a free public education for students with disabilities.The Hawaii Democrat is also looking to repeal a national school voucher program baked into the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law that’s set to launch in early 2027. The program allocates up to $1,700 in federal tax credits for people donating to organizations that provide K-12 scholarships, with 31 states having opted in so far. Hirono and Arizona Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, joined by more than two dozen of their colleagues, introduced legislation in April to repeal the program. Wisconsin Democratic Rep. Gwen Moore introduced a companion bill in June with Reps. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, Maxwell Frost of Florida, Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, Mark Pocan of Wisconsin and dozens more original cosponsors.

title: Trump’s DOJ demands California halt ballots to suspected noncitizens
text: The U.S. Department of Justice is demanding California not count ballots from voters it says are suspected noncitizens, a move by the Trump administration to apply last-minute pressure as voting begins in the midterm elections.The Justice Department on Tuesday gave California election officials 48 hours to remove voters on a list contained on a thumb drive provided to Los Angeles County, the most populous county in the country. The DOJ also wants election officials to withhold mail ballots from these voters. The demand appeared in letters to the California Secretary of State’s Office and the Los Angeles Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk. The DOJ gave the state until noon Eastern on Thursday to comply, threatening legal action if that deadline is not met.The letters set the stage for a courtroom confrontation between the Trump administration and the largest state in the country ahead of Election Day. The Justice Department’s demand marks an extraordinary effort to dictate to state officials who will be allowed to cast a ballot even as voting is underway.“The United States hopes that you share our commitment to ensure that only American citizens participate in our federal elections. Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes,” R. Trent McCotter, an acting deputy U.S. attorney general, wrote in a letter to California Democratic Secretary of State Shirley Weber.Questions lingerIt’s not clear whether the Justice Department plans to send letters to additional states. The Justice Department provided copies of the letters to States Newsroom on Wednesday but didn’t answer a question about whether other states would receive them.In the letters, McCotter asked California election officials to segregate the mail ballots of the suspected noncitizens until their citizenship status is determined. The individuals shouldn’t be sent mail ballots if they haven’t already been sent one, McCotter added, and any returned ballots should not be tabulated until citizenship can be determined.McCotter did not say how many individuals are on the DOJ’s list or how the federal government came to believe they aren’t citizens. He wrote that the Justice Department would “seek emergency relief” if California didn’t comply. Requests for comment to Weber’s office and the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk weren’t immediately returned. A request for comment to California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office was referred to the California secretary of state’s office.Voter roll changes prohibited during election seasonFederal law prohibits most states from conducting systematic purges of voters less than 90 days before an election. If the Justice Department sues to force California to remove the suspected noncitizen voters, a judge would likely grapple with whether the DOJ-provided list represents the kind of mass removal that’s not currently allowed.Voting rights groups and Democratic election officials, as well as some Republicans, have warned that Trump may try to interfere in the midterm elections. If Republicans retake control of the U.S. House or Senate, the final two years of the president’s term could be mired in investigations and legislative gridlock.Federal courts have uniformly blocked the department’s efforts to force states to turn over their voter rolls, including sensitive personal information such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. And a federal judge last week ruled against the DOJ’s use of voter data even from states that voluntarily provided the information.The U.S. Supreme Court also blocked Trump’s attempt to restrict voting by mail through the U.S. Postal Service, leaving the president with few remaining avenues to assert authority over elections, which are administered by the states under the U.S. Constitution.“Donald Trump’s attempt to invalidate votes in California is an attack on every voter across the country. The president is abusing his position in a callous attempt to take away the power of everyday people, but here in California we’re not going to let him,” Jonathan Paik, a leader with Can’t Stop California, a nonpartisan voter mobilization group, said in a statement.Trump has long complained about California elections, especially the speed of ballot counting in the state. California’s long count is a well-known feature of its elections, with election officials given about a month to process and tally all ballots and doesn’t indicate fraud.The Justice Department has followed Trump’s lead in scrutinizing California’s elections. The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles has linked suspicions about California’s elections to the state’s refusal to turn over its unredacted voter roll.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State office building to reopen after multi-year, $70M renovation
text:
The Jim Thorpe Building is pictured on the Oklahoma Capitol Complex on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — After three years and $70 million of renovations, state leaders announced Wednesday that the Jim Thorpe Office Building on the Oklahoma State Capitol Complex is reopening. 
The Oklahoma Corporation Commission, the state Election Board, the Oklahoma Arts Council and the Oklahoma Water Resources Board will occupy the building and lease space from the Office of Management and Enterprise Services. 
The building, located southeast of the Capitol at 2101 N. Lincoln Blvd., was renovated with funds appropriated in 2023. 
Mark Wood, director of OMES, said the project was focused on preserving what makes the Jim Thorpe building special while creating an accessible and functional government workplace.  
Mark Wood, director of the Office of Management and Enterprise Services, speaks about the reopening of the Jim Thorpe Office Building on the Oklahoma Capitol Complex on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
“Jim Thorpe’s name carries a remarkable legacy in Oklahoma,” he said. “… We hope this building continues to be a place worthy of his name and the example he left for future generations of Oklahomans and Americans.”
Thorpe, a Native American of Sac and Fox and Potawatomi descent, was a highly successful Oklahoma athlete who competed in the Olympics and played both professional baseball and football. 
Thorpe died in 1953, but some of his descendants were in attendance at Wednesday’s ribbon cutting ceremony. 
Budget chair Sen. Chuck Hall, R-Perry, said while it’s easy to focus on new ideas and projects in government, it’s also important to preserve what’s already been built. 
“We must balance investing in Oklahoma’s essential infrastructure with being responsible stewards of taxpayer dollars,” he said. “We also have a responsibility to preserve the places that tell Oklahoma’s storied history and pay tribute to Oklahoma legends, while ensuring our residents continue to benefit from the state assets that they paid for.”
Hall said the tenants of the building will use it to serve Oklahomans every day which makes it a worthwhile investment. 
“This building is going back to work,” he said. 
Bonnie Campo, director of outreach for OMES, said some finishing touches need to be completed, such as furnishing offices, before the building’s tenants move in. Agencies are expected to move in this winter, she said. 
Paul Ziriax, election board secretary, said their agency will maintain its public-facing offices at the Capitol and use space at Jim Thorpe for some administrative functions. 
New artwork was commissioned by the Oklahoma Arts Council through the state’s public art program, according to a news release.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Board of Regents adopts early warning rule for college athletics deals with private equity
text:
The Kansas Board of Regents adopts new policy guiding development of agreements between public university athletic departments and venture capital or private equity companies. Negotiations must be disclosed to Board of Regents leadership and the board will review deals prior to implementation. In this July 2025 image, a statute of University of Kansas coach Phog Allen stands outside Allen Fieldhouse. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Board of Regents amended policy to require officials at the six state universities to notify the higher education board’s leadership of discussions about partnerships between intercollegiate athletic departments and private equity or venture capital firms.
Text in the policy regarding disclosure of “material discussions” likely to lead to proposed agreements was left intentionally vague, but the rule required university officials at some juncture to notify the Board of Regents’ CEO and the board’s chair. In addition, the policy says all contracts and agreements between a university athletic department or athletic-affiliated corporation and entities engaged in private equity or venture capital must be approved by the Board of Regents before implementation.
It’s unclear why the Board of Regents convened a special meeting Friday to unanimously approve the policy rather than wait until a regular meeting Wednesday in Wichita.
The Big 12 Conference’s university presidents and chancellors in April ratified a five-year financial arrangement with College Athletic Solutions, which is a partnership between RedBird Capital Partners and Weatherford Capital. RedBird Capital is a private equity firm with ownership ties to networks offering sports programming. The investment firm Weatherford Capital has a stake in IMG Academy, a $102,000 per year boarding school for athletes in Florida.
The agreement didn’t transfer university or Big 12 governance authority, ownership interests or revenue rights to College Athletic Solutions.
The Big 12 office received $12.5 million to promote commercial development. Each of the 16 conference universities were given the option of taking a $30 million line of credit. The interest rate on the cash would be near 10% and repaid through conference revenue sharing. The partnership with the Big 12 could eventually serve interests of all parties when the conference negotiated a new media rights contract in 2031.
Kansas State University and most other Big 12 schools said they wouldn’t accept the $30 million credit line. The University of Kansas said it hadn’t decided whether to take the offer.
An earlier draft of the policy was revised to declare the Board of Regents wasn’t assuming oversight of coaches’ contracts, sports conference agreements or name, image and likeness deals involving athletes.
“We want to make sure, of course, that we are supportive of the universities … as we look at the fact that we do have a lot of critical short-term sort of financial issues in terms of athletics,” said Alysia Johnston, chairwoman of the Board of Regents from Edna in southeast Kansas. “We want to make sure, of course, that does not jeopardize anything that we should do long term.”
She said the board would be able to go into executive session to avoid disclosure of proprietary information or trade secrets of companies seeking to do business with university sports programs. Final votes by the Board of Regents would be subject to the Kansas Open Meetings Act.
“We’re just trying to make sure that down the road … we don’t somehow do something that would remove control or be a detriment to the finances or to the sustainability of not only the athletics programs but the universities in general,” she said.
Regent Blake Benson of Pittsburg asked about clarifying for university officials what was meant by policy text that says notice to the Board of Regents must occur “before engaging in material discussions that are likely to lead to a proposed transaction, agreement or arrangement” between a university and outside investment business.
He appeared concerned use of the phrase “material discussions” in the policy might not be universally understood.
Board of Regents general counsel John Yeary said the disclosure requirement wouldn’t be triggered during an initial meeting between a university and a private equity company.
“I think the idea is … if there is interest after an initial meeting and it’s, ‘Let’s talk further,'” he said. “Maybe when it gets a little more serious and looks like something that might proceed.”
Peter Johnston, a Salina attorney serving on the Board of Regents, said there was benefit to not refining the reporting mandate.
“From my vantage point, the language is, I think, fine. There’s some benefit in the ambiguity,” he said. “I really value flexibility in this space way more than in other spaces. I think the institutions need to have a free hand to a great degree.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Feds say New Mexico’s lobos are ‘nonessential’
text:
A Mexican wolf rests shortly after a release. (Evelyn Lichwa/Mexican Wolf Interagency Field Team /U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.)Ever since their reintroduction in the late 90s, wild Mexican wolves — a rare subspecies of gray wolf in the Southwest — have been labeled “nonessential” to the species’ overall survival by the federal government.
Conservationists objected in front of a panel of judges Tuesday, arguing that this legal distinction denies valuable protections often afforded to other endangered species.

This story originally published on KUNM.org.

As it stands, this definition means the genetically unique Mexican gray wolf population, which mainly live in New Mexico and Arizona, can be removed or lost without jeopardizing the existence of the broader species in the wild.
“The fundamental problem we have, in this case, is that the [U.S. Fish and Wildlife] Service never applied the correct definition of an ‘essential’ experimental population,” said Andrew Hawley, during oral arguments at the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit in Missoula. “This is a legal error.”
Hawley represents a slew of environmental groups appealing a 2025 decision in an Arizona district court that favors the federal government’s original definition designation. They first filed the lawsuit in 2022.
In Arizona and New Mexico, Mexican wolves are allowed to live under a special “experimental” management rule that restricts them below Interstate 40. It also governs specific conditions when they can be captured, removed, or killed by the federal government.
Conservationists argue labeling that population as “non-essential” means wolves miss out on critically protected habitat and federal consultation requirements.
“As a result, it [the wolf population] didn’t get all of the protections that it should have from day one,” said Hawley in an interview with KUNM.
In the courtroom, the government countered, pointing to a long-standing wolf breeding program as evidence they have the knowledge and expertise to restart the population if needed.
“The Fish and Wildlife Service, thanks to that program, has successfully established a growing Mexican wolf population that is progressing towards recovery goals year after year after year,” said attorney Kyle Gwen, on behalf of the federal government.
Creating the experimental management area was a compromise with the agricultural industry to ease livestock depredation tensions and other regulatory concerns.
Criticisms have long centered on how these boundaries are “arbitrary” and should be abolished to allow northern and southern wolf packs to intermingle.
Famously, a female wolf nicknamed “Asha” crossed north of the I-40 boundary twice – garnering the national spotlight as she searched for a mate in the southern Rockies.
After capture and relocation to the Sevilleta National Wildlife Refuge, Asha was placed with a mate. There, she gave birth to five pups.
Elsewhere, roughly 45 other lobos live separately in northern Mexico — and fewer than four are tracked with radio collars — which conservationists say is alarmingly low. They claim the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service cannot rely on this population across the border if numbers start to dwindle here in the United States.
Although the Mexican gray wolf lacks a habitat specifically set aside and protected for its recovery, federal law generally protects the species from being killed, harmed, or harassed by the public.
Attorney Gwen contends that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service applied the correct definition of essentiality after exercising reasonable scientific judgement. By doing so, they determined that losing Arizona and New Mexico’s lobos would not reduce the species’ likelihood of survival.
“So, the [U.S. Fish and Wildlife] Service had sufficient information to undertake this comparative analysis — at least in rough terms — even if it did not put a numerical point on it,” Gwen told the court.
Environmental groups in the Southwest have long maintained that the Mexican gray wolf’s genetic make-up is poor because the species was brought back from the brink of extinction by breeding just seven individual “founding” wolves together.
Often, any two random lobos are as genetically similar as brother and sister, leading to questions about how the Mexican wolf can live in the wild without human intervention.
Despite persistent concerns about the species’ future, its population has risen significantly. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s 2025 count, the minimum number of wolves on the landscape jumped from 286 in 2024 to 319.
While it’s nearly impossible to nail down an exact timeline for a judgment, a decision on the essentiality definition could come down sometime in the next six months.

name: Delaware
title: When Mom Needs More Help, New Options Are Changing Senior Care
text:
Senior Care Options: Technology is expanding what is possible at home. Assisted living communities are shifting their focus from managing decline to promoting wellness and a sense of purpose. And specialized advisers are helping families navigate the increasingly sophisticated choices. Image created on 10/14 using AI. 
Artificial intelligence, purpose-driven assisted living and new approaches to care planning are giving Delaware families more ways to keep aging parents safe, independent and engaged in life.
WILMINGTON, Del. — When Mom begins forgetting medications, struggling with daily routines or becoming less comfortable living alone, families face a familiar question: Can she safely remain at home, or is it time for assisted living?
The answer is changing, and families have more choices than ever.
“We’ve also shifted from reactive to proactive, anticipating challenges and guiding families to avoid pitfalls — delivering greater value and peace of mind,” said Lynn Paxson, owner of Oasis Senior Advisors of Delaware, reflecting on how her business has evolved over the past decade.
Technology is expanding what is possible at home. Assisted living communities are shifting their focus from managing decline to promoting wellness and a sense of purpose. And specialized advisers are helping families navigate the increasingly sophisticated choices.
For caregivers, the transformation offers opportunities to anticipate problems, preserve independence and potentially improve an aging parent’s quality of life while reducing some of the burdens on family members.
Artificial Intelligence Makes Staying Home More Practical
One significant advance involves artificial intelligence systems that can monitor a senior’s safety even when a professional caregiver is not present.
Griswold Home Care, which serves Delaware families, has partnered with Sensi.AI to introduce technology-enhanced services through its Griswold Care Plus program.
Small audio-sensing devices installed throughout a home use artificial intelligence to recognize patterns and identify possible falls, calls for help, unusual activity or changes in daily routines. The system does not require cameras or wearable devices.
Patrick Grey, who operates Griswold Home Care serving Wilmington, has described how the technology gives professional caregivers information they previously lacked.
In one example, repeated falls were identified during a client’s morning routine, allowing the care team and family to recognize the need for additional assistance.
The technology can help determine whether caregiving schedules should change or whether more intensive support is necessary.
Combined with hands-on assistance for bathing, meals, transportation and companionship, these tools can make remaining at home a more practical option for some families.
For adult children, they can provide greater awareness of what happens between visits and reduce uncertainty about a parent’s safety.
Easterseals Lets Families See the Technology for Themselves
For families uncertain about what technology might help an aging parent, Easterseals Delaware & Maryland’s Eastern Shore offers a practical place to explore the possibilities.
Its Resource and Technology Demonstration Center at 61 Corporate Circle in New Castle features hundreds of assistive devices designed to help people remain independent.
The approximately 3,000-square-foot center demonstrates everything from adaptive clothing, specialized eating utensils and medication aids to mobility equipment and voice-activated household controls.
Families can see how relatively simple tools might make eating, dressing, bathing and other daily activities easier and safer.
The center can also demonstrate Griswold’s AI-supported home monitoring technology for caregivers interested in understanding how newer systems can supplement traditional home care.
Easterseals staff help visitors explore appropriate options and understand where equipment can be obtained. The nonprofit does not sell the products, and virtual tours are available for people unable to visit.
The center provides a useful starting point for families who may not realize how many technologies and everyday adaptations are available.
Not every solution requires an expensive electronic system. Sometimes a modified utensil, adaptive clothing or simple home safety device can make a meaningful difference in a senior’s independence.
Assisted Living Shifts From Managing Decline to Encouraging Purpose
Assisted living is undergoing a different, but equally important, transformation.
Historically, many families considered assisted living primarily when an older adult could no longer manage independently. The emphasis was often on meals, medications, personal care and supervision.
Today’s model increasingly includes helping residents remain physically active, socially connected, and engaged in meaningful activities.
Harmony Senior Services, which operates communities in Delaware, is among the providers promoting this approach.
Its Living Life in Harmony programming emphasizes physical wellness, intellectual stimulation, social relationships, and opportunities to contribute to the community.
The emphasis on purpose is particularly important.
An older adult who spent decades working, raising a family or volunteering may struggle with isolation after retirement, the death of a spouse or the loss of the ability to drive.
Assisted living can provide opportunities to build friendships, participate in activities, mentor others, and rediscover interests that have become difficult to pursue independently.
Instead of spending the day managing household chores, meals, and transportation, residents may have more time for relationships and meaningful activities.
The approach also changes the conversation about when to move. Rather than waiting for a medical crisis, some families are considering assisted living earlier, while their parent can fully participate in community life.
For other seniors, remaining in familiar surroundings will continue to provide the greatest independence and quality of life.
AI Is Improving Memory Care, Too
Artificial intelligence is also finding a role inside residential communities.
Arden Courts, which specializes in memory care for people living with Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias, has introduced AI-supported fall detection in select communities.
The optional technology uses cameras and artificial intelligence to detect falls and preserve a short video record of the incident for authorized caregivers to review.
This can be particularly valuable for residents who may have difficulty explaining what happened.
Rather than simply responding to a fall, caregivers can review the circumstances and consider whether changes to furniture placement, mobility assistance or supervision might prevent another incident.
The technology can become part of an individualized care plan, combining specialized memory care with additional information about safety.
Arden Courts operates a memory care community in Wilmington, although availability of the technology at that location requires confirmation.
The larger development is that technology is no longer simply a tool for helping seniors avoid moving into assisted living. It is increasingly becoming part of improving care inside residential communities as well.
Senior Care Consulting Is Changing With the Choices
As options multiply, the professionals helping families make decisions are changing their approach, too.
Traditionally, senior placement services often focused on identifying assisted living communities, comparing costs and arranging visits.
Those services remain valuable, but determining where Mom should live is increasingly only part of the challenge.
Families may first need to understand whether home monitoring, adaptive equipment, professional caregivers, or household modifications could help a parent remain independent.
Others may need to evaluate cognitive changes, mobility limitations, or whether a residential community could improve their parent’s social engagement and quality of life.
Paxson said her Oasis Senior Advisors team now includes professionals with years of experience in physical therapy, social work, hospice care, assisted living and cognitive therapy.
Those backgrounds bring different perspectives to care planning, helping families consider physical limitations, memory changes, safety, emotional well-being and the practical responsibilities of family caregivers.
The advisers help families understand available services and appropriate next steps, while clinical evaluations remain the responsibility of qualified health professionals.
The growing range of options is also making early planning more important.
A family might begin with relatively inexpensive assistive devices demonstrated at Easterseals, add AI-supported home monitoring and professional caregiving as needs increase, and eventually consider an assisted living community that emphasizes wellness and social engagement.
Another family may decide that moving sooner will offer a better quality of life.
The decisions remain personal, and costs, safety needs and individual preferences all matter.
But the changing models give families something they did not always have: more opportunities to address challenges before they become emergencies.
For Delaware caregivers, the question is no longer simply whether Mom can stay home or needs to move.
It is what combination of technology, professional care, purposeful activity and experienced guidance will help her remain safe, independent and engaged in life.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Meta revealed as company behind controversial Mason County hyperscale data center
text:
Attendees gather at a Maysville-Mason County Joint Planning Commission meeting on Sept. 3, 2025, including members of “We Are Mason County” who expressed their concerns about a data center project. (Photo courtesy of Max Moran)
The technology company Meta will invest billions of dollars for a proposed Mason County hyperscale data center and will pay millions of dollars to local schools and the county but will also receive a 40-year tax break on local property taxes, according to a tentative agreement. 
During a regular Mason County Fiscal Court meeting Tuesday, Democratic Mason County Judge-Executive Owen McNeill revealed that Meta was the primary company behind the nearly 3,000-acre project, and the fiscal court had unveiled the tenative community benefits agreement with a subsidiary of the company earlier this month. 
Mason County Judge-Executive Owen McNeill. (Courtesy Mason County)
“I’m confident that this court will be able to continue to lower taxes and the tax burden on local citizens through investments like this,” said McNeill, who has been a local backer of the project since the project first started to gain attention last year.
The fact that Meta was behind the project had remained secret for more than a year until this week. Local officials signed non-disclosure agreements that prevented the release of specific information about the project, something that residents including with the group We Are Mason County had strongly criticized as being anti-transparent. 
Meta owns Facebook and Instagram and recently settled a multistate lawsuit over whether its products harmed young people. Kentucky will get $358 million in the deal. 
We Are Mason County executive director Max Moran told the Kentucky Lantern local residents should have known who was behind the project much earlier so they could research the company and “make sure they are a true good neighbor.” McNeill had previously defended non-disclosure agreements as a part of the economic development process.
“Of course they’re building a massive one in Louisiana and all over the country,” Moran said, referring to another Meta data center in Louisiana where Republican Gov. Jeff Landry had signed a non-discloure agreement with the company’s data center subsidiary. 
Moran is also concerned about a decades-long tax break on local property taxes that is a part of the agreement for the data center. 
The community benefits agreement with Meta’s subsidiary commits to a number of investments ranging from investing at least $130 million in water and wastewater infrastructure, roadway improvements and public safety enhancements. The agreement states thousands of workers will be needed during construction with 400 full-time employees as a part of the project. 
But the agreement also would have the county issue what’s known as industrial revenue bonds, lasting for up to 40 years, that would exempt the data center campus from paying local property taxes. In such cases, the government buys the property where a company site is to be located and leases the property back to a company, therefore allowing the company to avoid paying property taxes because a local government is exempt from paying property taxes on its own property. 
The agreement instead allows for payments to be made directly to the county government and county school district of $5 million a year and $2 million a year, respectively. Those payments would be on top of millions of dollars in tax revenue on electricity sales that would go to the county school district. 
Earlier this year, a progressive think tank in Kentucky had warned about the use of industrial revenue bonds as one of the ways data center developers could skirt having to pay their full share of local taxes. 
Jim Parsons, an attorney with Keating Meuthing & Klekamp PLL, discussed details about the community benefits agreement before the county fiscal court Tuesday. Parsons told the fiscal court that the payment agreement is “not perfect” but highlighted that it does ensure a floor of revenue for the local school district. 
“I will tell you that the company is getting an incentive on this particular project, and it is a benefit to the company here. But on the other hand, it’s good for the company, it’s good for the community,” Parsons said. 
Moran questioned whether industrial revenue bonds would meet the standard required in an executive order by Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear that data center developers pay their “full and fair share” of local taxes. 
McNeill did not immediately respond to a Wednesday text message and email sent by the Lantern requesting a response regarding concerns about the industrial revenue bonds. An email requesting commentary about the bonds sent to a media relations inbox for Meta was not immediately returned. 
A Beshear spokesperson did not immediately respond to a Wednesday email asking whether Beshear supports the use of local industrial revenue bonds for data centers and whether Meta is seeking additional state tax breaks for the data center. 
This story may be updated.

name: Maryland Matters
title: The most anti-labor law in Maryland you never knew existed
text:
The right to strike -- as United Auto Workers did in 2023 in this photo from General Motor’s Lansing, Michigan, Redistribution Center -- , is prohibited for public sector workers in Maryland. That needs to change, writes Tim Wright, if we value the work those employees do (Photo by Anna Liz Nichols/Michigan Advance)There’s a law in Maryland that’s standing in the way of teacher pay raises, smaller class sizes, and better and safer working conditions for all public sector workers, and unless you work in that public sector, you likely have no idea what that law is. It isn’t some obscure regulatory loophole buried in the tax code. Public employees in Maryland are legally forbidden from going on strike.
Under Section 22-205 of Maryland’s General Provisions code, the ban is stated in nine words: “Public employees are prohibited from engaging in a strike.” Teachers and other public school employees, library workers, transportation workers, sanitation workers,  city, state and county employees — an enormous swath of the people who keep our  state running are barred from the single most effective tool workers have ever had to win better pay and conditions. If they defy the ban, their unions run the risk of fines, decertification and, at worst, even firings.
“Essential services” is doing a lot of work
The traditional justification for strike bans is that public services are too important to interrupt — that a teacher walkout, unlike a factory strike, doesn’t just cost a company money, it disrupts children’s educations and families’ lives.
But if the work is so important that a strike is dangerous, don’t we want that work to be done in the best working conditions possible? These conditions will always end up being an afterthought without that basic fundamental right. The workers don’t truly have a seat at the table if they don’t have an exit from the room.




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




And in practice, the ban doesn’t eliminate labor unrest — it merely weakens workers’ leverage. When Baltimore County Public Schools have walked back negotiated raises, or when county budgets have squeezed school staffing, Maryland teachers relied on work-to-rule actions that helped with bargaining, but were unable to fully restore previously negotiated contracts.
In this environment, labor agreements can be made, but the underlying issues go unresolved year after year. No credible threat, no leverage, just public pleading to school boards and county councils who know the union’s hands are tied by law. That’s not labor peace. That’s labor powerlessness dressed up as public interest.
What the ban actually costs
The consequences aren’t abstract. When Philadelphia’s DC33 municipal workers went on strike for about a week, they won a 9% raise over three years — leverage Maryland public employees simply don’t have available to them, no matter how justified their case.
Maryland’s public sector workers have seen their real wages erode as cost of living increases outpaces negotiated gains even as Maryland institutes austerity cutbacks to social services every year.
There’s also a quieter cost: a workforce that knows its strongest tool is illegal negotiates differently — and loses differently. It’s harder to recruit and retain teachers and librarians in a state where, unlike nearly every private-sector counterpart, they have no meaningful strike leverage if a school board reneges on a deal.
Maryland is already grappling with education staffing shortages; a law that hands public employers the upper hand in every negotiation doesn’t help.
A ban that’s survived on obscurity
Part of why this law has endured is that it’s invisible until it isn’t. Nobody debates it at dinner parties. It doesn’t show up in campaign ads. It surfaces only when a specific group of workers — teachers in one county, librarians in another — run into a wall they didn’t know was there, and even then it’s treated as a one-off dispute rather than a symptom of a much broader structural imbalance written into state law.
That obscurity is precisely what has let it persist for decades without serious reconsideration. A right-to-work law would have unions in the streets. A strike ban that quietly took the streets away in the first place barely gets noticed.
If lawmakers are serious about supporting the state’s teachers and librarians, House Bill 1492, introduced in the 2025 state legislative session was a reasonable place to start. The Maryland Right to Strike coalition, consisting of dozens of public sector unions and community organizations from across the state has recently announced that it plans to continue this fight for a new public sector right to strike bill come this November.
But the larger conversation Maryland needs to have is simpler than any single bill: Why, in 2026, does the state still tell hundreds of thousands of its own workers that the most basic tool of labor power is one they’re not even allowed to consider?

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: In ‘purple’ Legislative District 12, swing-vote Riepe faces Democrat challenger Knorr
text:
The 2026 candidates for Legislative District 12, state Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston and Christy Knorr of Omaha, in the district on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — State Sen. Merv Riepe has racked up eight years of service in the Nebraska Legislature, but he is eligible for reelection because his two terms were not consecutive.
The retired hospital administrator was first elected in 2014 to represent District 12, encompassing Ralston and a portion of western Omaha. In 2018, he lost reelection to Democrat Steve Lathrop and returned to the Legislature in 2022 after Lathrop decided not to seek reelection.
This year, he faces another Democrat challenger, hospice nurse Christy Knorr, in one of the most politically diverse legislative districts in the state.
Riepe has consistently described District 12 as purple. The latest voter registration statistics posted on the Nebraska Secretary of State’s website show about 8,600 registered Republicans, 7,800 Democrats and 6,500 nonpartisan voters in the district.
This translates to a wide range of political opinions among voters in the area. Riepe said some constituents have expressed a desire for Nebraska to fully ban abortion, while Knorr said several voters have shared frustration with state officials’ resisting pleas to expand access to medical cannabis.
“People are angry about it,” Knorr said.
Riepe said he has been trying to appeal to Democratic voters by showing that he is not a platform Republican. He is known as a swing vote in the current Legislature. During his second term, he cast deciding votes to halt progress on a bill that would have returned Nebraska to a “winner-take-all” system for presidential elections and a bill that would have banned abortions at about six weeks of pregnancy. The latter earned him a censure from the Nebraska GOP.
“They know that I’m a little bit of a rebel,” Riepe said.
Proposed 12-week abortion cutoff hits sooner than Riepe’s, with no exception for fetal anomalies

In the Legislature’s 2023 abortion debate, Riepe said, he felt a six-week ban was too strict and instead proposed a 12-week ban to replace the 20-week ban in place at the time. His fellow Republicans eventually acquiesced to his request and passed a version of the 12-week ban.
However, it was this legislation that spurred Knorr to challenge Riepe. Knorr said that during the 2023 session, Riepe promised he would not support a 12-week ban if it didn’t include protections for medical providers. Despite this, Riepe ultimately did vote “yes” on the bill without protections, allowing the measure to pass. Though he introduced a bill in 2024 to add protections, it did not make it out of committee.
“That was the day when I let him know that I was coming to take his seat the next cycle,” Knorr said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Both Riepe and Knorr said they largely have gone door-to-door to have conversations with District 12 voters during their campaigns. Knorr said she did so much walking in the primary that she had total knee replacement surgery in June, and has been going door-to-door using a four-wheeled scooter since August.
Though party registrations among District 12 are mixed, Riepe and Knorr each said they have agreed more often than disagreed with voters they have spoken to on the campaign trail.
State Sen. Merv Riepe of Ralston, in his seventh year in the Nebraska Legislature, stands by a portrait in his Lincoln office memorializing his first campaign for the Legislature in 2014, including photos of his two grandchildren. Riepe served in the Legislature from 2015 to 2019, and he returned in 2023. March 11, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Riepe said he’s aware that some Republican voters in District 12 won’t vote in the November election because they disagree with his decisions. However, he said, a bigger fear is large Democratic turnout in the race because voters want to see a Democrat representing the district.
Assuming no other seats flip, if Knorr defeats Riepe, Republicans would have 32 of the 49 seats in the Legislature, just shy of the 33-vote threshold to overcome filibusters.
Riepe has argued that Knorr lacks the experience to get stuff done in the Legislature, while Knorr has said Riepe’s voting record does not align with his constituents. Voters want a representative who understands the current economic situation, she said, and Riepe was educated and worked under a different socioeconomic system.
“He got to retire with a pension, and that’s something that a lot of us don’t have these days,” Knorr said.
Both Riepe and Knorr have backgrounds in the medical field, but the two hold differing views on specific healthcare issues. For example, Knorr noted that she supports Medicaid expansion while Riepe has been hesitant.
On the debate about medical cannabis, Knorr said she has seen the benefits firsthand as a hospice nurse. She said it’s sometimes the only form of pain relief that works for her patients, and Nebraskans deserve the choice to use medical cannabis if they want.
Christy Knorr of Omaha, a 2026 candidate for Legislative District 12, outside her Omaha home on Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Knorr said medical cannabis is an issue that unites voters across the political spectrum in Nebraska. She criticized Gov. Jim Pillen, U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers for their attempts to restrict access to medical cannabis, saying this was “a hill I am willing to die on.”
“Somewhere along the line, we have lost our humanity and our empathy,” she said.
Riepe said he doesn’t support legalizing recreational marijuana, but supports medical cannabis with restrictions. He said he believes it would be a mistake to open too many distribution centers across the state, but acknowledged that excessive red tape would open the door for black-market distributors.
From his conversations with voters, Riepe said he believes their biggest issues are property taxes and Nebraska’s budget, which isn’t a surprise. He predicted that taxes will always be a major issue for voters, citing a 1975 political cartoon that depicted Uncle Sam throwing money at various government programs while a taxpayer looks on with empty pockets.
“People feel like their whole standard of living … is (in) quicksand,” Riepe said. “It’s just kind of slowly but surely escaping them, and they don’t know what the future is going to bring.”
Riepe said he is open to the controversial idea of increasing sales taxes — particularly on pop and candy — to make room to lower property taxes, though he also said he doesn’t believe voters want increased sales taxes. He said he is interested in ideas to reduce property taxes without shifting the burden somewhere else.
On property taxes, Knorr said she is honest with voters and won’t promise anything, though she wants to deliver on the issue. She noted that lawmakers are expected to face a budget deficit for the third year in a row when they enter the 2027 session.
If he’s reelected, Riepe predicted that 2027 might be “one of the least fun sessions” he’ll have taken part in, because the state budget will take precedence over all other issues. He said he hasn’t planned for specific legislation outside of budget-related issues because of this, though he would like to work on proposals for economic development.
Knorr said she also wants to focus on the budget. If elected, she said, she wants to go through the budget line-by-line to see exactly what the state is spending on. She said she suspects there are several areas of needless spending that could be cut, citing expenses for the governor’s mansion outside the state Capitol as one example.

title: Nonpartisan government watchdog recommends automated activation of ICE body cameras
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection need to improve oversight and guidance for federal immigration officers' use of body-worn cameras, according to a Wednesday report from independent federal investigators.Officials with the Department of Homeland Security, however, resisted a recommendation in the report from the Government Accountability Office that ICE change its current policy, in which agents choose when to manually turn on body cameras, as opposed to automatic activation. In a response to GAO, the department — which oversees both agencies — argued that automatic activation on a body camera presents a risk to ongoing operations, such as recording sensitive interactions with informants or victims or inadvertently filming bystanders.  GAO said that statement was insufficient. “However, DHS’s response did not include information on environments where automated activation could be effective, or other controls that could help ensure compliance with activating cameras when required by policy,” according to GAO. Multiple shootingsThe report came after multiple high-profile cases of federal immigration officers shooting and killing people during interactions and enforcement actions, prompting calls for wider body camera use.GAO made seven recommendations to the Department of Homeland Security to update its guidance for body cameras. The department agreed with six, but disagreed with implementing automated camera activation controls, arguing that ICE’s current policy  is sufficient. CBP does have automatic camera activation, which means the body camera turns on and starts recording when a weapon is drawn or emergency lights are turned on.“Without reliable control activities, ICE risks gaps in documentation and video evidence that can make reviews of incidents more challenging,” according to GAO. After federal immigration officers killed two U.S. citizens in January during an aggressive deportation drive in Minneapolis, the Trump administration directed body cameras to immigration agents. In June, there were two back-to-back killings of immigrants in Texas and Maine that prompted border czar Tom Homan to announce that during traffic stops at least one ICE officer will wear a body camera. Democrats have also pushed for all federal immigration officers to wear body cameras in the wake of the killings and violent interactions from agents that were recorded by bystanders. Thousands of body cameras distributedGAO investigators found that as of April, ICE issued 4,800 body cameras, splitting them evenly between its deportation wing of Enforcement and Removal Operations and the investigative law enforcement arm of ICE, Homeland Security Investigations. And in June, CBP issued approximately 11,500 cameras, mostly to Border Patrol.  But GAO found problems in the cameras’ deployment.“Most CBP and ICE offices have not developed specific operational guidance that explains how personnel should use, or not use, cameras under their unique operational circumstances,” according to the report. “The lack of guidance at this operational level increases the risk that CBP and ICE personnel will fail to use the cameras as required under policy.”DHS agreed to the recommendations from GAO that the leaders of ICE and CBP should update their body camera program to include changes in requirements and costs and plan for any contingencies based on current risk. The department also agreed that CBP and ICE should implement goals to ensure effectiveness for the body-worn camera program and that both agencies should ensure their sub-agencies are also given proper guidance on the expectations and appropriate uses of the body cameras.

title: Social Security benefits increase will hit 3.6% in 2027
text: WASHINGTON — The Social Security Administration announced on Wednesday that recipients will receive a 3.6% increase in benefits in 2027.The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, will begin for 72 million Social Security beneficiaries in January. It will apply for Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, recipients beginning on Dec. 31. Some individuals receive both types of benefits. SSI provides payments to 7.3 million people with limited income and resources.The COLA is based on continuing inflation, as recorded in the Consumer Price Index from the third quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026.On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by about $75 a month, the agency said. Tax rates to fund the program will stay virtually unchanged, at 6.2% of income up to a certain amount. The cap will increase slightly from $184,500 this year to $192,300 in 2027. Social Security is facing a shortfall, with payments to recipients outpacing tax collections. Without congressional action, that will mean benefits will automatically begin to decrease in 2032. Candidates in key U.S. Senate races this year, whose six-year terms would mean they’ll be in office when the benefits cliff arrives, have stayed relatively quiet on the issue.
