name: Alabama Reflector
title: Families want meeting with UAB officials over organ harvesting of loved ones
text:
Families of loved ones whose organs were harvested after they died in Alabama prisons prepare to speak with reporters after a hearing on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, at the Montgomery County Courthouse. The families want to meet with officials with the University of Alabama Birmingham. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Families of incarcerated Alabamians whose organs were harvested after their deaths demanded a meeting with University of Alabama Birmingham officials Tuesday as delays in their civil lawsuit continue to mount.
Speaking after a court hearing in Montgomery, in which UAB sought to have some counts dismissed, relatives said they wanted administrators to listen to stories of their relatives and demanded justice for their loved ones.
“If the attorneys for the Alabama Department of Corrections and UAB want to prolong this, they are the only ones who are benefitting financially,” said Simone Moore, whose brother Kelvin Moore died in Limestone Correctional Facility in 2023. “I don’t know what they are telling the trustees at UAB, but I believe the trustees should summon the attorneys and say to the attorneys, ‘Give us justification why you are prolonging this process and putting off the inevitable?’”
UAB declined comment on Tuesday.
In 2024, eight families sued the Alabama Department of Corrections, alleging that the department harvested the organs of their loved ones who died while in prison, and sent them to the University of Alabama Birmingham Heersink School of Medicine.
According to the lawsuit, a group of medical students from the school noticed that many of the specimens they worked with in the curriculum were taken from people who died while in Alabama’s prisons. The plaintiffs allege the organs were harvested without their permission, a violation of the law.
Montgomery Circuit Judge J.R. Gaines heard arguments Tuesday over UAB’s motion to dismiss but did not immediately rule on it. A trial in the case is tentatively scheduled to begin December 2027.
Since the original lawsuit, several other families have filed separate actions that have since been consolidated.
The university and the ADOC argued in February 2025 that state agencies enjoy absolute immunity and therefore cannot be held liable in civil lawsuits.
Gaines ruled against UAB and ADOC in April 2025 and allowed the case to proceed into discovery. However, defendants appealed the ruling for one of the lawsuits filed by the family of Charles Edward Singleton, 74, who died while in prison and whose organs were harvested without their permission.
Defense counsel appealed directly to the Alabama Supreme Court. In January 2026,  the justices dismissed six of the seven claims, and leaving one related to the Alabama Uniform Anatomical Gift Act (AUAGA). The justices wrote that attorneys for the defendants had not formally requested that it be dismissed in circuit court.
During the hearing Tuesday, UAB and ADOC attorneys argued that the statute of limitations to file a civil claim based on AUAGA had expired and that the officials who signed the agreement are individuals employed by the state and have immunity. Defense counsel also sought to dismiss the additional claims filed by plaintiffs against individuals on the grounds that the families filed their lawsuits after the two-year statute of limitations had expired.
Attorneys for the plaintiffs said defendants do not have immunity from their alleged wrongdoing and that the timeline on the statute of limitations did not begin until the family members knew they had a case, which did not happen until well after the autopsy had been done and was within the statute of limitations.
Several families Tuesday spoke about the grief they experienced knowing that their loved ones’ organs had been removed.
“It has been heartbreaking because every time we go to court, we get to live it and do not see that justice has been done,” said Tyrus Franklin, the brother of Kelvin Moore.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee GOP senator seeks one-month gas tax break
text:
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has approved a measure to allow farmers and loggers to use a lower-cost type of diesel through the October 2026 harvesting season, but now a state Senator wants a gas tax holiday for everyone. (Photo: John Partipilo/John Partipilo)A Tennessee Republican lawmaker is asking the governor to cut motorists some slack at the pump by calling for a one-month break on the state’s gas tax.
Sen. Tom Hatcher of Maryville sent a letter to Gov. Bill Lee requesting he suspend Tennessee’s 27.4-cent gas tax during November, with the average price of regular gas at about $3.90 per gallon in Tennessee.
“I believe the extraordinary circumstances facing Tennessee motorists warrant consideration of a temporary measure,” Hatcher said in an Oct. 7 letter to the governor.
The governor and lawmakers are likely leery about giving up a revenue stream as Tennessee struggles with a backlog of $58 billion to $87 billion in road and bridge construction projects over the next three decades and needs $3.6 billion annually to maintain and improve roads. But Hatcher said in his letter that he is seeking only a one-month suspension, which would allow for “minimal impact” on gas tax revenue, which “supports important transportation priorities” statewide. 
Hatcher told the Lookout the break would match the governor’s action on dyed diesel fuel, which is allowing farmers and loggers to use the cheaper, tax-exempt form of diesel normally allowed for off-road equipment on public roads during October’s harvest season and avoid record-high costs of more than $6 per gallon for regular diesel fuel. The diesel is dyed red to differentiate it from regular diesel for tax identification purposes.
The requested gas tax cut would take effect Nov. 1 and last 30 days, according to Hatcher.
“We’re allowing the farmers to use the different diesel that’s cheaper for them, and they need the help,” Hatcher said. “But also regular citizens need some help, and that would be right before Christmas time … and, hopefully, help them some also.”
Republican lawmakers asked Lee to allow the use of untaxed dyed diesel fuel on roads through Nov. 15, but he declined to extend the waiver past October. The ability to use dyed diesel for a full tank would save about $102 when filling up a 200-gallon semi truck tank.
House Democrats were rebuffed earlier this year when they urged the governor to put funds for a gas and diesel tax holiday in his budget. It’s unclear whether a Republican lawmaker will be heard. The governor’s office didn’t respond Tuesday to questions from the Lookout.
Lawmakers passed the IMPROVE Act in 2017, raising the gas tax by six cents and diesel by 10 cents over three years, a move designed to bring in hundreds of millions of dollars for road and bridge construction projects and put a dent in a $10 billion backlog. Simultaneously, the state decreased sales taxes on groceries to 4% as a way to ease the pain at the pump.
Despite that offset, the gas tax increase of nearly a decade ago has haunted lawmakers who supported it, costing Republican Rep. Barry Doss his seat in the following election and hurting veteran Republican Rep. Dennis Powers at the polls when he lost in this year’s primary.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Chesapeake Bay gets a C+ in overall health, its highest score in 20 years of records
text:
Heath Kelsey with the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science presents the 2026 Chesapeake Bay Watershed Report Card in Woodbridge, Virginia. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)The Chesapeake Bay earned a C+ on the annual report card that calculates improvements or losses in key indicators of health and conditions in the estuary and surrounding areas. This is the highest the Bay has ever scored since the record-keeping began in 2006. 
At the announcement in Woodbridge, Virginia, on Tuesday, leaders said the score reflects the impact continuous clean up efforts have in the Bay, however slow the progress may be.
“We are taking this as an opportunity to acknowledge that what we are doing is working, and that we have momentum moving forward,” said David Bulova, Virginia’s Secretary of Natural and Historic Resources.
A map of the Chesapeake Bay Watershed shows areas in 2026 that have improved in water quality over the last year. (Map courtesy University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences)
Eight of the Bay’s 15 regions showed improvement, including the Patapsco and Back Rivers, Upper Western Shore, Rappahannock, Lower Eastern Shore, Upper Bay and Lower Bay.
The highest-scoring area was the lower Bay region with a B plus. This part of the Bay, stretching between Cape Henry and Cape Charles in Virginia, is aided with water from the Atlantic Ocean. 
The lower Western Shore, which is bordered by the Patapsco River area on the north and extends down the coastline toward the Patuxent River, received the lowest score of  D minus. It suffers from heavy runoff from urban areas.
A map of the Chesapeake Bay Watershed shows areas in 2026 that have improved in water quality over the last year. (Map courtesy University of Maryland Center for Environmental Sciences)
The yearly report is conducted by the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science (UMCES). 
Researchers found that the level of pollutants that feed into the Bay have held steady or decreased. However the amounts of chlorophyll a, which causes harmful algae blooms, and the water clarity levels both worsened since last year.
A recent algae bloom in the Eastern Shore had devastating impacts on oyster farms in the area. The bloom is also reported to be connected to recent reports of fish kills, according to the Chesapeake Bay Foundation.
“This type of water quality data does take a long time to improve, and especially with the population pressure, development pressure that we have in our region, with large cities, large population centers, and also agriculture, and other types of pressures on the system like tourism,” said Alexandra Fries, program manager for UMCES. 
“Even though we are managing and trying to restore, there’s still a lot of threats. And so, the fact that we are seeing significantly improving trends is really promising.”
The progress in managing the Bay’s pollution levels is partly due to the Chesapeake Bay Watershed agreement that was first established in the late 1980s as a partnership between the six states and Washington D.C. whose waterways feed into the estuary.
The agreement set goals to reduce sediment and nutrients that end up in the Bay, make infrastructure improvements and follow agricultural best practices. The latest version of the agreement was signed in 2025, outlining new goals to meet by 2040.
“When you’re improving, when you’re on an upward trajectory, you don’t stop,” said UMCES President Fernando Miralles-Wilhelm. “You don’t cut funding, right? You double down on investments. And that’s what we need to continue to be doing.”
Earlier this month, The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency announced $37 million in grant funding, which would be matched by additional $53 million, for specific watershed and nutrient projects across the watershed. 
The report indicated some improvements manifested because much of the watershed experienced a very dry year, with many regions recording droughts.
This means less water was running off of agricultural land and out of stormwater systems that might have otherwise carried pollutants into the Bay and connected waterways.
But scientists who compiled the report emphasized that other factors weighed heavily in the Bay’s progress. 
“The score overall went up 6%. So having such a large increase, to me, is not just due to less precipitation,” Fries said. ”I think it’s also due to some of the restoration actions and best management practices that we’ve been putting in throughout the watershed.”
Key restoration wins that may have contributed to the improving scores include major investments in oyster habitat restoration. 
The hard-shelled mollusks are natural filters for water. Combined, Virginia and Maryland restored and protected about 2400 acres of oyster reefs since the 2014 signing of the watershed agreement. Over 7.5 billion oysters were planted as part of the effort and more are planned for in the latest iteration of the agreement.
The report card also outlined grave threats to water quality over the past year, including the sewage pipe that burst near Cabin John in Maryland sent an estimated 243 million gallons of raw sewage into the Potomac River. 
The disaster led to oyster harvest closures in some areas and demands from elected officials for more testing to be conducted.
The report card mirrors the continued efforts of state and local officials, scientists and communities to preserve and protect the Bay, the largest estuary in America and the third largest in the world. 
“I actually get a question all the time: ‘Why are you all investing so much money and restoring the Chesapeake Bay?’” Serena Mcllwain, Maryland’s Secretary of the Department of the Environment, said at the announcement event. 
“I just tell them, imagine if we didn’t spend any money. We wouldn’t progress, and we wouldn’t have the clean, beautiful Bay that we have today. Yes, it’s going to take continued investment. No, it’s not going to be solved tomorrow.  It means that we must continue to work in partnership.” 
More details of the Chesapeake Bay report card can be read here.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: PAC linked to Senate President Smith spends against Democrats challenging ‘Team Randy’ members
text:
Senate President Randy Smith, shown March 10, 2026 in the Senate chambers in Charleston, West Virginia, says he will seek another term in the powerful position. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Three weeks ahead of Election Day, a political action committee linked to Senate President Randy Smith is spending big opposing two Democratic candidates who could knock off two Republican members of “Team Randy.”
The Senate is in a precarious place after a divisive Senate president race, where Smith, R-Preston, won a competitive caucus vote in 2024 that split the upper chamber into clear factions. The contentious May Republican primary didn’t help the matter.
Republicans hold all but two seats in the Senate. 
Smith, a former coal miner, said he will run for reelection for the role that makes him second-in-line to governor. His path to victory could be reliant on Nov. 3 election results. 
Mountaineer Conservative Action, a political action committee tied to Smith, spent around $105,000 at the beginning of October opposing Democratic Senate candidates Shawn Fluharty and Richie Robb. The information was obtained through the West Virginia Secretary of State’s online campaign filing system. Mountain Conservative Action lists a P.O. box in Morgantown as its address.
Smith declined an interview for this story.
Fluharty, a current House of Delegates member, is running a competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Laura Chapman, R-Ohio in the Northern Panhandle. Pollsters have flagged the seat as one that could flip to blue this November. 
Mountaineer Conservative Action recently circulated a mailer against Fluharty, saying he was the wrong choice for Wheeling. The group has spent around $55,000 against Fluharty at this time.
Del. Shawn Fluharty, D-Ohio, addresses fellow members of the House of Delegates during a discussion about House Bill 4951 Tuesday, Feb. 3, 2026. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Fluharty said the move was “expected.”
“They want puppets in Charleston to push their fringe agenda that has resulted in one of the worst economic performances in the country. That’s why I have been supported by both business and labor, recently receiving Chamber of Commerce support,” Fluharty said. “Meanwhile, they sit on the fringe, trying to divide people so that they are distracted from the fact that those in power can’t govern. I’m nobody’s puppet. I believe in merit-based elections on actual policy, they push their own dark money DEI candidates. Sad!” 
Chapman has held the seat since 2022. She did not respond to interview requests for this story. 
She left Senate leadership in January, resigning from her position as Senate Health Committee chair due to conflict with Smith and his agenda. In May, Chapman told West Virginia Watch that she believed Smith had done a fine job in the role. 
Mountaineer Conservative Action has spent $50,000 so far opposing Richie Robb, a Democrat challenging Sen. Ann Charnock, R-Kanawha. Charnock was appointed last year by Gov. Patrick Morrisey to the Senate seat; this election is for the seat’s unexpired term. 
Charnock declined an interview request in a text message. She was tapped by Smith to serve as chair of the Committee on Confirmation. 
Robb, former mayor of South Charleston, said money coming from PACs like Mountaineer Conservative Action can “distort the election.”
“Whether they’re attacking someone like me, or they’re promoting someone else, there’s a lot of generalities without specifics,” he said. “I think it’s generally done to reach a sort of a visceral response from certain voters.”
Groups like Mountaineer Conservative Coalition, another PAC linked to Smith, and PACs linked to Morrisey unusually spent millions of dollars in the May primary to influence statehouse races for Republicans.
“We’ve got plenty of needs out there and political issues to talk about instead of your superficial, knee-jerk type influencing type ads that are in many respects pretty silly,” Robb said. “I’ll just grin and bear them for the next couple of weeks.”
Sen. Tom Takubo, R-Kanawha, (front) sits in the Senate Chamber waiting on the final night of 2026 legislative session. Behind him are (from right to left) Sen. Glenn Jeffries, R-Putnam, Sen. Zack Maynard, R-Lincoln, and Sen. Eric Tarr, R-Putnam. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Senate president nomination to be held in December 
The Senate president’s nomination process will occur in December within the Republican caucus ahead of the 2027 legislative session. 
Sen. Jay Taylor, R-Taylor. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Sen. Jay Taylor, R-Taylor, said he expects Smith to maintain his power position with his number of backers in the Senate. Taylor is on “Team Randy.”
“He’s a good friend, and he’s a good leader, and I’m looking forward to what we can do for the future of West Virginia,” Taylor said when reached by phone. 
Taylor said Smith and others have begun working on the Senate’s agenda for the 2027 legislative session. The public school funding formula, workforce participation and addressing the benefits’ cliff are expected to be key items, according to Taylor. 
“I definitely think (Smith) has been the one to support our ideas that we’re hoping to get across,” Taylor said. 
Political groups linked to Smith were active during the contentious Republican primary in May. 
Mountaineer Conservative Coalition, which MetroNews reporter Brad McElhinny traced to Smith, was behind political messaging against Republican Sen. Tom Takubo.
Takubo, R-Kanawha, had vied for the Senate president position in 2024 against Smith and Sen. Eric. Tarr, R-Putnam. The fallout from that intra-caucus vote made Takubo a de facto leader of the Senate’s other faction, which tends to lean more moderate Republican and regularly opposes Morrisey’s leadership decisions. 
Smith’s team often aligns with Morrisey. 
Sen. Joey Garcia, D-Marion, speaks on the Senate floor about Senate Bill 641 on March 4, 2026. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Sen. Joey Garcia, D-Marion, said the current breakdown of Republicans who won in the May primary favors Smith as leader, but Democratic challengers could disrupt those numbers if they’re successful in November.
“If people who have committed to him are beaten in the general election by Democrats, there’s a chance that the Senate presidency is decided on the Senate floor next January,” Garcia said. “I feel very confident that Democratic candidates for state Senate are going to overperform and potentially surprise some people in races in November.”
Garcia is the only guaranteed Democratic senator to return in 2027 — a major shift from the once Democratic stronghold in the state Legislature. The Senate’s other Democrat, Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, is retiring. 
“Leadership has not paid attention to kitchen table issues and the things that matter most to people’s pocketbooks,” Garcia said. “We need to have accountability and focus towards the issues West Virginians care about, and I hope the next Senate president will take that to heart.”
Early voting in the 2026 general election begins Oct. 21 and ends Oct. 31.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado affordability tax credit most effective tool to lift children out of poverty, report says
text:
A mother and her son hold hands on a swing set. This year, more state and local leaders are pushing to hold parents accountable for their children’s behavior, particularly when it involves serious criminal offenses. (Photo by Troy Bennett/Maine Morning Star)Colorado’s most effective tool for reducing child poverty is a state-level family tax credit that’s in jeopardy for the current tax year, according to a new report from a Colorado nonprofit that aims to improve the wellbeing of children.
The Colorado Family Affordability Tax Credit, created by the state Legislature in 2024, pulled 22,500 children out of poverty in its first year of implementation, researchers estimated in the “Proof It Works” report from the Colorado Children’s Campaign and Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy. Denver-based Gary Community Ventures helped fund the research that went into the report released Tuesday.
Low-income families who met certain requirements could claim a credit for each child in their household for the 2024 and 2025 tax years. The credit will likely not be available for families in the 2026 tax year, and if it is, it will be underfunded, nonpartisan state analysis predicts. The availability of the credit will be officially determined during the December economic forecast.

Maya Gould, vice president of research at the Colorado Children’s Campaign, who led the research in the report, said it’s encouraging to see a state investment successfully help kids. 
Other state and federal programs helped reduce child poverty by increasing household resources that make it easier to afford basic necessities like food, housing and health insurance. But since their research found that the most effective tool is the state tax credit, which state leaders have complete control over, Gould said she hopes the report will convince those who control the budget that the tax credit is a worthwhile investment even in a tight budget year. 
“That’s a place where we are able to make the decisions about how we want to invest, and how we want to support Colorado families in a way that … we don’t always have control over changes at the federal level,” Gould said. 
Lawmakers on the bipartisan Joint Budget Committee had to cut about $1 billion to balance the budget this year, and future years are also projected to have significant budget challenges. 
A separate report that evaluated the state tax credit found that it helped lower child poverty by 37% in Colorado.
Tax credits and government assistance programs like housing assistance, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families also help bring kids out of poverty. Others including the Colorado Earned Income Tax Credit, The Colorado Child Tax Credit, the Women, Infants and Children program, and school lunch programs helped reduce poverty rates too. 
The report found housing assistance, including federal subsidies and vouchers, brought almost 15,800 children out of poverty, and SNAP did the same for 11,600 children.
Data in the report is based on a measure the Center on Poverty and Social Policy developed that considers factors specific to Colorado, like cost of living and state programs, using data from the census bureau and state agencies. It goes further than federal poverty metrics to include the local context in Colorado, Gould said. 
The federal government measures poverty based on income thresholds that vary by family size. If a family’s household income is less than the income threshold, they are considered in poverty. For example, according to 2026 guidelines, a family of four with an annual income of $33,000 or less is considered in poverty. 
U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet, a Colorado Democrat, has led the push to renew a federal child tax credit enacted for one year as part of the American Rescue Plan Act in 2021. The federal tax credit allowed more low-income families, including those with no income at all, to claim up to $3,600 for each child up to age 6, and up to $3,000 per child ages 6 to 17. For the first time, families received the funds in monthly installments.
U.S. Census Bureau data found that the expanded tax credit cut child poverty nearly in half, with the rate falling from 9.7% in 2020 to a record low of 5.2% in 2021. But after the tax credit expired, it spiked again, rising to 12.4% in 2022.
Gould said while policies like the federal child tax credit also helped, state leaders from Colorado can only do so much to advocate to reinstate it, again emphasizing the state’s full control over the Family Affordability Tax Credit.
With the tax credit projected to lapse in the 2026 tax year, Democrats in the General Assembly advanced three bills during this year’s legislative session to fund a similar credit by rolling back certain corporate tax breaks. Together, the bills would have established a new credit of up to roughly $2,000 per child. But two of the three bills died in the final days of the session amid veto threats from Gov. Jared Polis, capping the new credit at $260 for children under 6 and at $195 for children ages 6 to 16.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Healthcare changes, affordability worries highlight race for US House seat in Arkansas
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman (right) is being challenged by Democrat James Russell (left) to represent Arkansas' 4th Congressional District. (Photos courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State's office)Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman said he wants to continue working on forestry and healthcare concerns for constituents in Arkansas’ 4th Congressional District, even as he acknowledged the challenge his party faces nationally with voter discontent over affordability.
“They drive by our biggest network of campaign signs, I think, in the country when they drive by gas stations every day and they see the price of gasoline and diesel,” he said.
His opponent, Democrat James Russell, said the work the Republican from Hot Springs has done in his 11 years representing the rudy-red district doesn’t justify another term.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Westerman, a licensed engineer and forester who has represented the 33-county district since 2015, is a Garland County native and former state legislator who played football for the University of Arkansas Razorbacks. After receiving his bachelor’s degree he went to work for Riceland Foods, then later obtained a master’s degree in forestry from Yale University. 
The district covers large parts of south, west and north Arkansas. Westerman defeated his 2024 opponent, Democrat Risie Howard, with more than 72% of the vote and President Donald Trump won the district by nearly 40 percentage points.
Forestry needs, fuel prices
Westerman, who chairs the House Natural Resources Committee, said he’s running for a seventh term because he has a proven track record and there’s still more work to be done, including efforts on reforming the National Environmental Policy Act that he hopes will make it into law by the end of the year. 
The measure, which passed the House last year, is awaiting Senate approval. He said he also wants to work on reauthorizing the Great American Outdoors Act, first passed in 2020, to continue addressing the maintenance backlog at national parks and forests. 
Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman chats with Col. Matthew Mason, commander of the Pine Bluff Arsenal, before a news conference at the U.S. Army facility on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)
“I will continue working on forestry issues,” he said. “Having the forestry expertise gives me a lot of stuff to work on in that space.”
Russell, who is waging his second bid for public office, said he decided to run because he “got tired of not finding a politician that I could believe in, and I wanted to go and be that politician.” If elected, Russell said he will work to reassert Congress’ power over tariffs and “getting corporate money out of politics.”
“For me that means getting in there and taking back control as a co-equal branch of government, restricting executive overreach like we’ve had, and enacting things like the War Powers Act to make sure that the aggression we’ve got going on with Iran gets shut down,” Russell said, while also “tackling the affordability crisis that we’re running into.”
Russell served in the Arkansas National Guard and has owned and operated a mental health business with his wife in Little Rock for more than 10 years. The Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol drove him to seek the Democratic nomination for Arkansas governor in 2022. 
He lost in the gubernatorial primary to Chris Jones, who is challenging Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill to represent central Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District.
Affordability is a top concern weighing on voters in an election cycle where polling shows the cost of everything from gasoline to housing has left Americans angry, two years after Trump was elected on promises to lower prices. 
The mood has raised Democrats’ hopes that they can win the U.S. House in November, though political forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Larry Sabato have rated Westerman’s race as safely Republican. Still, Arkansans have soured on Trump and his handling of the war in Iran, according to an August poll from Talk Business and Politics and Hendrix College. 
US House and Senate split on ending Trump’s war in Iran, as gas prices rise

The conflict in Iran in February spiked gas and diesel prices, increasing the cost of moving goods worldwide. Diesel currently averages nearly $6 a gallon in Arkansas, up from $3.33 a year ago, according to the AAA.
Westerman acknowledged the difficult electoral environment, and said his party’s failure to address the cost-of-living concerns that won them control of the government in 2024 could cost Republicans nationwide in November. 
“Cost-of-living is front and center on people’s minds, and it very well could cost our party across the country in the election,” Westerman said. “People were sick and tired of inflation and high prices with the Biden administration, and they got a new administration. Republicans are in control in the House, the Senate and the White House, and prices are still high.”
Still, Westerman said prices aren’t increasing “as much as they were,” and he believes the economy is stronger now than it was during the Biden administration. He also said the tax and spending cut legislation Trump signed last year known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act would help “alleviate” the impacts of the war in Iran.
“There’s a tremendous effort being made to produce more domestic oil right now, and gas, but it takes a long time to get those projects up and running,” Westerman said.
James “Rus” Russell III, Arkansas candidate for the U.S. House, District 4, introduces U.S. Senate candidate Hallie Shoffner at the Ballots, Blue Jeans, & BBQ fundraiser on Thursday, October 1, 2026 in North Little Rock, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Russell said he supported enacting a war powers resolution that would halt military action without congressional approval. Westerman and the rest of the state’s Republican U.S. House members have voted against such a measure.
Russell said Congress must also tackle the rising costs of fuel and healthcare.
“The war hawks have just gone nuts,” the Democrat said. “We need to get everything back under control because we’re causing escalation of crises that we had no business creating in the first place.”
Healthcare changes
Healthcare ranks at the top of costs voters are worried about according to a poll released by KFF last week. Westerman and Russell both pointed to it as an area that they considered a priority — though for different reasons.
Westerman linked the ballooning cost of healthcare to the nation’s growing debt, an area he hopes to pay more attention to if reelected. Westerman said constituents tell him the increased cost of healthcare isn’t leading to more benefits.
US House Dems’ campaign chief predicts they’ll gain majority control in midterms

“If we’re ever going to address the debt, we have to address healthcare spending,” Westerman said. The U.S. government spent $1.8 trillion on Medicare in fiscal year 2025. Stabilizing the Medicare and Social Security trust funds, both of which are currently expected to run out in the 2030s, is crucial to resolving America’s longstanding deficit, Westerman said. 
If the Medicare trust fund runs out of money as it’s expected to do in the 2030s, the program could reduce benefits but Westerman said he believes the more likely scenario is that the government would borrow more money to make up the shortfall. The Fair Care Act, which Westerman has introduced every Congress since 2019 but hasn’t yet made it out of committee, “addresses a lot of these things,” the Republican said.
“Congress is the world’s best organization at kicking the can down the road until they get in a crisis situation, and we have a crisis situation on the horizon,” he said, adding that he is considering swapping some of his committee assignments if reelected to be in a better position to push for the bill’s passage.
The 434-page Fair Care Act would end the Affordable Care Act’s requirement for large employers to offer health insurance. The legislation would also allow for pre-tax dollars in a health savings account to be used for insurance premiums, among other changes.
But Russell said Westerman’s solution for the nation’s healthcare cost woes would not solve the multitude of problems that have made the cost of care one of Americans’ top affordability concerns. 
“You’re trying to promote something that’s a health savings account to people who are already so economically strapped that they cannot afford to put anything into savings,” Russell said. “That’s not a genuine solution.”
Russell supports a Medicare-for-all system instead, arguing it would save trillions in taxpayer dollars and thousands of lives. The only reason America didn’t have one when other developed countries did, Russell said, was due to a lack of political will.
“It would start helping the healthcare deserts that we’re seeing cropping up because people would be able to go and get the healthcare they need,” Russell said. “That would incentivize and keep rural healthcare facilities opened up.”
Russell said such a system could be paid for using a 1% “progressive wealth tax” on incomes starting at $200,000 — though he said a universal healthcare system would ultimately pay for itself by lowering health costs and keeping people in the workforce. 
“We have this habit of anytime we’re talking about making sure that everyone is covered with healthcare, we’re constantly talking about how are we going to afford it?” Russell said. “Nobody questioned how are we going to afford going to war with Iran again. Nobody questioned how are we going to afford arming countless ICE agents and throwing them out into the street.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Ethics questions arise for North Dakota lawmaker who also leads charitable gambling group
text:
Rep. Mike Motschenbacher, right, is also the executive director of the North Dakota Gaming Alliance. Pictured here: The Republican lawmaker from Bismarck reviews hearing handouts next to Scott Meske, center, lobbyist for the North Dakota Gaming Alliance, and Rudie Martinson, executive director of the North Dakota Hospitality Association, during an administrative rules hearing on charitable gambling on Feb. 18, 2026, at the North Dakota Capitol. The hearing was outside of a legislative session. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A Bismarck-area lawmaker says he is “completely separated” during the legislative session from his job heading a trade group for charitable gambling, a critical topic and burgeoning area of state law in recent years.
An ethics expert said Rep. Mike Motschenbacher could do more to better navigate the two jobs and potential conflicts of interest. A Democratic-NPL leader said he hasn’t been totally transparent with voters and should recuse himself from certain bill votes. 
Motschenbacher, R-Bismarck, is seeking a second four-year term for District 47, an area of north Bismarck. Since late 2020, he has been the executive director of the North Dakota Gaming Alliance, which calls itself “your voice for all those in the charitable gaming industry in North Dakota.” 
Charitable gambling is an ongoing topic in front of the Legislature following the proliferation of electronic pull tabs since 2018. The Legislature has dealt with many gambling-related bills, including regulations, since Motschenbacher was first elected in 2022.
Motschenbacher said he visited with the secretary of state, Ethics Commission and attorney general’s office before he first put his name on the ballot. He takes a four-month, unpaid leave of absence from his job during the regular biennial session and does not sponsor or speak on gambling-related legislation, he said. The Gaming Alliance hires a lobbyist, Scott Meske, who handles legislative matters, he said.
“I am completely separated. I concentrate solely on the issues that are important to District 47 and the state of North Dakota. I don’t do any lobbying or anything like that, so I have done everything that was asked of me and even above and beyond, I would say,” Motschenbacher said in an interview with the North Dakota Monitor.
He has not recused himself from votes on gambling-related bills, saying he does not uniquely or personally benefit from the legislation.
Rep. Mike Motschenbacher, R-Bismarck, speaks on the House floor during a special session of the Legislature on Jan. 22, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Motschenbacher hasn’t been upfront with voters about his job, said Bob Valeu, the Bismarck-Mandan Democratic-NPL director. He cited a District 47 GOP mailer that lists details and credentials for all three candidates, but did not include Motschenbacher’s Gaming Alliance job. He also pointed to Motschenbacher’s candidate statement of interest, which lists his principal occupation as a “professional” for the Gaming Alliance.
“It’s just so frustrating that there isn’t more disclosure and accountability with regards to potential ethical questions on a member of the Legislature voting on legislation that directly or indirectly impacts the association that he works for,” Valeu said.
Motschenbacher said his campaign website lists his Gaming Alliance job, which he said “just wasn’t pertinent to the mailer we put out.” 
“I’m not hiding behind it. Everybody knows what I do,” he said.
Motschenbacher clearly realizes he has an issue and is trying to deal with it, said Dennis Cooley, a professor of philosophy and ethics, and director of the Northern Plains Ethics Institute at North Dakota State University.
“That’s always a positive in regards to talking about somebody’s action and character,” he said.
But Cooley wondered what direction the Gaming Alliance lobbyist takes from Motschenbacher. 
“What he’s doing on its face looks fine, but as I said, it depends on whether or not there’s anything going on at all with him instructing that lobbyist, so when he steps away, is it a clean step away?” Cooley said.
Motschenbacher said Meske “is pretty much on his own during the session” as to lobbying and provides information on bills to lawmakers. Meske will ask him questions and give updates, he said.
North Dakota lawmakers work to refine which groups can conduct charitable gambling

The Gaming Alliance has a board that develops policy positions and directions for Meske before the session, Meske said. Motschenbacher is involved in that as executive director, Meske said. 
“That’s standard,” Meske said.
Meske said he gives the Gaming Alliance weekly updates and testimony during the session. When the session starts, Motschenbacher is not involved, Meske said.
“During the session, it’s like, nothing. If I see him in the hallway, I say, ‘Hey, how’s it going?’ but there’s no other interaction with that,” Meske said.
In the Legislature’s interim period, Meske will handle matters if the Gaming Alliance has a position on rules or is asked to testify, he said.
Earlier this year, Meske testified on behalf of the Gaming Alliance at a rules hearing of the state Gaming Commission. Motschenbacher sat in the audience and talked with Meske at times. Motschenbacher said he was being paid by the Gaming Alliance at the time, and sat in on the meeting to see how it went.
“I don’t want to be construed as trying to influence anybody because I do know I have my legislative duties and I separate them completely from my professional duties,” he said. 
The next month, Motschenbacher testified on behalf of his association at a meeting of a panel reviewing state boards and commissions, in which he expressed support of keeping the Gaming Commission. The panel, which includes other lawmakers, initially recommended eliminating the Gaming Commission but later changed course and indicated the commission would be studied in the upcoming legislative session.
Motschenbacher said normally Meske would have made the presentation as the organization’s lobbyist, but he was unavailable, so Motschenbacher did it in his official Gaming Alliance capacity. He didn’t speculate on whether his testimony helped the Gaming Commission.
Meske said, “I’m disappointed that this continues to be an issue, the fact that people criticize his position that he is employed by, just because he’s a legislator, and the only reason the issue is coming up is because it’s charitable gaming.”
In 2025, Motschenbacher voted for bills that would have lowered tax rates for charitable gambling, and would have restructured the state Gaming Commission to include groups that operate charitable gambling. Neither bill ultimately passed. The Gaming Alliance lobbied for both bills.
The same year, he also voted against a bill opposed by the Gaming Alliance that sought to restrict which organizations qualify to conduct charitable gambling. The bill passed the Senate but was overwhelmingly defeated in the House.
Motschenbacher cited a rule that lawmakers with personal or private interests in legislation must disclose their situation to the House, which then decides whether to allow the member to abstain from voting — but such interests are defined as “directly, individually and uniquely” affecting the legislator.
“I do not benefit whatsoever, personally or uniquely, by any bill I vote on,” he said. He gets no paycheck or bonus, but would recuse himself if a bill did uniquely benefit him, he said.
North Dakota House votes against revising rules on charitable gambling eligibility

Motschenbacher might be following the law, but perhaps the law isn’t what it should be, one of his opponents said.
“I mean, if he’s working for an organization that essentially benefits from the passage of certain things or from the failure of certain bills, then whether that’s impacting him directly is still in my mind a conflict,” Democrat Rosann Jacobs-Fode said. 
Valeu wondered how Motschenbacher would vote on a likely bill to regulate charitable organizations owning bars. 
“Is he going to vote on the basis of his employer, or is he going to vote on the basis of what his constituents want?” Valeu said. 
The ethical thing to do would be for Motschenbacher not to vote on legislation that would directly benefit the Gaming Alliance, Valeu said.
Cooley said a person doesn’t have to have money going into his or her pocket to have a conflict of interest. He suggests lawmakers consider how certain votes might look to their constituents. Does it look like self-dealing, for instance? And what do Motschenbacher’s constituents want him to do, he added.
Motschenbacher said every other lawmaker who works could be portrayed as having a conflict, given the “citizen legislature” North Dakota has.
“I would say I’m less conflicted just because of the fact that I take a four-month leave, and I don’t deal with gaming whatsoever during the session,” he said.
Motschenbacher’s Gaming Alliance job is in an inherently controversial business, Cooley said. That’s different from farming, teaching and other occupations Motschenbacher said could present conflicts for lawmakers in those professions.
Jacobs-Fode, a teacher and one of the Democrats running for House, said she has questioned voting on education-related bills. How would she approach voting on a teacher pay raise, she wondered.
“I totally understand the conflict that Mike is in and the difficulty of it, because I feel like I’m going to find myself in a similar boat. So it’s about following the law, making sure that we’re being as ethical as we possibly can be and double-checking ourselves,” she said. 
House Majority Leader Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, said each legislator is responsible for assessing possible conflicts on bills. He pointed out that a number of lawmakers recused themselves in the 2025 session, more than in years previously.
“My two cents would always be, ‘When in doubt, be open, be transparent,’” he said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Last year, other lawmakers routinely recused themselves from bill votes, citing employer ties to the topic or business with the state government. The House and Senate often excused lawmakers but also allowed some to vote.
There’s more understanding to be done regarding conflict procedures in legislative rules and visiting with the Ethics Commission, Lefor said.
Motschenbacher said he met with Ethics Commission Executive Director Rebecca Binstock three times “to make absolute sure that I am doing things correctly.”
Binstock said she met with him in 2023 but didn’t recall specifics. The Ethics Commission can’t function as lawmakers’ attorneys but can educate them on what the law says, Binstock said. It’s common for lawmakers, especially new ones, to ask questions, she said.
Motschenbacher has not ever sought an advisory opinion or “anything formal” from the ethics panel, Binstock said.
Motschenbacher said he has never heard from the Ethics Commission about complaints against him.
State laws on legislative lobbying, including registration and what activities define lobbying, don’t apply to lawmakers.
Even when wrong information is given in a House floor debate, he doesn’t rise to correct it “just due to how I’m hamstrung on this,” he said. 
Motschenbacher previously was a registered lobbyist for the Gaming Alliance until mid-2022 and for the North Dakota Hospitality Association and Citizens for Responsible Government until 2009.
Motschenbacher’s daily Gaming Alliance duties include dealing with memberships, listening to concerns in the industry and meeting with people all around the state, he said.
The Gaming Alliance gets most of its revenue from membership dues and assessments, according to the organization’s tax filings. The organization highlights on its website that its accomplishments include killing bills that would have restricted charitable gambling.
Motschenbacher confirmed he earns a $65,000 salary from the Gaming Alliance. His legislative salary was $34,926 last year, according to Legislative Council.
Motschenbacher is running with former Bismarck School Board President and past Bread Poets owner Jon Lee. Jacobs-Fode and fellow Democrat Cole Montoya also are running for the two District 47 House seats. Independent candidate Andrew Alexis Varvel suspended his House campaign but will still appear on the ballot.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com. Monitor reporter Michael Achterling contributed to this story.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: What to know as early voting begins in Iowa for 2026 general election
text:
A voter submits a ballot for the 2024 general election on the first day of early voting, Oct. 16, 2024, at the Polk County Election Office in Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Early voting has officially begun in Iowa, as of Wednesday, Oct. 14, for the 2026 general election.
Iowans will have an early chance to weigh in on their choice for Iowa governor, U.S. senator and representative, as well as a number of state legislative and local races and a constitutional amendments in the Nov. 3 election.
County auditors are able to begin sending out requested absentee ballots Wednesday. To participate in the election by mail, voters must submit an absentee ballot request, which can be downloaded from the Iowa Secretary of State’s website, to their local county auditor’s office. When requesting a ballot, Iowa voters must provide proof of identification through the ID number on their driver’s license or non-operator’s ID, or by using the four-digit PIN found on their voter identification card.
Iowans could begin submitting their absentee ballot requests August 25. The final day to submit the request is Monday, Oct. 19 — the form must be received by the county auditor by 5 p.m. in order for the request to be fulfilled. In order for completed mail-in ballots to be counted, the county auditor’s office must receive the ballot by 8 p.m. Nov. 3, the time polls close on Election Day.
In addition to mail-in ballots going out, Wednesday is also the first day Iowa voters can begin voting early at in-person locations. Iowa county auditors are able to host in-person early voting sites at their county auditor’s office and designated satellite polling locations. Locations, information and hours can be found on the websites of voters’ county auditor’s offices. Find your local county auditor here.
Voters must be registered to participate in early voting and they can register at the polling place. Iowa offers same-day registration for both early voting and on Election Day.
To register to vote in person, Iowans must bring an accepted form of identification as well as proof of residence through documents like a residential lease or utility bill to their polling location. People who do not have these required documents can still vote if a registered voter from their precinct attests for them, with both parties signing an oath that the statements made were true.
Voters whose ability to cast a ballot is challenged, such as for a lack of identification or proof of residency, can cast a provisional ballot. They would have until noon on the Monday after Election Day to supply proof of their identity and residency so their vote can be counted.
When participating in both early and Election Day voting, Iowans already registered to vote are also required to bring valid identification, like a driver’s license, U.S. passport, or signed Iowa Voter Identification Card.
Additionally, Iowans can register to vote online through the Secretary of State’s website with their Iowa driver’s license or non-operator ID information, or can register by filling out and returning a registration form to their county auditor’s office. Eligible voters must be U.S. citizens, Iowa residents and 18 years old by Election Day to register.
In addition to voting on candidates in the election, voters will have the chance to weigh in on a constitutional amendment. The proposal would add to the Iowa Constitution a requirement for future increases to personal and corporate income taxes to require a two-thirds majority vote of state lawmakers in order to go to the governor’s desk. If a simple majority of voters approve of the language in the ballot measure, the state constitution will be amended.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Doug Jones tells Montgomery town hall he wants to ‘phase out the CHOOSE Act’
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones talked about his education policy plan and other topics during a town hall in Montgomery on Oct. 13, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones Tuesday fielded questions about education and other topics at a town hall in Montgomery
Speaking to a crowd of at least 100 people, Jones talked about giving teachers and retirees a cost of living adjustment and said he wanted to “phase out the CHOOSE Act,” the state’s effective school voucher program. Income caps on eligibility for the program will end on Jan. 1.
“It’s (the CHOOSE Act) going to ultimately, if it doesn’t kill public schools, it’s going to just cripple and such that we do the public, and then we are seeing that in the numbers of kids that are in public schools this year,” Jones said. “The first year of the CHOOSE Act, 5,000 to 6,000 folks dropped fewer kids. The next year it was 12,000. Why do you think it’s going to be next year when the income caps are gone and we start giving handouts to people who make a lot of money?”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alabama State Schools Superintendent Eric Mackey said during the Alabama State Board of Education meeting last week that preliminary numbers showed 12,000 students were unenrolled from public schools. Mackey said while CHOOSE Act recipients made up some of the loss, the large drop in enrollment can’t be attributed to the voucher program alone.
Jones’ plan to phase out the program differs slightly from his earlier talks of ending school vouchers in the state entirely. Jones said he “started out candidly talking about eliminating it,” but because there are students already taking advantage of the program, he wants to phase out school vouchers instead.
“Those kids made a decision and their parents to change schools and benefited,” he said. “They believe so, and the income caps were on, so we’ll phase it out. But we’ll let those kids graduate.”
Jones also said he was “committed to making sure teacher raises go up,” but that his focus will be split with ensuring that educators have access to healthcare.
“Healthcare delivery in this state is a challenge. It’s really in a crisis right now because of the cost of health insurance, the fact that we didn’t expand Medicaid, and it is really crippling,” Jones said.
The Public Education Employee Health Insurance Plan (PEEHIP) board plans to ask the Legislature for a $222 million increase in the fiscal year 2028 budget due to rising health care costs.
One public school teacher asked what Jones thought about the Ten Commandments being displayed in schools because of how it could impact non-Christian students. Gov. Kay Ivey this spring signed SB 99, sponsored by Sen. Keith Kelley, which requires local school boards to display a poster of the Ten Commandments in fifth through 12th-grade classes and within common areas, in April. The bill went into effect on Oct. 1.
“I think we’ve got to have an attitude in this state that is more open and honest about who our neighbors are and where they are and what they are and have that respect. The Bible that I grew up with, the Sunday school lessons I grew up with, taught Christianity, but they also taught respect for others,” Jones said.
A kindergarten teacher asked if Jones would be willing to split money in the Education Trust Fund for turnaround schools, an initiative to help struggling schools in the state, to provide for all schools in the state and bring back teacher’s aides if elected.
Jones said the RAISE Act, which aims to create a needs-based funding model for K-12 schools, is on the right path to ensuring schools remain funded.
“There’s school systems that have foundations that help them because their residents will contribute to those foundations, and I don’t think they should be denied state funding. I’m not saying that, but there are, and I think the RAISE Act is a real good start of identifying those schools and putting extra money there,” he said.
Jones also addressed questions about data centers, repeating his call for a moratorium on new data center construction to give time to develop plans for the facilities. 
“I believe that a moratorium would probably not even last a year. I think if right now the governor, the Legislature, whoever said we’re not going to build these things until we get it all together, I think people are going to come to the table, and they’re going to see what we need to do,” Jones said.
Jones used Lowndes County, which approved plans for a hyperscale data center Tuesday despite community members disapproval, as an example of why a moratorium is needed. 
The data center in Lowndes County, called Project Red Clay, is a 800-acre facility that would be placed near a residential area.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee puts constitutional amendment questions near top of the ballot next to governor’s race
text:
Tennessee will have three constitutional amendment questions on the November 2026 ballot. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee officials placed the three constitutional amendment questions on the first page of the November 2026 ballot as required by law, pushing U.S. Congressional and state legislative races further down the ticket.
The legally required ballot design keeps Tennessee’s gubernatorial race at the top, with the constitutional amendments coming next. In Davidson County’s sample ballot, the amendments take up nearly three pages before voters get to the rest of the ballot. On Shelby County’s, the questions are more condensed. 
Tequila Johnson, co-founder of the Equity Alliance and a strategist helping Tennessee Democratic candidates, said that pushing U.S. Congress and state House races further down the ballot makes voters more likely to skip them. 
“We’ve lost state House races because people who voted for the Democrat at the top of the ticket didn’t vote down ballot,” Johnson said. 
In 2020, former President Joe Biden won the majority in the Memphis state House District 97, garnering over 17,000 votes. But the Democratic candidate in that district received about 14,000 votes, losing to the Republican by about 500. 
District 97 in the Tennessee state House is one of the party’s top targets in 2026, as it’s the only state House seat held by a Republican that voted for former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 Presidential election. 
Voters last took up constitutional amendments statewide in 2022, but those amendments were shorter. 
State officials placed the amendments near the top of the ballot because of a legal requirement, said Ben Hill, spokesperson for Tennessee Secretary of State Tre Hargett. Under Tennessee’s constitution, a majority of voters in this fall’s gubernatorial election would have to support the amendments for them to be added to the constitution. This means that even if they receive a majority of the votes cast, they may not pass if voters leave them blank. 
Voters face three constitutional questions in November election

What are this year’s constitutional amendments
Constitutional amendments end up on Tennessee’s ballot only after they pass the state legislature in two consecutive legislative sessions. This process means the questions appear only after the Republican supermajority approves them. 
The first constitutional amendment question seeks to remove the right to bail for defendants charged with one of 73 felony crimes that require at least 85% of the sentence to be served.
The second question is to prohibit lawmakers from implementing a statewide property tax, which Tennessee does not currently have. 
The third constitutional question focuses on crime victims’ rights, allowing them to be more involved in the judicial process before and after a conviction.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Amendment 82 is a dark-money attack on Colorado’s clean energy leadership
text:
A flare stack burns at a natural gas facility in Garfield County on May 16, 2023. (Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)With election season here, Colorado voters will decide on a wide range of ballot measures. Now is a good time to think about what makes a good ballot measure and what makes a bad one.
A great example of a good one was Amendment 37, which we passed back in 2004. It required Colorado’s large utilities to provide 10% of their electricity from clean, renewable sources by 2015. It was the first such measure in our nation to come from the citizens themselves and not the state government. Not only was that original goal achieved well ahead of schedule, but its success encouraged the state legislature to keep upping the requirement. Colorado’s largest utility, Xcel Energy, is now on track to provide close to 80% of our electricity from solar and wind, now the lowest cost sources of electricity, in just the next four years.
Amendment 37 had important features that make for a good amendment: first, it was a grassroots effort by Colorado citizens, not an industry effort funded by dark money; second, it moved our state forward, not backward; and third, it provided benefits to all Coloradans, not some special interest group.
This year, there is another ballot measure related to energy, Amendment 82, “Right to Purchase and Sell Natural Gas,” that manages to fail all three of those qualifications that you look for in a good amendment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Amendment 82 is funded by a dark money group, Advance Colorado, that is behind a whole slew of this year’s ballot measures. It would move us backward toward an old polluting fuel, natural gas, and hinder our efforts to take advantage of the clean electricity we now have available to heat our homes. And it would only benefit the natural gas industry while undermining our progress in addressing air pollution, which benefits all Coloradans. It would provide the gas industry with widespread pollution protection and would likely result in costly court battles.
Decades ago, the natural gas industry touted methane gas as a clean fuel compared to burning coal or oil to heat our homes. But, just as with burning gasoline in our cars, the burning of natural gas in our homes results in nitrogen oxide emissions, which are precursors to ground-level ozone production — a major cause of Denver’s serious air pollution problem.
This air pollution has real impacts for both our health and our pocketbooks. A study by the Colorado School of Public Health of the Denver Metro and North Front Range concluded that if we had simply met the federal ozone requirement over the five-year study period, we would have avoided 390 excess respiratory hospitalizations, 35,000 missed school days due to asthma and 170 deaths, and would have saved up to $580 million each year in healthcare costs. If we fully take advantage of our clean electricity to electrify our cars and homes, the benefits will be much greater still.
Colorado has been a leading state in terms of the percent of new car sales that are electric vehicles, so we are making great progress in that regard. And we are also starting to make good headway in electrifying our homes. Xcel Energy now has excellent rebates for purchasing today’s high-performance cold-climate electric heat pumps that can both heat and cool our homes and operate in the coldest weather without requiring any back-up heat. These heat pumps are marvels of modern technology and use energy about three times as efficiently as gas furnaces. Geothermal heat pumps, which extract heat from the ground instead of the outdoor air are even more efficient and are especially well-suited to new home developments.
A modern, all-electric home not only reduces outdoor air pollution but provides clean air to breathe inside our homes as well. This is especially important for homes with children, as recent studies have shown that the pollution from a gas stove significantly increases the incidence of asthma in children. Switching to today’s induction stovetops not only avoids both outdoor and indoor gas pollution but also provides very efficient, controllable and fast stovetop heating.
Amendment 82 would not give us a new right to purchase natural gas. We already have that right, thank you. What it would do is undermine our state’s efforts to reduce both air pollution and climate change emissions and cost our state money in legal battles. Its purpose is to benefit one special interest group: the methane gas industry. It’s a bad deal for the rest of us.
