name: Connecticut Mirror
title: High costs limit access to abortion in CT, research finds
text:
Nonprofit funds bridge access gaps for low-income people seeking abortions in Connecticut, according to recent research by students at Trinity College.
The findings show that more than 80% of the 969 respondents to an anonymous survey reported they delayed abortions due to costs.
The research project, conducted in partnership with the REACH Fund of Connecticut, a group that funds clinics to pay for abortion care, found that uninsured people almost always had a delay to get an abortion due to financial reasons.
Findings showed 83% of Medicaid patients that were surveyed, and about 76% of people with private insurance, also reported delays — in some cases a month or longer.
“The longer you wait, the more it’s going to cost,” said Alyce Coleman, board president of the REACH Fund. “Abortion pills work up to 10 to 12 weeks, and then it’s going to be a more complicated procedure.”
Planned Parenthood reports the average price for an in-clinic abortion at one of its facilities is about $600 in the first trimester, and rises to $2,000 or more later in the second trimester.
Those costs can rise as high as $20,000, Coleman said.
The REACH-Trinity project called for greater funding for abortion access and related costs, such as transportation, childcare and support for lost wages.
Jasmine Winters, lead community engagement coordinator at The Women’s Centers, and patient advocate for Women’s Centers in Connecticut, New Jersey, and Pennysylvannia, said although Connecticut’s Medicaid system covers abortion services at Connecticut clinics, patients can still face out-of-pocket costs in cases involving telehealth services, private providers, travel, delayed appointments or other logistical complications.
“As the cost of housing, groceries and gas continues to strain household budgets, we see patients every day who simply don’t have room for an unexpected medical expense,” Winters said.
Winters added that more than 100,000 people in Connecticut could lose Medicaid coverage under new federal work requirements.
“We’re deeply concerned that even more patients will face financial barriers to care,” Winters said. “At a time when families are already struggling to make ends meet, protecting access to affordable abortion care has never been more important.”
This story was first published Oct. 2, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Habitat for Humanity NC and pastors strike deal on ‘deeply affordable’ housing
text:
Rev. Cameron Barr, left, and Rev. Tony Boss discuss a new housing initiative in Hillsborough, Oct.11, 2026. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)After 18 months of sometimes uncomfortable conversations about race, a group of Orange County pastors and Habitat for Humanity of Orange County have reached agreement on a plan to help 10 low-income families buy homes in Habitat’s new Auman Village townhome community under construction in Hillsborough.
In February, crews had begun clearing the site where the Auman Village townhome project will be built. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
The pastors, who are also members of Orange County Justice United, and Habitat are longtime affordable housing allies, but had been at odds over a minimum income requirement of more than $60,000 to purchase an Auman Village home. The pastors told NC Newsline in February that the requirement would price low-wage earners out of the 75-unit townhome development, which is located near an historic African American community.
“It’s been my hope and desire that when you are planning to build within the community, allow the community to live in the community,” said Rev. Tony Boss, senior pastor of the 138-year-old Piney Grove Missionary Baptist Church, which is about a mile from Auman Village.
Boss initially asked for homes to be set aside for members of his congregation, but said in February that all African Americans with modest incomes should have a chance to buy homes in Auman Village.
Jennifer Player (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
Jennifer Player, Habitat’s president and CEO, said Habitat and the pastors made progress on a plan to serve low-income residents after she stopped looking at the issue as a math problem.
“In my mind, we had to start connecting our heart and our brain,” Player told NC Newsline. “Our brain was saying this is a math problem, but our heart was saying, gosh, it really feels — you know, we really wish we could do the work for this group of people.”
As housing prices climb due to higher land and construction costs, Habitat officials in Orange County and across the country say it’s becoming increasingly difficult to serve people earning 30% of area media income, which is about $34,350 for Orange County. 
They expressed reservations about lowering the minimum income requirement out of concern that a homebuyer would later be unable to pay the mortgage.
But Boss noted that some low-wage earners pay more in rent than he pays for his mortgage and still manage to “keep a roof over their heads.”
“It lets me know that if they had that opportunity to the American dream, if it was presented to them, they would be able to afford it because they are already doing it,” Boss said.
A large crowd gathered at Mt. Zion AME Church to hear about a new affordable housing initiative, Oct. 11, 2026. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
On Sunday, Boss and other pastors joined Habitat officials at Mt. Zion AME Church to announce the “Heaven Practice Housing” initiative to raise $2 million to subsidize mortgages for low-income families who buy homes in Auman Village. The money raised will offset the sales price for 10 townhomes to keep mortgages for them affordable for families. 
Rev. Cameron Barr, senior pastor of United Church of Chapel Hill, reminded the crowd that Orange County is one of the wealthiest in the state.
“So this isn’t good, and it doesn’t look good and it doesn’t feel good to any of us,” Barr said. “There are people suffering in Orange County, and it’s looking like we don’t care enough to do anything to change it.”
Habitat for Humanity and area pastors at odds over affordable housing

Barr said the goal is to make “deeply affordable” housing available to people who earn well under the Habitat’s minimum income requirement.
He said that the money raised would help, for example, a family of three earning $34,350 or a family of two with an annual income of $40,000 to afford to purchase a home in Auman Village. Those are the salaries of nursing assistants, the housekeeping staff at UNC Chapel Hill, and assistant teachers and school nutrition service managers in Orange County Schools, Barr said.
He also pointed out that the median income for a white family in Orange County is $99,961, while it’s just $52,121 for African American households.
“That is almost a $50,000 spread between the median white and the medium black household income in our county,” Barr said. “This is not right, and we know that as the cost of housing goes up, the effects on African American households are especially severe, and that is followed by the effects on Hispanic households and Latino households.”
Judit Alvarado (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
Judit Alvarado, a current Habitat homeowner, said homeownership changed her life.
“It gave us peace of mind, security and the ability to focus on our future instead of constantly worrying about housing,” Alvarado said.
Becoming a homeowner also deepened her family’s connection to the community, she said.
“The one thing that I wish more people understood is that families who need deeply affordable housing are not looking for a handout,” Alvarado said. “We are looking for a chance to create stability for our families and to put down roots and build a greater future.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Former Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback steps into US Senate campaign to endorse Roger Marshall
description: Former Gov. and U.S. Sen. Sam Brownback endorsed GOP Sen. Roger Marshall's reelection campaign. Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton pounced.
text:
Sam Brownback, ambassador for international religious freedom, delivers remarks at the State Department on June 21, 2019, in Washington, DC. (Photo by Sarah Silbiger/Getty Images)TOPEKA — Former U.S. Sen. and Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback endorsed the reelection of Republican Roger Marshall in the toss-up U.S. Senate campaign with Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton.
Brownback, with a 30-year record as a Kansas conservative, said he was puzzled people approached him to inquire about who he intended to vote for in the Nov. 3 showdown. He took to social media to share unequivocal support for Marshall. In doing so, Brownback exhibited no fondness for U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer, the New York Democrat, and aligned himself with President Donald Trump.
“Not sure why people keep asking,” Brownback said. “Kansas voters have a clear choice between Marshall and a liberal Democrat who wants to make Chuck Schumer majority leader and block President Trump’s judicial nominees.”
Hamilton told CNN that he wouldn’t support election of Schumer as Democratic leader if Kansas voters sent him to Washington, D.C., to replace Marshall.
Marshall’s campaign didn’t offer a direct response to the endorsement from Brownback posted to X. It’s unclear whether Marshall sought the backing of Brownback, who won a 1996 special election to assume the U.S. Senate seat previously held by Bob Dole. Brownback won a full term in 1998 and was reelected in 2004. In 2010, he was elected governor of the deep-red state, but his popularity cratered in his second term. Brownback resigned as governor in 2018 to accept President Donald Trump’s appointment as U.S. ambassador of religious freedom.
Campaign staff working for Hamilton, the Methodist founder of the Church of the Resurrection, seized upon the Brownback endorsement to remind voters that six of the eight living Kansas governors endorsed Hamilton. The Hamilton group included four Democrats and two Republicans.
“Congratulations to Roger Marshall on earning the support of one of Kansas’ least popular politicians,” said Tyson Brody, a Hamilton spokesperson. “Kansans remember the days of the Brownback experiment that devastated our public schools, left our roads in disrepair and financially ruined our state.”
 
Governor endorsements
Hamilton has been endorsed by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly and former Democratic Govs. Mark Parkinson, Kathleen Sebelius and John Carlin. Former Govs. Mike Hayden and Bill Graves, both Republicans, endorsed Hamilton.
Graves, who was governor from 1995 to 2003, said on PBS NewsHour that he appreciated the middle-of-the-road path sought by Hamilton. Graves said his confidence in Marshall eroded after Marshall voted Jan. 6, 2021, not to certify election results from Arizona and Pennsylvania that affirmed President Joe Biden beat Trump in 2020. He said Marshall subsequently failed to stand up for the interests of Kansans.
Hayden, who was governor from 1987-1991, said in a three minute video he had “supported Roger Marshall before, but he has put party and politics ahead of the people of Kansas.
“It’s time for a change,” Hayden said. “Kansas needs a senator willing to stand up and say ‘This isn’t working.’ ”
In response to the request for comment about the Brownback endorsement, Marshall spokesperson Payton Fuller said Kansans had a “clear choice” on Election Day.
Fuller pointed in the statement to Marshall’s allegation that Hamilton didn’t do enough in 2005 to address complaints that a Church of the Resurrection volunteer abused children at a church camp. In 2006, the church received more information and reported allegations to law enforcement.
“Kansans have a clear choice this election: A senator who has fought and delivered major wins for our farmers, cut taxes for the middle class and secured the border or a Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat who protected and enabled a pedophile preying on children at his church camp,” Fuller said.
The Senate Leadership Fund, the top super PAC aligned with U.S. Senate Republicans, plans to devote $14 million to Marshall’s candidacy. The PAC aligned with U.S. Senate Democrats, the Senate Majority PAC, committed $5 million to Hamilton’s cause.
 
Brownback legacy
Brody, the spokesperson for Hamilton, said Brownback signed legislation in 2012 that lowered state income taxes. The state didn’t cut spending to balance the revenue losses. That led to years of budget shortfalls. Brownback responded by increasing borrowing, retaining part of a temporary sales tax increase, cutting funding to K-12 education and postponing highway projects.
In 2017, a coalition of Republicans and Democrats in the Legislature passed a bill repealing much of the Brownback tax agenda. Brownback vetoed the bill but was overridden by two-thirds majorities in the House and Senate.
Brownback’s popularity suffered until he resigned to work in the first Trump administration. National polling by Morning Consult showed that at one point he was the least popular U.S. governor with an approval rating of 23% and a disapproval rating at 70%.
Brody said Brownback and Marshall “took our state backward” and that it was “time for something different.”
Trump endorsed Marshall’s reelection and Vice President JD Vance traveled to Kansas to boost voter enthusiasm for Marshall. Vance’s visit followed reporting by The New York Times that attorneys for Marshall, who worked as a physician in Kansas, filed lawsuits against more than 700 of his patients for nonpayment of medical bills. The process led to the arrest of approximately 80 patients. Marshall also has been criticized for assessing delinquent patients an 18% annual interest rate on unpaid debt.
 
The cookie bill

On Saturday, Marshall’s campaign paid $1,300 to settle a six-year-old debt to Holly’s Sweet Treats. The company provided cookies and treats for Marshall’s Senate primary campaign celebration party in 2020.
Store founder Holly Thomas said she attempted for more than a year to convince Marshall’s representatives to pay the $678.75 bill. She didn’t receive a response until after her recent viral Facebook post documented the debt owed by Marshall and explained why she wouldn’t vote for him in November.
“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020 — double,” Marshall said on social media.
Marshall’s campaign paid $57.50 less than double, but Thomas confirmed receipt of the payment: “Better late than never, right?”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Pete Buttigieg to campaign for Scott Colom in Mississippi
description: U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg visited the city for the groundbreaking of a $20 million rebuilding project of Medgar Evers Blvd, Friday, June 21, 2024 in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will campaign for Scott Colom, Mississippi’s Democratic Senate nominee, in cities along the Gulf Coast on Oct. 27, one week before the federal midterm elections.
Buttigieg, in a statement, said that he is looking forward to joining Colom on the campaign trail and “seeing him elected as the next U.S. Senator from Mississippi.” 
“Scott Colom is the kind of leader we need in the U.S. Senate: rooted in his community and ready to work with anyone to deliver results,” Buttigieg said. “He knows that it is not too much to ask for safer communities, good-paying jobs, and a government that works for people.” 

Buttigieg last visited Mississippi in 2024 while he was transportation secretary to help break ground on a $20-million renovation of Medgar Evers Boulevard in Jackson. He also toured the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument and visited the Mississippi Delta. 
Buttigieg, a potential presidential contender in 2028, has visited traditionally conservative states such as Kansas, South Carolina, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Florida, and Montana recently to campaign for Democratic candidates. 
The announcement marks the latest national Democratic figure to campaign for Colom. Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey visited Mississippi in recent weeks to campaign for the Mississippi Democrat.
Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia will host a fundraiser, conduct a conversation with faith leaders and headline a campaign rally on behalf of Colom in Jackson on Wednesday. 
Former President Barack Obama cut an ad on Monday urging Mississippians to vote for Colom ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 
“Mississippi, it’s time for a change,” Obama said in the ad. “And that’s why you need to send Scott Colom to the U.S. Senate.”
Colom is competing against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and independent candidate Ty Pinkins. 
Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, said in a statement that Colom “will suffer the same fate as the last two candidates President Obama endorsed in Mississippi.” Monssen was referring to Obama’s 2020 endorsement of Mike Espy for U.S. Senate against Hyde-Smith and his 2019 endorsement of Jim Hood for governor. 
President Donald Trump has endorsed Hyde-Smith, saying the Republican incumbent would never let Mississippi down.

name: Daily Montanan
title: I-194 seeks to remove ‘dark money’ from politics
description: An initiative seeking to limit spending by corporations, nonprofits and other organizations in elections, I-194, will be on the ballot this November. The initiative, which is being spearheaded by the Transparent Election Initiative, is using Montana’s ability for citizens to propose state laws to ask the question: Whether “artificial persons” can contribute[...]
text:
Former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg speaks at the Mother Lode Theater on Sunday, May 17, 2026 in Butte, Montana during an event highlighting the Montana Plan, an effort to create a state law to remove corporate spending from elections. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)An initiative seeking to limit spending by corporations, nonprofits and other organizations in elections, I-194, will be on the ballot this November.
The initiative, which is being spearheaded by the Transparent Election Initiative, is using Montana’s ability for citizens to propose state laws to ask the question: Whether “artificial persons” can contribute to elections to voters statewide.
In Montana law, “artificial persons” include groups such as nonprofits, trusts, partnerships, corporations, trade associations, or unincorporated associations. 
Since corporations are regulated by states, the idea behind the initiative is: Montana could limit corporate powers when it comes to contributing to elections, candidates and political parties. The plan grew out of frustrations about the huge amount of money flowing into political campaigns, as well as dissatisfaction with the “Citizens United” decision which equates campaign donations with political speech, afforded the highest protection by the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.] 
“We’ve never given up the authority as a state to determine what powers corporations have,” said Jeff Mangan, a former Montana Commissioner of Political Practices who has been pushing the effort for years. “So, what I-194 does simply is basically redefine those powers.”
Mangan is the president and founder of Transparent Election Initiative, an organization seeking to address the issue both in Montana and nationally. 
If passed, I-194 would mean that anyone who wants to contribute to a political campaign has to do so with their name attached. Advocates for I-194 have said that shell corporations have washed Montana in political cash and this pushes back against it. There’s nothing in the initiative that prevents businesses from advocating for candidates, but that they can’t contribute money. Businesses that fail to abide by that law would lose their right to do business in Montana.
There has been some opposition to the plan, including the Montana Chamber of Commerce and industrial interests such as the Montana Mining Association. The state Republican party has also added opposition to it to its platform.
Todd O’Hair, President and CEO of the Montana Chamber of Commerce worries that it could make it difficult for businesses to band together and fight regulations or candidates they don’t like. One worry, O’Hair said, is that it would not prevent a wealthy person from individually bankrolling a specific candidate.
“If I-194 passes, I think you can rest assured that there will be some of those folks coming in here to attack the things that are important to us and attack the values and our way of life because the business community will not be able to defend itself,” O’Hair said.
He also said the state has a relatively cheap media market, and there’s also a similar worry that someone with an axe to grind against a specific policy could theoretically blanket the state in ads regardless. And O’Hair worries businesses in the state wouldn’t be able to push back under I-194.
“It’s not hard to imagine someone coming in and saying, ‘This is a cheap media market. We can move the needle. We can ban a certain practice or a certain sector in the state of Montana, and we can do so in a way knowing that the opposition, the business community, is not going to be able to fight back and try to provide a different educational sort of narrative on this,’” O’Hair said. “So they would be free to make all sorts of misstatements, misconstrue facts, and completely lie about activities going on.”
Russell Cleveland, who is the Executive Director of Partnerships for TEI, says this levels the playing field between small businesses and large corporations. Cleveland finished third in the Democratic primary for Montana’s First Congressional district in June and made dark money a major facet of his campaign.
“One of the three pillars for me was getting ahold of this corruption issue that we have in politics and in government,” Cleveland said. “I really preach: You have to start at the source, which typically starts with campaigning and campaign finance.”
If passed, Montana would be the second state to introduce such a law, following Hawai’i. The idea has picked up steam nationally, as frustrations with spending in political races continue to mount — more than $1.7 billion has been spent on the 2026 midterm elections, according to Mother Jones.
“There’s an overwhelming need for reform and to get some regulation around it,” Cleveland said. “And this Montana Plan allows a different method to do that.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: A new owner took over central Missouri hospital. 9 days later, it cut labor and delivery
description: For pregnant women living north of Interstate 70 in central Missouri, there weren’t many places to deliver a baby. Fitzgibbon Hospital in Marshall was one of them. Now it isn’t. Fitzgibbon delivered 252 babies in 2025. In April, the hospital filed for bankruptcy protection and began sale negotiations for its 60-bed hospital and its 99-bed […]
text:
Fitzgibbon joins the ranks of nearly a dozen hospitals in Missouri that have shuttered labor and delivery services since 2010 (Fitzgibbon Memorial Hospital/Facebook).For pregnant women living north of Interstate 70 in central Missouri, there weren’t many places to deliver a baby. Fitzgibbon Hospital in Marshall was one of them.
Now it isn’t.
Fitzgibbon delivered 252 babies in 2025. In April, the hospital filed for bankruptcy protection and began sale negotiations for its 60-bed hospital and its 99-bed long-term care facility.
Just nine days after the sale closed in early September, Fitzgibbon’s new operator announced the hospital would end labor and delivery services at the end of the month.
Now, Fitzgibbon joins the ranks of nearly a dozen hospitals in Missouri that have shuttered labor and delivery services since 2010.
New owners Strawberry Fields REIT and operators American Medical Administrators are keeping prenatal and postpartum care running at Marshall Women’s Care, but their patients will have to leave Marshall to deliver their babies.
The closure comes as maternity care continues to disappear across rural Missouri. More than half of Missouri’s counties have no local labor and delivery services or obstetric clinicians, according to a recent March of Dimes report.
Bothwell Regional Health Center in Sedalia and Western Missouri Medical Center in Warrensburg are set to absorb the patients who were planning on delivering at Fitzgibbon. But both hospitals come with increased travel time for families, ranging from 30 minutes to over an hour.
 Preserving care was meant to be part of the deal 

Along with new owners and operators, Fitzgibbon is getting a new name: Missouri Valley Regional Medical Center.
But the brand refresh doesn’t erase the financial difficulties that the sole hospital in the town of roughly 14,000 is facing.
As the need to sell became more obvious, Fitzgibbon said it did what it could to make sure care would remain available to patients under new ownership.
Fitzgibbon said it had offers as high as $14.5 million to purchase the hospital, but accepted the lower $10.5 million offer from Strawberry Fields and American Medical Administrators partly because the groups had expressed a commitment to continue care, preserve jobs and participate in Medicare.
But those commitments got more complicated as the deal risked falling apart.
While finalizing the sale, the prospective owners raised concerns about Fitzgibbons’s finances and operations, according to court records. Then the sale missed its Aug. 31 deadline.
To avoid the potential of closing the hospital, Fitzgibbon sued American Medical Administrators  and Strawberry Fields to force the sale through. In that lawsuit, Fitzgibbon alleged American Medical Administrators had proposed cutting services, reducing outpatient care and backing away from Medicare commitments.
It only took days for services to be cut after the sale was finalized.
Dr. Abdullah Arshad, the chief medical officer at American Medical Administrators, said the company’s clinical team struggled to get enough visibility into Fitzgibbon’s operations during the sale process. Once the sale was closed and the company could closely examine the hospital’s finances, it became clear labor and delivery could no longer be sustained.
For former labor and delivery staff at Fitzgibbon, the news didn’t come as much of a surprise.
“I was not shocked, though I was sad,” said Rachel Leavitt, a nurse who worked in labor and delivery. “For me, it is mostly a concern for the community. One couple in one of our last births, they were already over an hour away,” Leavitt said. “She said with this it would be at least a two-hour drive. It’s mostly north of us that we really get into problems.”
 Is labor and delivery a losing game?

It’s getting more challenging for hospitals across the country to maintain their labor and delivery services, and to justify their cost.
Labor and delivery require constant staffing, including an obstetrician, anesthesiologist and specialized nursing staff on any given day, even if births aren’t happening.
Fitzgibbon’s maternity ward wasn’t sitting empty, but ultimately was still seeing fewer than one birth a day on average, which wasn’t enough to sustain the service in the face of the hospital’s broader financial problems.
“You have over 100 days in the year that you have to maintain services, without having the ability to bill for those services,” said Arshad.
Arshad said larger hospitals can often offset financial losses from labor and delivery with other services delivered across the hospital. But Fitzgibbon has spent years shuttering services, including its intensive care unit, leaving fewer profitable services to pad those losses.
Medicaid’s lower reimbursement for births makes the situation more complicated.
In Missouri, over 38% of the state’s births are covered by Medicaid. In areas outside a metropolitan hub, the number jumps to over 47%.
Despite an average of less than one birth a day, Leavitt said the unit felt relatively busy to those working there.
Nurses generally had several scheduled inductions or C-sections each week, in addition to unexpected deliveries and other emergencies. On slow days, nurses helped elsewhere in the hospital.
“We always had something to do,” Leavitt said. “It’s not like we were twiddling our thumbs.”
 Labor and delivery service cuts following acquisitions

The problems at Fitzgibbon predated the bankruptcy filing and the following sale. Fitzgibbon previously shut down its inpatient behavioral health services, its intensive care unit and some of its primary care offices.
But September brought a change in who was overseeing the books.
The timing at Fitzgibbon mirrors a trend researchers have found nationally: Rural hospitals are more likely to lose maternity care after they are acquired.
Eilidh Geddes, a health economist and assistant professor at the University of Georgia, and her colleagues studied what happened to obstetric care at hundreds of rural hospitals after an acquisition.
Overall, they found that acquired hospitals were 11% less likely to offer obstetric care five years after an acquisition.
“When rural hospitals are acquired, they are substantially more likely to close down their obstetrics units,” Geddes said.
Geddes said that compared to hospitals with no acquisition, maternity wards in hospitals that have been acquired are closing at higher rates.
And they found OB units that closed following acquisitions tended to be larger than OB units that closed without an acquisition.
“It is suggestive that a hospital that has not been acquired is going to continue on with an unprofitable service longer than an acquired hospital,” Geddes said.
She said that the maternity units they studied were generally small, at around 200 births annually. Geddes cautioned that the research doesn’t establish that an acquisition necessarily caused any individual hospital’s maternity ward to close.
 What’s next for Fitzgibbon? 

Arshad said his company will retain the hospital’s equipment needed to handle emergency deliveries if they happen. The hospital’s emergency room will stay staffed with on-call midwives and OB-trained nurses, and prenatal and postpartum care will still be available.
“Our ER is going to have a 24/7 OB-trained nurse, which is rare in rural hospitals,” Arshad said. “We are doing everything we can within our resources to staff our ER with a higher level of OB services than typical rural ERs.”
Eventually, he added, the operator hopes to reopen labor and delivery for Marshall and the surrounding areas, although Arshad did not provide a timeline for when that may be.
For Leavitt, many of her patients have chronic conditions or may not make it to all of their prenatal appointments, which can be associated with worse maternal or infant health outcomes.
“We have a high Micronesian population that typically don’t get a ton of prenatal care. They’ll have maybe one appointment, then show up at the hospital,” Leavitt said. “I’m way more concerned about the populations that we serve.”
Overall, more than 120,000 Missouri women live more than 30 minutes from a hospital offering labor and delivery services.
For Leavitt, losing the unit is less about whether babies can be delivered at other hospitals. A lack of specialized care in an emergency room can make a risky birth even more dangerous.
“I don’t think people realize how much we need maternal health. It is such a specialized field,” Leavitt said. “This is increasingly happening across the United States.”
“I love birth,” Leavitt said. “To be with women in birth is one of the most amazing, humbling experiences. But it is also one of the most dangerous times for women and children.”
This article first appeared on Beacon: Kansas City and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana death row inmate seeks execution delay for brain scans ahead of clemency hearings
description: Indiana death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit is asking the state’s highest court to move his execution from Nov. 5 to Nov. 19 so experts can analyze brain scans his attorneys say would give Gov. Mike Braun a fuller account of his impairments before deciding clemency. A federal judge approved funding for the testing but ruled […]
text:
Jeffrey Weisheit’s attorneys are seeking a two-week delay of his Nov. 5 execution to obtain brain scans and present additional evidence in his clemency case. (Mugshot provided by the Indiana Department of Correction)Indiana death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit is asking the state’s highest court to move his execution from Nov. 5 to Nov. 19 so experts can analyze brain scans his attorneys say would give Gov. Mike Braun a fuller account of his impairments before deciding clemency.
A federal judge approved funding for the testing but ruled she lacked authority to order prison officials to transport him for the scans.
In two emergency motions filed Monday with the Indiana Supreme Court, the lawyers asked the justices to direct Indiana State Prison officials to transport him to a nearby medical imaging center and postpone his execution and clemency proceedings by two weeks. The Indiana Parole Board is scheduled to interview Weisheit on Friday and hear public testimony Monday.
The Indiana Department of Correction did not immediately respond before publication.
The requests come days before an Oct. 15 deadline for written clemency materials. His attorneys contend that additional imaging and expert analysis could help establish that brain injuries affecting his behavior preceded the 2010 murders of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb.
Weisheit was convicted in 2013 of killing the children in a fire at their Evansville home. The Indiana Supreme Court set his execution in August, after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to review his case in June.
His attorneys argue that evidence about his brain injuries, mental illness and childhood trauma was not adequately developed or presented during his trial and appeals. They are now seeking that evidence for Gov. Mike Braun, who will decide whether to grant clemency after receiving the parole board’s recommendation.
“A 14-day extension would realistically afford a narrow but sufficient window — far short of the years available in prior recent cases — for Mr. Weisheit to develop this critical evidence,” the attorneys wrote in their motion to reschedule the proceedings.
The motions were filed by Joseph C. Welling, an attorney with the nonprofit law practice Phillips Black, and Indiana Public Defender Amy E. Karozos, who represent Weisheit.
The Indiana Supreme Court in 2018 previously rejected Weisheit’s challenge to his sentence based on the brain-injury evidence presented during post-conviction proceedings.
Weisheit’s attorneys said their request for more time to obtain brain scans is separate from an anticipated challenge to the execution method and a separate stay request tied to further post-conviction proceedings.
 Funding approved —but transportation denied
Weisheit’s lawyers emphasized that the immediate obstacle is getting him from Indiana State Prison to the nearby Franciscan Health Diagnostic Imaging Center in Michigan City for magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, and positron emission tomography, or PET, scans.
U.S. District Judge Sarah Evans Barker authorized funding for defense investigative services Sept. 16. According to the defense filings, that authorization included brain imaging and expert analysis.
Story continues below.
JAW-2026.10.12-mtn.short.stay.
 
The lawyers initially requested a federal transportation order Sept. 21 and filed a revised, public version of the request Sept. 25.
Attorneys from Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita’s office opposed the request, arguing that the federal court’s authority to fund clemency work did not give it authority to compel prison officials to transport Weisheit. His federal challenge to his convictions and sentence had already ended, they said.
“This Court has no authority to order transportation in this closed case,” the state wrote in its Oct. 5 response. “Nothing in (federal law) provides the authority for a district court to order anything beyond money for reasonably necessary investigative or expert services.”
Barker denied the transportation request Oct. 7. She distinguished the court’s authority to approve funding from its authority to direct state officials to help obtain evidence for a state clemency proceeding.
“In an abundance of caution, the Court did pre-approve Mr. Weisheit’s request for funding for potential new brain scans and other matters … ,” Barker wrote. “However, that order does not require the Court to issue a subsequent order compelling a state official to take certain action to ensure that the scans take place.”
Her ruling cited decisions limiting federal courts’ authority to order evidence gathering for state clemency cases. She also noted that Weisheit had not suggested he intended to use the new scans to support a claim that he lacks the mental capacity to be executed.



Quotation







Mr. Weisheit seeks the opportunity to present relevant information to the parole board. Absent a transport order to secure the brain imaging, this reporting would be unavailable.


– attorneys for Jeffrey Weisheit


The defense has now turned to the Indiana Supreme Court, arguing that a transportation order would allow Weisheit to present relevant information through the state’s clemency process.
“Mr. Weisheit seeks the opportunity to present relevant information to the parole board,” his attorneys wrote. “Absent a transport order to secure the brain imaging, this reporting would be unavailable.”
They asked the justices to require transportation within five days of an order, at a time coordinated between the prison and imaging facility. The center has indicated appointments could be arranged on approximately three days’ notice, according to the motion.
The request also specifies that metal restraints cannot be used in the scanning room because of the equipment’s powerful magnets.
Dispute over earlier brain injuries
The proposed testing concerns a longstanding dispute over the extent and timing of Weisheit’s brain injuries.
His attorneys contend that he experienced repeated head injuries during childhood and early adulthood, along with mental illness and abuse. They argue that those impairments affected his behavior long before the killings and were compounded by another head injury during his arrest.
Earlier MRI and PET scans were performed in 2012, according to Barker’s order. The defense is seeking new imaging and more detailed analysis to evaluate damage that might not be apparent through a visual reading of the scans alone.
Monday’s filings include a 2021 declaration from Ruben Gur, a University of Pennsylvania professor whose work focuses on brain function and behavior.
Indiana plans to proceed with execution after botched Tennessee attempt

Gur said quantitative analysis can identify abnormalities that are not readily visible and compare them with a database of other brains. Combined with neuropsychological testing and a person’s history, he said, the analysis could help distinguish older injuries from damage sustained during Weisheit’s arrest.
“There is a substantial likelihood that this data, including the Quantitative Analysis will show that Mr. Weisheit’s brain abnormalities pre-dated his arrest,” Gur wrote in the declaration.
He also explained how the imaging could be assessed alongside other evidence.
“Such integration can provide strong evidence of correlations between behavior exhibited throughout the person’s life history and the documented brain abnormalities,” Gur continued.
A 2018 Indiana Supreme Court opinion questioned how reliably Gur’s testimony established earlier concussions or lasting injuries. It also cited a state expert’s opinion that medical evidence did not establish traumatic brain injuries other than the injury during Weisheit’s arrest.
The defense argues that additional analysis could address those concerns. Gur said in his declaration that earlier testimony describing potential results as speculative reflected uncertainty about what testing would reveal before it had been conducted.
Hearings approaching
Under the current clemency schedule, the parole board is set to interview Weisheit at Indiana State Prison on Friday at 10:30 a.m. Central, or 11:30 a.m. Eastern.
Public testimony is scheduled for Monday, Oct. 19, at the Indiana Government Center in Indianapolis, with supporters of clemency appearing in the morning and opponents in the afternoon.
The defense wants the deadline for written materials moved to Oct. 29 and the public hearing moved to Nov. 2, along with the requested Nov. 19 execution date.

The parole board’s notice to Weisheit says hearing dates will not change unless the execution is stayed or rescheduled.
Braun has the final say on clemency. He denied requests from Benjamin Ritchie and Roy Lee Ward before their executions last year. Weisheit’s execution would be Indiana’s fourth since the state resumed carrying out death sentences in December 2024 after a 15-year pause.
The new requests also come amid separate, mounting questions about Indiana’s lethal injection preparations.
Indiana prison officials said earlier this month that they intended to proceed with Weisheit’s execution — even after Tennessee halted an attempted execution using pentobarbital, the same drug Indiana has used in its three most recent executions.
Indiana officials said the state has purchased but not yet acquired drugs for Weisheit’s execution.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Large majority in NJ backs voter ID requirements, poll finds
description: Strong majorities trust New Jersey's election results will be accurate, but even larger majorities want voter ID, per a new Rutgers poll.
text:
Strong majorities trust New Jersey's election results will be accurate, but even larger majorities want voter ID, per a new Rutgers poll. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Voter ID measures, including restrictive measures requiring proof of citizenship, enjoy broad support in the Garden State, a new Rutgers-Eagleton poll found.
More than 4-in-5 New Jerseyans, 82%, said they support or strongly support a voter ID requirement that allows voters to prove eligibility using a driver’s license or state ID, while 71% said they back more severe requirements to mandate voters prove citizenship by providing a birth certificate or passport.
The poll results come as Republicans in the New Jersey Legislature have renewed their push to pass voter ID legislation amid revelations from Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s administration that thousands of people who told the state Motor Vehicle Commission they were noncitizens were registered to vote anyway, and about 340 of them cast ballots.
Sherrill (D) has said she has no issue with voter ID requirements, but the GOP measures have not advanced in the Democratic-controlled Legislature.
Despite broad support for voter ID, majorities of voters expressed confidence in the security of New Jersey elections, the Eagleton poll says.
Nearly three-fourths of New Jersey adults, 74%, said they were somewhat or very confident about the accuracy of in-person and early vote counts. A little under three-in-five, 59%, said the same about mail voting.
Still, despite similar levels of support, the poll’s respondents were more likely to strongly support voter ID measures than they were to express strong confidence in voting results’ accuracy.
“Majorities would both support these hypothetical voting requirements and are confident about how November’s election will be run, but the intensity behind those two views is not the same,” said Ashley Koning, director of Rutgers’ Eagleton Center for Public Interest Polling.
Majorities expressed strong support for both voter ID requirements generally (63%) and a proof of citizenship requirement (51%), while only a plurality of voters (40%) said they were very confident in-person results would be accurate. Even fewer (29%) were confident mail votes would be counted accurately.
The parties were split when asked whether they believed only eligible voters would cast ballots in New Jersey.
Democrats overwhelmingly said they were very (59%) or somewhat confident (28%) that only the eligible would vote, while Republicans were more likely than not to doubt voter eligibility. Just 12% said they were very confident only eligible New Jerseyans would vote, compared to 28% who said they weren’t confident at all.
“Republicans are the most emphatic about tightening the rules and the least sure the system is working as it stands,” Koning said. “Ninety-five percent strongly support an identification requirement, and 12% are very confident that only eligible voters will cast ballots. Those two numbers are telling the same story from opposite ends.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. abortion shield law takes legal fire
description: The legal challenge comes as the country considers the messy legal question of whether reproductive care services are being provided where the patient is — which may be a state with a ban — or where the abortion medication is issued.
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Jennifer Smith
GUESTS: Nicole Huberfeld, Boston University law professor, chair of the BU Health Law Program, and co-director of the BU Program on Reproductive Justice








THREE RED STATES have launched a broadside against laws in Massachusetts and two other states that protect providers of abortions.  
The attorneys general in Louisiana, Arkansas, and Alabama filed a lawsuit at the end of September against California, Massachusetts, and New York. The suit asks the US Supreme Court to strike down the “shield laws” allowing providers in the three blue states to send abortion medication to people in states with stricter abortion laws. 
There are two lawsuits taking aim at the shield laws. One is filed against individual providers, including the Massachusetts Medication Abortion Access Project, and one is targeting the states themselves.  
The “extremity” of the inter-state clash was expected, said Boston University law professor Nicole Huberfeld on The Codcast. Huberfeld is chair of the BU Health Law Program and co-director of the BU Program on Reproductive Justice. 
“The fact that the states have drifted so far apart in their positions and are so willing to make it part of their political theater and culture wars — maybe that part of it wasn’t quite as predictable,” she said, “but the high degree of conflict and its intractability was entirely predictable.” 
Shield laws, Huberfeld noted, are a relatively new creation. After the US Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade in June 2022, Gov. Charlie Baker issued an executive order prohibiting executive branch cooperation with out-of-state investigations targeting lawful abortions in Massachusetts.  
The Legislature codified the order into law that fall, and Gov. Maura Healey signed an updated shield law in 2025 expanding protections. Massachusetts’ challenged law not only prevents cooperation with other states looking to discipline Bay State providers, it also limits the release of sensitive data, allows prescription labels to display a practice name instead of an individual physician’s name, and codifies a state requirement for abortion care to be provided in emergencies when medically necessary.  
States with strict abortion laws have been trying to enforce their laws against providers in other states. It’s thrust the country into the messy legal question of whether the reproductive care services are being provided where the patient is — which may be a state with a ban — or where the abortion medication is issued.  
“I wish I didn’t have to make this analogy, but I have researched it and it’s the best I can come up with,” Huberfeld said. “This is a lot like the way state laws looked before the Civil War, where slavery was either legal or banned, and there was litigation over this question of who could reach into the borders of other states over trying to, for example, retrieve enslaved people back to the place where they had been enslaved.” 
The US Supreme Court may take up the question directly or allow it to play out in the lower courts first, Huberfeld said, but the nation’s highest court will likely be faced with this high-stakes jurisdictional puzzle. 
“There is no clear answer as to what happens when states refuse to cooperate,” she said, “and in fact have laws that are not only incontrovertibly but irreconcilably in conflict with one another.” 
On the episode, Huberfeld discusses the history of shield laws (3:00), the messy nationwide legal landscape (14:00), and the main arguments in the case filed with the US Supreme Court (22:00).

name: Alaska Beacon
title: As King Cove road issue heads to federal appeals court, Peltola reiterates her support
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola reiterated her support for construction of the proposed Izembek road between Cold Bay and King Cove during a visit to King Cove this month. Peltola’s position is identical to the one held by incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola is challenging in the November general election. In […]
text:
An aerial view, taken by drone, shows the King Cove area where the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities is seeking to start construction on a road to Cold Bay. (Photo by Gabe Strong/Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities)

 Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola reiterated her support for construction of the proposed Izembek road between Cold Bay and King Cove during a visit to King Cove this month.
Peltola’s position is identical to the one held by incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola is challenging in the November general election.
In the weeks before the election, Peltola has limited her debate appearances against Sullivan and is campaigning in rural Alaska. On Tuesday, when President Donald Trump is scheduled to rally in Wasilla with Sullivan, Peltola is expected to be in Kotzebue. 
Petersburg’s Dan J. Sullivan and Republican candidate Gerald Heikes are also on the November U.S. Senate ballot.
In a prepared statement released Oct. 2, Peltola said that if elected, she will “ensure completion of the Izembek road.” The road is also commonly referred to as the King Cove road.
King Cove’s runway is frequently limited by weather, and Cold Bay, 19 miles away, has a long paved runway occasionally used as an emergency landing point for trans-Pacific flights.
But between the two is the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge and several miles of federally designated wilderness. 
Environmental groups have opposed the construction of a road between the two communities, frequently fighting it in court. In August, U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason overturned a land trade that would have permitted road construction to take place. 
Two days before Peltola’s visit, the federal government, state of Alaska and the local Alaska Native Corporation, King Cove Corp., appealed Gleason’s decision to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which is expected to rule by spring.
“A road would provide safe, reliable, and affordable access to the Cold Bay airport, which would give King Cove residents access to quotidian necessities, like fresh groceries, which most of us take for granted,” the appellants stated in their filing. “But most relevant for this motion, the road would facilitate medical evacuations.”
They said construction on the road could begin by April and be completed next summer if the 9th Circuit overturns Gleason’s ruling.
In an August forum hosted by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, Peltola said she isn’t happy with the way the federal government has blocked development in Alaska wetlands.
For example, she said, she opposes the EPA’s pre-emptive veto of Pebble Mine even though she disagrees with the project.
That veto, and federal obstacles to the Izembek road, she said, are indicators that “DC’s one-size-fits-all policy just doesn’t fit the needs of Alaskans.”
“We’re talking about an 11-mile gravel road, and this is a life-and-death issue for the people of Cold Bay, and it is being completely precluded because of the wetlands,” she said.
At the AOGA event, Sullivan said, “I just want to mention I do agree with my opponent on King Cove.”
He has visited the community several times while in office, including earlier this year.
He went on to add that if Peltola is elected, it increases the chances that Democrats will take control of the U.S. Senate, and Democratic administrations have opposed the Izembek road.
“The senators who she would empower … if she got elected, they’re all the ones against the King Cove Road. So you can’t have it both ways. You can’t empower the people who want to shut us down and then say, ‘I don’t want to shut you down,’” Sullivan said. 
In a statement Monday, a spokesperson for Peltola’s campaign said, “The people of King Cove can’t afford to wait any longer to access the healthcare and services they need, and Mary will stand up to anyone to help get this project across the finish line. Mary stood up to her own party to support this life-saving road on behalf of the Alaskans in King Cove, and in the Senate she’ll keep fighting to advance projects that are important to Alaskans.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Jake Johnson is collecting receipts — can he collect enough votes against Rep. Brad Finstad?
description: Jake Johnson stood at a small park tucked within the hills of North Mankato, his dinged-up Toyota minivan parked just behind him, armed with a solid gimmick: He would collect the receipts brought to him by people across Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District to document the rising price of everyday life.  If elected in November, he […]
text:
Jake Johnson, DFL candidate for Minnesota's 1st Congressional District, greets an attendee at the kick-off event to his "Receipts Tour” in North Mankato, Minn. on Oct. 4. (Photo by Maya Betti/Minnesota Reformer)Jake Johnson stood at a small park tucked within the hills of North Mankato, his dinged-up Toyota minivan parked just behind him, armed with a solid gimmick: He would collect the receipts brought to him by people across Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District to document the rising price of everyday life. 
If elected in November, he said he plans to bring those receipts to Washington — in his minivan.
The event underscored Democratic hopes for a Johnson upset victory in the 1st District, which President Donald Trump carried comfortably in three straight elections and which has been represented by a Republican in Congress since 2019. But rising prices — particularly the cost of fuel after Trump launched an attack on Iran in March — are giving Democrats like Johnson an opening to make the election a referendum on the cost of living. 
Johnson laid out the argument: “Costs continue to rise, and Washington doesn’t seem to care about it,” Johnson said. “Whether it’s the cost of gasoline or diesel because of the Iran war, whether it’s just the cost of doing business, building houses because of tariffs or the massive health care cuts that we’ve seen championed by our congressman — it seems to have no end in sight.”
The event also highlighted Johnson’s challenge in a district where Trump won by nearly 12 percentage points in 2024. Just six supporters managed to show up — his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad, has more children than that.
In order to win, Johnson, 43, has to prove to voters — Republicans, independents and Democrats alike — that he represents something different, rather than a typical blue state Democrat. 
Finstad, who didn’t respond to interview requests, has avoided obvious mistakes and scandal and would typically be able to rely on Republicans’ numerical advantage, but this is not an ordinary year. 
Home to Mayo Clinic and some of the Midwest’s richest farmland
Drive across Minnesota’s 1st District spanning the southern part of the state and the landscape changes, sometimes within a few miles. 
There are fields filling the horizon, small towns with modest church houses and dusty farm roads cutting through some of the state’s richest agricultural land. Then there is Rochester, where the skyline rises around the Mayo Clinic. Minnesota’s third largest city has grown by roughly 41% since 2000.  
The combination of farm country and growing cities like Rochester, Mankato and Winona has created a dynamic political mix in the 1st. 
Jim Cottrill, a Winona State University political scientist, points out that over the past 100 years, the congressional seat has been held by just two Democrats — Gov. Tim Walz, from 2007 until 2019, and Tim Penny, who retired in 1995. 
Rochester, a solidly Democratic outpost, is the region’s economic center, fueled in part by the expansion of the Mayo Clinic and the Destination Medical Center initiative. Around 50% of the city’s residents ages 25 and older have a bachelor’s degree or higher, and 13% are foreign-born — that’s more than twice the share in the rest of the district, and fertile territory for Democrats’ standard bearer Johnson, who is on leave from his job as a Rochester Public Schools teacher. 
Outside its cities, the district is dominated by agriculture. 
The district contains more than 6.6 million acres of farmland — about three-quarters of its total acreage — and accounts for roughly 36% of Minnesota’s agricultural sales. In 2022, the district ranked ninth nationally in agricultural sales, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.  
In years past, Republicans could rely upon this rural base to turn out on Election Day. Finstad, who has a family farm and worked for the U.S. Department of Agriculture during Trump’s first term, has been well positioned to dominate among these voters. 
Now, however, the farm economy is facing pressure from several directions: tariffs, inflation driven by the Iran War and cuts to federal farm programs — all under the leadership of a Republican president.  
“Bill Clinton, when he ran, he talked about ‘It’s the economy, stupid,’” Cottrill said, referring to the famous motto of the 42nd president’s political advisor, James Carville. “Those kinds of economic issues — how much groceries cost, how much gasoline costs — tend to hit people in their pocketbook, and it tends to motivate them.” 
With the tide of national politics turning against the president, whose approval rating is hovering just above 30%, and an energetic opponent, Finstad is confronting more of a real race than in years past.
Johnson shares working-class roots
This summer, Johnson traveled across Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District for a town hall tour that took him to all of its 21 counties. At each stop, he invited local residents to ask questions and raise their concerns.
And at each one, he started with the same story of uplift from working-class roots. 
His father was a garbage collector. His mother was a meter reader for a gas company. He grew up in Stewartville with 10 siblings, relying at times on SNAP and Medicaid and, later, on Pell grants and subsidized Stafford loans to afford college. 
Before his time on the campaign trail, Johnson spent 20 years as a high school math teacher. There, he worked to improve wages and working conditions for teachers through union activism. 
As a teacher at John Marshall High School he helped campaign for a Rochester Public Schools funding referendum in 2024, getting his first taste of politics. The referendum passed, providing more than $19 million a year in funding for the district for the next 10 years.
Now, Johnson is trying to translate that background into a campaign built around affordability for a candidate who understands the pressures middle-class families are facing.
At the “Receipts Tour” event in North Mankato, Johnson framed the election as a fight between working families and the wealthy.
“There’s two sets of rules,” Johnson said. “There’s a set of rules for the rich, powerful, well-connected folks in D.C. and then there’s a set of rules for the rest of us… working families doing more and more and making less and less.”
Johnson has gingerly tried to separate himself from other Minnesota Democrats, including Walz, given the metro party’s association with progressive social issues and the defrauding of the state’s social safety net. The party has nonetheless embraced his campaign. Walz and U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar have both extended praise to him, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added him to its “Red to Blue” program that seeks to promote promising candidates in historically hostile districts. 
Despite the attention from party leaders, Johnson insists he is not much different from the people he is asking to vote for him.
“I am the most real, boring person that maybe has done this for a while,” Johnson told the Reformer in an interview. 
Boring or not in the classroom, he’s engendered loyalty from his former students. 
Nik Marda, Johnson’s campaign manager, was once his student. Oftentimes at his town halls, young faces familiar to Johnson from his years in the classroom can be seen taking photos, recording video and handling microphones for the campaign. 
Jake Johnson, DFL candidate for Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District, answers questions at an “extra credit” town hall in Harmony, Minn. on Sept. 26. (Photo by Maya Betti/Minnesota Reformer)
For some voters at these events, Johnson’s appeal lies in his distance from current national politics, particularly Trump. 
“I think that Brad Finstad is just out of touch with this district,” said Maggie Jones, who came to Johnson’s North Mankato event. “He’s supported Trump in too many budget things, and it’s just gotten out of hand.”
Jim Davison, an elementary school principal at Fairmont Area Schools, calls himself a “proud independent” and said Johnson’s willingness to compromise is part of what drew him to the candidate. 
“He’s shown up,” Davison said. “He’s not bought and sold by somebody… I believe that he will work hard to really represent both sides.”
Davison introduced Johnson at a town hall in Martin County; he stressed that he wouldn’t have done so for any other candidate.
As Johnson has traveled across southern Minnesota, logging nearly 20,000 miles on his vehicle, he has turned his conversations with residents into policy, including a call for a data center moratorium and a plan to stop what he calls “data center exploitation.” 
Finstad has said that data centers can bring jobs and revenue to communities that want them. 
If elected, Johnson said he plans to continue holding his town halls, in every term, in every county. 
Finstad counts on his record
Finstad, like Republicans across the country, has been forced to take a different approach.  
While Johnson spent the summer driving from town to town, Finstad has largely kept his head down, relying on the advantages of incumbency: name recognition, a slight cash advantage and all the favors that members of Congress can do for constituents.
Finstad, 50, who is from New Ulm, has spent much of his career inside Republican politics. He served as an agricultural policy adviser to U.S. Rep. Mark Kennedy and spent three terms in the Minnesota House. In 2017, Trump appointed him to lead USDA rural development in Minnesota, a position he held until running for Congress.
He first won the seat in a 2022 special election following the death of Rep. Jim Hagedorn. Later that year, Finstad won the general election by over 11 percentage points — the best showing for a Republican since 2004. He was reelected in 2024 with almost 60% of the vote, outperforming even Trump. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Finstad has focused his work on issues that affect Minnesota’s agricultural economy. He voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions from his FARMER Act, which increased premium subsidies and extended benefits for new farmers and ranchers, among other provisions. That bill also kept in place income tax cuts passed in 2017, while cutting taxes on tips and overtime. To pay for it, Congress cut $1 trillion from Medicaid, the state-federal program of healthcare for low-income, disabled and elderly Minnesotans in nursing homes. 
Finstad has also championed a 2026 farm bill that would improve producers’ access to credit and make crop insurance more affordable. It passed the House in April, but has yet to pass the Senate.
Finstad is running a low-key incumbent’s campaign. 
“It’s not strategically wise for him to open himself up to opportunities to misspeak or to say something that will be taken out of context or misheard,” said Cottrill, the Winona State political scientist. “Incumbents are going to try to be judicious about where they go and what they do and what they say.” 
And Finstad has apparently been judicious with public events. 
U.S. Rep. Brad Finstad, pictured here during his first campaign for Congress. (Photo courtesy of Finstad)
Throughout his time in Congress, Finstad has opted against in-person town halls in favor of  “tele-town halls” —  phone calls in which his office “randomly selects” constituents from across southern Minnesota to speak with him for about an hour.
Dial-ins are not allowed, his office says, to prevent outsiders from infiltrating the conversation. One such tele-town hall purportedly drew 7,000 participants. 
He’s also been selective when it comes to press. 
Over the course of reporting for this story, the Reformer contacted Finstad’s congressional offices and campaign seeking an interview. There was no response. Multiple calls to his New Ulm and Rochester offices went unanswered. The Reformer also contacted state Republican officials and local Republicans seeking a comment about Finstad. Also, no response. 
Finstad hasn’t ignored his opponent entirely, however. His campaign website includes a “Jake Johnson vs. Reality Claims” section, which leads to a document devoted to Johnson’s political associations. It highlights Johnson’s past criticism of Trump, his ties to Walz and a $20 donation Johnson made to Sen. Bernie Sanders in 2020.  
There is no contact form on the Finstad website, but there is an email address at the bottom. The Reformer sent an email, but received no response. The website’s “news” section has not been updated since 2023.

name: California
title: At Alcatraz, Native advocates criticize Newsom’s vetoes of tribal bills
text:
Aztec dancers perform in front of a crowd at the Indigenous Peoples Day Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco on Oct. 12, 2026. Photo by Melanie Henshaw, CalMatters/ICT




Roughly a mile north of San Francisco, on Alcatraz Island, thousands gathered in the early hours of Monday to celebrate Native American resilience, reports CalMatters’ Melanie Henshaw.
The event, which took place on Indigenous Peoples Day, commemorates the 19-month occupation of Alcatraz from 1969 to 1971 by the Indigenous advocacy group, Indians of All Tribes. At one point, as many as 400 people lived on the island and ran their own basic services to protest federal policies targeting Native American communities and religions.
During the observance, organizers and attendees highlighted the challenges facing California Native people. Several criticized Gov. Gavin Newsom’s recent vetoes of bills that would have required state agencies to address tribal water shortages, and strengthened protections for tribal religious practices and sacred sites.

Morning Star Gali, executive director of the advocacy group Indigenous Justice and a citizen of the Pit River Tribe: “I’ve gone into state parks with all of our relatives to go in to be able to gather medicine and to be able to pray, to be able to pray at the sacred waters — I’ve been kicked out of those spaces.”

Sixty-two tribes in California lack federal recognition, which among other things would provide protections for sacred sites. Tribal leaders have argued that without additional protections, they are limited in their ability to safeguard sacred sites that could be damaged as a result of state and federal policies.
Attendees also criticized Newsom’s veto of a bill that would have established a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Justice Program within the California Department of Justice. In his veto message, Newsom said existing efforts rendered the proposal “unnecessary.”

Teyana Viscarra, co-founder of Way of the Sacred Mountain, an advocacy group focused on missing and murdered Indigenous women: “It’s ridiculous, our sisters continue to be ignored even as they go missing and die.”

Read more.



CalMatters and the UC Student and Policy Center are hosting a lunchtime conversation today in Sacramento on the ballot propositions shaping California’s future. We will break down what each measure would do and what’s at stake before you vote. Register here.

Other Stories You Should Know


Grappling with ICE in Central Valley and college campuses


Detention officers escort a handcuffed person from a white van into a federal immigration office in downtown Fresno on Oct. 7, 2026. Photo by Larry Valenzuela for CalMatters




As federal agents continue to crack down on immigrants, CalMatters’ reporters examine how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is rattling two different California communities:

Central Valley: In California’s agricultural heartland, residents are reporting a surge of ICE arrests. Unconfirmed social media videos in recent days appear to show uniformed agents in Madera and Chowchilla, as well as cars with missing drivers and smashed windows parked alongside the region’s farmlands. Workers in Mendota are carrying immigration documents in case they’re stopped. Democratic Assemblymember Esmeralda Soria, whose district covers Fresno and Madera, said her office heard about a family whose parent was detained on his way to cash his work check, leaving them unable to pay their rent. Said Soria: “They’re out there terrorizing our families.” Read more from Wendy Fry.


Community colleges: ICE agents have been making arrests near community college campuses, including at parking lots and public streets, inciting panic among students. Though college presidents say they’re doing everything to keep students safe, they admit that they have limited power. Some colleges have installed or plan to install signs outside building entrances telling agents they need approval to enter. In Santa Barbara, one college has partnered with a local immigration advocacy organization to help alert the college of ICE agents. Read more from Adam Echelman.




Where do CA gubernatorial hopefuls stand on water?


Birds flock over the San Luis Canal, part of the State Water Project, in Kettleman City on March 8, 2025. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo




California’s next governor will have to grapple with the state’s thirst for water, including groundwater overuse, lack of access to safe drinking water and ongoing water usage conflicts involving farmers, tribes, water districts and environmentalists. 
So what would the candidates, Republican Steve Hilton or Democrat Xavier Becerra, do to address these challenges?
As CalMatters’ Rachel Becker explains, Hilton is outspoken about his plans to build more ways to store and move water to farms and cities. He supports the Sites Reservoir to store Sacramento River water and the Trump administration’s controversial proposal to build Shasta Dam higher. 
Meanwhile, Becerra offers no specific proposals, but his record as former California attorney general can be telling: His lawsuits halted an effort to raise Shasta Dam, and he contested President Donald Trump’s proposal affecting water delivery systems that state officials feared would harm salmon and other species.
Read more.



And lastly: Fallout from $600K travel scandal


Ian Choudri, chief executive of the California High-Speed Rail Authority, at a board meeting at the California Natural Resources Agency in Sacramento on Oct. 9, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




The board that oversees the California High-Speed Rail Authority voted to restrict the spending power of the agency’s chief executive, after a state investigation found that consultants billed the agency $600,000 in travel expenses that were unauthorized or poorly justified. Some consultants flew first class, hailed luxury rides and traveled to night clubs. Read more from CalMatters’ Yue Stella Yu.






California Voices
Proposition 2 is about fiscal responsibility, and would double the size of the state’s rainy day fund so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next economic downturn hits, write Jesse Gabriel and Josh Hoover, Democratic and Republican California assemblymembers, respectively.
