name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas AG has a history of using unreliable expert witnesses in high-profile cases
description: TOPEKA — A woman told a Lawrence court earlier this month about using a bathroom in the Kansas Statehouse when she was a 19-year-old intern for a state representative.  “As I was using the restroom, it was apparent to me that the person who was in the stall right next to me was quite clearly […]
text:
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach appears at a Sept. 14, 2026, rally by Vice President JD Vance at Webco Manufacturing in Olathe. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A woman told a Lawrence court earlier this month about using a bathroom in the Kansas Statehouse when she was a 19-year-old intern for a state representative. 
“As I was using the restroom, it was apparent to me that the person who was in the stall right next to me was quite clearly a man,” said the woman, who testified anonymously during an Oct. 2 hearing on a law that restricts bathroom use based on sex assigned at birth. 
“I could tell this by the way that the individual was clearly standing to pee,” she said, according to court transcripts, adding that “they were facing towards the wall as opposed to facing outward, like as if you were sitting to pee.”
When the woman saw Kansas’ first transgender lawmaker, Stephanie Byers, come out of the stall, she told the court, she felt uncomfortable.
The trouble with that testimony, Byers said, is that she received gender affirmation surgery in 2019 in Thailand, roughly two years before she began serving in the Legislature. Her anatomy makes it impossible for her to stand to use the restroom, she said.
“Standing to pee is not something that is comfortable to do,” Byers said in a phone interview. “That is not something I do.”
The woman who testified anonymously is one of several witnesses Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach has brought forward in state cases whose bias and credibility has been questioned. 
Byers, a Democrat who lived in Wichita when she served in the House from 2021-2023, directly challenged the woman’s truthfulness.
But federal and state judges have deemed expert witnesses brought forth by Kobach, or on his behalf, not credible or unreliable in more than a dozen instances since 2016 across four court cases involving state laws.
A spokesperson for Kobach’s reelection campaign attributes the courts’ rejection of his witnesses to political pandering from the bench.
“Some judges are political,” said Danedri Herbert, a spokesperson for Kobach’s campaign who is also the chair of the Kansas Republican Party. “When an expert’s opinion stands in the way of a judge’s agenda, he will declare the witness not credible.”
A retired district judge found the pattern troubling.
“What’s concerning is he keeps using the same people over and over again,” said Kevin Moriarty, a retired Johnson County district judge, who was the first to permit same-sex marriage in Kansas.
“There is a pattern throughout the country,” he said, that indicates witnesses know what they’re going to say before they take the stand.
“The only thing the judges agree on is, frequently, they don’t have the experience to testify,” Moriarty said.
In a high profile 2016 case on voting rights involving then-Secretary of State Kobach, a federal judge, Julie Robinson, sanctioned Kobach and reprimanded him for “flaunting disclosure and discovery rules that are designed to prevent prejudice and surprise at trial,” she said in a 2018 ruling that also blocked a law Kobach supported that required proof of citizenship to vote.
“For most attorneys, they would be devastating comments,” Moriarty said.
Robinson also found Kobach in contempt of court before her 2018 verdict. Before that, a federal magistrate demanded he pay a $1,000 fine for presenting misleading information about voter fraud.
In a 2023 case challenging state-imposed abortion restrictions dating back to 1997, then-Johnson County District Judge Christopher Jayaram questioned the credibility of seven witnesses who testified for Kobach’s team of attorneys during a two-part trial in 2025. 
Jayaram said the opinions of a retired neonatologist, Robin Pierucci, on fetal development and fetal pain were “unlikely to be accurate and are certainly outside of the medical mainstream, which is not surprising, given her lack of experience in the subspecialities that actually deal with fetal development, health, and well-being.”
He said testimony from Farr Curlin, an internal medicine and palliative care physician, was “obviously biased and ideologically based.”
He gave Curlin’s testimony “no weight whatsoever,” he wrote in a 261-page decision issued in August, hours before he was sworn in as a Kansas Supreme Court justice. But Kobach ultimately used Curlin as a witness again months later.
Jayaram also gave little weight to testimony from three abortion patients, who “appeared biased and untrustworthy to the court, when considered either independently or in totality.”
Two, he said, gave testimony that was “significantly influenced” by “obvious philosophical biases” developed in the decades since they received their abortions. Another had three abortions, none of which occurred in Kansas. Jayaram said her testimony at times “seemed unbelievable and coached, given her demeanor while on the stand.”
Herbert, Kobach’s spokesperson, said Jayaram’s findings about the women’s credibility was “based on their religious faith,” which she speculated was a violation of the First Amendment.
On the other side, Jayaram called the plaintiff’s witness testimony in the case “extremely competent,” “compelling and impressive,” “equally powerful and credible,” “compelling and persuasive,” and with “no particular ‘bent’ or agenda to pursue, other than to testify objectively to the views of the mainstream medical and scientific communities in this particular subspecialty area.”
The case is in the process of being appealed.
In a case challenging a gender-affirming care ban for minors, Douglas County District Judge Carl Folsom disputed most of the witnesses Kobach put forth in a May ruling.
Folsom said the vast majority of the state’s witnesses were “not credible” or gave their testimony little to no weight in articulating his decision to temporarily block the ban. Kobach said at the time Folsom’s decision was “a stark example of judicial activism.”
The state’s eight witnesses included a plastic surgeon, a medical ethicist, an endocrinologist who treats adults and a neuroscientist. Folsom gave little weight to three of the eight, some weight to one and little-to-no weight to another. 
One of the witnesses was Curlin, the physician and medical ethicist who testified months earlier in the abortion restriction case.
Folsom said Curlin’s opinions were “inconsistent with the weight of medical research in his field, and his opinion appears motivated by his personal views as opposed to a methodology applicable in the field of medical ethics.”
He gave his testimony little to no weight.
Kobach also brought to the stand James Cantor, a neuroscientist-psychologist who has testified in favor of gender-affirming care bans in cases across the country. He has been criticized in the past for his specialized research on pedophilia.
Folsom said Cantor’s opinions were “supported only by cherry-picked information, conjecture, and research taken out of context,” and he gave his testimony little weight.
“Judge Folsom’s ruling on Dr. James Cantor was an aberration,” Herbert said. “Dr. Cantor was deemed credible and the court relied on his testimony in Missouri, North Dakota, and Kentucky. In that case, Folsom literally copied and pasted the proposed finding of fact from the ACLU, a leftwing New York advocacy group. He did no independent thinking at all.”
A judge in North Dakota used pieces of Cantor’s testimony to back up his opinion to uphold a gender affirming care ban. Gender affirming care bans were also upheld in Missouri and Kentucky, but other courts, including in Alabama and Tennessee have given Cantor’s testimony little weight. Folsom’s office did not respond to Kansas Reflector’s request for comment.
Despite Folsom’s ruling, Kobach brought Cantor to the stand again in early October.
During the four days of hearings over the anti-trans law, where the anonymous witness mentioned her experience in a Statehouse restroom with the state’s first trans lawmaker, Cantor testified before Douglas County District Judge James McCabria. 
Cantor said in a deposition for the case that he reviewed Folsom’s opinion before testifying. 
“I think he applied the wrong criteria for what determines the appropriate qualifications for expertise in the matter,” Cantor said.
Leah Rymer, a spokesperson for Democrat Chris Mann, who is running for attorney general against Kobach in the November election, said taxpayers are footing the bill for state witnesses.
“It’s reasonable to expect the state’s top attorney to bring credible witnesses, not ones who push a political agenda,” Rymer said.
Byers, the trans former state lawmaker, said honest assessments of trans people are necessary, especially in court. 
“You can’t let someone else tell your story,” she said. “The narrative is being told by people who don’t know and are not trans, and they are writing their own narrative in such a way to cast aspersions and fear on trans people.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Complexity isn’t the issue. The Legislature’s dysfunction is.
description: The complexity of our few bills tells us very little, if anything, however, about the quality of the bills or of the process that produced them. In fact, the complexity of bills covering multiple topics often only adds to the dysfunction and underperformance of our Legislature.
text:
A recent commentary piece by Massachusetts Senate counsel James DiTullio arguing that criticism of the Legislature’s productivity is misplaced because we are one of just seven states that allow for multi-issue “omnibus” bills drew considerable attention, including three op-eds written in response that we are publishing. In addition to the commentary below by former state representative Jay Kaufman, there are responses by Scotia Hille of Act on Mass and Jonathan Cohn of Progressive Mass.
IN HIS COMMENTARY piece, “Critics of the Legislature’s productivity ignore a key legal distinction setting Mass. apart from nearly all other states,” James DiTullio castigates critics of the Massachusetts Legislature’s productivity for failing to see the virtues of the complex bills passed by our lawmakers. DiTullio, the counsel to the Massachusetts Senate, correctly points out that 43 states have a single-subject limitation for any bill to be considered, and Massachusetts – like six other states and the federal government – does not.  
This distinction, he argues, makes claims that our Legislature is among the country’s least productive very misleading when based solely on a tally of the number of bills passed, since we are one of a handful of states that can enact omnibus bills covering many issues.      
The complexity of our few bills tells us very little, if anything, however, about the quality of the bills or of the process that produced them. In fact, the complexity of bills covering multiple topics often only adds to the dysfunction and underperformance of our Legislature. And DiTullio never addresses the question that really matters. 
For six of my 24 years in the Massachusetts Legislature, I had the privilege of serving on the board of the National Conference of State Legislatures, the professional association serving legislators and legislative staff. I came to appreciate the wide diversity of practices and cultures in our 50 states. That experience leads me to suggest that the right question to raise is how our practices and culture translate into the quality of work produced and the quality of the exchange of ideas and information, both within the capitol and with the public. By these metrics, the Massachusetts Legislature is failing miserably. 
DiTullio overlooks the Legislature’s practice of assigning bills to a “study” – a euphemism for making them disappear – or the cynical and intentional exploitation of multipurpose legislation to control the pace and outcome of what, in a well-functioning legislature, is called debate and deliberation, the democratic process. We, the public, don’t get to see committees grappling with complex and difficult issues, taking public action, and then sending bills to the floor of the House and Senate for active consideration and a vote.  
Instead, if bills don’t vanish into alleged “studies,” they head to the all-powerful Ways and Means Committee or secretive conference committees. From there, if they appear at all, they emerge changed and blended with other similarly disappeared bills into new bills which, under the Legislature’s rules or practices, are simply voted “aye” or “nay,” with no amendments considered.   
These long, multi-layered bills, written behind closed doors, are almost always released immediately before the chambers are asked to vote on them, certainly without adequate time for legislators, much less the public, to know what is in them or give them due consideration.  
Sadly, few members, lobbyists, or advocacy organizations are willing to speak out against this and risk the access and goodwill that comes with staying quiet. In the silence, the anti-democratic practices continue unchallenged. 
Perhaps requiring single-subject bills would make the omnibus bill sleight of hand harder to pull off. Perhaps requiring that any bill sent to “study” lead to a real report – complete with a recommended action to be taken by a real deadline. This would result in manageable and realistic action items in place of what are currently thousands of faux studies.  
But these, however valuable, wouldn’t begin to address the underlying issues.  
Perhaps eliminating the Legislature’s much-abused and corrupting leadership stipend practice would weaken the Speaker and Senate president’s hold on members and encourage more independence of thought and action. Perhaps having a nonpartisan office for policy and budget analysis (as most states do) would enhance the quality of the work and empower members to better understand and evaluate proposals before them.  
Perhaps it makes sense to curtail the pay-to-play culture the results of which can be seen in legislative leaders’ campaign coffers filled by those seeking access and influence. Perhaps Ranked choice voting and serious campaign spending limits would change who runs for election and who serves in our name on Beacon Hill. Perhaps term limits for legislators (leadership positions in particular) could undermine the wait-your-turn and go-along-to-get-along culture that encourages members to surrender their independence and power to the person at the top. 
Each of these reforms would make a positive difference. Would any or all make the Legislature more effective, transparent, accountable, and democratic? Let’s dare to find out. Allowing multi-subject bills is an interesting procedural distinction that sets us apart from most states, but it’s a distraction from the real issues that should be at the heart of any evaluation of how our Legislature functions.  
Jay Kaufman is a former Democratic state representative from Lexington.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Rather than a defense of their productivity, the Legislature’s reliance on omnibus bills should be an indictment
description: Democracy depends on being able to give positive and negative reinforcement to elected officials. Constituents should be able to praise legislators for what they do right and criticize them for what they do wrong. Omnibus bills weaken that ability, and that’s the point.
text:
A recent commentary piece by Massachusetts Senate counsel James DiTullio arguing that criticism of the Legislature’s productivity is misplaced because we are one of just seven states that allow for multi-issue “omnibus” bills drew considerable attention, including three op-eds written in response that we are publishing. In addition to the commentary below by Jonathan Cohn of Progressive Mass., there are responses by Scotia Hille of Act on Mass and former Democratic state representative Jay Kaufman.
IN A RECENT piece for CommonWealth Beacon, Massachusetts Senate counsel James DiTullio defends the Legislature’s productivity against statistics that show Beacon Hill passing far fewer bills than other states. He points out that Massachusetts is one of just seven states that allow omnibus bills covering multiple issues, a structure that he says reduces the number of bills in comparison to the vast majority of states, which only permit single-issue legislation.   
But his piece ignores the way that such statistics can be artificially padded at the same time that they are artificially limited in comparison to other states, and raises questions about the way that Beacon Hill’s lawmaking norms evade transparency and accountability.  
Given our paternalistic home rule system, in which Beacon Hill acts as a gatekeeper for cities and towns seeking to pass their own laws, many of the bills signed into law end up being home rule petitions. The first bill signed into law this year was approving a charter change for Malden, and the most recent was about Natick’s deputy police chief. Why does Beacon Hill need a role in either?  
The total count is also bloated by administrative matters like sick leave banks, in which state employees are able to benefit from unused sick leave from their colleagues.  
Last year, for example, there were 20 sick leave banks and 61 home rule petitions signed into law out of a total of 101 new laws. Of the 231 bills signed into law this year, 200 were home rule petitions and 6 are sick leave banks. If we were to look at laws of statewide import, the national statistics DiTullio rails against would be even worse.  
But DiTullio is correct that the Massachusetts General Court’s embrace of omnibus bills and policymaking through budgets and supplemental budgets makes simple bill tallies an imperfect yardstick. It was through last year’s budget, for instance, that Beacon Hill passed a new immigrant legal defense fund and banned tenant-paid broker’s fees, both significant wins. Bills can also be subsumed into thematic omnibus bills— say, for example, the PROTECT Act, which combined a number of important provisions from other standalone bills.  
However, you would never know this from the Legislature’s website. It records many of those individual bills as dead for the session, to be mourned today and to rise like a phoenix from the ashes in January. Indeed, understanding which bills have become law in the Legislature through budgets and omnibuses requires expensive paid subscriptions to companies specializing in bill tracking. Pity the poor engaged constituent, or even legislator, simply trying to understand what’s going on.  
Rather than a defense of the Legislature’s productivity, the reliance on omnibus bills should be an indictment. Congress has faced criticism in recent years for overly relying on budget reconciliation to pass legislation, creating mega bills containing a full agenda that get negotiated behind closed doors. Beacon Hill deserves the same criticism. Indeed, the reliance on omnibus bills is a breakdown of legislative process, not a sign of its efficiency.  
From the perspective of a rank-and-file legislator, you are forced into decisions about whether or not to support a bill that contains provisions you fought for and provisions you may despise. These trade-offs become pronounced when more and more unrelated items get cobbled together into one.  
For advocates and everyday voters, such a practice eliminates basic mechanisms of accountability. Consider the recent economic development bill. Both the House and Senate included important progressive policy changes as part of their bills, which passed near unanimously as “must-pass” bills always do. But can you praise individual legislators for what the bill included? Did they even know what policy riders were in there? Would they have voted for them as standalone bills, or even amendments? Constituents don’t know. Many legislators simply vote for the economic development bill for the sake of the earmarks.  
Democracy depends on being able to give positive and negative reinforcement to elected officials. Constituents should be able to praise legislators for what they do right and criticize them for what they do wrong. Omnibus bills weaken that ability, and that’s the point.  
Such omnibus bills also disempower rank-and-file legislators and empower the handful of high-ranking legislators who craft these bills and then negotiate them in conference. Fewer people making an ever-larger number of decisions is bad for democracy, and it’s also one of the biggest causes of inertia. Even if you assume the best of intentions of all, centralization slows things down.  
However, at the end of the day, the true test of productivity will never be based on the number of bills or outside sections of omnibus bills. Nor should it even be compared to other states. We need to judge the Legislature based on whether we are meeting our climate goals and our housing goals, whether we are making a more affordable and more equitable Commonwealth, and whether we are removing arbitrary hurdles to participation in our democracy. In all of that, we still have a lot of work to do.  
Jonathan Cohn is policy director at Progressive Massachusetts.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Omnibus bills enable opaque lawmaking
description: The modern trend of relying on omnibus bills for routine legislative work is not a neutral choice. It turns a simple democratic process into a labyrinthine ordeal.
text:
A recent commentary piece by Massachusetts Senate counsel James DiTullio arguing that criticism of the Legislature’s productivity is misplaced because we are one of just seven states that allow for multi-issue “omnibus” bills drew considerable attention, including three op-eds written in response that we are publishing. In addition to the commentary below by Scotia Hille of Act on Mass, there are responses by Jonathan Cohn of Progressive Mass and former Democratic state representative Jay Kaufman.
IN HIS RECENT op-ed regarding legislative productivity in Massachusetts, Senate counsel James DiTullio actually adds credence to the movement for reform.   
As executive director of Act on Mass, a nonprofit focused on transparency and civic engagement with our Legislature, I have criticized our Legislature’s lack of productivity. DiTullio contends that critics like me ignore Massachusetts’s lack of a “single subject” rule, which forces most other states to write bills pertaining to only one policy matter. Criticisms that Massachusetts is unproductive, he claims, can be explained by a unique ability to use “omnibus bills” and policy riders to combine multiple policies into large legislative packages.  
Those other states have something else in common: Their legislative output is clear enough that it does not require the chief counsel of a legislative chamber to spend extra time defending it to the public. Their output can be viewed and understood plainly by considering the number of bills enacted by the legislature and their contents. If this is not the case for Massachusetts, it is not the fault of “critics,” but of a broken legislative system that prefers opacity over transparency and unanimity over debate.  
Although Massachusetts’s peculiarities can make it difficult to compare to other states, it can be measured against our own historical record. During the 1997-1998 legislative session, the earliest available on the Legislature’s website, Massachusetts enacted 725 new laws. As is typical, most of these were local bills, commemorative bills, appropriations, or sick leave banks for individual state employees. An Act on Mass analysis found that 252, or roughly 35 percent, were general policy laws.  
In the most recently completed legislative session, 2023-2024, Massachusetts enacted just 496 new laws. Of these, just 79 were general policy laws, representing 16 percent of legislative output. Repeating this analysis for all sessions since 1997 reveals a consistent decline in overall legislative output. Although the current session is unfinished, it is not on track to reverse this trend.  
Results of Act on Mass analysis of the Massachusetts Legislature’s historical output.  
The decrease in overall output has coincided with a significant decline in passing general policy bills. If this decline in output is not due to a lack of productivity, as DiTullio claims, then the frequency and size of omnibus bills must have dramatically increased in the last 30 years. Put differently, a dependence on omnibus lawmaking is not an inherent feature of our state’s constitutional system, but a choice made by our current political leadership.  
The current Legislature has one of the largest Democratic supermajorities in the country. Unlike Congress, it cannot blame “gridlock” for its reliance on large omnibus bills and policy riders. If it’s true that our state legislators—unlike any other in the country—increasingly need such tactics to be “productive,” we should be concerned about why, not patting ourselves on the back.  
Indeed, the modern trend of relying on omnibus bills for routine legislative work is not a neutral choice. It turns a simple democratic process into a labyrinthine ordeal. For a window into what this costs us, here’s a slide from an Act on Mass “State House 201” workshop, concerning a bill that passed through DiTullio’s chamber. 

Slide from Act on Mass “State House 201” workshop, covering omnibus bills. 

Before even reaching the House, the Senate Data Privacy Bill (S.2619) was assigned six different numbers, each with its own unique page on the Legislature’s website. After a single  public hearing, the bill absorbed the contents of three different bills, swelled in size, and then shrank by half.  
In order to track the fate of an individual policy change from S.29, an interested constituent would have to manually search for it among the 34 pages of S.2619—and then hope it makes it through negotiations with the House. With a process this convoluted, it’s hard not to envy Virginians, whose system DiTullio points to for its “painfully narrow” bills.  
For another example, DiTullio touts the Legislature’s economic development bill for “effectively” addressing “many separate policies and topics” in one bill. That 225-page bill contains policy measures as diffuse as piloting psychedelics as mental health care, wage law adjustments for minor league baseball players, legalization of historic horse race betting machines, and authorizing multifamily housing on land owned by religious institutions, among others. 
In praising this system, DiTullio and his colleagues overlook a key purpose of our Legislature: representative democracy. Each of the bill’s “policies and topics” are distinct issues, which a constituent may care about and want to know their representative’s position on in order to inform their next vote for representative. Blending these issues into one bill, passed with a single vote, is not clever lawmaking; it’s a system that keeps constituents in the dark.
The last few decades have also seen more and more legislative work shifting to the second year of a session, even well past the traditional July 31 deadline. At the end of the most recent legislative session, legislators enacted a whopping 95 laws on the session’s final day; State House News pointed out that this constituted 20 percent of all laws enacted in the 2023-2024 session. In the first six months of this session, in 2025, just eight new laws were enacted.  
Now, 20 months into this legislative session and a year after Act on Mass first used it as a workshop example, the Data Privacy Act (S.2619) has still not been enacted into law. It is one of many outstanding priorities still languishing on Beacon Hill, including energy affordability, primary care reform, and the economic development bill discussed above.  
This procrastination has consequences. Currently, it means that the Commonwealth’s schools have started another academic year without knowing if they may need to implement a ban on cellphones. Although Gov. Healey named it an early-session priority in May 2025, we are heading into another winter season without a solution on energy affordability. And although it is the number one concern for Massachusetts voters, the Legislature failed to produce a single standalone bill tackling the housing crisis. Some might describe this delay and inaction, from a full-time Legislature, as a lack of productivity.  
Massachusetts residents don’t need to read a 50-state analysis to feel that our Legislature is failing to deliver. They feel it when they open their utility bills. They feel it when they struggle to find affordable housing. They feel it when considering this year’s record-tying nine ballot questions, many of which result from years of frustration trying to pass things on Beacon Hill.  
If Beacon Hill wants accolades for their productivity, they should spend less time defending undemocratic tactics and more time passing laws to improve the lives of Bay Staters. For greatest clarity, they could consider doing it one at a time.  
Scotia Hille is executive director of Act on Mass.

title: Nevada lawmakers propose alert system for missing Indigenous people
description: Nevada lawmakers are aiming to introduce a bill that would help address the ongoing crisis surrounding missing and murdered Indigenous people in the state. Nevada state Assemblymember Shea Backus (D-Las Vegas), a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, on Monday announced a bill draft request she sponsored that would establish a statewide Missing and Murdered Indige[...]
text:
(Right) Nevada Assemblymember Shea Backus, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, speaking at press conference on Indigenous People's Day. (Left) Nunie Harjo, an enrolled member of the Muscogee Creek Nation, waves Las Vegas Paiute Tribe flag. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Nevada lawmakers are aiming to introduce a bill that would help address the ongoing crisis surrounding missing and murdered Indigenous people in the state.
Nevada state Assemblymember Shea Backus (D-Las Vegas), a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, on Monday announced a bill draft request she sponsored that would establish a statewide Missing and Murdered Indigenous Peoples (MMIP) Alert.
Bill draft requests (BDRs) are not official bills, they are requests by lawmakers for a draft of the proposed bill they can further amend and discuss during the legislative session.
The intent of the BDR is to create a coordinated statewide system to rapidly share information with law enforcement, Tribal Nations, media, and the public when an Indigenous person goes missing under qualifying circumstances. 
The alert would function similarly to existing alert systems, like Amber and Silver alerts. Colorado, Washington, New Mexico, and California have similar alert systems for missing Indigenous people.
The proposed bill was announced on Indigenous People’s Day in front of the welcome to Las Vegas sign.
“When someone goes missing, we know how important time is,” Backus said during a press conference. “When an Indigenous person is reported missing and meets the established criteria, an MMIP alert would help get critical information out to the public, so that more people can be on the lookout and share information that may help locate them.”
More than four out of five Indigenous people in the U.S. have experienced violent crime, according to national data. Those are some of the highest rates of violence for any demographic, with Indigenous women nearly three times more likely to be murdered than white women.
The proposed bill would also serve as an omnibus bill, said Backus, adding that it would address several issues affecting Native American communities, including cleanup language to protect Indian children subject to the Indian Child Welfare Act.
Native Voters Alliance Nevada helped author the bill and is making passage of the legislation a priority in 2027.
Barbara Hartzell, executive director of Native Voters Alliance Nevada, said Indigenous people are impacted by disproportionate rates of violent crime. Hartzell recalled growing up listening to her grandfather talk about aunts, sisters, and cousins who went missing without a proper investigation.  
“No family should have to become an investigator, an advocate, and a public relations campaign just to convince someone to look for the person they love, yet to many Indigenous families that is the reality of missing and murdered Indigenous peoples’ crisis,” Hartzell said. 
Nevada Democratic U.S. Reps. Steven Horsford and Dina Titus spoke at the event in favor of the proposed legislation. 
“Every missing loved one deserves an urgent response, and every family deserves answers,” Horsford said.

name: California
title: One area Democrats, GOP agree: California needs a larger rainy day fund
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Jesse Gabriel
Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino, represents California’s 46th Assembly District and chairs the Assembly Budget Committee.


Josh Hoover
Josh Hoover, a Republican from Folsom, represents California’s 7th Assembly District and is vice chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee.


At a moment when Californians can’t agree on much, we’ve found common ground on something that matters: how the state saves for hard times.
One of us is a Democrat. The other is a Republican. We are united about Proposition 2, because this measure isn’t about partisan politics. It’s about basic fiscal responsibility, and it was developed by the people who understand California’s budget best.
California has one of the largest and most dynamic economies in the world. It’s also one of the most volatile. The state ranks fifth in the nation in revenue volatility because of our tax structure, but only 29th in the size of its budget reserves.
When the good times roll, state revenue pours in. When the economy faces challenges, the state is often forced into abrupt, painful cuts to programs Californians rely on: healthcare, higher education, public safety and safety net services.
Seniors, students and working families bear the brunt, often with little warning.
Prop. 2 fixes that imbalance. It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits. 
This is a structural budget fix without raising taxes to save more. It’s the type of budgetary planning we need to protect our future.
This isn’t a new or radical idea. It builds directly on a framework voters approved in 2014. And it reflects more than a decade of experience with how that fund has actually worked. 
Prop. 2 didn’t start with politicians. It was born from budget experts, not special interests. 
The Legislative Analyst’s Office, California’s nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, recommended its reforms, which developed during legislative hearings with input from the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts and business leaders.
But its earliest supporters were firefighters, small business advocates, healthcare providers and education leaders — people who see firsthand what happens when reserves run dry and cuts land on hospitals, schools and emergency response. 
That list has since grown because state leaders and fiscal experts from across the political spectrum have lived through what happens when California doesn’t save enough.
A stronger rainy day fund would make California more fiscally credible to taxpayers. States that save responsibly don’t just weather downturns better; they also borrow more cheaply and give families and businesses more confidence that the state can keep its commitments, even when the economy turns. 
That’s the real case for Prop 2. California is safer, steadier and more trustworthy when it saves like it means it.
Saving responsibly is not a partisan value. It’s common sense. California’s budget shouldn’t lurch from boom to bust. Prop. 2 gives us a better way forward.

name: California
title: Thousands mark Indigenous Peoples Day on Alcatraz as tribes decry Newsom’s vetoes of tribal bills
text:
In summary
Organizers and attendees at the twice-yearly sunrise ceremony criticized the governor’s vetoes of bills on water, sacred sites and missing and murdered Indigenous people.


Thousands gathered around a roaring bonfire on Alcatraz as the sun rose above the San Francisco Bay on Monday for a gathering to celebrate Indigenous resilience. 
The observance, which highlights the struggles of Native communities worldwide, takes place twice a year at sunrise, on Indigenous Peoples Day and Thanksgiving. 
In press materials before the event, organizers criticized Gov. Gavin Newsom’s relationship with California tribes and repeated those concerns in an interview with CalMatters/ICT.
“Our resilience in our continued fight for our religious freedom connects us to being here today,” organizer Morning Star Gali, executive director of the advocacy group Indigenous Justice, told CalMatters/ICT. 
The group sponsored Assembly Bill 1881, which would have strengthened protections for tribal religious practices and sacred sites. Newsom vetoed the bill on Sept. 30.
His office did not immediately respond to requests for comment Monday.
The event commemorates the 19-month occupation of Alcatraz from 1969 to 1971 by the Indigenous advocacy group Indians of All Tribes. At one point as many as 400 people lived on the island and ran their own basic services to protest federal policies targeting Native American communities and religions. The protest helped catalyze the Red Power movement of the 1970s.
The event, now nearly half a century old, was co-hosted by the International Indian Treaty Council. It  comes as the Mukwema Ohlone tribe, whose homelands encompass much of what is now the Bay Area, continue to seek federal recognition. 
“It’s more important now than ever to be here and to be present,” Gali said. “Every day as a California Indian woman is a fight against erasure and a fight against invisibility.”
Speakers included Matonth Brown, an Elem Pomo and San Carlos Apache whose ancestors include some of the 19 Hopi men from what is now Arizona whom the federal government imprisoned on Alcatraz in 1895, when the island housed a military prison. Authorities charged the men with seditious conduct for resisting the government’s removal of their children to federally operated boarding schools. The schools tried to forcibly assimilate Native Americans by stripping them of their identities, beliefs and languages, a policy experts now consider an act of genocide.
From a fire to an occupation
The occupation was “the spark that lit the fire” in the Native American rights movement, Gali said. It began in November 1969, six years after the prison closed, and days after an unexplained fire destroyed the American Indian Cultural Center of San Francisco, a critical service hub for Native residents of the area.
The fire galvanized activists, who were led by Richard Oakes and LaNada War Jack, to seek a new space for the urban Native American community.
On Nov. 9, 1969, Oakes swam across the bay’s chilly waters to reach Alcatraz. He declared it “Indian Land” and offered to buy it for $24 in glass beads and red cloth, recalling the sham purchase of the island of Manhattan by the Dutch in 1626. Oakes wrote his speech, later known as the Alcatraz Proclamation, in the style of treaties the U.S. had offered tribes. The group, which included many students, asserted control of the island under the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, which provided that surplus federal property would return to Native tribes. 
The Coast Guard removed the first activists in less than a day. Oakes and around 90 others returned Nov. 20 and over the next 19 months, the group established a school, radio station and a health clinic. Federal agents forcibly removed the remaining occupants on June 11, 1971.
Dancers converse with men tending the ceremonial fire after an intertribal round dance at the Indigenous Peoples Day Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco on Oct. 12, 2026. Photo by Melanie Henshaw, CalMatters/ICT
The legacy endures, said Irvin Whekins, a Shawnee youth counselor with Elevate Youth California, who brought nine Native youth from Chico to the ceremony. Sipping a coffee as the ferry crossed the inky black San Francisco Bay, he said the gathering is an opportunity every year to honor Indigenous diversity and resilience.
Changes may be coming to the island itself. President Donald Trump has repeatedly vowed to reopen the prison, and in April he requested $152 million for it in his fiscal 2027 budget, which Congress has yet to finalize.
“It’s a scary world we live in — scary president,” Whekins said. “He’s still trying to get rid of us.” 
Tribes challenge Newsom’s vetoes
In highlighting the challenges facing California Native peoples organizers pointed to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s recent vetoes of AB 1881 and another bill, both of which would have strengthened tribal protections for water rights and sacred sites.
In a statement, one of the groups hosting the event, International Indian Treaty Council, called the vetoes a “shocking action.”
The vetoes came less than a week after Newsom signed a law designating Sept. 30 as a Day of Remembrance for Indian Boarding Schools. The law identifies 13 California boarding schools that housed children from tribes across the country, subjecting them to “harsh conditions” and burying those that perished in unmarked graves. 
Gali, a citizen of the Pit River Tribe, and others criticized Newsom for promoting the proclamation before vetoing the water rights and sacred-sites legislation days later. 
Assembly Bill 1881 would have strengthened protections for sacred Native religious and cultural sites in California. 
“I’ve gone into state parks with all of our relatives to go in to be able to gather medicine and to be able to pray, to be able to pray at the sacred waters — I’ve been kicked out of those spaces,” Gali said.
Aztec dancers perform in front of a crowd of more than 2,000 spectators  at the Indigenous Peoples Day Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco on Oct. 12, 2026. Photo by Melanie Henshaw, CalMatters/ICT
Sixty-two tribes in California lack federal recognition, which among other things would provide protections for sacred sites. Tribal leaders say that, without additional state-level protections, they have limited ability to prevent significant damage to sacred sites.  
Newsom also vetoed Assembly Bill 2218, which would have required state agencies to address tribal water shortages. The bill would have required disputes between tribes  and state water agencies over projects in tribal ancestral territories to go through a mediation process facilitated by the Governor’s Office of Tribal Affairs. 
Jackie Fielder, a San Francisco supervisor and citizen of the Three Affiliated Tribes of North Dakota, is the first Native American woman to serve on the city’s Board of Supervisors. She emphasized the need to protect California Native communities’ access to clean water.
“We know water is life,” she said. “It must be protected.”
Calls for justice, and a veto amid a crisis
Several attendees also criticized Newsom’s veto of Senate Bill 891, which would have established a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Justice Program within the California Department of Justice. In his veto message, Newsom said existing efforts rendered the legislation “unnecessary.”
Teyana Viscarra, co-founder of Way Of The Sacred Mountain, an advocacy group focused on addressing issues facing Indigenous communities, attends the Indigenous Peoples Day Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco on Oct. 12, 2026. Photo by Melanie Henshaw, CalMatters/ICT
Native American women in California face disproportionate rates of criminal violence, including homicide. The bill would have increased funding and data collection and added victims advocates for Indigenous families. 
“Who else is going to stand up and be visible for our sisters? No one,” said Teyana Viscarra, a Piro-Tewa Pueblo, Apache and Kumiai woman who is a co-founder of Way Of The Sacred Mountain, an advocacy group focused on missing and murdered Indigenous women. “It’s ridiculous, our sisters continue to be ignored even as they go missing and die.”
Viscarra’s organization runs the Red Tipi Healing Project, which sets up bright red tipis covered with white handprints at events across the country to raise awareness of missing and murdered Indigenous women and provide spaces of healing and prayer. After the Alcatraz gathering, Viscarra and others reconvened to place a red tipi at Yerba Buena Gardens in San Francisco, and hold a separate celebration. 
She says the organization will continue draping the country in red cloth as long as Indigenous mothers and sisters go missing.  
This story is co-published by CalMatters and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in California.

name: Nevada Current
title: Hit to NV economy from Trump immigration policies could top $400 million by year-end, report says
description: The Trump administration’s anti-immigrant agenda could lead to roughly 15,000 people in Nevada losing legal protections and cost the state’s economy an estimated $441 million by the end of this year, according to a recent Fwd.us analysis    The report released by the immigrant advocacy organization earlier this month found that about 7,000 people in Nevada [[...]
text:
Protesting Trump's immigration detention and deportation policies in Las Vegas on Jan. 30, 2026. (Photo: Matthew Mondschein/Nevada Current)The Trump administration’s anti-immigrant agenda could lead to roughly 15,000 people in Nevada losing legal protections and cost the state’s economy an estimated $441 million by the end of this year, according to a recent Fwd.us analysis   
The report released by the immigrant advocacy organization earlier this month found that about 7,000 people in Nevada have government-authorized work permits. Construction and hospitality sectors make up the top industries, and each could lose roughly 2,000 workers.
The analysis warned the volume of people losing their immigration status won’t only destabilize Nevada’s economy but also harm mixed-status families, threatening the stability of households accounting with as many as 4,000 children in Nevada who are U.S. citizens.
Nevada, like most states, has seen a drastic spike in deportation and immigration enforcement since Trump took office in January 2025.
In addition to a surge in deportations as part of his campaign promise, the administration has made rapid changes to who is eligible for temporary protected status, stripping protections away from individuals from Haiti, Venezuela, Afghanistan, and Cuba. 
Around 80,000 immigrants in Nevada have some form of protected status, including DACA, TPS, asylum or U-Visas, which applies to survivors of violent crimes. 
Of that, about 52,000 people rely on work permits and “contribute an estimated $1.8 billion to the state’s economy each year,” according to the analysis.
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services notified Salvadorans –  6,000 of whom live in Nevada – that their temporary protected status would expire Sept. 9. It was the latest group of people to learn TPS would end. 
Immigration experts say federal law requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to decide whether a country still qualifies for a TPS designation at least 60 days before it expires. TPS protections for Salvadorans remain intact until DHS makes an official decision.
Nationally, roughly a million people have lost temporary protected status as of August 2026, according to FWD.us. Roughly 3.5 million immigrants are projected to lose status by the end of 2028.
By the end of Trump’s first year back in office, an estimated 2,000 people in Nevada lost their immigration status. Half of them had been in the state with work permits.  
The state could lose about $40 million in annual state and local taxes this year as well as $48 million in federal and payroll taxes under current projections from the 15,000 people losing immigration status. 
On the current trajectory, roughly 34,000 people in Nevada could lose immigration status by the end of 2028. 
Of that, about 21,000 people could lose work authorization with the top industries impacted being construction with 7,000 jobs and hospitality with 5,000. Health care and education make up another 2,000.
“In Nevada, total losses are projected to reach 21,000 workers, an $849 million loss in annual economic contributions and an annual loss of $220 million in combined taxes,” the report found.

title: Family Court incumbent challenged by former Clark County DA candidate
description: Judge Charles Hoskin has been on the Family Court bench for 17 years and is seeking another term. He faces a challenge from Timothy Treffinger, who ran for Clark County District Attorney in 2022 and lost.  Treffinger has little campaign presence and did not respond to requests for an interview.  Hoskin was appointed to the […]
text:
Charles Hoskins, Timothy Treffinger.Judge Charles Hoskin has been on the Family Court bench for 17 years and is seeking another term. He faces a challenge from Timothy Treffinger, who ran for Clark County District Attorney in 2022 and lost. 
Treffinger has little campaign presence and did not respond to requests for an interview. 
Hoskin was appointed to the Family Court Department E by Gov. Jim Gibbons in 2009. He was elected in 2010, 2014, and 2020. 
 by Gov. Jim Gibbons in 2009. He was elected in 2010, 2014, and 2020. 
Hoskin, who could retire if he desired, says he’s seeking reelection at the urging of family law attorneys “wanting to make sure we have some stability and some experience on the bench, as we’ve got a lot of new judges or fairly new judges.”
Family court, he says, deals with “probably the most emotional area of the law. It’s a rough situation for individuals who find themselves in those circumstances,” he said of litigants. “They  didn’t really ask for it most of the time, and they’re not really prepared for it. Essentially, they’re asking a third party to make decisions that will affect them and will affect their children.” 
Hoskin, who has practiced family law for 35 years, says he strives to ensure a professional and informed environment, which he credits with keeping the drama at a minimum in his department.  
“I had a really good idea of how the process works and how people deal with it before I even put on the robe, so I think that probably helps me,” he said, noting some judges “don’t have that experience before they come in, and it takes them a minute to to learn how that works and the overwhelming emotions that people are going through during that process.”
Between 70% and 80% of Family Court litigants represent themselves. Hoskin helped the Supreme Court create rules for an informal, opt-in trial program that allows parties to bypass some of the confusing protocol that dominates court proceedings.
The court is designed for unrepresented litigants  “who don’t understand court processes, don’t understand the rules of evidence, or the procedures. It creates a way for them to get all the evidence they need into the court and not have to jump through those hoops. We’re able to consider the totality of what they want to present, rather than what they are able to get in using the rules of evidence.”
The use of artificial intelligence in motions is complicating matters for Hoskin and other judges who say the pleadings don’t always reflect what the party is requesting. He says he’ll ask pro se litigants for additional information, when needed, and give them an opportunity in court to clarify.
“With attorneys, I’m a little less lenient, but I still want to make sure I understand their argument,” he says, adding he has at times read cases prepared by a lawyer “and I’m still not clear on what it is they’re asking me for. I just have higher expectations for someone who’s been to law school and passed the bar than somebody who hasn’t.” 
Of the 108 attorneys who evaluated Hoskin in the Las Vegas Review-Journal’s Judging the Judges 2025 survey, 83% recommended that he be retained.
According to Our Nevada Judges, which tracks judicial records, appeals courts found Hoskin to be in error in 42 of 80 cases. 
Statistics don’t always tell the story, Hoskins says, noting appellate judges “have a different job than I do. My job is to take the evidence and apply it against the law to the specific circumstances. Their job is to look at what was presented and determine whether they believe that something didn’t go the way that it should have gone.”
Appeals courts, Hoskin says, also have the luxury of time to analyze what happened, while he is “dealing with everything in the moment that is happening.” 
Statistics don’t always tell the story, he adds.
“If I’ve made a mistake, I want to learn from it and be able to change it in the future,” he says. “The frustrating part for me is when I will get a reversal in one case and an affirmance in another case with very similar facts, and have to figure  out what they want me to do in the future.”
Hoskin is endorsed by the Professional Fire Fighters of Nevada, the Las Vegas Police Protective Association, the Culinary Union, Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, IATSE 720, Teamsters Nevada, and Nevada Veterans United. 
As of Oct. 5, Hoskin had raised $20,800 and had just under $11,500 in the bank. He says he’s not trying to raise money. 
“My opponent really isn’t doing anything,” Hoskin asserts. “I haven’t seen him at any events. He didn’t even file a second quarter contribution report.”
Treffinger filed one report for the first quarter in which he reported no contributions or expenses.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: What’s up with amendments A & B? Lawmakers are asking voters to change the Utah Constitution (again)
description: In addition to all the congressional, legislative and local races Utahns will need to sort through after they get their by-mail ballots starting this week, there are two wonky but important questions for them to answer.  The questions titled Amendment A and Amendment B, depending on what voters decide, will have long-term implications for the […]
text:
People watch from a packed gallery as the Senate discusses a proposed constitutional amendment related to citizen initiatives during a special legislative session at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Wednesday, Aug. 21, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)In addition to all the congressional, legislative and local races Utahns will need to sort through after they get their by-mail ballots starting this week, there are two wonky but important questions for them to answer. 
The questions titled Amendment A and Amendment B, depending on what voters decide, will have long-term implications for the state’s foundational governing document: the Utah Constitution. 
Amendment A will strip out the explicit requirement for all other future proposed constitutional amendments to be published in newspapers before the election, instead replacing it with a more flexible rule set by lawmakers. 
Amendment D still void: Utah Supreme Court upholds district court decision

Amendment B — the more controversial of the two — would set a higher bar for Utahns to enact certain laws at the ballot box, requiring a 60% approval threshold for ballot initiatives that would come with a tax increase. 
The amendments mark the Utah Legislature’s latest attempts to change the state Constitution — something that’s become fairly common. 
Over Utah’s history, the Legislature has referred 192 measures to the ballot — nearly seven times the number of citizen-initiated measures, which have totaled 28 since 1895. Measures put on the ballot by the Legislature (which requires a two-thirds majority vote), have had a higher likelihood of passing — nearly 70% — compared to just 25% of citizen-led ballot initiatives, according to an analysis done by Ballotpedia. 
Over the past 10 years, since 2016, Utah lawmakers have proposed 20 changes to the Utah Constitution. Most have passed at the ballot — but not all. And in 2024, two of those questions were voided by the courts, in part because state leaders failed to follow the newspaper publishing requirement and in part because they used misleading and inaccurate ballot language. 
Here’s what you need to know about this year’s pair of proposed amendments and the debate around them:
Amendment A 



				Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to change how proposed constitutional amendments are published, requiring publication for 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner established by state law instead of in newspapers?			


Under this proposed constitutional amendment, newspapers would no longer be the required way for state officials to spread the word about all future proposed constitutional amendments. 
If voters approve Amendment A, the Utah Constitution would be changed to remove its explicit requirement that state officials publish proposed constitutional amendments in “at least one newspaper in every county of the state, where a newspaper is published for two months” immediately before the election. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Instead, the constitution would require they be published “in a manner provided by statute, for 60 calendar days” immediately before the election. 
If voters approve Amendment A, state law would be changed through HB481, which was approved during the 2025 legislative session, to require the lieutenant governor to publish the full text of all proposed constitutional amendments (and other ballot questions from the Legislature) on the state’s Public Notice Website and on the lieutenant governor’s website for 60 days before the election. 
This proposed amendment was put on the ballot after a unanimous vote to approve it in the Utah House and Senate. There is no known organized effort to oppose the amendment.
However, it has a history that stems from controversy over previous constitutional amendments that were halted by the courts. 
Utah lawmakers proposed it after two proposed constitutional amendments were voided from the 2024 ballot amid lawsuits, in part because the courts determined state leaders failed to meet the constitutional publication requirements and in part because lawmakers used misleading and inaccurate ballot language to describe their effects. 
If voters approve Amendment A and HB481 takes effect, it could reduce state costs by up to $1.4 million every two years, according to a fiscal analysis included in the state’s voter information pamphlet. 
Utah legislative leaders express regret over Amendment D’s ‘misleading’ ballot language

“The savings from changing the publication requirement for proposed constitutional amendments from newspapers to publicly operated websites would vary depending on the length of each proposed constitutional amendment and newspaper publication rates,” the analysis notes. 
Proponents of the amendment have argued that in the digital age, print newspapers are becoming more scarce and not the primary way most Utahns get their information anymore. 
“While that made sense when newspapers were the primary source of information, most Utahns now rely on digital sources, mobile devices, and online platforms to stay informed,” Rep. Anthony Loubet and Sen. Daniel McCay, both Republicans, wrote in an argument in favor of the amendment included in the voter information pamphlet. 
They argued it would “modernize” Utah’s public notice practices and allow them to “adapt as technology evolves.” 
“By modernizing an outdated constitutional requirement, Utah can maintain transparency, improve accessibility and save taxpayer dollars,” they wrote. 
Because Amendment A was put on the ballot by a unanimous vote, no rebuttal to the argument in favor was included in the voter pamphlet. 
Amendment B



				Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to require that citizen-proposed laws that increase taxes compared to existing law be approved by at least 60% of voters, instead of a simple majority?			


This constitutional amendment would make it harder for certain statewide ballot initiatives — or laws approved by Utah voters — to pass at the ballot box. 
Under Utah’s Constitution, currently most ballot initiatives need a simple majority (more than half, or 50%) to pass. The one exception is thanks to a constitutional amendment Utah voters passed in 1998, which requires two-thirds approval (66.67%) for voters to approve ballot initiatives related to the “taking of wildlife,” or hunting. 
If approved by Utah voters this year, Amendment B would raise the bar to 60% for ballot initiatives that increase taxes, either by creating a new tax, expanding an existing tax, hiking an existing tax rate, or changing a property tax rate in a way that results in a smaller decrease in the property tax rate than would occur under existing law. 
What would that mean for ballot initiatives? It helps to look back to 2018, when Utah saw a flurry of ballot initiative efforts. 
Utah lawmakers want a higher bar for ballot initiatives that raise taxes. Will voters sign off?

That year, no initiative received more than 60% of the vote, though three passed and two increased taxes. An initiative for full Medicaid expansion passed with 53.3% of the vote, and an initiative to legalize medical marijuana passed with 52.7%. A Better Boundaries’ initiative to create an independent redistricting commission also passed, but by a slim 50.3%. 
The Medicaid expansion and medical marijuana initiatives both created new revenue streams to pay for themselves, so if they were subject to the new 60% requirement in Amendment B, neither would have passed.   
Proponents of Amendment B — including the Utah Taxpayers Association — have argued the change would help protect taxpayer money. The question’s sponsor, Sen. Lincoln Fillmore, R-South Jordan, argued during this year’s legislative session that voters should decide whether to set the higher threshold or not. 
Critics, however, have launched a political issues committee, Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, to finance a campaign urging Utah voters to vote down Amendment B. They have argued the change would be an “unnecessary and permanent rewrite of Utah’s founding document that would weaken one of the most important tools citizens have to hold government accountable.”
Utahns Protecting Our Constitution argues that the Utah Constitution should only be changed when absolutely necessary, and if voters approve Amendment B, they’ll be taking away their own power “and giving politicians control over the rules.” 
In arguments in favor of Amendment B included in the election’s voter information pamphlet, Fillmore and the question’s House sponsor, Rep. Jason Kyle, R-Huntsville, said with Amendment B, Utah voters will decide “how easy should it be for your neighbor to raise your taxes?”
Voter Guide: 2026 General Election

“Any proposal that will take more money from Utah families, workers and businesses should have widespread agreement from the people who will pay for it,” Fillmore and Kyle wrote. “Amendment B provides that safeguard by requiring statewide tax-related ballot initiatives earn 60% voter approval before becoming law. The amendment does not prevent voters from approving tax hikes they support. It simply ensures proposals affecting taxpayers statewide have broad backing before they take effect.”
The Legislature’s top Democrat from Salt Lake City, Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla and House Minority Leader Angela Romero wrote the argument against, saying it really asks “should elected officials have more power than you?”
“Requiring 60% approval for tax-related initiatives does not create accountability,” Escamilla and Romero wrote. “It creates an unequal system where voters face stricter rules than the Legislature itself. Lawmakers can raise taxes with a simple majority. The people should have that same power.”
Fillmore and Kyle argued that taxes imposed by the Legislature “can be reversed by new legislators at any time, but statewide initiatives operate differently.” They contend they “cannot be revised or adjusted once passed, other than by another costly initiative.” 
It’s worth noting, however, that Utah lawmakers repealed and replaced all three of the 2018 Medicaid expansion, medical marijuana and independent redistricting initiatives, making changes to the voter-approved laws. A lawsuit over the redistricting repeal and replacement led to a 2024 Utah Supreme Court ruling that made clear Utah lawmakers’ ability to change “government reform” ballot initiatives has limits.
