name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Criminal justice advocates disappointed by GOP attacks, Crowley’s cancellation of  jail tablets
description: For weeks, a stream of ads has attacked Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor, for allowing  access to tablets in the Milwaukee County Jail. In some high-profile cases, incarcerated people used the tablets to harass people on the outside. The ads, which recycle footage of a disgruntled local judge, have kept […]
text:
David Crowley, Milwaukee County Executive, speaks to media after he relaunches his campaign to become Wisconsin's next governor. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)For weeks, a stream of ads has attacked Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic candidate for governor, for allowing  access to tablets in the Milwaukee County Jail. In some high-profile cases, incarcerated people used the tablets to harass people on the outside. The ads, which recycle footage of a disgruntled local judge, have kept Crowley on the defensive while casting his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, as a protector of crime victims. 
The ads focus on individual cases of people using their jail-issued tablets to harass witnesses and victims. Many feature Milwaukee County Circuit Court Judge David Borowski, who asked,  “Why is the sheriff’s office handing laptops and iPads to defendants?” Borowski was presiding over a hearing involving Thomas Zollicofer, who is accused of killing three people in a spree. Zollicofer used his tablet to tell a witness to “stop lying,” WISN 12 News reported. Some of the ads also mention Ameir Jones, who is also accused of homicide and of attempting to call a victim in his case over 1,500 times, with prosecutors saying 300 of those calls were answered.
The Wisconsin Examiner’s Criminal Justice Reporting Project shines a light on incarceration, law enforcement and criminal justice issues with support from the Public Welfare Foundation.
Over a short span of time, the anti-Crowley ads have made tablet access a big issue in the governor’s race. Late last week, Crowley suspended instant messaging on digital tablets at the Community Reintegration Center. The facility, formerly known as the House of Correction, is under more direct oversight by Crowley and the county board than the jail, which is overseen by the sheriff’s office. 
On Monday Brian Schimming, chairman of the Wisconsin Republican Party, issued a press release accusing Crowley of protecting himself from a scandal. “This program should’ve never been allowed in the first place, and Crowley resisted ending it for months after victims were threatened and laws were broken,” said Schimming, going on to call Crowley “a craven politician who only cares about his own political future, not the safety of our state’s citizens.”
Milwaukee-based Black Leaders Organizing Communities (BLOC), which supported Crowley when he re-entered the race for governor and won the primary race, expressed disappointment at the suspension of messaging services. “We have to be careful in giving in to the narrative of Republicans and their methods to make incarcerated people as uncomfortable as possible,” their statement warned. The group added that “this form of communication seems to be the best and safest form that there is currently.”
As the political controversy over tablets grew, the sheriff’s office attempted to clear the air. Joshua Briggs, director of the Milwaukee County Jail, said that the devices are not iPads but a “generic tablet.” Briggs explained that the tablets cannot be used to make calls out of the jail, and are not connected to the internet. The devices use a network maintained by the vendor, ICSolutions, which allows for keyword flagging and other guardrails. Briggs estimated that 98% of the people held in the jail use the tablets responsibly.
U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany speaks to reporters after his launch event in Wausau in September. (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
The ads don’t mention that Republican-dominated counties including Waukesha and Ozaukee also give people housed in their jails access to tablets. 
The tablets are important, advocates say, because they allow incarcerated people to maintain connections with loved ones and others on the outside. 
“I understand what it means to have a connection to home,” Marianne Oleson, co-executive director of Ex-Incarcerated People Organizing, told the Wisconsin Examiner. Oleson, who spent four years in prison before being released in 2017, explained that tablets give incarcerated people access to recovery resources, employment preparation, parenting classes, and other rehabilitative services. 
Tablet use  has become commonplace in jails and prisons tablets. “This technology is being used on a significant scale,” Oleson said. “Edovo reports that its educational platform was available in 1,483 correctional institutions across 47 states in 2025, with participants completing 46 million hours of learning. Those are the provider’s reported numbers, but they show how much programming can be delivered through these tools.”
Shannon Ross, a founding member of Justice Forward, wrote in August in an op ed for Wisconsin Watch, that tablet-type devices are used in 48 state prison systems, the federal prison system and in county jails nationwide. “Correctional officials have credited tablets with reducing violence and disturbances inside correctional facilities,” Ross wrote in the August op ed. “Some jurisdictions have reported declines of up to 40%, and the director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons described the agency’s tablet program as reducing administrative burdens and allowing staff to focus more on institutional safety, not as a security risk it was forced to accept.”
The Milwaukee County Jail. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
“Providing tablets is an established practice today,” Oleson told the Examiner. “Wisconsin DOC says that each person residing in an adult facility will be issued an ICS tablet as its transition moves forward. Ozaukee County’s own website says that personal letters, pictures and drawings are delivered digitally through tablets available in all living units. This is happening across jurisdictions, regardless of politics.”
Other criminal justice advocates raised similar points about the use of tablets in jails and prisons. “Allowing tablets inside jail facilities is particularly important because it allows more in-depth communication with family and friends,” BLOC said in a statement to the Examiner. “Inmates can see messages and pictures from their families and loved ones. It enables them to maintain a closer connection than that of regular phone use. Sometimes, persons in custody need their families to advocate for them for their health, treatment and more that the jail staff cannot assist with immediately.”
Oleson was also disappointed by Crowley’s move. “My reaction to Crowley’s decision is concern for the people and families who are losing legitimate communication because of someone else’s misuse,” she wrote. “Victim harassment and witness intimidation are serious, and they must be addressed. We support holding people accountable for that behavior and holding facilities and vendors accountable for enforcing protections.”
Roy Rogers, a minister, board member of the Wisconsin Justice Initiative, and leader of the Onesimus Group of Milwaukee, wrote in a statement to the Examiner that electronic communication is one of the main ways his ministry can keep in touch with incarcerated people. “For us, a message is an opportunity to encourage someone, share our faith, or help them think through their next steps,” wrote Rogers. “For families, it means maintaining a connection with a parent, spouse, or child. We say ‘reentry begins with relationship’ because those connections need to grow before someone comes home.” 
 Getty Images
Rogers said that he cares about the safety and security of victims. “No one should have to fear threats or harassment through this technology,” wrote Rogers. “My understanding is that Crowley’s action pauses messaging at the CRC until stronger safeguards are in place, rather than eliminating tablets altogether. My hope is that those protections allow safe communication to continue. These tools have a meaningful place in family connection, ministry, daily facility operations, and preparation for reentry.”
“If a suspension is necessary while those changes are made, there should be a clear timeline and an explanation of what must happen for access to resume,” wrote Oleson. “I am concerned when the needs of incarcerated people and their children become talking points in a political campaign. These decisions affect real families. They should be guided by evidence, safety, and what will help people return home successfully.”

title: Ohio voters are deeply concerned about corruption, poll shows
description: As the midterm elections near, another poll is showing that Ohio voters and Americans generally are deeply concerned about corruption. In Ohio, respondents said they didn’t particularly trust either party to fix the problem. And huge majorities said they’d consider voting for candidates who said they’d fight corruption in specific ways. The survey was an […]
text:
Getty Images.As the midterm elections near, another poll is showing that Ohio voters and Americans generally are deeply concerned about corruption.
In Ohio, respondents said they didn’t particularly trust either party to fix the problem. And huge majorities said they’d consider voting for candidates who said they’d fight corruption in specific ways.
The survey was an online poll of registered voters conducted between Sept. 8 and Sept. 23. It was conducted by YouGov on behalf of the reform group End Citizens United.
When asked, “How much of a problem do you think corruption in government is in the United States today?” two-thirds of Ohio voters said it was a very serious problem. 
Another 28% said it was a somewhat serious problem. That’s 94% of voters who think it’s a problem.
Zero said it wasn’t a problem at all.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ohio has its own recent history of corruption, but the poll didn’t ask specifically about it.
When Ohio voters were asked to pick three of eight issues they found most pressing, “corruption in Washington” came in at No. 2. “Economy and rising costs” was No.1, and “threats to democracy and elections” was No. 3.
The Ohio results roughly matched those in an identical national poll.
While the Ohio poll didn’t ask respondents to define corruption, another national poll conducted this spring did. 
The Brennan Center for Justice, which sponsored the poll, said respondents “understand corruption broadly, centered in part on the perception that government primarily works for the ultrawealthy and well-connected and doesn’t prioritize the interests of most voters.”
Other survey data show that Americans see partisan gerrymandering as another form of corruption because it also thwarts the will of the voters.

The portion of respondents to the Brennan Center poll who said corruption is a major problem was similar to that in the Ohio poll that was conducted in September.
When it comes to solving corruption, the Ohio respondents in September appeared to view both parties with suspicion. 
Thirty five percent said they trusted Republicans more to address the issue than Democrats. That compares to 32% of Ohioans who said they trusted Democrats more to clean up corruption.
That leaves a full third of respondents in the “neither” camp. And this appears to create opportunities for reform-minded candidates.
Asked if support for certain reforms would make them more likely to support a candidate, huge majorities said they would. The reforms:

Ban Congressional stock trading — Seventy percent said it would make them more likely to support a candidate, 10% said it would make them less likely and 20% were uncertain.
Ban corporate political action committees from giving to campaigns — Sixty four percent said it would make them more like, 9% said it would make them less likely and 27% were undecided.
Require donor disclosure, or get rid of dark money — Seventy two percent said they were more likely to support that candidate, 8% said they were less likely and 19% were undecided.

title: Wisconsin doesn’t have to accept new gas plants as inevitable
description: Wisconsin is facing another major test of how it plans its energy future. We Energies has proposed a new 750-megawatt natural gas plant in Wrightstown, the Fox North Energy Center. If approved, it could begin operating around 2032 and run for 30 years or more. With Fox North added to the queue, We Energies now […]
text:
The XTO energy oil and gas plant is seen at night on March 24, 2024 in Coyanosa, Texas. (Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)Wisconsin is facing another major test of how it plans its energy future.
We Energies has proposed a new 750-megawatt natural gas plant in Wrightstown, the Fox North Energy Center. If approved, it could begin operating around 2032 and run for 30 years or more. With Fox North added to the queue, We Energies now has roughly 4.25 gigawatts of methane gas generation awaiting Public Service Commission approval.
The utility says the buildout is needed to meet rapidly growing electricity demand and maintain reliability. Data centers are a major part of that growth.
But projected demand does not make new gas plants inevitable.
Wisconsin is being asked to make decades-long energy decisions based on electricity demand forecasts that are changing faster than our regulatory system. That is exactly why new methane gas plants must first prove they are the cleanest, lowest-cost, lowest-risk option before customers are committed to paying for them.
Before Wisconsin commits customers to decades of fuel costs and long-lived infrastructure, regulators should ask a more important question: What combination of resources can meet that demand reliably, affordably and with the least long-term risk?
That means comparing new gas plants not just with one solar farm or one battery project, but with complete portfolios of solar, wind, storage, energy efficiency, transmission, distributed resources, nuclear power and demand flexibility.
Other states, including Minnesota and North Carolina, have already shown that regulators can challenge utility assumptions and require closer examination of alternatives rather than treating new gas plants as the default response to projected load growth.
Wisconsin can do the same.
That approach is already gaining support in Wisconsin, including among labor leaders who see comprehensive energy planning as an opportunity to create good-paying jobs.
Climate Jobs Wisconsin, whose leadership includes representatives of Wisconsin building trades and construction unions, recently advanced a “35 by ’35” clean-energy and good-jobs agenda. The proposal envisions roughly 35 gigawatts of new clean-energy resources by 2035, including storage, utility-scale solar, wind, nuclear generation and networked distributed power. A plan  developed by the PSC would map what gets built, where and when, establish resource targets and create a grid-investment roadmap.
That is exactly the kind of planning Wisconsin needs.
Whether policymakers ultimately adopt those exact numbers is less important than the principle behind them: Evaluate the whole system before locking customers into decades of costs.
And expanding clean energy does not have to mean sacrificing Wisconsin’s best farmland or open space.
Renewable development can be directed toward brownfields, marginal and previously disturbed lands, rooftops, parking structures, industrial parks, sites near substations and existing infrastructure. Solar can also be integrated with agricultural production through agrivoltaics, allowing farming and energy production to coexist rather than compete.
Wisconsin should be able to protect prime agricultural land while dramatically expanding clean energy. Those goals are compatible if we plan carefully.
The jobs case matters, too.
Climate Jobs Wisconsin’s agenda is built around creating clean-energy careers with prevailing wages, registered apprenticeships and local hiring. It proposes tying those labor standards to PSC approvals and expanding Wisconsin’s ability to build new energy infrastructure with skilled union labor.
That is important because Wisconsin’s energy transition should not be framed as a choice between workers and the environment.
Done well, it is an industrial green growth strategy.
It can create careers for electricians, operating engineers, laborers, carpenters, pipefitters and other skilled trades while reducing exposure to volatile fuel costs and strengthening Wisconsin manufacturing.
The rapid growth of data centers makes this kind of comprehensive planning even more important.
Wisconsin families, farmers, manufacturers and existing businesses should not become the financial backstop for those investments.
If a gas plant is justified largely by projected data-center demand, regulators should determine how certain that demand really is, what alternatives were considered, who will pay for the plant and who bears the stranded-cost risk if forecasts change.
Transparency is equally important.
That means disclosing projected electricity and water use, infrastructure requirements, tax arrangements and long-term impacts before commitments become difficult to reverse.
It also means using transparent Community Benefit Agreements, so benefits are public, measurable and enforceable.
Transparency is not anti-development. It is how responsible development earns trust.
Wisconsin does not have an electricity shortage. It has a planning challenge.
The choice before us is not new gas or reliability. It is whether Wisconsin evaluates all available resources together before committing customers to another generation of long-term fossil fuel infrastructure costs.
The Fox North proposal gives Wisconsin another opportunity to get that right.
A new gas plant should have to prove it is necessary. It should not be treated as inevitable.

title: Ramaswamy loans campaign $5 million more as Acton outpaces him with donors
description: Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton out-raised her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy nearly 2-to-1 in September. She outpaced him in July and August as well. However, Acton’s success with donors got swamped by Ramaswamy’s personal wealth. In August and September, Ramaswamy made $5 million-plus in loans to his campaign. In all, Ramaswamy has st[...]
text:
Vivek Ramaswamy and Amy Acton. (Photo by WEWS.)Ohio Democratic candidate for governor Amy Acton out-raised her Republican opponent Vivek Ramaswamy nearly 2-to-1 in September. She outpaced him in July and August as well.
However, Acton’s success with donors got swamped by Ramaswamy’s personal wealth. In August and September, Ramaswamy made $5 million-plus in loans to his campaign.
In all, Ramaswamy has staked more than $36 million of his personal fortune on his bid for governor. Because those funds are structured as loans, he can pay himself back with money from donors.
Ohio’s monthly reports cover contributions for statewide candidates in July, August and September. Campaigns aren’t required to share their expenditures over that timeframe. Still, the reports offer a glimpse of a campaign’s finances during the months between the post-primary and pre-general reports.
Acton’s latest figures
During the month of September, Acton’s campaign raised slightly more than $6 million. In August, the campaign raised $4 million, and in July it brought in $5.8 million.
The campaign’s biggest donor in September was the Ohio Democratic party. The state candidate fund gave her $232,000 across three different donations. Aside from that, Acton collected several contributions organized labor, fellow candidates and interest groups.
Unions representing bricklayers, auto workers, teachers and firefighters all gave $10,000 or more. Emily’s List, which backs female candidates who support abortion access, and the PAC for America’s Future, which supports Democratic state candidates, both effectively maxed out for Acton.
Among others, she got big donations from the CEO of the major league soccer team FC Cincinnati, a vice president at Oracle, and a couple of nursing home executives.
More than $5.5 million of Acton’s September contributions came from individuals, and $3.5 million, or 63%, of that total came from Ohioans.
Ramaswamy’s contributions
In September, Ramaswamy’s campaign raised a little more than $3 million. Its August fundraising was just shy of $2.6 million and in July the campaign brought in nearly $4 million.
Where Acton’s donations from political action committees lean toward labor, Ramaswamy’s lean toward business.
Committees representing Ohio hospitals and contractors both maxed out for Ramaswamy. The Ohio Chamber of Commerce gave $16,000, and American Property Casualty Insurance gave $16,600. Two groups representing home builders gave a total of $10,000.
Ramaswamy also got significant backing from OHCANN, a trade group representing licensed cannabis companies in the state. In September, the group gave $15,000 between two donations.
The cannabis industry shows up in Ramaswamy’s big ticket individual donations as well.
The President and CEO of Illinois-based Green Thumb, which operates Rise Dispensaries, both maxed out in September.
Ohio Chamber executives Steve Stivers and Rick Carfagna, both former lawmakers, tapped funds leftover in their previous campaign accounts, giving Ramaswamy $5,000 and $2,000 respectively.
Ramaswamy also cashed big checks from the CEO of NetJets, a partner with the commerical real estate firm the Daimler Group, and leaders for the car dealerships Ricart Automotive and Kerry Automotive group.
Ramaswamy even got max donations from a father and son running an antiquarian book and photograph shop in New York.
A bit more than $1.6 million, or 57%, of the $2.8 million Ramaswamy raised from individuals in September came from Ohioans.
Ramaswamy’s loans
The campaign’s most substantial influx of cash, however, came in the form of Ramaswamy’s personal loans.
On the one hand, his largesse makes good on an early campaign promise. In July last year, he pledged to put at least $30 million behind his election effort.
Acton has outraised Ramaswamy on a regular basis, but the sum total of her donations since entering the race still fall about $5 million short of Ramaswamy’s personal contributions alone.
In addition to his $5 million loans in the two most recent monthly reports, Ramaswamy has made several highly specific loans ranging from $39,984.22 to $136,749.
The Ohio Capital Journal requested comment from Ramaswamy’s campaign but got no response.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Gen Z women want politicians who can make the ‘American dream’ feel attainable
description: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th.  Strike up a conversation with a Gen Z woman about politics, and affordability will likely come up within the first 30 seconds. The cost of doing anything, whether it’s renting a home, staying in college or getting a […]
text:
Comedian Michelladonna interviews New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani while he visits Court Side Deli in the Bronx on April 7, 2026. (Michael Appleton/New York Mayoral Office)This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th. 
Strike up a conversation with a Gen Z woman about politics, and affordability will likely come up within the first 30 seconds.
The cost of doing anything, whether it’s renting a home, staying in college or getting a drink, is the top issue motivating young women this election cycle. In a new The 19th/YouGov poll, a majority of Gen Z women said they were worried about paying for the cost of healthcare, housing, groceries and utilities — and in each category Gen Z women were more worried than Gen Z men. Last year, 90 percent of Gen Z women said the cost of housing and everyday expenses was a critical or important issue — ranking it just above healthcare, abortion and immigration issues, according to a September 2025 poll by the Public Religion Research Institute and the Brookings Institution.
For politicians, it should be an easy way in — affordability is the top issue for just about every group of voters this year. But organizers around the country say the messaging around affordability is not breaking through with Gen Z women.
Reach is important if candidates want to tap into this group of engaged voters ahead of the next presidential election. Gen Z women turn out to vote at consistently higher rates than young men and in the last presidential cycle turned further to the left, creating an opportunity for Democrats.
But instead, the prevailing feeling among Gen Z women is one of disillusionment with a political establishment rarely willing to get radical with their solutions to a growing affordability crisis, young women told The 19th.
“They are fed up, I think, with the way that the political system is kind of just not doing anything for them,” said Molly Metz, a 19-year-old student leader with the political organization NextGen America at Penn State. “Especially for Gen Z women, candidates need to be more direct, and they need to take action — very concrete, very immediate action.”
When Metz talks to students on campus, they bring up how hard it is to live in State College, Pennsylvania, where the school is located. They talk about how rent averages about $2,000 for a one-bedroom apartment, and how they stock up on food when they go home during break to save on groceries.
Standard-issue political messages around lower taxes — “that does not appeal to us. It has no reason to appeal to us. We are not concerned about taxes. We’re concerned about the fact that we can’t afford to eat or pay rent,” Metz said.
There’s evidence Democrats have been trying to get less ideological and more practical when it comes to economic issues. This midterm cycle, they’ve been focusing more on tangible day-to-day issues, like the cost of groceries, because it’s an area where President Donald Trump’s approval rating has been tanking. Republicans, too, have tried to center affordability in their campaigns, but the message has been mixed; at one point, Trump called affordability a fake narrative and a “con job by the Democrats.”  The problem for both parties is that so little of that affordability message is breaking through to young people.

“A lot of candidates just kind of talk about affordability, but it’s all in very loose terms,” Metz said.
At college campuses across her state, recent graduate Sydney Ball, an organizer with the Ohio Student Association, said students bring up the cost of gas, weighing things like if it’s cheaper to commute from home and pay for the gas or live on campus. They talk about the cost of medical treatments and getting an internship. In some of the majors Gen Z women dominate, like education, students are required to do an internship to graduate but many are unpaid.
“They’re having to choose between: ‘Do I take the unpaid internship on top of the other jobs and the school that I’m doing and sacrifice some other costs in my life, whether that’s food or gas or whatever it is, or do I set myself up to not get a job post-grad?’” Ball said.
Unemployment rates for young women ages 16 to 24 have been ticking up since 2024, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
In January 2024, the unemployment rate for young women got as low as 5.9 percent but then rose until it peaked at 10.3 percent in August 2025. As of September 2026, the rate was 9.9 percent; for working women over the age of 20, the rate is 3.6 percent.
Over the past several years, young men have had higher unemployment rates than young women, but theirs has been coming down all year, from 11.5 percent at the end of 2025 to 10 percent in September.
Under those conditions, young women, who attend college at higher rates than men, have started to wonder if they can even bank on a good education giving them a secure future.
Cheyenne Hunt, one of the first Democratic Gen Z women to run for Congress, said for women of her generation it feels like the American dream that was promised is slipping away, but “it doesn’t seem like people actually care.”
“We’re living the nightmare that was always used to fearmonger in politics for generations before, which was the idea that there could come a generation that is less prosperous than ours, and that is our lived reality,” said Hunt, 29. She lost in the primary for California’s 45th Congressional District in 2024, when she was 26. She is now the executive director of a nonprofit against gender bias called Reckoning Action.
In Hunt’s view, political messaging is failing to address the unique ways that young women are being affected by the current economic climate. It’s the young women bearing the majority of student loan debt, entering a labor market with a persistent gender pay gap, who are now becoming a generation of women that feels much more anxious about its financial future than men of the same age.
“They are feeling [the economic slowdown] in a unique way, and yet there’s this really strange unwillingness to acknowledge that,” Hunt said.
Affordability feels like an existential issue that politicians must address because even the simple things feel under attack, said Jessica Siles, a spokesperson for Voters of Tomorrow, a Gen-Z-led advocacy organization that promotes civic engagement.
“It really is like the cost of a drink,” said Siles, who is also Gen Z. “Young people are just really feeling priced out of day-to-day life, a night out with their friends, a concert ticket.”
On campuses, students say they want candidates who are willing to meet with young people, hear their concerns — and then meet those concerns with really specific policies. It’s much more about the individual candidate’s message than it is about the party they represent.

“This is a generation that doesn’t really believe in just blind party loyalty, and I think the two-party system has to get comfortable with being a little bit uncomfortable,” said Mary-Pat Hector, the CEO of Rise, a student-led organization focused on lowering tuition costs and expanding voter turnout.
This election cycle, there is some excitement among Gen Z women around candidates including Abdul El-Sayed, who is running to represent Michigan in the Senate on a platform that lists Medicare for All as a key pillar, and Angie Nixon, who is running to represent Florida in the Senate on a platform that includes universal childcare. Both are Democrats. But for the best example of who is doing it right, one name came up again and again over more than a dozen interviews The 19th conducted with young women and organizers: Zohran Mamdani.
What New York City’s mayor did to capture the support of 82 percent of young women voters in the 2025 mayoral election, compared with 65 percent of young men, came up repeatedly as an example of how to excite a disillusioned group.
“Mamdani is on my timeline every day. Whether it be social media or just the things he’s saying — childcare for all, that type of thing — he’s really setting an example for what people should be thinking about,” said Jasmin Lopez, 29, who works at Cisco Systems and is based in New Jersey.
Key to his success was his ability to be chronically online and reach young people on the platforms they were on. But the other part was directness: People outside New York City could cite what Mamdani wanted to do. Free buses. Free childcare. A rent freeze. His policies were not only clear, they were tangible. And he spread his message by being out in the park, on the subway, on street corners. He flew past his goal of knocking on 1 million New Yorker’s doors (with the help of volunteers). The final count was more like 3 million.
“Mamdani went to neighborhoods of people who don’t vote frequently, talked to them about issues they cared about, like how they’re going to pay their rent, how they’re going to pay their bills, how they’re going to get to work — but with free buses,” said Mariah Ross, the ballot initiative director at One Fair Wage, an organization working to raise the minimum wage to at least $25 an hour.
That is what young women want, Ross said, rather than a crop of Democratic candidates that are “trying to appeal to everyone.”
“They want to hear: ‘I have a solution for you to be able to ultimately help take care of your family,’” she said.

They want radical.
“That’s what the other side does,” Ross said. “They tell us their radical, crazy agenda —verbatim — and their base rallies for that.”
Of course, young women are not a group of single-issue voters, nor are they a monolith. They care about other things, like reproductive health and climate, but many can’t put their focus on other causes until their own livelihood feels secure.
When Ross talks to Gen Z women about the national push for a $25 or $30 an hour minimum wage, up from the federal wage floor of $7.25 an hour, the response is resounding, she said.
“People are like, ‘Hell yeah. Yes. I need that.’”

 Catching Our Eye

• Brown on possibility of impeachment. The Columbus Dispatch’s Cole Behrens reports, “Sherrod Brown says he would not support Trump impeachment if elected.”
U.S. Senate candidate Sherrod Brown says he would not support impeaching President Donald Trump if Brown is elected in November.
Republicans have said Democrats will try to impeach Trump if they retake Congress in the midterms. In an Oct. 9 interview, Brown told The Dispatch he would not be in favor of impeaching the president.
“I can’t speak for everybody else, but I would not support an impeachment of Trump. There’s just simply no reason for that, no matter what happens in the midterms,” Brown told The Dispatch.
• AG race. The Toledo Blade’s Danny Eldredge reports, “State auditor, longtime litigator face off in race for Ohio attorney general.”
Ohio’s next attorney general will be someone with decades of relevant experience regardless of which candidate voters choose in November.
Republican Keith Faber is serving the final year of his second term as state auditor. He previously served 18 years as a state legislator in both chambers of the Ohio General Assembly — including four years as Ohio Senate president. He is also a senior partner at Celina, Ohio-based law firm Faber & Associates. He earned his law degree from the Ohio State University Moritz College of Law.
Democrat John Kulewicz, an Upper Arlington city councilman, worked as an attorney for Columbus-based law firm Vorys, Sater, Seymour, and Pease for 44 years where he argued cases in the U.S. Supreme Court and courts across Ohio. He earned his law degree from Yale Law School, where he served as an editor of the Yale Law Journal.
The candidates discussed their views on a range of issues during separate interviews.
• Free and fair elections. WVXU’s Lilley Halloran reports, “‘Ohio does it right’: Local boards of elections say the midterms will be free and fair.”
NPR reporting suggests that, while more voters trust their state and local officials to run a free election, there is still a fair amount of distrust this midterm season.
But Nicole Unzicker, director of the Butler County Board of Elections, is confident voters can trust the process… Unzicker said all of Ohio’s boards of elections must adhere to strict guidelines.
“It doesn’t waver between elections,” Unzicker said. “If 10 people turned out for an election, or 50,000, it’s the same work that we’re doing for every election.”
Key to the integrity of an election is bipartisanship, Unzicker and other election officials said.
In every county, the elections director and deputy director are members of opposite parties. And there must be an equal number of Democratic and Republican poll workers.
• Prediction markets. The Dayton Daily News’ Jamie Dupree reports, “Ohio presses for U.S. Supreme Court hearing on ‘prediction markets’.”
A bipartisan coalition of 39 states led by Ohio’s attorney general has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to step into a growing legal dispute involving sports gambling on prediction markets, and whether states — or a federal agency — should be allowed to regulate those bets.
“Prediction markets say that classic sports bets — things like whether Joe Burrow throws three touchdowns or Ohio State beats Michigan — are not bets at all,” Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson argued in a written brief submitted to the Supreme Court.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Scholarship tax credit vouchers, a wolf in sheep’s clothing
description: I have seen firsthand the disparity in resources among school districts in Fairfield County. This tax credit codifies and deepens those inequities.
text:
For months, governors across the country have awaited U.S. Treasury guidelines on the use of a Federal Scholarship Tax Credit set to launch January 1, 2027. Those guidelines have now been released, and the picture they paint for public education is worse than we could have imagined.  
The FSTC would release tens of billions of federal dollars to scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs) to provide services ranging from special education and autism support to private school tuition and high-dosage tutoring for students. Taxpayers who donate to SGOs would receive a dollar-for-dollar credit up to $1,700 per individual, or $3,400 per household, with no income limits.  

Joslyn DeLancey

The Trump administration has said that federal tax credit funds would not be limited to private schools; public school students could, ostensibly, benefit. The Treasury’s newly released guidelines tell a different story. 
SGOs act as middlemen for private equity firms, and the FSTC’s launch will provide these brokers with a strong, steady, reliable cash flow. The guidance around the FSTC tax scheme not only lets SGOs keep a 10 percent cut of every contribution, but it also gives them full decision-making power over where that money goes. They could decide every dollar they receive, for example, goes to religious schools.  
Under those same guidelines, states cannot impose a single guardrail on these funds. They cannot earmark them for students from low-income families or ensure they don’t discriminate. They cannot ensure these funds go where they would do the most good. 
The newly released guidelines only underscore widespread concerns about tens of billions of taxpayer dollars pouring into private schools and private-equity-owned education service providers. Education decisions would no longer be in the hands of public school parents, teachers, and boards of education; they would transfer to wealthy financial and tech investors.  
On the face of it, a $1,700 tax credit, especially one that’s reported to help all students,  seems hard to argue against. Look at the fine print, though, and you’ll see that it’s another voucher scheme designed to almost exclusively benefit the wealthy, direct money to private schools and service providers, and leave students and families with the greatest need behind.  
As a Stamford resident, longtime public school teacher in Darien, and vice president of the Connecticut Education Association, which represents educators all over the state — including Bridgeport and Danbury— I have seen firsthand the disparity in resources among school districts in Fairfield County. This tax credit codifies and deepens those inequities.  
Under this new initiative, high income families in Fairfield County will have the luxury of choosing to divert their tax dollars to private educational programs. These programs don’t have to follow the same rules, and taxpayers will have little to no say over what happens with those scholarships. There’s no guarantee of equitable distribution, and one thing is for certain: those dollars will not find their way to our public schools.  
Governors have until December 31 to opt into this voucher scheme, and those who care about preserving and improving the quality of their state’s education system will take a hard pass.  
We don’t need a crystal ball to know how this private equity scheme will play out in Connecticut’s public schools.  We’ve had a front-row seat to private equity’s destruction and abandonment of local hospitals and nursing homes, saddling them with enormous debt, stripping services down to the bare minimum, cutting core staff and resources, then cashing out and leaving.  
This has already happened with private equity-owned education service providers as well, including FEV tutoring, which closed overnight, leaving families across 30 states scrambling.  
For those who are undecided about the tax credit, the following questions are helpful:  

How do we ensure smaller class sizes, equitable funding, and accountability in our public schools under this initiative?  
Public schools are already underfunded by the federal government, especially special education. If tax dollars are diverted to public programs, won’t we pay for the tax credit either in property or state taxes to make up the difference? 
This program will create winners out of a few private companies selling educational services. Wouldn’t that raise the cost for services delivered to public schools? 
Fairfield County has some of the best public-school systems in the state, and we pride ourselves on that. Do we want to risk the quality of our public schools?  

Tax credits and scholarships may sound really exciting. In this case, you’re not saving money, and you’re not necessarily helping kids in need. You’re just playing a shell game: moving public dollars into private systems. Connecticut could and should do better. Imagine if we truly committed to investing in our public schools instead of buying into gimmicks.  
If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.  
Say no to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit.  
Joslyn DeLancey is vice president of the Connecticut Education Association.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: One AI-enabled school shooting is far too many.
authors: Abbey Clements and U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes.
description: AI chatbots are the newest and most dangerous front in the fight against gun violence, and Congress cannot afford to look away.
text:
As former teachers from Connecticut, we have helped hundreds of students go on to become productive citizens. While we’ve worked on opposite ends of the school system, one as an elementary school teacher, and another as a high school history teacher, we have many common experiences as teachers.
First and foremost, we’ve learned all the different hats teachers wear in addition to their primary job to help students learn. We serve as informal caretakers, mentors, coaches and more.

Abbey Clements and U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes.

We’re proud of the things our students have gone on to do after leaving our classrooms. Ultimately, students face increased challenges inside and outside of school when navigating the fear and impact of gun violence. We know this especially keenly because we saw how the aftermath of the Sandy Hook tragedy and the everyday gun violence in Connecticut cities changed the lives of so many people forever.
What is even more tragic is how normalized gun violence has become since then. According to a 2024 study by the Trace, an average of 57 shootings happen near schools every day. Unfortunately, we can see the cause clearly. We live in a nation with more guns than people. A study by the U.S. Secret Service found that as many as two-thirds of school shootings happened because a student had access to an unsecured firearm from a friend or relative.
When students have easy access to firearms, the last thing we need is anything that makes our gun violence problem worse. Unfortunately, that is a real risk if we do not have more direct action from both Congress and big tech companies.
CNN reported recently that in hundreds of tests, AI chatbots were helping teens plan to carry out acts of violence and “are actively assisting users by giving them information that could be used in preparing attacks.”
Tragically, this isn’t just a theoretical issue confined to user testing. In February, reports emerged that an AI company did not alert law enforcement regarding an account it banned that belonged to an alleged 18-year-old mass shooter who carried out one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history, an attack at a school that left eight victims dead and dozens wounded.
Meanwhile, in the United States, there’s already at least one lawsuit filed against the maker of ChatGPT after reports show that the Florida State University shooter asked ChatGPT a series of questions that allegedly helped him carry out the April 2025 shooting.

This photo provided by Leon County Sheriff’s Office shows suspected Florida State shooter Phoenix Ikner.  Credit: Leon County Sheriff's Office via AP

According to local media, Phoenix Ikner asked ChatGPT “how to take the safety off of a shotgun” three minutes before he began firing. The chat bot reportedly “answered, giving a detailed description of how to make the shotgun operable. As a result, two people died, six more were injured. Countless lives were changed.
The big tech companies that produce AI are some of the most valuable in the world, and their employees are some of the most highly compensated in the country. And they are failing us.
 In February, OpenAI hired Dylan Scandinaro, a former AI safety researcher at Anthropic, to serve as the company’s new head of preparedness, a role that has broad responsibility for company safety protocols. He earns a salary of more than $550,000 annually plus equity in the company.
These companies have the resources and capacity to do better. It’s time that they be compelled to do so. The Canadian government took an important first step into investigating the role AI  platforms played in the shooting there. Congress can and should do the same here.
Lawmakers have shown this kind of accountability is possible on gun violence before.
They have pressed the Secretary of Health and Human Services until he went on the record acknowledging gun violence as a public health crisis, introduced legislation to close the loophole that leaves preschools without the same gun-free protections K-12 schools have, and pushed for a federal Office of Gun Violence Prevention and a public database to track gun violence research. 
AI chatbots are simply the newest and most dangerous front in the same fight, andCongress cannot afford to look away.  Until Congress takes real action, our advice to parents if we were still in the classroom would be clear: Don’t allow your children unsupervised use of AI products. The risk is just too great.
Jahanna Hayes was named 2016 National Teacher of the Year and now represents Connecticut’s Fifth Congressional District. Abbey Clements is a survivor teacher of the Sandy Hook School tragedy in 2012, and was an  elementary school teacher for 32 years. She is co-founder and executive director of Teachers Unify to End Gun Violence.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Lauren Boebert, Eileen Laubacher appear in lone televised debate ahead of midterms
description: Democrat Eileen Laubacher said during a debate Monday night that if her party regains control of Congress during the upcoming midterm elections, it should not use that power to impeach President Donald Trump. “I do not want us to waste two more years trying to impeach the president. I do not think that that is […]
text:
Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert (left) and Democrat Eileen Laubacher appear at a congressional debate hosted by 9News on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)
Democrat Eileen Laubacher said during a debate Monday night that if her party regains control of Congress during the upcoming midterm elections, it should not use that power to impeach President Donald Trump.
“I do not want us to waste two more years trying to impeach the president. I do not think that that is a good use of our time,” she said during a debate with U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert of Windsor, whom she is running to unseat as the representative of Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.
“I think it is important for people to be held responsible for the things that they do that are unlawful and unethical, and I hope that happens,” Laubacher added. “But I think that what we really need to do is to be a more effective Congress than we see right now.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Her comments came in response to a question from moderator Kyle Clark of 9News about what Democrats should do, if anything, amid potential calls to investigate Trump and his administration during the next Congress. The debate was the only scheduled televised meeting between Laubacher and Boebert ahead of the Nov. 3 election, and thousands of voters in the district already have their mail-ballots.
Boebert is running for her second term in the district and her fourth term as a representative from Colorado. She previously served two terms in the 3rd Congressional District, representing the Western Slope, but moved across the state to her current district, which includes Douglas County and the Eastern Plains, following a near-defeat by her Democratic challenger in 2022. Boebert won the solidly-red seat in 2024 with 53.6% of the vote, but the congressional campaign arm of the Democratic Party is targeting the district this year as a possible flip.
Monday’s televised debate between two Colorado candidates for Congress was a relative rarity this election season. In the battleground 8th District, incumbent GOP U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans and his Democratic challenger, state Rep. Manny Rutinel, did not agree to any televised debates, and met for their only scheduled face-to-face event in Berthoud last week. The race in the 3rd District is likewise set to have only a single, untelevised meeting between Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd and Aspen business owner Dwayne Romero — the two candidates shared a stage for 30 minutes at a Club 20 event last month — after Hurd declined an invitation to a televised debate.
Boebert touted some of her recent congressional accomplishments, such as securing funding for the Arkansas Valley Conduit through the House version of the Water Resources Development Act and advocating for disaster relief for sugar beet farmers. She said that since arriving to Washington, D.C. five years ago, she has worked on an approach to “disagree better,” and acknowledged that she is often one of the most outspoken members of Congress.
Laubacher is a first-time candidate and 34-year Navy veteran who retired as a rear admiral in 2024. She then served as senior director for South Asia at the National Security Council under former President Joe Biden. She is also a recent arrival to the district after moving there two years ago.
House Democrats want to win every Colorado congressional seat this year

On the war in Iran, Boebert said she “never wanted” the country to be involved, but stands by Trump’s decision as commander in chief, as well as her votes against multiple Democrat-led war powers resolutions that have passed the House of Representatives.
“I do agree that this is expensive, and I hear from Republicans, unaffiliated (voters) and Democrats that they want this to come to an end, and so do I,” she said. “We are having conversations with the Department of War and with the president on a regular basis about how to come to an end with this. A symbolic procedural vote put on by progressive Democrats is not going to be the answer.”
Laubacher pushed back, however, saying that Boebert’s votes against those resolutions contradict her job to “raise the voices” of the people in the district opposed to the war.
‘The loudest voices on both sides’
The candidates also sparred over Trump’s ongoing tariffs, with Boebert defending the president’s use of the trade policy as a “tool” to bring in revenue. Laubacher said she supports some, but not all tariffs.
“There are different kinds of tariffs that are effective, like pushing back on China to ensure our semiconductor industry has the opportunity to grow,” she said. “But the tariffs that we’re seeing right now — for example, the ones with Canada — those are not being paid by foreign governments. Those are being paid by Americans.”
They both said they oppose Trump’s plan to pause tariffs on beef from countries including Argentina and Brazil to bring the price down for consumers. The 4th District is home to most of Colorado’s ranching industry.
Laubacher was a longtime Republican and switched her party affiliation, first to unaffiliated, and then to Democratic in 2024. She defended that action by claiming her belief in personal liberties is currently found in the Democratic Party, and that the GOP she historically supported is “nearly unrecognizable.”
“Being registered a Republican or registered a Democrat, it doesn’t define me as an individual. I’ve always voted for a person, not a party,” she said. “I changed my party because my view of what the parties represented changed.”
She also defended her recent move into the district, saying she and her husband downsized to a house in a community they already interacted with — 10 miles, she said, from their former house in Littleton.
On Monday, Laubaucher gave Trump credit for stronger immigration policies at the southern border, and declined to name the “extremists” in the Democratic Party that one of her campaign advertisements alludes to.
“I believe that we have way more in common across the aisle than we do that separates us,” she said. “But I believe that the loudest voices on both sides are the ones that are making the most noise, and people think that that is what we should be listening to. And I do not think so.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Bottoms faces empty podium on debate stage while Jackson campaigns with Kemp
description: Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, debated against an empty podium Monday night after GOP nominee Rick Jackson declined to participate in the Atlanta Press Club’s debates.  The Loudermilk-Young debate series, organized by Atlanta Press Club in partnership with Georgia Public Broadcasting, is a two-day event featuring statewide candida[...]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms stands next to an empty podium during the Atlanta Press Club Loudermilk-Young Governors Debate at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. (Abbey Cutrer for the AJC)Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, debated against an empty podium Monday night after GOP nominee Rick Jackson declined to participate in the Atlanta Press Club’s debates. 
The Loudermilk-Young debate series, organized by Atlanta Press Club in partnership with Georgia Public Broadcasting, is a two-day event featuring statewide candidates on the ballot in the general election. Early voting for the Nov. 3 election starts Tuesday. 
Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, instead spent the day flying around the state talking to reporters and supporters, with stops planned for Columbus, Macon and Savannah, and ended the day with a rally near Augusta.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks during the Atlanta Press Club Loudermilk-Young Governors Debate at the Georgia Public Broadcasting studio in Atlanta on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. (Abbey Cutrer for the AJC)
Bottoms and Jackson appeared together on the same stage last week for a town hall-style debate that will likely give Georgia voters their only side-by-side look at the candidates competing to be the state’s next top leader. 
Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, used the half-hour forum Monday night to promote her platform, such as expanding Medicaid, fully funding pre-K and creating a fund for affordable and workforce housing. And, except for a few instances, she largely veered away from attacking her opponent, rarely gesturing to the empty podium as candidates often have in past debates when their opponents are absent.
During the debate, Bottoms had the opportunity to ask the podium a question she would have asked Jackson had he been there. She took the opportunity to discuss Georgia’s six-week abortion ban, which hasn’t been a big topic on the campaign trail so far. And she pointed to comments Jackson made over the summer, which were reported by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, that a doctor would need to have evidence to prove an abortion was necessary to prevent facing legal consequences under the Georgia law. His campaign has disputed that as a mischaracterization.  
“If he were here, I would ask, how do you prove that you have been raped in order to get an abortion?” Bottoms said at the debate. “He’s not here because he’s on his private jet flying around the state rather than having to answer to the people of Georgia about this irresponsible position.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Bottoms did ramp up her attack on Jackson when taking questions from reporters after the debate, calling Jackson a “coward” for declining to participate in the debate and saying that skipping a debate that is televised statewide is a disservice to voters. Jackson is the first candidate for governor in a general election to opt out of the Atlanta Press Club debate series since 1994.
“Rick Jackson refuses to show up and answer unscripted questions before the public and even before the press. And if he is doing that as a candidate, what is it that we should expect from him if he were ever to be elected as governor? There’s no reason he should not have been here tonight,” Bottoms said.
Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for governor, answers a reporter’s question Monday at the first stop of a fly-around tour. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder
Shortly before Bottoms’ solo act, Jackson stood on a stage in Grovetown just outside of Augusta for a rally with Gov. Brian Kemp. 
Jackson defended his decision to skip Monday’s debate when talking to reporters in Atlanta, also with Kemp at his side. 
“I have visited thousands of Georgians for the last nine months. I’ve gone hundreds of places. I’ve not had one voter ask me a question about debate. That’s not what’s important to them,” Jackson said. “What’s important to them is affordability, and gas prices going up, and paying bills, and our property taxes, and so forth.
“My priority is not the media and what they want. My priority is what Georgians want,” he added. 
At the same stop in Atlanta, Jackson was asked to give an example of an issue where he disagrees with President Donald Trump. Jackson said he departs from Trump on data centers but didn’t offer specifics. Trump has opposed attempts to curb data centers and the advancement of artificial intelligence the facilities help support. 
But Jackson said his position would also depend on the specifics of a situation. 
“My priority is Georgia. It’s not the United States. What happens in D.C. we don’t have control of. What happens in the world? What happens in the weather? The question is, how are we going to respond to it?” Jackson said. “And just like Gov. Kemp, he responded and always did what was best for Georgians. That is my priority. No other priority is higher than representing Georgians. And I don’t care who comes here and says anything, but we will work with people.” 
Jackson was endorsed by Trump after Jackson defeated the president’s first choice, and Jackson’s campaign confirmed that the Republican will campaign with Trump during the president’s visit to Dalton this Friday. 
“Rick will be in Dalton and looks forward to reminding Georgia voters that bad mayors do not make good governors,” said Jackson campaign spokesman Garrison Douglas.

title: Indigenous Peoples Day event at Alaska college showcases tradition, food and fellowship
description: Alaska has for years designated the second Monday of October as a holiday to honor the nation’s Indigenous cultures and acknowledge the harms of colonialism instead of observing Columbus Day. In Alaska, Indigenous Peoples Day has been an official holiday since 2015. Gov. Bill Walker’s  yearly proclamations were followed by a 2017 bill passed by […]
text:
Members of the Ida'ina K'eljeshna dance group, also known as the Friendship Dancers, perform Monday at the Indigenous Peoples Day celebration at Alaska Pacific University. The Dena'ina group was one of three dance groups performing at the celebration, which has become an annual event at the Anchorage college. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaska has for years designated the second Monday of October as a holiday to honor the nation’s Indigenous cultures and acknowledge the harms of colonialism instead of observing Columbus Day.
 

Alaska Pacific University President Janelle Vanasse speaks to the audience at the start of the school’s Indigenous Peoples Day event on Oct. 12, 2026. With her on the state is Oliver Iqitainguq Tyrrell, a Yup’ik and Iñupiaq social work student at the Unviersity of Aalska Anchorage, who served as the event’s emcee. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	In Alaska, Indigenous Peoples Day has been an official holiday since 2015. Gov. Bill Walker’s  yearly proclamations were followed by a 2017 bill passed by the Alaska Legislature thatthat made the state holiday permanent. In 2023, the Anchorage Assembly made the day a paid holiday for municipal workers. Alaska is one of 17 states, along with the District of Columbia, that celebrate Indigenous Peoples Day, according to the Pew Research Center.
 

Fish heads are arrayed in a dish at the Indigenous Peoples Day celebration on Oct. 12, 2026, at Alaska Pacific University. Attendees were also served moose stew, another traditional food. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Alaska Pacific University in Anchorage hosted a midday celebration that featured dances, traditional foods like moose stew, a Native sports demonstration, arts and crafts vendors and information booths. It was one of several events in the city and around the state.
The private Anchorage university, which has a goal of becoming a tribal college, hosts Indigenous Peoples Day events annually.
APU President Janelle Vanasse, in remarks to the audience at the start of the celebration, spoke of the college’s programs, including a scholarship that is available for Native students.
 

Curtis Silook, a member of the Sivuqaq Dance Group of Anchorage, plays a drum during a performance at the Indigenous Peoples Day celebration held Oct. 12, 2026, at Alaska Pacific University. The dance group members are from St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Strait region, though residing in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Vanasse spent two decades in education in Alaska’s Yukon-Kuskokwim region, followed by service as principal of Mt. Edgecumbe High School, a public state-run boarding school in Sitka that was once an Alaska Native boarding school, before coming to APU.
In comments after her welcoming address to the attendees, Vanasse said her experience in the Yukon-Kuskokwim region helps inform her understanding of community needs there a year after the disaster wrought by ex-Typhoon Halong. The flooding and other damage from the storm prompted the evacuation of more than 1,500 village residents who are now contemplating their futures.
Vanasse said it is important for the residents that the storm-hit communities survive, even if they do so in different configurations.
 

A shopper examines handmade jewelry on display at the Oct. 12, 2026, Indigenous Peoples Day celebration at Alaska Pacific University. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“I just think there’s so much strength in those communities,” she said.
It is important for Alaska as well, she said. “Our state is ultimately enriched when we have those communities that are keeping so many of their traditions alive,” she said.
Fittingly for a college venue, the performers used their time on state to educate the audience.
One of the performing groups, the Yurapik Drummers and Dancers, encouraged audience members to follow along to learn how to do a traditional Yup’ik morning dance.
 

Quentin Odomin, a Native Youth Olympic athlete, demonstrates the traditional seal hop at the Oct. 12, 2026, Indigenous Peoples Day celebration at Alaska Pacific University. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“In this song we’re going to be greeting the day. So you’re going to claim yourself to be a part of this world,” Valerie Tony, a leader of the dance group, told the audience.
It is a ritual done even while traveling, she said.  “This is where — pay attention — this is where you get your directive from your ancestors,” she said.
And she had another piece of instruction: Audience members trying to follow along should give each other plenty of space, “because we don’t want you to be accidentally on purpose whacking your neighbor.”
One-year-old Hector Triplett is held by his mother, Hannah, as they watch a dance performance at the Oct. 12, 2026, Indigenous Peoples Day celebration at Alaska Pacific University. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana Democratic Party chairperson steps down, endorses independent US Senate candidate
description: Montana Democratic Party chairperson Shannon O’Brien announced Monday she was resigning her leadership position with the party “effective immediately” to endorse independent U.S. Senate candidate Seth Bodnar. In a statement to MS NOW, O’Brien described the reasons she supports Bodnar, and she also expressed reservations about Alani Bankhead, the Democratic n[...]
text:
O'Brien speaks at a political rally at the Capitol in 2023. (Photo by Blair Miller, Daily Montanan)Montana Democratic Party chairperson Shannon O’Brien announced Monday she was resigning her leadership position with the party “effective immediately” to endorse independent U.S. Senate candidate Seth Bodnar.
In a statement to MS NOW, O’Brien described the reasons she supports Bodnar, and she also expressed reservations about Alani Bankhead, the Democratic nominee.
In an email, Bankhead said O’Brien already has been working against her.
“Shannon didn’t switch sides today,” Bankhead said in a statement from her campaign. “She’s been working against the Democratic nominee since the summer.”
Political analysts point to Republican Kurt Alme as the frontrunner in the Senate race. Libertarian Kyle Austin is also running.
O’Brien, who described herself in the statement as “a lifelong Montana Democrat,” said Alme does not share Democratic values and must be defeated.
“I know Bodnar to be someone who listens,” O’Brien said. “He is kind, hardworking and bright. I can say with confidence he has what’s best for Montana’s future in mind.”
O’Brien joins other Dems
O’Brien is the latest high-profile Democrat to sign onto the campaign of Bodnar, a military veteran and former University of Montana president.
In a social media post last week, Denise Juneau, former superintendent of public instruction, said Bodnar was among the candidates she and her mom, former longtime state lawmaker Carol Juneau, were supporting.
The Juneaus are Democratic stalwarts whose opinions are sought by Montanans.
O’Brien told the Daily Montanan she became convinced Bodnar is the only shot Democrats and independents have of beating Alme.
She said she initially worried her resignation might harm other Democratic candidates, whom she supports, but she took the step after discussions with advisers assuaged her concern.
O’Brien told the Daily Montanan she believes many Democrats remain undecided in the Senate race, and she wants to help.
“Maybe I have the opportunity to communicate to them (undecided Democrats) that ‘It’s OK. You can be a good Democrat and you can vote for an independent who will fight for our values,’” O’Brien said.
Bankhead fights back
For months, O’Brien said she has been taking calls asking if she could persuade Bankhead to step out of the race. She said Bankhead has been unresponsive to discussion.
“She hasn’t returned my calls since June,” O’Brien said.
A spokesperson for Bankhead’s campaign said the record shows Bankhead communicated with the party in June and July.
In a statement, Bankhead said O’Brien tried to undermine her campaign, partly by investigating whether the party could legally “refuse to replace me (on the ballot) if I quit.”
“If Ms. O’Brien called, she was calling a nominee she was working to remove from the ballot,” said Bankhead spokesperson Kaight Meyers in an email.
In the statement to MS NOW, O’Brien said she was taking the uncomfortable step of airing concerns about Bankhead because “the future of our state and our country is at stake.”
She said Bankhead refused advice from political leaders in the state despite being “almost brand new to Montana,” and she questions Bankhead’s commitment to protecting a woman’s right to choose.
Bankhead’s stance is pro-choice. Her campaign site said her position “distinguishes between matters of personal faith and the role of the government.”
Bankhead said the only “advice” she received from “the party’s old guard” was to quit: “That was a pressure campaign, not advice.”
In the statement, O’Brien also said Bankhead doesn’t have “the momentum, resources, or will to win this race.”
“Montanans can feel that Washington, and our democracy, stopped working for them a while ago,” O’Brien said. “This needs to be fixed, and Bodnar has built his entire campaign around it.”
Democratic Party regroups
In a news release announcing a new chairperson, the Montana Democratic Party said its work “continues with focus and determination.”
It named Bruce Knutson, formerly vice chairperson, as its new leader, but did not directly address O’Brien’s decision.
Knutson, of Helena, said Democrats want leaders who will “lower costs, protect health care and stand up for working families,” and the party has voters to reach and “seats to win.”
“Our strength has never rested with one person,” Knutson said.
Other members of the Democratic Party board have expressed support for Bodnar in the past including in a letter in August asking Bankhead to drop out of the race.
In a statement, Bodnar said he was grateful for O’Brien’s courage and lifetime of service to Montanans.
“Montanans of every political stripe are coming together in this race because they know what’s at stake, and they’re ready to send an independent senator to Washington who answers only to them,” Bodnar said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin Democrats’ lawsuit joins broader attack on taxpayer-funded Trump ads
description: A Wisconsin Democratic Party lawsuit is part of a broader response to the Trump administration’s use of taxpayer funds to pay for partisan ads, a lawyer whose organization is handling the case told reporters Monday. “It is important to pursue multiple angles of attack and ensure that there is a clear court order” to block […]
text:
President Donald Trump appears in a taxpayer-funded public service announcement that critics say is indistinguishable from a 2024 campaign ad. The Democratic Party of Wisconsin, Common Cause, and the Democratic National Committee have all filed separate lawsuits to stop the ads. (Screenshot from video posted to Truth Social)A Wisconsin Democratic Party lawsuit is part of a broader response to the Trump administration’s use of taxpayer funds to pay for partisan ads, a lawyer whose organization is handling the case told reporters Monday.
“It is important to pursue multiple angles of attack and ensure that there is a clear court order” to block the administration’s action, said Norm Eisen, a co-founder and board member of Democracy Defenders Action, during an online news conference Monday afternoon.
Democracy Defenders Action and the law firm Hecker Fink are representing the Democratic Party of Wisconsin in a lawsuit filed Friday. The ads, aired on broadcast, cable and streaming platforms, were labeled as paid for by the U.S. government but promoted the actions of the Trump administration and criticized opponents of President Donald Trump, the lawsuit charged.
“Using that taxpayer money to pay for political ads is illegal, unconstitutional, and just wrong,” Eisen said Monday. Other ads “actually were recycled Trump campaign ads simply relabeled ‘paid for by the United States government.’”
Despite Trump administration claims that the payment for the ads was being shifted from the federal government to a Trump-supporting super PAC, Devin Remiker, chair of the Democratic Party of Wisconsin, said he saw some of the government-funded ads as recently as Sunday’s Green Bay Packers football game.
“It is very clear that we cannot take this administration or Republicans at their word and we have to hold them accountable through the courts,” Remiker said.
The Wisconsin Democrats’ lawsuit is one of three that have been filed against the ad campaign. The political watchdog group Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee filed suits last week demanding that the taxpayer-funded ads stop. A New York federal judge issued an order Sunday blocking the ads.
Eisen said a hearing to seek another temporary restraining order against the ads is scheduled this week in Washington, in the Democratic National Committee’s lawsuit, and that the Wisconsin plaintiffs would join that effort.
He said the state party’s lawsuit reflected the fact that elections are not merely national, but are administered at the state and local level as well. “We felt it was very important even though other litigation was going on to have a state party that was speaking out, to have a state candidate that was speaking out,” Eisen said. “Ours is the only case involving a state party and a state candidate.”
Along with the Democratic Party of Wisconsin, the Democratic candidate for state treasurer in November, Yee Leng Xiong, is also a plaintiff in the lawsuit. He joined the lawsuit “to hold the Trump administration accountable for using your taxpayer dollars for ads promoting himself,” Xiong said. “Our tax dollars should serve the people, not promote a politician.”
