name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana US Senate candidates share debate stage
description: All four candidates for Montana’s open U.S. Senate seat shared a stage Sunday for a 90-minute debate to distinguish themselves in the eyes of Montana voters.  The event, sponsored by the Montana Broadcasters Association and the Greater Montana Foundation, took place at the Field and Stream Lodge in Bozeman and candidates discussed their views on […]
text:
Seth Bodnar, Kurt Alme, Alani Bankhead and Kyle Austin attend a debate for U.S. Senate candidates in Bozeman on Oct. 11, 2026. (Screenshot via CSPAN)All four candidates for Montana’s open U.S. Senate seat shared a stage Sunday for a 90-minute debate to distinguish themselves in the eyes of Montana voters. 
The event, sponsored by the Montana Broadcasters Association and the Greater Montana Foundation, took place at the Field and Stream Lodge in Bozeman and candidates discussed their views on a range of issues, including foreign policy, affordability issues in Montana, the environment, and artificial intelligence. 
It was the first time all major candidates made an appearance together, as Republican Kurt Alme, the frontrunner in the race, has declined other invitations.  
Four panelists from various broadcast news agencies took turns asking questions of the candidates. There was no direct back-and-forth conversation between the candidates, but they still took a few shots at each other’s platforms, backers and bonafides, with Libertarian Kyle Austin spending the most time attacking his opponents. 
 The candidates: 

Kurt Alme is the Republican replacement for Sen. Steve Daines, who bowed out of his reelection campaign minutes before candidates filing closed in March, letting Alme slip in without additional Republican or major Democratic candidates getting notice. 
He is a former U.S. Attorney and served under two Republican governors heading the state’s budget and revenue departments. 
“I’m the only candidate up here with a proven record of cutting taxes, balancing our state budget, and locking up violent criminals,” Alme said. “I’ve spent my career serving and protecting Montana families, and I’m ready to step up and serve again to make our lives more affordable, make our communities safer, and protect our Montana way of life.”
Democrat Alani Bankhead has made headlines as a political unknown who won the Democratic primary boosted by millions of dollars from progressive dark-money organizations and Republican political actions committees, successfully elevating her over the primary field. 
A former U.S. Air Force lieutenant colonel who spent time on antitrafficking task forces and investigating internet crimes against children in Hawai’i, Bankhead has committed to staying in a race despite trailing an independent candidate in many polls. 
“I’m the only one on the stage who has trust built with D.C. folks who I’ve grown up with since the ‘90s, who are now in charge of things in government, and we’ve spent the last 20 years protecting you from corruption. I’m not beholden to D.C.,” Bankhead said. “I will absolutely fight for the people of Montana because I’m unbought and unbossed and unafraid.”
Seth Bodnar, a Green Beret and former University of Montana president, bucked the hopes of many state Democratic party members and entered the race as an independent back in March. He has consistently outraised all candidates, has support from elected officials from both parties, but was unable to manage a one-on-one race against Alme, which would have put Montana’s Republican-held seat onto a competitive list with other independents making coalition waves across the country. 
“This country was founded on a promise — the promise that we govern ourselves, and that those that we elect work for us. I put my life on the line to defend that promise, but that promise has been broken today,” Bodnar said. “Washington D.C. is filled with cowards who answer to their party bosses, their corporate donors… We have a chance in Montana to tell Washington D.C. that neither party owns the state and that nobody gets to take us for granted, because you know what? Montana is my party.”
Kyle Austin won the state’s Libertarian primary even as the Montana Libertarian Party said he doesn’t share their values. He has tried to paint himself as the true conservative in the race, and pointed to having experience in agriculture and healthcare as reasons he’ll be effective in Washington D.C. 
Austin has consistently shown single digit support in polling done in the state. 
“Who is the real Montana conservative out there with Montana values? Who is the candidate with the most integrity and who has the deepest roots that can serve you day in and day out? I feel I can be that candidate,” Austin said. 
A poll by the non-partisan health research organization KFF released March 7, 2025, found 82% of those surveyed said Congress should keep spending on Medicaid about the same or increase it. (Photo by Ariel Skelley/Getty Images)
 On addressing healthcare costs:

Alme said that the Affordable Care Act failed to make health care affordable and instead served to subsidize pharmaceutical and insurance companies. 
“We need to hold them accountable, and we need to make healthcare more affordable by making it more transparent, more competitive, and by putting patients first,” Alme said. “And we can do that with things like being sure prices and costs are more transparent, being sure that healthcare dollars get distributed out to patients so that they can shop and buy the best quality policy that they can get.”
Bankhead has repeatedly said she favors universal healthcare and points to the nation’s military healthcare system, TRICARE, as a model for covering primary care, dental, eyecare and mental health under a single system. 
Paying for universal healthcare is possible, Bankhead said, by ending the war in Iran and funneling those funds elsewhere. Having citizens in the richest country on earth unable to afford healthcare is “completely unacceptable.” 
Austin said his 18 years as a pharmacist showed him the impending healthcare crisis the country is facing. His plan, “Healthcare 2.0” would transform the system  “to create one set of rules, to get the payers to clean up their mess and actually pay our providers what they’re worth.”
Bodnar said healthcare is a prime example of where Washington politicians have failed. He said a universal coverage option should be available for all Americans while “maintaining choice and competition.”
He also said restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies which expired last year is key to lowering costs. He pledged to protect Medicaid expansion and eliminate hoops to receive health care.  
 On Social Security: 
By 2034, it is estimated that incoming payroll taxes will only cover around 83% of the program’s  benefits. 
Pointing to his time as a state budget director, Alme said he knows how to pay off debt and balance a budget, and would focus on eliminating waste, fraud and abuse across the federal budget to help bolster Social Security funding. 
He said he will work with any member of Congress to strengthen the program and “will never support a cut in benefits for seniors.”
Bankhead said on the campaign trail she’s heard “the horror stories of retirees who are not able to retire with dignity, which I find completely unacceptable because nobody works harder than a Montanan.”
The solution, she said, is to remove the wage limit for contributions — which in 2026 kicks in at $184,500 — and require all income to be subject to Social Security taxes. 
“This race is not about Democrat versus Republican. It’s about the 1% versus everybody else. And what we need to do is tax the wealthy, and it starts by ensuring that they pay their fair share of Social Security,” Bankhead said. 
Austin shared his own update to the “outdated” Social Security program. His plan includes putting together trust funds for individuals where contributions will stay with them, rather than paying for current retirees. 
“At the end of the day, when you’re ready for retirement, it’s your money, not the government’s money,” he said. 
Bodnar also focused on using taxation tweaks to fix Social Security, saying that higher earners paying more into the system will help shore it up. 
He also took shots at the Republican Party, and Alme, for talking about fiscal responsibility when he said the current party running D.C. is focused on “reckless spending” for ballrooms and wars. 
 On AI:

Bodnar said Congress needs to step in and regulate artificial intelligence companies, but can’t because it’s “paid for by big tech.” 
“The reality is that we need to stop any AI data center that wants to come into this state and exploit Montana communities, taking our water, driving up utility rates,” he said. 
He also said protecting kids from “unfettered, unsupervised access” to chatbots should be a priority as well as protecting workers from being displaced. 
Alme said when it comes to AI companies building data centers in Montana, they should be “transparent, clear about their cost to the community and other effects.” 
He said data companies need to pay their own way, create local jobs, and have no adverse effects on water users, water quality, and electricity bills for Montanans. 
“I’ll work to be sure that we have transparency, we have clear guardrails, and that Montana communities are heard,” he said.
Bankhead cited her experience on an internet crimes task force as proof she is willing to stand up to big tech firms and prevent exploitation. She also voiced the strongest opposition to the industry. 
“Make no mistake that this entire election, all roads lead to AI data centers, and I am the loudest on this stage about being opposed to them,” she said. “We don’t currently have AI being held accountable, and our public lands are being opened up for AI data centers… if you want more of the same, you can expect that from the Republican candidate.”
Austin said there is no stopping AI and data centers, but there needs to be safeguards. He says putting data centers in space or in the ocean is the way to move forward, as opposed to putting them in Montanans’ backyards. 
“This is an AI race not only for national security, but for the future of America,” he said, adding that tech companies will “drive energy, drive jobs, and drive our economy.”
Along the Nez Perce National Historic Trail, Bitterroot Valley Trapper Peak, near Sula, Montana. (Photo by Roger Peterson/ U.S. Forest Service)
 On Montana’s public lands: 
 
The Trump administration proposed rescinding the Roadless Rule, which means opening large tracts of wilderness to development, logging or other uses which some groups say will harm endangered and sensitive species. 
“We need a U.S. senator who’s going to stand up and fight like hell to defend our public lands, not be the servant of Mike Lee down in Utah, who’s going to do everything he can within the Republican Party to sell off our public lands,” Bodnar said. 
He touched on the Roadless Rule, which the Trump administration has proposed to rescind, which will change how around 6 million acres of Montana is managed. 
“We need to make sure that we’re protecting key habitat areas, key species, and that we’re funding the agencies responsible for smart management, proactive management of our forests, and we’ve seen those agencies gutted in the past year,” he said. 
Alme did not touch on specific policies of the current administration, such as rescinding the Roadless Rule, but talked about how important the state’s public lands were for his family, having grown up in Montana. 
“I will always fight to keep our public lands in public hands, and all fight against anyone who tries to sell them off,” he said. 
“All roads lead to AI data centers,” said Bankhead, adding that the current Republican administration has relentlessly opened up public lands for additional “exploitation.” 
Changing how land management agencies are structured, relocating offices across the country and rolling back rules is “all about chipping away” protections to eventually put data centers on more public land. 
 “Public lands will remain public lands,” Austin said.
But he said the “far left agenda” adds too much red tape and rules that prevent good management of public lands — leading to problems like more wildfires.
“We need access to our wilderness, so we can bring back responsible management of our forests,” he said. “The Roadless Rule will open it up so we have access for responsible logging. We can bring back the mills so we can build affordable lumber to build affordable houses, but we will gate that so it does not turn into an interstate and it does not ruin our environment.”
 
The debate can be viewed in full online.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska candidates for governor address growing gap in childcare
description: One of the many issues before the next governor of Alaska will be the growing gap between available providers and the demand for childcare, which some advocates are calling a “childcare crisis.”  Many Alaska families are grappling with finding reliable care due to a lack of childcare facilities and workers that contributes to fewer slots, […]
text:
Children's bicycles are parked outside of the Interior Alaska Center for Non-Violent Living in Fairbanks, Alaska on September 14, 2023. (Photo by Claire Stremple for the Alaska Beacon)One of the many issues before the next governor of Alaska will be the growing gap between available providers and the demand for childcare, which some advocates are calling a “childcare crisis.” 
Many Alaska families are grappling with finding reliable care due to a lack of childcare facilities and workers that contributes to fewer slots, long waitlists and rising costs for families. 
An estimated half of Alaskan families cannot fully participate in the workforce because they lack access to childcare, according to thread, a statewide childcare resource and referral organization. The organization estimates that’s more than 25,000 Alaskans that could be more active in the workforce. 
The average cost to Alaska families is estimated at over $14,000 per year, thread estimates, sometimes surpassing the monthly cost of rent.  
Advocates say a patchwork system of federal, state and local funding is insufficient in providing Alaska families with adequate childcare, with childcare providers reporting struggles to complete licensing requirements to open new facilities, provide competitive wages to workers and keep daycare operations going. 
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins and Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor said they would seek to reduce state regulations for childcare providers and promote incentives for employers to provide childcare, if elected.
Kreiss-Tomkins and Bronson also said they would support recurring state funding for childcare. 
The three are among four candidates running for governor in the November election, along with Republican Bernadette Wilson. Wilson’s campaign declined to comment on her platform on childcare issues after numerous calls, texts and emails over the course of a week. 
Kreiss-Tomkins, Bronson and Taylor said their administrations would prioritize expanding access to childcare, especially in rural Alaska. 
Bronson called childcare “essential infrastructure” for the state’s economy. “I would work with local communities, tribes, employers, school districts, and existing providers to expand the options that fit each community. So whether that’s a licensed center, a home-based provider, a cooperative, or an employer-supported program,” Bronson said. “Rural Alaska needs solutions designed locally, because a model that works in Anchorage may not work in a village.” 
Kreiss-Tomkins also said he would support opening smaller, home-based providers and for childcare workers in rural areas, which would also boost rural employment opportunities. “Making training available to providers creates jobs for people who already live and work in rural communities and lets parents go to work, go hunting, or back to school,” he said.
Currently, only some Alaskan families receive childcare assistance based on available funding and eligibility. The non-profit thread estimates that 23% of children receive a subsidy from the government or employer.  
Kreiss-Tomkins cited a true cost study commissioned by the Dunleavy administration in 2024 that showed a wide gap between childcare assistance and the cost of care — which is significantly larger in rural areas — in his support for boosting state childcare funding.
“Besides direct investment in programs like Child Care Assistance at the state level, I think one aspect we should clearly do more with is investment in the child care workforce, and partner with unions, tribes and universities to make those investments,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. 
Bronson also said he supports recurring state funding, as well as “targeted employer partnerships” and pursuing federal grant programs.
But Taylor disagreed, saying before more state funding he would look to federal funding and tax credits for families and employers. “Any state support would come from the existing budget, not new taxes, and be tied to one result: more open slots for Alaska families,” he said.
All three candidates said they would pursue state incentives, like tax credits, for employers to provide childcare. 
The three candidates split in views on expanding statewide childcare through implementing a statewide “universal” pre-Kindergarten program. Currently some Alaska school districts provide preschool and early education programs, but not all. 
Kreiss-Tomkins said it would be a long-term intention of his administration to “get to a place where pre-K is something all parents in Alaska can count on.” 
“That’s a lofty goal, and maybe a ways away, but I want to bring local governments, the state government, and other partners to the table to work toward it,” he said. Kreiss-Tomkins said he would also aim to expand paid family leave to reduce the demand for infant childcare.
Bronson and Taylor said they do not support a statewide pre-K program. Bronson said instead he supports families’ choices for public, private, tribal and community-based options. Taylor said he supports existing pre-K for children who qualify and choices for families, including homeschool programs. 
Likewise the Democratic and Republican candidates split on their approaches to supporting childcare worker recruitment and retention. 
Kreiss-Tomkins said he would support childcare workers through loan forgiveness programs, and “robust” apprenticeship programs. Bronson also said his administration would “work with employers and  training institutions to recruit and prepare new workers.” Taylor said his administration would “lower barriers to entry” by reducing credential and education requirements for childcare jobs. 
The Trump administration has announced plans to roll back regulatory requirements for Head Start programs, which serve children ages three to five years old, including changing provider ratios to allow more children per adult.
Bronson said he opposes an increase in ratios “as a quick fix,” citing safety. Kreiss-Tomkins did not say directly that he was in opposition of a ratio increase, but said he wants to be “thoughtful” with changing staffing ratios. “I think for infants, especially, there should be reasonable ratios on the number of infants any one caregiver is responsible for,” he said.
Taylor said he supports increasing staff ratios, in order to expand childcare programs, “with safety as the line I won’t cross,” he said. “The bigger threat to providers today is rules that make it impossible to staff a room or make the business pencil out. More flexibility helps them stay open.” 
All three candidates who responded to the Alaska Beacon expressed support for reducing regulations for childcare providers licensed under the Alaska Department of Health to help ease barriers and help expand new childcare centers. 
Wilson also indicated at an October candidate forum in Juneau that she would focus on cutting regulations in order to expand childcare capacity. 
“For this administration, our first day in office, we’re going to come back and we’re going to roll those pages of bureaucratic regulations off the books. If they shouldn’t have been there, and the governor’s got the ability to do it, then by God, we’re going to get in there, and we’re going to do it,” she said. “We’ve got to roll those back and get them out of the way.”

title: Cotton’s absence takes center stage at debate between Arkansas’ US Senate candidates
description: Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton was not in the room as his Democratic and Libertarian challengers debated Monday, but criticism of the Arkansas lawmaker’s record and his absence from the debate took center stage. Cotton, who is seeking his third term in the Senate, didn’t participate in the Arkansas TV debate with Democrat Hallie Shoffner […]
text:
Moderated by Steve Barnes, U.S Senate candidates for Arkansas Jeff Wadlin (L), and Hallie Shoffner (D), debate in the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton was not in the room as his Democratic and Libertarian challengers debated Monday, but criticism of the Arkansas lawmaker’s record and his absence from the debate took center stage.
Cotton, who is seeking his third term in the Senate, didn’t participate in the Arkansas TV debate with Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin. Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, instead attended a birthday party for World War II veteran and family friend Jock Davis Monday, campaign spokesperson James Arnold said in an email.
Shoffner and Wadlin barely acknowledged each other during the debate, and their focus on Cotton was apparent from the get-go.
“Where is Tom Cotton? He’s not here, because he either thinks he’s too good or he’s too scared, and neither one of those works for Arkansas,” Shoffner said in her response to the first question.
Hallie Shoffner (D), candidate for the U.S. Senate race in Arkansas, answers questions during the debate against Jeff Wadlin (L) on Monday, October 12, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
The second question was about Cotton’s absence. Jeff Wadlin, the Libertarian candidate, took the opportunity to call the incumbent “a coward and a hypocrite.”
“Twelve years ago he badgered Senator (Mark) Pryor about not showing up to debate him. Well, where is Senator Tom Cotton today?” Wadlin said. He said he’s travelled to all of Arkansas’ 75 counties as part of his campaign, and the message he’s heard has been consistent: “The consensus I’ve heard from Arkansans is that they want (Cotton) fired.”
Cotton has repeatedly criticized Shoffner on immigration issues and his campaign has vastly outspent hers. Shoffner and Cotton accepted an invitation to debate by conservative Christian news outlet Salem Media. Wadlin said during the debate Monday that he was excluded.
Jeff Wadlin (L), candidate for U.S. Senate for Arkansas, answers questions during the debate with opponent Hallie Shoffner (D) at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Monday, October 12, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
The Cook Political Report sees the Senate race as solidly Republican, though local polling found Shoffner with a slight edge over Cotton in August — though still within the margin of error for the poll. 
Panelists’ questions touched on topics ranging from the war in Iran to immigration to economic development to college athletics. 
Shoffner, a sixth-generation farmer, frequently steered the conversation back to criticism of Cotton on issues like his past votes against the Farm Bill that sets policy for an array of food and agriculture programs. Wadlin frequently quipped that many of the issues plaguing Americans were a result of Democrats and Republicans “somehow working together to generate terrible outcomes.”
Both candidates also worked to differentiate themselves from their parties. Shoffner said that she would have voted to advance the Farm Bill out of the Senate Agriculture Committee  that Senate Democrats voted against because of cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance program.
Wadlin put distance between himself and the Libertarian Party’s preference for less economic regulation when responding to a question about the Protect College Sports Act, which would grant the NCAA a limited anti-trust exemption to enforce eligibility and transfer rules if it passes the House. It passed the Senate last month.

While Wadlin was opposed to the legislation, he said that in general “we need to stand up to industry consolidation because monopolies and oligopolies are costing Arkansas farmers.”
The candidates also decried the war in Iran, with Shoffner saying she would vote to end the war if elected and Wadlin saying Congress needed to exercise its authority under the Constitution to rein in the war. Cotton has defended the Trump administration on the war and has voted against war powers resolutions aimed at blocking military action against Iran.
“As I travel around the state, people don’t ask me the details of the war in Iran. They wanna know why we’re there,” Shoffner said. “Tom Cotton can’t give us a good answer.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Roger Marshall, La Confusa Frontera Entre Fondos Públicos y De Campaña
description: Traducido por Claudia Amaro. Nota del editor: Esta historia es una colaboración entre Kansas Reflector y MS NOW. Mientras el senador Roger Marshall lucha por su vida política en Kansas, un asistente del demócrata Adam Hamilton — oponente de Marshall — ha estado molestando al equipo del senador republicano con una pregunta inusual: ¿Alguno de […]
text:
El senador estadounidense Roger Marshall aparece en el debate del 12 de septiembre de 2026 en la Feria Estatal de Kansas en Hutchinson. (Foto por Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
Nota del editor: Esta historia es una colaboración entre Kansas Reflector y MS NOW.
Mientras el senador Roger Marshall lucha por su vida política en Kansas, un asistente del demócrata Adam Hamilton — oponente de Marshall — ha estado molestando al equipo del senador republicano con una pregunta inusual: ¿Alguno de ustedes está recibiendo pago?
Según los registros más recientes de Marshall ante la Comisión Federal de Elecciones presentados en julio, nadie que trabajaba para la campaña de Marshall había recibido un cheque de pago en los últimos cinco años, una situación que expertos en financiamiento de campañas dijeron que era potencialmente sin precedentes en la era moderna de la política.
Pero según el jefe de gabinete de Marshall, Brent Robertson, la campaña ahora cuenta con algunos empleados pagados, aunque se negó a ofrecer pruebas o detalles, como cuántas personas están siendo pagadas o cuándo comenzaron a trabajar.
Aun así, expertos de campaña dicen que la situación plantea dudas sobre la línea entre la campaña de Marshall y su oficina en el Senado, financiada con fondos de los contribuyentes.
En una investigación conjunta, Kansas Reflector y MS NOW obtuvieron grabaciones de audio, fotos, videos, capturas de pantalla de mensajes de texto y elementos del calendario de 2020 — cuando Marshall se postuló por primera vez para su escaño en el Senado — que parecen mostrar al senador y a su principal asesor usando repetidamente al personal del Congreso y recursos gubernamentales de maneras que, según los expertos, probablemente cruzaron la línea entre asuntos oficiales y campaña.
Según el Manual del Congreso de los Miembros, si el “propósito principal” de un viaje es un evento o propósito no oficial, “la oficina no puede programar actividades oficiales alrededor del evento/propósito no oficial para que el viaje sea elegible para que las oficinas congresionales sean reembolsadas.”
Pero los materiales obtenidos por Kansas Reflector y MS NOW muestran que la oficina puso a prueba repetidamente ese principio durante la campaña de Marshall en 2020 — y varios exmiembros del personal relataron ocasiones en las que la oficina parecía funcionar más como un brazo de campaña que como una oficina del Senado financiada con fondos de los contribuyentes.
Después de prometer responder “de manera significativa” a una lista detallada de preguntas si Kansas Reflector y MS NOW extendían la fecha límite para comentarios, Ryan Dollar, abogado de la campaña de Marshall, envió una declaración que no abordaba dichas preguntas.
“La campaña de Marshall no compartirá ni tiene ninguna obligación de compartir información sobre operaciones de campaña con los reporteros de nuestro oponente, y los habitantes de Kansas saben que el senador Marshall y su equipo cumplen plenamente con las reglas de la FEC y la ética del Senado mientras luchan por Kansas”, escribió Dollar, afirmando que la historia provino de “un empleado descontento.”
Sin embargo, existen dudas reales sobre si Marshall y su equipo han cumplido plenamente con todas las normas éticas de la FEC y del Congreso.
En un momento, de los más de 200 textos revisados, Robertson logra organizar una sola reunión oficial en Chicago y luego instruye al personal para que todo el viaje de campaña ahora sea considerado “Oficial”, permitiéndoles reservar vuelos para Marshall con fondos de los contribuyentes.
Según los ítems del calendario de 2020, muchos de los viajes que Marshall pagó con su Subsidio de Representación de los Miembros — la cuenta financiada por los contribuyentes usada para operar oficinas del Congreso — incluyeron eventos de campaña. El personal tenía un sistema codificado por colores para distinguir entre lo que era una reunión oficial y lo que estaba relacionado con la campaña.
Durante un viaje a Oklahoma a finales de septiembre de 2020, según notas tomadas por un exasistente, Marshall utilizó su PAC de liderazgo para pagar sus vuelos. Sin embargo, Robertson reservó hoteles y pagó comidas en restaurantes con fondos de la MRA.
Un viaje a Dallas el mes siguiente, en octubre de 2020, justificó que Marshall usara fondos de campaña para reservar vuelos, según las notas. Pero usó dinero de los contribuyentes para una comida, a pesar de que el único evento oficial en su calendario era una reunión por Zoom. En contraste, una captura de pantalla de su calendario codificado por colores muestra su asistencia a un partido Cowboys vs. Giants, a tres reuniones y a una cena de recaudación de fondos, todos marcados como eventos políticos.
Cuando el personal se opuso en un momento a reservar lo que parecía ser un viaje de campaña con fondos oficiales del gobierno, Robertson les dijo que podrían culparlo si alguna vez los interrogaban, según un mensaje de texto que un exmiembro envió a su madre en ese momento.
Durante un intercambio de mensajes, tras preguntarle a Robertson si el propósito principal de un viaje era oficial o de campaña, el jefe de gabinete escribió: “El propósito principal es lo que decimos que es.”
Durante otro intercambio, un miembro del personal solicitó más detalles sobre una cena en un restaurante de carnes en Dodge City, Kansas.
“¿Algún otro miembro del personal estaba comiendo en el Prime de Nine? ¿Están cuestionando el precio de $170 para 2?”, preguntó el miembro del personal a Robertson.
“¿Quiénes son?”, preguntó Robertson. Finalmente declaró: “No existe un límite legal para lo que puedo gastar en comidas.”
“Apruébalo”, escribió.
Los expertos señalaron que existe un límite legal sobre lo que los empleados gubernamentales pueden gastar en alimentos, y que “no debe exceder la tarifa diaria para las comidas” que establece anualmente la Administración de Servicios Generales. Para Kansas en 2020, fue de $55.
En otro intercambio de mensajes de texto, Robertson afirma que recibió una aclaración de que la oficina solo necesita una reunión oficial para poder usar fondos públicos y viajar a una serie de eventos de campaña.
“Tenemos mucha más correa de la que pensé. Adelante, reserva Philly para Doc”, escribió Robertson sobre un viaje a Filadelfia en marzo de 2020 para Marshall, a quien el personal llama “Doc.” “No existe ningún sistema de ratios.”
“Literalmente necesitaremos una reunión oficial por viaje”, escribió Robertson.
Los expertos en financiamiento de campañas disputaron la interpretación de Robertson.
Craig Holman, experto en financiamiento de campañas y ética gubernamental de Public Citizen — un grupo sin fines de lucro de derechos del consumidor y buen gobierno fundado por Ralph Nader — dijo que estos relatos sobre el “flagrante desprecio” de Marshall y su oficina por las reglas éticas del Congreso son “tanto impresionantes como aparentemente muy condenatorios para el carácter de Marshall.”
“No solo muchos de los eventos de viaje sugieren fuertemente violaciones deliberadas de la ley, sino que incluso comentarios improvisados del personal evidencian la intencionalidad de estas infracciones y los esfuerzos por ocultarlas de la vista pública”, dijo Holman.
“La ley federal y las reglas éticas del Congreso son muy claras: los recursos gubernamentales pagan los viajes oficiales relacionados con deberes del Congreso, y los fondos de campaña y presupuestos personales deben usarse para pagar la campaña o los componentes personales de los viajes al Congreso”, dijo Holman, agregando que Marshall parece haber usado dinero de los contribuyentes para “todos los aspectos de los viajes de campaña y los viajes personales.”
Brett Kappel, abogado en Harmon Curran y autoridad en financiamiento de campañas, dijo, en contraposición a la afirmación de Robertson, que “el personal no tiene, en realidad, una correa larga” sobre el uso de fondos oficiales con fines de campaña.
“Hay algunas excepciones, muy limitadas y específicas, que permiten el uso de recursos oficiales con fines de campaña”, dijo Kappel, citando un memorando de ética de la Cámara sobre la actividad de campaña.
Los mensajes de texto también se refieren al traslado de Marshall a Florida, donde su casa en Sarasota se ha convertido en un tema de campaña.
En un momento de los mensajes, Robertson instruye al personal a volar a Marshall, “de Kansas a Sarasota, con escala en el futuro.”
El lugar donde vive Marshall se ha convertido en un tema en su campaña de reelección. Durante un debate el mes pasado en la Feria Estatal de Kansas, mientras Marshall hablaba de su casa de 1.2 millones de dólares en Florida, una multitud combativa coreó: “¡Tú no vives aquí!”
Los mensajes muestran al personal navegando repetidamente por las demandas únicas de viaje de Marshall. El Kansas City Star informó en agosto que Marshall realizó al menos 14 viajes oficiales a Sarasota entre 2021 y 2024, que costaron a los contribuyentes $18,886, según el análisis de gastos de viaje del Star, reportado por la oficina de Marshall al Secretario del Senado.
La oficina de Marshall le dijo a MS NOW el jueves que, aparte de que Marshall había vendido su casa en Florida, era una historia aparte. Hasta el viernes, el anuncio de la casa en Zillow , que tenía un precio de lista de $1.45 millones, decía “aceptando ofertas”.
Robertson también ha sido objeto de controversia propia por su transporte diario. Una investigación de Politico el año pasado reportó que cobró a los contribuyentes $44,000 durante dos años por gastos relacionados con el traslado desde su casa en Lynchburg, Virginia, hasta su lugar de trabajo en Washington, D.C. Los registros públicos muestran que el total ahora supera los $71,000.
Stanley Brand, un abogado que se desempeñó como asesor jurídico general de la Cámara bajo el presidente de la Cámara Tip O’Neill, dijo a Politico que “nunca” había oído hablar de un acuerdo similar, aunque la oficina de Marshall dijo que el gasto estaba “en plena conformidad y aprobación de la ética, las reglas y los lineamientos del Senado.”
Sin embargo, una reunión de 2020 que Kansas Reflector y MS NOW pudieron revisar ofreció un ejemplo de que el propio Marshall podría vulnerar esas normas éticas, reglas y directrices.
 
El senador estadounidense Roger Marshall aparece en un mitin del vicepresidente JD Vance el 14 de septiembre de 2026 en Webco Manufacturing en Olathe. (Foto por Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
El ‘discurso motivacional’ de Marshall
El 13 de octubre de 2020, Marshall envió mensajes de texto al personal senior de su lado oficial y de campaña para organizar una “charla motivacional” con “todos”.
“Sí, todos”, escribió Marshall.
Expertos en ética gubernamental dijeron que esa reunión parece haber violado las reglas federales de ética que prohíben el uso de “recursos oficiales” con fines de campaña.
Tanto el personal del Congreso como el de campaña — muchos usando equipo financiado por los contribuyentes, como celulares y computadoras — fueron convocados a la “LLAMADA OBLIGATORIA DE TODO EL PERSONAL”, tal como figuraba en sus calendarios oficiales de correo electrónico. Y un video de la llamada de Zoom del 14 de octubre de 2020 muestra a Marshall y sus asistentes del Congreso discutiendo el estado de su campaña.
A lo largo de la llamada, Marshall habla de la escasez de letreros de campaña y de lo que los llamadores de puerta escuchan en el terreno. También le pide a su gerente de campaña “puntos de conversación” y “consejos útiles” para tratar con votantes preocupados por la salud.
Algunos empleados consideraron que la llamada de Zoom fue una violación tan clara de las reglas éticas que se vieron obligados a documentar sus preocupaciones.
“Enviando este mensaje como referencia de que nos oponíamos a esta actividad ilegal y que yo lo planteé a nuestros superiores y señalé que no es permisible según el estatuto de ética mencionado”, envió un mensaje de texto el director legislativo de Marshall en ese momento, Michael Brooks, a otro miembro del personal del Congreso.
Brooks no respondió a las consultas sobre esta historia.
Holman dijo que la reunión del 13 de octubre “claramente cruza la línea hacia un comportamiento ilegal.”
“Los miembros del Congreso y todo su personal están completamente informados de no mezclar el tiempo de oficina y los recursos oficiales con deberes de campaña”, dijo. “A todo el personal se le dan instrucciones paso a paso para respetar el límite entre las funciones oficiales y las actividades de campaña.”
“Por eso, el personal de Marshall era muy consciente de que el ‘discurso motivacional’ sobre la campaña en horario oficial no estaba permitido por ley”, continuó Holman. “Tanto Marshall como el personal pueden ser considerados responsables de esa violación.”
Actualmente, Marshall está en una reñida contienda por el Senado con el pastor demócrata Adam Hamilton, quien lidera la congregación metodista unida más grande del país. Encuestas recientes han mostrado que la contienda está esencialmente empatada, convirtiendo un escaño en el Senado, confiablemente republicano, en una contienda competitiva. Y aunque la campaña de Hamilton ha recaudado más en donaciones que la de Marshall, los republicanos nacionales están invirtiendo dinero en Kansas para proteger a Marshall. Ningún demócrata de Kansas ha ganado un escaño en el Senado desde 1932.
Marshall también ha enfrentado un intenso escrutinio tras un reporte del New York Times sobre demandas presentadas contra expacientes por facturas médicas impagadas. Su campaña ha respondido de manera contundente a las acusaciones, con una vocera de Marshall diciendo que pasó décadas cuidando a pacientes sin importar su capacidad de pago.
“Los jueces emiten órdenes cuando las personas faltan repetidamente a las fechas de la corte, no los doctores”, escribió Payton Fuller, director de comunicaciones de la oficina de Marshall, en un comunicado.
Pero incluso esa respuesta subraya la inusual superposición entre la oficina oficial de Marshall y su campaña: Fuller es tanto asesora actual del Congreso — ganando un salario financiado por los contribuyentes — como vocera voluntaria de campaña sin sueldo. Para esa historia separada relacionada con la propiedad de Marshall en Florida, MS NOW contactó un correo genérico de prensa para la campaña. Fuller respondió desde su correo de campaña como “directora de comunicaciones del senador Roger Marshall.”
En medio de la reñida contienda de Marshall, la idea de que no tendría personal remunerado hizo que los expertos en ética gubernamental y en financiamiento de campañas dudaran.
Un experto señaló que Marshall había estado operando una campaña con sorprendentemente pocos gastos. Según sus informes de la FEC, Marshall solo gastó $206,869 en su campaña desde principios de 2025 hasta agosto, el último periodo de reporte.
“Para una campaña al Senado, es extremadamente raro que no haya gastos para el personal de campaña ni muchos otros gastos habituales de campaña”, dijo Kedric Payne, vicepresidente y asesor general del Campaign Legal Center.
Agregó que los senadores pueden estar sujetos a sanciones penales si ellos o cualquier persona en su oficina hacen un uso indebido de fondos oficiales con su conocimiento. Y si la oficina de Marshall “usó fondos de los contribuyentes para actividades de campaña disfrazadas de asuntos oficiales, es una clara violación de una de las reglas éticas más básicas.”
“Estas acusaciones tan graves merecen, al menos, una explicación inmediata y creíble por parte de la oficina del senador”, dijo Payne. “De lo contrario, se requiere una investigación por parte del Comité de Ética del Senado.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas State Arts and Sciences facing $2.6M budget shortfall, raising worries about possible layoffs
description: TOPEKA — The Kansas State University College of Arts and Sciences faces a $2.6 million annual budget shortfall in addition to millions owed for loans from the administration, a situation that may eliminate academic programs and cause faculty layoffs.  K-State officials presented a plan to address $13.5 million the college owes to the school’s administration,[...]
text:
Kansas State University College of Arts and Sciences is undergoing an assessment process to determine how to save money as its budget sits in the red, according to university officials. (Photo by K-State Division of Communications and Marketing)TOPEKA — The Kansas State University College of Arts and Sciences faces a $2.6 million annual budget shortfall in addition to millions owed for loans from the administration, a situation that may eliminate academic programs and cause faculty layoffs. 
K-State officials presented a plan to address $13.5 million the college owes to the school’s administration, as well as the projected annual shortfall, at a September town hall, the Collegian reported. 
The reverberations from that meeting, where employees were told about likely layoffs and an assessment process that will occur to determine a reorganization plan, worried professors.
“The college has held two all-college meetings to discuss these challenges and has been transparent that potential options may include departmental mergers, discontinuation of academic programs and workforce reductions,” said an unattributed statement from K-State in response to Kansas Reflector questions. “No decisions have been made yet.”
The budget announcement came as state universities struggle to make up state funding shortfalls — some tied to requiring proof the universities eliminated diversity, equity and inclusion education. Fort Hays State University announced last month it was closing the Sternberg Museum of Natural History because of state budget cuts.
 
Ongoing budget issues
The College of Arts and Sciences budget problems aren’t new, said English professor Dan Hoyt. 
“If we’re going to make these drastic budget cuts, healthy programs might be lost,” he said. “There is lots of talk from administration about us losing departments and maybe even the college, and forming schools. That will mean, though, fewer choices for students and less autonomy for programs, and it also will mean lots of job losses for staff.”
In university organizational structures, colleges are broader with multiple subjects while schools are smaller and more specialized. 
Jesse Perez Mendez, K-State provost and executive vice president, announced a new organizational process at the town hall, which involves input from faculty. Hoyt and other professors said it will require significant time and paperwork from faculty. 
Hoyt and Philip Nel, an English professor, said they are concerned about the speed with which the university is tackling the organizational process. 
“The A and S budget has been in deficit for years, so it’s not actually news,” Nel said. “What is new is that it’s now being treated as if it’s a crisis. Arts and Sciences serves the entire university in terms of the courses that we teach, and it doesn’t bring in the same kind of grant money that perhaps other colleges do.”
Faculty in Arts and Sciences teach 40% of all the credit hours at the university, Hoyt said.
Nel, Hoyt and David DeFries, an associate history professor, all question the budgeting process used in the past and the assessment process being proposed.
“The budget model we were presented last year was built on assumptions that are hard to verify,” Nel said. “For example, it was built on the sustained increase of students at the time that we’re facing a demographic cliff. That’s a great narrative to promote, and even an aspiration to have, but it’s not something on which I would build the math of the budget.”
The “cliff” Nel referred to is the decrease of college-age students in the next decades because of lower birth rates.
The College of Arts and Sciences decreased freshman enrollment from 713 in fall 2025 to 624 in fall 2026, according to a university dashboard.  
Nel said decisions are being made without consulting faculty.
“There is an attempt to move power away from the faculty into central administration in order to serve what I perceive as a different mission than the one that I signed up for,” Nel said. “I see a university as a public good that encourages people, students, faculty, to pursue truth wherever it may lead, and it may lead to disagreement.”
DeFries said the assessment process asks questions such as what can be done to bring more students into Arts and Sciences.
He offered an answer: “Not much.”
“I mean, they are the ones who have been engineering the curriculum and public relations to drive people away from our programs,” he said. “They’re the ones who have given the engineering school and the business school and the grain science all these shiny new buildings, and left the humanities and the College of Arts and Sciences in the old buildings that need renovation.”
A slide at the town hall shared with Kansas Reflector said one-third of the college’s 22 buildings need 50% of replacement value in deferred maintenance. The example given said if it would cost $10 million to replace the building, and $5 million was needed in maintenance.
Jean Folkerts is a retired professor, former interim dean of the K-State journalism school, and a member of the Kansas Press Association hall of fame. News of proposed cuts to the college’s budget didn’t surprise her because financial challenges were ongoing. 
“For starters, Arts and Sciences has always been a stepchild at K-State,” she said. “It’s dominated by agriculture, business, architecture and engineering. Arts and Sciences has always existed as something that they never really, I think, put a lot of effort into.”
Folkerts said past budgeting processes weren’t appropriately designed for a college like Arts and Sciences that offered prerequisites that students in other colleges needed. In 2017-18, “big budget cuts” were needed and the school cut across the board without trying to reinforce strong programs, she said.
Other changes affected Arts and Sciences, such as students beginning to take prerequisite courses like Composition I and Speech at community colleges.
Folkerts would like to see K-State officials work through the assessment process of what’s next for Arts and Sciences by talking to former deans and associate deans to gather insights. Arts and Sciences is a “very large college,” which was challenging in many ways, and there could be ways to split it up effectively.
“My absolute clear statement that I want to make is: No university is a decent university if it does not have a strong college or collection of colleges of Arts and Sciences,” she said. “It’s an underpinning of the university.”
 
Looking long-term
K-State officials said the current process to address the budget will look at long-term strategies. 
“The goal is not simply to resolve an immediate budget shortfall, but to build a sustainable foundation that protects the college’s academic strengths, supports student success and creates opportunities for future growth,” K-State’s statement said.
The Arts and Sciences Renewal Committee is the assessment process designed to “examine the college’s current structure, engage faculty and staff, explore potential organizational models, and develop recommendations for a path forward that enables the college to invest in its future,” the statement said.
An aggressive student recruitment campaign with student incentives is also planned.
The university statement said the debt to the administration was accrued after the university allowed the college to spend in excess of its allotted budget for the past three years to hire new faculty and additional adjunct instructors and pay other expenses.  
That loan will be repaid in annual installments beginning in 2029 through 2043.
“Although the college is reimbursed for all student credit hours it teaches, during the three-year period, student credit hours continued to decline while related expenses were not reduced in accordance,” the statement said. “The college is now facing a structural deficit.”
 
Student worries
Lily Hansen is a sophomore majoring in English and social transformation, which she described as an umbrella term for gender and women’s studies and ethnic studies. Last year, she found out Arts and Sciences was discontinuing the social transformation degree, but those already enrolled are allowed to complete it, Hansen said. 
“We’re having a lot of cuts in humanities-based fields,” she said, adding that students received little information about what was happening with the degree program and that same lack of communication is happening now.
Hansen, who began her college experience as a biology major, said she values STEM degrees, too, but believes there is an attack on humanities, which she called a focus on “anti-intellectualism.”
“As people in general, we’re devaluing thinking so much, with the rise of AI and all that,” she said. “It’s so frustrating to see these majors — their entire purpose is to teach you how to think, teach you the baseline of how to be a capable human being — face the most backlash.”
 
Higher ed challenges
DeFries, Hoyt and Nel all said what is happening at K-State is part of the controversial landscape occurring nationally in higher education, including disagreement on cultural issues.
“We encourage students to ask questions that will challenge dominant assumptions about gender, about race, about sexuality, about capitalism,” Nel said. “If you are working to dismantle or, excuse me, reorganize, the College of Arts and Sciences, you are also reorganizing the area of the university where critical thinking is key.
“It’s key everywhere but it’s particularly key in terms of how can we make our democracy work better? What would justice look like in America? How can we ensure that we act for the good of the many and not just the few? Questions that are ethical, that are moral, and that can guide us to one hope: build a better society, make the current one that we live in work better, and make people’s lives more fair, make people’s lives ones that have greater access to opportunity, and that is not the direction that either the university or the country is currently headed in.”
Correction: Updated to correct number of credit hours taught by Arts and Sciences faculty.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: How the Alaska Beacon covers elections
description: The Alaska Beacon’s election coverage is aimed at informing the state’s electorate with timely, nonpartisan news and information that they need to cast their vote. We think our work connecting Alaskans to their state government is key to a healthy democracy.
text:
The Alaska State Capitol is seen from the steps of the Alaska State Office Building in downtown Juneau on August 18, 2026. (Photo by Claire Stremple for the Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Beacon’s election coverage is aimed at informing the state’s electorate with timely, nonpartisan news and information that they need to cast their vote. We think our work connecting Alaskans to their state government is key to a healthy democracy.
Readers often have questions about how we do that work, and the decision-making process that undergirds our coverage. You can find the answers to some common questions below, and on our elections page, which has all of our elections stories and resources. 
When we’re covering elections, we use the “citizen’s agenda” approach. The basic idea is that we focus our coverage on what voters want to hear from candidates, rather than trying to determine who’s ahead before the votes have been cast or counted. [Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Because all our work is centered on state government and politics, we get a lot of new readers during elections. If you’re new here, Alaska Beacon is an independent, nonpartisan news organization. All of our reporting is produced by a four-person team of Alaskans based in Juneau and Anchorage.  
Our newsroom is part of States Newsroom, the nation’s largest nonprofit news organization, whose aim is to support newsrooms in each state capital. Our funding comes from States Newsroom — you can see all national supporters and financial disclosures here — and local donations from readers like you.
In addition to reported stories about candidates and ballot measures, we produce a voter guide. This year, the Alaska Beacon collaborated with Anchorage Daily News, Alaska Public Media and KTOO. We asked every Alaska candidate for U.S. House, U.S. Senate, governor and legislature their positions on several questions, drawing from input from readers. Most candidates responded to the questionnaire. 
Along with their answers, the guide includes some basic biographical information, their party affiliation, whether they are incumbents and links to their campaign sites. The guide also includes information about each district, as well as the term length and salary for each position.
How we explain voting
We have an election page devoted to the information voters need to successfully cast their ballots, including relevant dates, a how-to guide and a video that explains ranked choice voting. Additionally, we partnered with other Alaska outlets to create a voter guide that includes biographical information and policy positions of candidates on issues that matter to our readers.
How readers inform our work
We started asking what you want to hear from candidates this election season at the beginning of the year, and we updated our call this summer before the primary election. We renew that query in every morning newsletter. Don’t like filling out forms? Email us at info@alaskabeacon.com.
How we hold politicians accountable
We ask politicians the questions we know our readers are asking, and we don’t just report their responses — we also look into their records to give readers context. The candidate responses to the questions in our voter guide are useful for helping voters make their pick, and also for keeping candidates accountable to the promises they made on the campaign trail once they’re elected.
How we choose which races to cover
We prioritize our coverage where we can be most useful. Our four-person team isn’t able to closely cover all 50 state legislative races, so we use our best judgement to decide which races to focus on. We strive to cover races that are the most competitive, or whose outcomes may have a significant effect on politics and policy in Alaska. We also factor in what interests our readers.  
How we work with other journalists and outlets
We choose collaborations that serve our aims of connecting Alaskans with their state government and providing a forum for commentary on state issues. We will seek out partnerships and collaborations that increase readers’ access to information, expand access to our nonpartisan reporting and that elevate the political discussion in the state. We think our citizens initiative approach is valuable, so we want to be wherever Alaskans are seeking information about elections candidates or issues. We are a non-profit newsroom and do not take any financial compensation for collaborations.
How we cover misinformation
In our reporting, we seek the documented, verifiable facts on issues. In elections, candidates make claims that do not always match what we can verify. In cases where political claims may mislead Alaskans, we will use documentation and context to bring the full picture. While we strive to verify facts through multiple sources, we sometimes get it wrong, and we commit to transparency by noting factual corrections in our stories. We do not use AI as a source and you can find our full ethics policy on our website.
Does this align with what you see in our coverage? Can you think of something we missed? Please let us know at info@alaskabeacon.com.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah House speaker says he’s open to repealing controversial development law
description: Amid ongoing controversy over a state law that allows landowners to essentially self-form a new city or town, one of Utah’s top Republican lawmakers says he’s open to a change — or even a full repeal of the law.  House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, told Utah News Dispatch in an interview Monday he’s supportive of […]
text:
A new housing subdivision is under construction in the Heber Valley on Sept. 19, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)Amid ongoing controversy over a state law that allows landowners to essentially self-form a new city or town, one of Utah’s top Republican lawmakers says he’s open to a change — or even a full repeal of the law. 
House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, told Utah News Dispatch in an interview Monday he’s supportive of addressing issues with SB258 that passed in 2024, and he fully expects a repeal or substantial changes to the law to be discussed in the upcoming legislative session scheduled to begin in January. 
“There should be a broader discussion, and I think, you know, a full repeal should be part of the conversation,” said Schultz, who has worked in residential and commercial real estate and owned development companies. “We will be open to all options right now, including a full repeal.” 
In response to a request for comment and a question asking whether the governor would be supportive of a repeal or alterations to SB258, Cox issued a prepared statement Monday indicating he would be open to changes. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We’re committed to making Utah a place where our children and grandchildren can afford to live and raise their families. That means exploring all options to address housing affordability,” Cox said. 
In a formal resolution approved last month, Wasatch County leaders called on state lawmakers to walk back SB258 because they said it allows developers to “entitle large-scale projects while sidestepping the infrastructure, housing, oversight and accountability standards every other community in Utah must meet.” 
The law created a pilot program that allows up to three landowners in mostly undeveloped, unincorporated areas to petition to create a “preliminary municipality,” which Wasatch County leaders described as “a step toward eventual full incorporation.” 
“The process requires a feasibility study but sets a comparatively low bar for what that study must show and grants the applicant substantial entitlement and development authority well before the community it describes has any residents, tax base, or independent capacity to deliver services,” Wasatch County officials wrote in a report listing the flaws they see in the law. 
What led the issue to ‘blow up’
Outcry over SB258 has been particularly sharp in Summit and Wasatch counties, where the issue recently caught more attention after Utah Gov. Spencer Cox’s senior housing adviser, Steve Waldrip, issued a threat to withhold state road funding from Wasatch County because leaders rejected a 144-lot proposal about six miles east of Heber. 
After Wasatch County rejected the project, Philo Development partner Greg Whitehead told a local radio station, KPCW, that it “sounds like we’re getting some retaliation” for pursuing a preliminary municipality under SB258. 
“We’re getting punished because we are considering a preliminary municipality,” Whitehead told the station. “Because we considered it, we’re not welcome to develop in Wasatch County, is what that sounds like.”
‘Threat’ to block state funds from Wasatch County stirs anger over ‘top down’ development pressure

In an interview with Utah News Dispatch last month, Wasatch County Manager Dustin Grabau said Waldrip’s comments appeared to be a reaction to an “untrue rumor” that Wasatch County was somehow “going to collude with other counties to defy state law related to preliminary municipalities.”
Since then, after meeting with Wasatch County leaders, the threat to withhold state funding over the issue has been dropped and state and local leaders say they’re now working together. But some Wasatch Back residents continue to be frustrated with the governor’s tactics, and local leaders continue to push for SB258 to be repealed.
It’s also been a top campaign issue in the House District 59 race between Democrat Celeste Johnson and Republican Luke Searle. Both candidates oppose the law, The Park Record reported earlier this month. 
Schultz noted that the Utah House earlier this year unanimously approved a bill, HB510, to create more requirements for preliminary municipalities, but that bill failed on a narrow, 14-12 vote in the Senate on the final night of the 45-day session. 
Schultz said he’s been talking with Searle and listening to all of the concerns with the law, which he said have become more widespread after Waldrip’s comments. 
“We in the House have been supportive … of making changes and modifications to it and feeling like the proper balance hadn’t been struck,” he said. “But now to see it kind of blow up to the extent that it has, is it time to just do a full repeal and start over? I think those are all options that are on the table.” 
Utah housing market remains among most expensive in U.S., with 91% of renters priced out

Schultz added that until now, “we really didn’t understand how much pushback there is inside Wasatch County on this particular issue.” 
Since longtime Senate President Stuart Adams, R-Layton, lost his primary election, he won’t be returning to Capitol Hill next year — and it’s not yet known who will be in Senate Republican leadership. However, Schultz said he’s been talking with some senators who are “on all sides of this.”
“Some are open to a full repeal. Others want to make modifications to it,” Schultz said. “So we’ll see kind of where that lands. … I think most everybody sees that there needs to be changes. Now, is that a full repeal? You know, that’s something that we’re certainly open to, or (should we) make modifications? Those discussions are going to be had.” 
The House speaker noted that lawmakers have tried to balance local planning authority with a push to increase more affordable housing stock across the state, but he said the Philo Development proposal and the “preliminary municipality” law didn’t seem to do much to advance that goal. 
“These are very large lots, very expensive homes. And, you know, it obviously really has people upset up there,” he said. 
Property owned by the Utah Trust Lands Administration in Wasatch County, east of Heber City, is pictured on Sept. 19, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
‘Everybody makes mistakes’
As for Waldrip’s comments and the controversy about an apparent threat from the governor’s office to withhold state funding over the issue, Schultz said “everybody makes mistakes.” 
“I’m not going to be too critical of that,” Schultz said. “I appreciate Steve and the governor in recognizing that they could have had a different approach that may have had a better outcome. You know, I think that’s what’s kind of caused the stir that’s brewed up at this point.” 
Waldrip, in an interview with Lindsay Aerts for ABC4’s Inside Utah Politics show last week, said the governor was “frustrated” with Wasatch County and he wanted Waldrip to “make sure that they understand we’re very serious about these issues.” However, Waldrip said they took the wrong approach.
“Fortunately, out of the back end of that, we’ve got really productive conversations that are going on right now,” Waldrip said in the interview with Aerts. “And yeah, we could have done a better job of delivering that message.”
The issue has also prompted a larger debate around top-down development pressures from state leaders and whether other entities like the Military Installation Development Authority — which was behind the highly controversial Stratos data center proposal in Box Elder County and a major Deer Valley resort development in Summit County — drive economic development that add to housing pressures without enough local planning. 
Schultz noted that local authorities must first give a nod of approval before entities like MIDA can create project areas in their communities. However, he agreed that the state and local officials need to work together, not against each other. 
“I do think the state and local elected officials need to work together to provide housing opportunities for our kids and grandkids. That’s what I think is important, and that’s what we should be focused on,” Schultz said. “I don’t think it should be a top-down, heavy-handed approach. I do think it ought to be a collaborative approach.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: More SC schools get top scores than ever, but education leaders say there’s still work to do
description: Although 90% of students attend a school considered average or better, education leaders want to improve the remaining 10%.
text:
State Superintendent Ellen Weaver announces school report card results at the Statehouse in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — More schools got top scores on South Carolina’s 2026 state report cards than in any year since the rating system began, according to data released Monday.
Schools continued to improve across all metrics used to grade them, including test scores, classroom surveys and student progress. Education officials pointed to statewide changes in education policy and funding as the reasons behind the improvement.
“We have so much to celebrate,” state Superintendent Ellen Weaver told principals, superintendents, teachers and reporters at the Statehouse. “We have a lot of important work ahead.”
Nearly a quarter of the state’s schools, or 320, received an “excellent” rating, the highest possible score. That’s an improvement of 50 schools over last year and the highest number since the rating system was revamped in 2018, according to the Department of Education.
The number of unsatisfactory schools also declined. This year, 24 schools received the lowest possible rating, compared with 31 last year, according to report card data.
More schools moving out of the unsatisfactory rating means more children receiving more than a bare-minimum education, said Patrick Kelly, lobbyist for the Palmetto State Teachers Association. At the same time, having two dozen schools still in that category means some students continue to get a subpar learning experience, he said.
Education leaders aren’t done working until every school is out of the lowest categories, Kelly said, also referring to the 103 schools rated “below average.”
“As long as we have any schools rated in the bottom two categories, that’s concerning,” he said.
Overall, though, he considered the results promising, especially after several years of sustained improvement, he said. More than 90% of students are attending schools rated average or better, he pointed out.
“There’s a lot here that’s encouraging,” Kelly said.
Reasons for improvement
Several policy changes at the state level helped push schools out of the lowest categories and toward excellence, Weaver said.
Legislators have made strides in teacher recruitment and retention over the past several years. This year, the state budget increased the minimum starting pay for a first-year teacher to $50,500, surpassing the governor’s goal set four years ago.
Other laws, such as the sweeping Educator Assistance Act passed last year, were meant to improve working conditions for teachers, including dedicated planning days and more transparency about their salary before they sign contracts for the next school year.
Those changes helped drop the number of teacher vacancies statewide, said Kelly, who also teaches advanced government classes in Blythewood. And when the state invests in educators, student performance improves, he added.
“That’s what students are showing right now,” he said.
Policies also changed how and what students are learning. Teachers in kindergarten through third grade had to complete a two-year training program on “the science of reading,” with the goal of improving reading scores. Education leaders say they’re already seeing improvements, and statewide test scores used in report cards reflect that.
While the number of students reading on grade level surged in end-of-year standardized tests taken last spring, more than half of students still couldn’t do math as expected for their grade. A similar training program on math, called the Palmetto Math Project, launched this year with the hopes of similarly springboarding students’ math skills.
“Our philosophy is simple,” Weaver said. “High expectations paired with high support are the winning formula for student success.”
Also helping is a 2024 law included in the state budget that bans cellphones during the school day, Weaver said.
“Our Free to Focus statewide policy is giving students new freedom from the constant distraction of cellphones and giving our teachers freedom to focus on instruction and what they’re there to do: teach,” Weaver said.
For Jenifer Seymour, principal at Centerville Elementary School in Anderson School District 5, jumping from below average to excellent this year was the result of years of hard work and changes in attitude among students and teachers, she said.
“There were no changes in policies,” Seymour said. “It was just really about our whole staff coming together and looking at every single student, where they are, making sure we’re meeting them where they are for them to be successful.”
Holding onto the excellent rating will take a lot of work, Seymour said.
The same is true for the state as a whole, Kelly said.
After Gov. Henry McMaster leaves office in January, the state’s scores could start to backslide unless the incoming governor picks up the mantle, he said.
“For all the positive momentum we have now, we could fly backward,” Kelly said.
Areas for improvement
The on-time graduation rate increased slightly this year, from nearly 87% to close to 88% of students graduating in four years. That means students are still graduating at the highest rates they have in a decade, Weaver said.
While a high graduation rate is good, that doesn’t always reflect the reality of how much students have learned, Kelly said.
Some students receive a diploma without the same rigor as their peers, he said. Incentivized to get as many students as possible across the finish line, some schools offer easier remedial classes for students who failed a class the first time, Kelly said.
“I think that’s well-intentioned in getting students to the finish line, but we also need to make sure there’s value to getting a high school diploma,” he said.
Grade floors may also inflate graduation rates. Some schools still set minimum grades for students and bar teachers from giving lower scores — often a 50 in a state where 60 is a passing grade.  That allows students to scrape by in class while doing little to no work. Legislators passed a law this year banning the practice. That might cause graduation rates to dip next year as fewer students pass their classes, Kelly said.
Just over a third of high schoolers were considered college-ready, a metric based on their college entrance exam results, college credit earned through dual-enrollment, and scores on Advanced Placement tests.
The number of students who received a passing score on an AP test, which can earn them college credit, increased this year, according to report card data. But the percentage of those hitting benchmarks on SAT or ACT college entrance tests dropped.
The report card also measures career readiness, which includes passing a test gauging workplace skills, getting a technical education certificate, completing a state-approved internship, or getting approved to enlist in the military.
Roughly 77% of students met that criteria this year, according to the report card data.
A solid foundation
If the state really wants to improve student outcomes, officials should start at the very beginning, said Dena Crews, president of the South Carolina Education Association.
Roughly 39% of kindergarteners started school prepared last school year, meaning they tested ready for their age on language, math concepts, basic social skills and dexterity, such as the ability to hold a crayon, according to scores on the Kindergarten Readiness Assessment.
That means more than half of students started kindergarten behind their peers, Crews said. While some students can get on track, others fall further and further behind in a snowballing effect that’s increasingly difficult to correct.
“When students aren’t coming in ready, they are already behind, and teachers need to play catchup,” Crews said.
Preschool programs are highly beneficial in helping students learn the necessary foundational skills, studies have found. But not everyone has access to those programs, Crews said.
Last year, hundreds of eligible 4-year-olds sat on a waitlist for state-funded preschool, despite the state having thousands of open spots, a report found. Some parents may not know why preschool is important or how to enroll their child, Crews said, adding the state can do more to educate parents.
The state Department of Education will continue pushing programs meant to improve the state’s public school system and student scores, Weaver said. She noted the agency has turned in its funding request for the year, though she didn’t go into detail about what it included.
“Our goal is a better future for every single one of our South Carolina children,” Weaver said. “And so, while we celebrate these historic results, we are not declaring victory. We’re building momentum.”
