text:
President Donald Trump , shown here at an August event, says in a social media post that he plans to rally in Kansas for Sen. Roger Marshall's campaign .(Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)TOPEKA — President Donald Trump said Monday he will host a “Kansas Style rally very soon” to support U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in his reelection campaign for U.S. Senate.
Numerous polls have shown the race between the Republican Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton to be a virtual tossup, and national parties are pouring millions of dollars into the race.
In a long post on Truth Social, Trump lauded Marshall and criticized Hamilton, calling him a “Dumocrat” and a “Trump Deranged Phony who pretends to be a ‘Moderate.’ ”
Trump called Marshall one of his favorite senators and said Marshall was given a “bum rap” by people who criticized him for taking patients to court to collect on past-due bills. 
“A judge ordering a patient’s arrest for not showing up to court many, many times is not Roger Marshall’s fault — IT IS THE LAW, and his Crooked Opponent is using that against him,” Trump wrote.
Trump claimed Hamilton wants high taxes, open borders and men in women’s sports, among other things.
“I won the Evangelical Christian Vote IN A LANDSLIDE, a Record Number, the Highest in History, and am more popular with them now, than ever before, because of what I have done, and gotten them — And I wouldn’t want Adam Hamilton being my pastor,” Trump wrote. “He’s caused nothing but turmoil in his church, which has broken up, and is virtually at war with each other because of him.”
Trump said Marshall has fought hard for Kansas farmers and agriculture, to secure the border and to cut taxes and regulations. 
“I will be having a Kansas Style Rally, in Roger’s honor, very soon. See you there!” Trump wrote.
Hamilton’s campaign spokesman said Trump’s post was a sign that Washington is panicking over “desperate failing politician Roger Marshall.”
“They’re saying anything to try to distract from Marshall’s record of supporting the war in Iran, gutting healthcare, and raising prices on everything from gas to groceries,” Tyson Brody said in an email to Kansas Reflector. “Marshall is turning to these desperate lies and false attacks because Kansans have learned Roger Marshall had pregnant mothers arrested and jailed over small medical debts, and voted to block the release of the Epstein files.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma state board again rejects Jewish charter school in ‘shocking’ vote
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Despite a federal court ruling in favor of a Jewish charter school, an Oklahoma state board again rejected the school from opening. The 4-3 decision Monday fell one vote short of the five needed for the Statewide Charter School Board to approve Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School. One member of the nine-person […]
text:
The Statewide Charter School Board meets Monday at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Despite a federal court ruling in favor of a Jewish charter school, an Oklahoma state board again rejected the school from opening.
The 4-3 decision Monday fell one vote short of the five needed for the Statewide Charter School Board to approve Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School. One member of the nine-person board was absent. Another seat is vacant.
None of the board members explained their reasoning before casting their votes. The board met in a closed-door executive session with attorneys for more than an hour Monday before voting publicly. 
“Welcome to the rollercoaster ride,” Board Chairperson Brian Shellem, who voted in favor of the school, said in the moments after the vote. “Unfortunately, that’s where we stand.”
Board member William Pearson said after the meeting that the local Jewish community’s opposition to the school weighed heavily in his decision to vote against Ben Gamla. 
Statewide Charter School Board member William Pearson listens during a board meeting Nov. 10, 2025, at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma Jewish faith leaders have publicly criticized the school as an out-of-state initiative that lacks local support, raising doubts about its viability. The school’s leading founder, Florida charter school leader and former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, has acknowledged he expects only 10 students to enroll in its first year.
Pearson similarly voted against a Catholic charter school, St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School, that applied for approval in 2023. St. Isidore, which had backing from local Catholic leaders, was later struck down in an Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling. A deadlocked U.S. Supreme Court upheld the state Court decision.
“I think it all goes back, to me, with the Jewish community in Oklahoma that actually had submitted letters to the board recommending that we not approve it,” Pearson said. “That, in conjunction with the fact that with St. Isidore we saw a lot of parent support for that. We saw none of that with the Ben Gamla issue, and that’s what played mostly in my mind.”
Board members Marshall Baker and Courtney Anderson, who acts as state Superintendent Lindel Fields’ proxy, also voted against the Jewish charter school. They declined to comment after the meeting. Fields’ office did not immediately return a request for comment.
The statewide board denied Ben Gamla’s application earlier this year in light of the state Supreme Court’s rejection of religious charter schools, but it still supported Ben Gamla’s case in Oklahoma City federal court.
Statewide Charter School Board Chairperson Brian Shellem attends a board meeting Monday at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Federal District Judge David L. Russell decided last month it would violate the First Amendment to deny a charter school solely because of its religion. The judge’s decision prompted the board to reconsider its vote on Ben Gamla.
Shellem, the board chairperson, said the school’s founders could apply again to open a religious charter school, but they would have to bring a new application. He said other faith groups also are welcome to apply in light of the federal court decision.
The vote Monday, though, “subjects our board to more litigation,” he said.
“We have a preliminary injunction that says we can’t discriminate against them based on their religious character,” Shellem said. “Obviously, I didn’t poll any of the board members. I don’t know why they voted a certain way. They had the same information that I had. I thought Ben Gamla’s application was strong and thorough. I think they would have been a great addition to our charter school network.”
Monday’s vote is “a setback,” said Brett Farley, a member of Ben Gamla’s founding board. The founders hoped to open Ben Gamla in August 2027 as an online school teaching both the tenets of Judaism and secular subjects.
Brett Farley, of the Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School founding board, prays before a Statewide Charter School Board meeting Monday at the Oklahoma History Center in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Farley, also of the Catholic Conference of Oklahoma, said the founders will consider their options for appeal, either before the board or in court. This result, he said, was “a little shocking.”
“We expected after the court decision that they would approve,” he said. “So, we’re just taking assessment here of this decision and where we’re going to go from here.”
The board’s attorney, A.J. Ferate, was similarly unsure what steps lay ahead. He suggested the school’s founders could try to have the board held in contempt of court, given the vote seemed to contravene the federal judge’s decision.
“Being a lawyer, I presume that’s probably what’s going to come,” Ferate said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Will AI make work easier or workers obsolete? A new NC survey looks at what workers think
description: There have been many predictions about how artificial intelligence will impact the way in which people work, and a new report by Elon University’s Imagining the Digital Future Center takes a deeper dive into how workers are adapting. The national survey of 775 adults employed full- or part-time found that large majorities anticipate a future […]
text:
As AI is deployed in more professions, workers are finding the need to adapt. (Photo: Getty Images/Johner Images/Royalty Free)
info@johner.se
sales@johner.seThere have been many predictions about how artificial intelligence will impact the way in which people work, and a new report by Elon University’s Imagining the Digital Future Center takes a deeper dive into how workers are adapting.
The national survey of 775 adults employed full- or part-time found that large majorities anticipate a future in which there are fewer jobs, inadequate wages and work becomes less satisfying.
Of those surveyed, 83% of adults expect AI to eliminate more jobs than it creates, and more than two-thirds (68%) believe most jobs will pay too little to afford a decent lifestyle.
Lee Rainie, director of Imagining the Digital Future Center, says while half of workers are highly confident that they can adapt their own skills to changing demands, they are concerned AI will “hollow out” the meaning of work and threaten people’s sense of purpose.
Lee Rainie is director of the Imagining the Digital Future Center at Elon University (Photo: Elon.edu)
“If you ask an American who they are, in many cases, they’ll tell you what they do,” said Rainie. “And there’s a very interesting dynamic emerging now as people worry about becoming lazy. They worry about deferring too much to AI tools.”
Eighty-one percent of those surveyed said paid work is extremely important to their role in their family, while 70% of workers said paid work is very important to their personal sense of meaning and purpose.
And 65% of adults polled agree that if AI makes work less meaningful, people will lose their sense of dignity.
A majority of those currently using large language models like ChatGPT said these models and chatbots are already smarter than they are.
“We’ve never faced an entity that’s smarter than we are,” Rainie told NC Newsline. “There’s a sense that as we have to share this essential part of human nature, our intelligence, our social wits and wisdom, what are we going to be good for as we see these things march through our workplaces and even our personal lives?”
Rainie said the survey found having familiarity with AI somewhat softens that pessimistic outlook. Still, jobholders want more guardrails as employers are accelerating AI adoption. Fifty-two percent of respondents said training about AI’s limits would be beneficial, and knowing when human judgment should take priority.
“People have little faith that businesses, schools and communities will step up to effectively assist them in the AI transition, “said Janna Anderson, senior researcher at the ITDF Center.
Among workers surveyed, only 11% said they felt government agencies would provide support if AI significantly affects their jobs in the next few years.
North Carolina lawmakers dipped a toe into the debate in May as they questioned whether restrictions should be placed on AI’s use in insurance and medical billing.
A controversial bill to rein in AI use in medical billing advances in NC Senate

Among those entering the working world, there’s a hunger for professional advice. Nearly half of those surveyed said they would appreciate advice about which professions will decline and which human skills will complement AI.
“One of the most interesting things about being a pollster in this area is that for years and years, young people have been the most enthusiastic about technology compared with others. That’s not the case with AI,” said Rainie. “Younger people, even if they’re using these systems, are very anxious about their futures, in part because of the implication for jobs.”
The findings will be presented Tuesday at the Tech Rising Summit in Charlotte.

title: New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich touts bipartisan permitting reform bill amid environmentalist criticism
description: U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Monday held back-to-back meetings in Albuquerque with labor leaders, manufacturers and renewable energy companies to tout his new, bipartisan permitting reform bill, which has drawn criticism from local and national environmental advocacy groups. Heinrich, who serves as the top Democrat on the U.S. Senate’s Energy and Na[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Oct. 12, 2026, convened a group of renewable energy company leaders in Albuquerque to tout a new permitting reform bill he co-sponsored with a fellow Democrat and two Republican senators. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Monday held back-to-back meetings in Albuquerque with labor leaders, manufacturers and renewable energy companies to tout his new, bipartisan permitting reform bill, which has drawn criticism from local and national environmental advocacy groups.
Heinrich, who serves as the top Democrat on the U.S. Senate’s Energy and Natural Resources Committee, described the 417-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 on Monday as a “very fine balancing act” achieved over months of negotiations with Committee Chair U.S. Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) and other Republican leaders. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“It was not easy,” Heinrich said Monday before a roundtable discussion of renewable energy company leaders. “It took longer than we would like, but everyone was committed to getting there. And I think we’ve come up with a really defensible product that, if we can get it passed, I think will age very well over time.”
The sweeping permitting reform bill aims to greatly reduce the amount of time energy projects, including solar arrays, wind farms or transmission lines, idle while awaiting federal permits. It imposes additional deadlines on parties that seek to litigate once a project is approved, an effort to stop approved projects from being further delayed in the courts. 
Jeremy Turner, the senior director New Mexico development and strategy for the Pattern Energy Group, told Heinrich on Monday that the company’s 500 miles of transmission lines for its wind farms took more than a decade due to lags in the permitting process. 
The company’s New Mexico wind turbines generate more than 1,400 megawatts of power across 800,000 acres of land, according to Turner’s comments Monday and the company’s website. The company has leased an additional 1 million acres of land that could produce as many as 5,000 megawatts of power, Turner said, but only if the approval process proceeds quickly and reliably.
“A reasonable timeframe for review by the federal agencies, and then also a timeframe for when people can actually challenge that decision, is absolutely imperative,” Turner said. “Without those, we’re going to continue to stay stagnant.”
Heinrich’s bill, which he announced alongside three co-sponsors at a news conference on Oct. 1, has received praise from labor unions, as well as both the American Petroleum Institute and the American Clean Power Association. Groups touting bipartisan policy have also lauded it as a step forward on a policy matter that has long frustrated advocates for all types of energy production in the United States. 
But some environmental advocacy groups have sharply criticized Heinrich, whom they say undermined his long record as an advocate for renewable energy and environmental protection by crafting the compromise bill with Republicans. 
And now, because he is a co-sponsor, Heinrich can’t honestly describe the negative impacts of the bill when he goes on a tour “hyping” it, Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center, told Source NM. 
New Mexico U.S. Sen. Heinrich and colleagues announce bipartisan regulatory reform bill

“We feel betrayed by Sen. Heinrich on this bill,” Schlenker-Goodrich said. “We think he has effectively boxed himself into silence about what the harms of this permitting deal are to New Mexico and the people and places we love in this state.”
Schlenker-Goodrick also said he is “perplexed” by Heinrich announcing the bill just weeks before midterm elections, in which Democrats are projected to gain seats and potentially change the dynamics in both chambers. 
Heinrich told Source NM on Monday that he disagrees that waiting for potential Democratic gains once Congress convenes in January would have resulted in a better bill or one with better chances of passing. 
“In the next Congress, we’re still going to have the same White House; we’re going to still have the same need to build a bipartisan coalition, and frankly, we probably won’t have the same chairs and ranking members,” he said. “And some of the secret sauce in this was just the fact that we had four people who were genuinely committed to a balanced package that both sides could support.”
Heinrich also called criticisms that the bill weakens environmental protections “unfounded and misguided,” saying the bill simply ensures federal agencies review projects more quickly, not that they approve them.
“We’re going to get to ‘yes’ faster. We’re also going to get to ‘no’ faster when a project is harmful,” he said. “And we’re going to be able to actually solve the climate crisis. It shouldn’t take 18 years to build a project that actually has value cleaning up the grid.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma voter registration system malfunction expected to have minimal impact, official says
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Some Oklahomans, who waited until the final day to register to vote for next month’s election, experienced problems after the state’s system unexpectedly malfunctioned, officials said. Some people who attempted to register electronically through the Oklahoma State Election Board online voter portal on Friday received an error message and were[...]
text:
A sign points voters to the polling place at the Millwood High School Field House on June 16, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Some Oklahomans, who waited until the final day to register to vote for next month’s election, experienced problems after the state’s system unexpectedly malfunctioned, officials said.
Some people who attempted to register electronically through the Oklahoma State Election Board online voter portal on Friday received an error message and were told to try again later, officials said.
The Oklahoma State Election Board said the interface between the Online Voter Registration System and Service Oklahoma’s data experienced communication issues for a couple of hours Friday afternoon. Service Oklahoma provides driver and motor vehicle services, and the information is used to verify addresses of people seeking to register. 
Paul Ziriax, election board secretary, speaks about candidate filing during a media briefing on Tuesday, April 2, 2024. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)
State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax called the issue an “isolated incident” that didn’t seem to have much of an impact.
Friday was the deadline to register to vote in the Nov. 3 general election or to update voter information.
Once the issue was resolved, nearly 800 applications, or about 40% of the daily total, were successfully submitted to the Online Voter Registration System.
“We regret that there was a brief issue with the interface, but it appears to have had minimal impact on voter registration applications,” Ziriax said. “Literally, hundreds and hundreds of electronic applications were submitted after it was fixed.”
Ziriax said there is no legal authority to extend the deadline for those who were unable to register. Voters had other options to register, he said. They could also submit a registration at their local county election board.
“It is our hope and our belief that anyone who received the message to try again later did so and it successfully went through,” Ziriax said.
Despite the issue, a record 1,906 people successfully electronically submitted applications, the most of any single day in 2026. A comparable figure for four years ago was not available.
Misha Mohr, an agency spokesperson, said once an application is submitted online, it still must be approved by the local election board.
Ziriax said his agency is working with Service Oklahoma and the Office of Management and Enterprise Services to determine what occurred and to plan for the future to avoid it. The Office of Management and Enterprise Services handles information technology and other functions for the state.
Andy Moore is CEO of Let’s Fix This, an organization that promotes voting and civic engagement.
“We would love to see the state expand the window for voter registration up to and including election day,” Moore said. “A number of states allow for same day voter registration and we think Oklahoma should be one of them.” 
Oklahoma Republican Party Chairperson Charity Linch and Oklahoma Democratic Party Chairperson Erin Brewer did not immediately respond for a request for comment as of publication.

name: WyoFile
title: No black-footed ferrets found in Meeteetse, 40 years after a rescue saved the species
description:
Combination of plague and drought-ravaged prairie dog population are the primary culprits for missing mustelids. 
The post No black-footed ferrets found in Meeteetse, 40 years after a rescue saved the species appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming wildlife managers are reporting that no black-footed ferrets are being detected in the cradle of the species’ conservation: the Absaroka Range foothills outside of Meeteetse, where the ferrets were saved after presumed extinction in the 1980s.
A tough combination of plague and drought — both big issues for the embattled western species — are suspected causes of a population collapse in the Meeteetse area, where wildlife managers returned ferrets to the wild in 2016 after a three-decade-long absence. It’s not assured that the reintroduced population is completely gone, but it’s not looking promising, Wyoming Game and Fish Department small carnivore biologist Andy Gygli said. 
“We spent a couple hundred hours of effort surveying 4,000 to 5,000 acres of the Meeteetse reintroduction area,” Gygli said. “We didn’t see any ferrets.”
The complete absence of ferrets during the late August surveys wasn’t wholly surprising. Sylvatic plague flared in the region in 2018 and 2019, and ferret numbers plunged to just one confirmed animal in 2020. Subsequent releases of captive-raised ferrets, including 18 animals in 2022, helped the small population temporarily recover, but plague struck again in 2023. By 2025, spotlighting surveyors again detected just a single ferret. This summer there were none.
Ferrets bottoming out and potentially disappearing struck Meeteetse rancher Allen Hogg as a big letdown. 

John Hogg poses with his blue heeler, Shep, the dog that rediscovered black-footed ferrets after the species was presumed extinct in the 1980s. (Courtesy/Hogg family)

“I’m really disappointed, of course,” Hogg told WyoFile. “They might be gone. But just because they didn’t find them doesn’t mean they’re not there, either. I’m not saying all hope is lost.” 
The Meeteetse rancher’s family name became synonymous with black-footed ferrets 45 years ago, when a blue heeler owned by his parents brought a dead weasel-like critter home. Subsequently, biologists found more than 100 other black-footed ferrets — presumed extinct for the two years prior — on and near the family ranch. 
The exact cause of the ferrets’ absence during the surveys is unknown, but recently drought in the Bighorn Basin walloped their primary prey species, prairie dogs. In many corners of the West, there just hasn’t been enough vegetation growth to sustain strong numbers of the grass-eating mammals. 
“We’ve heard a lot about deer, elk, pronghorn and cattle having hard times,” Gygli said. “It’s the same with our other herbivores. Prairie dogs also have to eat, and lack of [vegetation] coverage can result in low recruitment, which can result in downstream effects.” 
For ferrets, those downstream drought effects are severe. They, too, haven’t had enough to eat. Indirectly, drought caused the numbers of rare mustelids in the world’s largest wild black-footed ferret population, in South Dakota’s Conata Basin/Badlands, to plummet from 250 to 70 animals between 2024 and 2025, according to biologist and ferret expert Travis Livieri, who studies that population.
“In my 30 years of doing this, I’ve never seen [drought] this bad, where prairie dogs failed to reproduce at a high rate,” Livieri said. “The prairie dogs don’t do well, the ferrets won’t do well.”
Prairie dogs trip on a remote motion-triggered camera in the Meeteetse black-footed ferret reintroduction area in June 2023. Densities and distribution of the rodents have been greatly impacted by plague and drought, in turn affecting ferrets. (Wyoming Game and Fish Department)
Prairie dogs in the Meeteetse area also continue to struggle, Gygli said. After the 2023 bout of sylvatic plague, Game and Fish surveys mapped prairie dog colonies and found only 3,800 acres in active use — down from the 6,000-plus acres that were mapped around the time of the 2016 reintroduction. Densities of prairie dogs per acre aren’t great, either. 
The habitat conditions were bad enough for black-footed ferrets this summer that Gygli diverted 10 captive-raised animals that were going to be released in Meeteetse to the Shirley Basin, site of a rare ferret reintroduction success story. His rationale was that keeping ferrets out of the reintroduction area would relieve predation pressure on prairie dogs, helping them recover — and ultimately again support ferrets.
“There are prairie dogs there,” Gygli said. “They just need some time and some good conditions to come back. Rodents reproduce. That’s part of their strategy — they reproduce really quick.” 
Wildlife managers are also assisting the recovery with prophylactic insecticide treatments to kill fleas and guard against plague. On average, they treat roughly 4,000 acres annually — a roughly $100,000 expense, with the lion’s share covered by the Bureau of Land Management, Gygli said.
For now, the Meeteetse reintroduction area might stay free of ferrets intentionally. The last time that happened, in 1986, there were wildly different circumstances. It was a rescue mission to save the species. Although the federal and state wildlife officials found 124 black-footed ferrets after Shep the ranch dog’s remarkable rediscovery, the population plummeted in 1985 from a combination of plague and canine distemper. 

Wyoming Game and Fish Department small carnivore biologist Andy Gygli handles a captured ferret in the Shirley Basin in September 2025. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Retired Game and Fish Nongame Wildlife Supervisor Bob Oakleaf was on the front lines at the time, and he helped develop a contingency plan that outlined when wildlife officials should step in and whisk the remaining animals from the wild. Taking every last ferret into captivity from their only stronghold was a controversial decision, he recalled. 
“There was a lot of blockage in the Game and Fish,” Oakleaf told WyoFile. “Back then, the Game and Fish really wasn’t oriented towards captive breeding.”
Then-Game and Fish Director Bill Morris halted the ferret capturing operation “halfway through,” he said, leading to a series of meetings. Oakleaf and others talked him into allowing them to resume. 
“Thank God for the agreement on the contingency plan, because it allowed us to catch a few more ferrets,” Oakleaf said. 
After the last known wild ferret, a male known as Scarface, was captured in early 1987, there were a total of 18 black-footed ferrets remaining in the world — all from Meeteetse. Ferrets didn’t return to the area for another three decades. They went back into the wild on the same private ranchland where they were rediscovered. 
“All of the releases and all of the recovery efforts have all been concentrated here on our ranch and the Pitchfork,” Hogg said. “Lenox Baker, the current owner, was probably the most instrumental person in getting them brought back here — he really made the push.” 
Late Wyoming Game and Fish Department Director Scott Talbott poses with Allen and Kristine Hogg during the 2016 release of black-footed ferrets back into the area that saved the species. (Courtesy)
Hogg’s hopeful that the Meeteetse reintroduction area’s prairie dogs stage a comeback and the black-footed ferrets reappear — even if it takes continuous intervention. 
“It might be a situation where, to maintain it here for historical reasons, we have to keep supplementing that population,” Hogg said. “Sometimes it just is what it is. You can only spend so much money on a project. If it doesn’t work, it doesn’t work, but we certainly hope it will work.” 
There are some skeptics that Meeteetse will ever be home to self-sustaining ferrets. Oakleaf, the Game and Fish retiree, says he understands the desire to restore the historically significant population, but he worries that it’s just not the right place — it’s too small and has too much plague, he said. 
“Everybody involved feels obligated to put them back in Meeteetse.” Oakleaf said, “But, man, I don’t know how you do it. It just hasn’t shown over the years that it could support a ferret population.”
For now, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department is not giving up.
“This is a place that we’re going to continue to work on,” Gygli said. “It’s the place where ferrets persisted.” 
In an ideal world, prairie dog populations would bounce back enough to support a captive-raised ferret release in 2027, he said.

text:
Mill Creek as it flows under High County Road in Cherokee County. (Photo via Google Earth) The Iowa Department of Natural Resources is investigating a manure discharge in Cherokee County that reached a tributary of Mill Creek
A news release from the department said manure came from an open feedlot with an overflowing effluent basin.
DNR staff responded to the site Friday and said the producer had taken measures to “mitigate the impact of the discharge.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Franklin County coroner announces measles-associated death, state Health Dept. still investigating
description: If confirmed, it would mark the sixth measles-associated death in Pennsylvania this year.
text:
Photo of a single dose of the MMR vaccine. (Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)A 39-year old woman has reportedly died in Franklin County after being diagnosed with measles, according to the local coroner’s office.
If confirmed, it would mark the sixth measles-associated death in Pennsylvania this year. That’s the most in a single year since 1991, when there was an outbreak in Philadelphia.
According to the Franklin County coroner, Jordan F. Conner, the woman was unvaccinated and had multiple underlying conditions, though her primary cause of death was “a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.”
“This is the first death in Franklin County in many years with a patient with a recent history of a measles diagnosis and meets the definition set forth by the Pennsylvania Department of Health for a measles-associated death,” his office said in a press release.
More details were not provided out of respect for the deceased and her family’s privacy, Conner said.
A spokesperson for the state Department of Health said the department is “conducting a thorough review of the reported death. We will update the public after our investigation is finished.”
The department defines a measles-associated death as one that “occurs within 30 days of symptom onset in an individual with clinical evidence of a measles infection and a positive laboratory test and that is not due to unrelated causes (e.g., motor vehicle accident.)”
Coroners and state health officials have disagreed over causes of deaths before.
Pennsylvania has become the epicenter of a nationwide measles outbreak that, as of Friday, sickened 4,080 people this year, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In Pennsylvania alone, there have been over 1,130 cases, about one in five of which have required hospitalization.
Less than 1% of measles cases in Pennsylvania have been in vaccinated people, according to the state Department of Health. 
Two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine provide 97% lifetime protection. 
Pennsylvanians can contact their doctor or local health department for more information on where and whether they should get vaccinated.

title: Green, Hatley, Pinkston to participate in Tennessee Press Association governor’s forum
description: The Tennessee Press Association announced Friday it will hold a gubernatorial debate on Oct. 27 with the Democratic nominee and two independents agreeing to participate.  The Republican nominee U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not respond to the press association’s invite, according to a news release. Blackburn is considered the frontrunner as Tennessee has el[...]
text:
Gubernatorial candidates, clockwise from top, Lauren Pinkston, Democratic nominee Jerri Green and  David Hatley will participate in an Oct. 27 sponsored by the Tennessee Press Association. (Photos: Pinkston and Hatley, John Partipilo; Green, Karen Pulfer-Focht)The Tennessee Press Association announced Friday it will hold a gubernatorial debate on Oct. 27 with the Democratic nominee and two independents agreeing to participate. 
The Republican nominee U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn did not respond to the press association’s invite, according to a news release. Blackburn is considered the frontrunner as Tennessee has elected Republicans to statewide office in every election since 2010. 
The event, to be held at Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro, will likely be the only nonpartisan, fully public forum of the 2026 gubernatorial campaign. 

“Members of the press have a duty and public service to inform Tennesseans about government and public affairs, including elections,” said Dave Gould, publisher of Main Street Media and president of the Tennessee Press Association . “This is the first time in eight years Tennessee voters will elect a new governor and it’s important the public hear from the major candidates in an open forum.”
Democratic nominee Jerri Green and independent candidates David Hatley and Lauren Pinkston confirmed their participation, according to a press release.
In a statement, Green’s campaign said she “looks forward to a robust discussion on how we lower costs, strengthen our schools and make Tennessee government work for everyday people.
Blackburn, who has been in elected office since her election to the state Senate in 1998, has done no public forums throughout the campaign. She refused challenges from her opponents in the Republican primary, U.S. Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts, and in September told WDEF-TV in Chattanooga she would not debate Green, calling her a “socialist.”
She has not participated in a public forum or debate since her 2018 Senate campaign against former governor, Democrat Phil Bredesen.
The event, scheduled for 7pm CDT/8pm EDT, will be held in a studio setting and live streamed by a student-led video production team in the Department of Media Arts at MTSU’s Scott Borchetta College of Media and Entertainment. 
It will not be open to the public but will be live streamed by Tennessee Press Association member newspapers throughout the state.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Supreme Court sides with school board on principal firing
description:
Supreme Court upholds civil court decision.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Supreme Court sides with school board on principal firing.
text:
Brattleboro Union High School. File photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

This story by Chris Mays was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Oct. 8. 2026.
BRATTLEBORO — The Vermont Supreme Court upheld the school board’s firing of a high school principal.
The court said that after an internal investigation into complaints that former BUHS principal Steve Perrin “mistreated a female student on multiple occasions and attempted to prevent a mandatory report of child abuse,” the Windham Southeast School District Board terminated his employment. The Bennington Superior Court, Civil Division upheld the decision in November 2025 and Perrin appealed. 
In its Oct. 2 decision, the Vermont Supreme Court said it finds “no constitutional deficiency in either the termination or discovery process and conclude[s] that sufficient evidence supported the Board’s termination decision.”
Perrin was employed at BUHS from 2011 through Nov. 14, 2022. During an investigation into staff misconduct throughout the district, a former BUHS student came forward and Perrin was placed on administrative leave. The student is referred to as Jane Doe in court documents and has spoken with The Commons weekly newspaper about the experience and recent ruling.
“I am grateful to the Vermont Supreme Court for affirming what the school board, witnesses, survivor accounts, and now multiple court rulings have made clear: Steve Perrin’s conduct was serious, harmful, and grounds for his removal from BUHS,” she told the paper. “The courts have now said so repeatedly, and the Vermont Supreme Court’s decision explicitly recognized that the record was consistent with the Board’s findings and that there was substantial corroboration.
“The court has rejected Perrin’s attempts to undermine the findings against him and affirmed that he should never again be in a position of authority over students. I thank them for recognizing the seriousness of his misconduct and for refusing to allow his efforts to shift blame and erase what happened.”
The Supreme Court said Perrin’s firing was supported by a “harmful investigation of a sexual assault,” which involved interviewing the student alone, not notifying her parents despite her request, and threatening to tell the police she had made a false report when she refused to answer his questions. He was found to have engaged in a pattern of harassment, abuse and unprofessional conduct toward Jane Doe from 2009 until she graduated in 2012, which included repeatedly calling her to his office without specific reasons, making her wait outside his office to shame her, saying unwelcome comments about her appearance and touching her hair. He also instructed an employee not to make a report of suspected child abuse even though she believed she was legally required to do so as a mandated reporter, according to the decision.
Perrin argued that the board denied him due process in the pre-termination stage because it did not provide him with the evidence supporting the charges and that the investigation was “one-sided and stacked against him.” Without being given a copy of the evidence, he claimed he could not respond accurately to the allegations. He also told the courts he felt the board was biased against him and questioned how it could act as both investigator and adjudicator in the process.
His attorney Theodore Kramer called the recent decision “a bitter pill to swallow.”
“The reality is that it is very difficult to overcome findings made by a school board, as the Supreme Court is extremely deferential in those circumstances,” he said in a statement. 
Kramer said he hopes “the community will remember, when reflecting on Steve, that despite the accusations made against him, he had the unwavering support of all three superintendents under whom he served, as well as his staff and colleagues, both male and female.” 
“During my many, many, many hours with him, he never had a single unkind word to say about anyone,” Kramer said. “He was the epitome of resolute calm, knowing that he had always, always, always conducted himself with the best interests of our children at heart.”
Doe told The Commons that Perrin “did not act in a vacuum.”
“What happened to me happened inside a school, over years, in plain view of adults whose job was to keep students safe,” she told the newspaper. “When an institution lets someone in power treat a student this way for so long, it has failed its students and the public.”
Doe told The Commons that she hopes “this is the end of a painful chapter and that our community can move forward, but that can only happen when institutions believe survivors, protect their students, and make sure that what happened here is never allowed to happen again.”
School Board Chairwoman Deborah Stanford did not immediately respond to a request from the Reformer for comment. She told the Commons, “I am unable to comment in detail regarding the recent court ruling. I am sure that I speak for many in stating that I am relieved to move beyond this issue.”

title: Independent US Senate candidates from Plains states say they would not caucus with either party
description: Three independent U.S. Senate candidates from Great Plains states said Monday they will not caucus with Republicans or Democrats if elected, while the National Republican Senatorial Committee accused them of being Democrats in disguise. Brian Bengs of South Dakota, Seth Bodnar of Montana and Dan Osborn of Nebraska made the commitment during a virtual press [[...]
text:
U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs speaks to supporters on Nov. 7, 2022, at the Washington Pavilion in Sioux Falls. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)Three independent U.S. Senate candidates from Great Plains states said Monday they will not caucus with Republicans or Democrats if elected, while the National Republican Senatorial Committee accused them of being Democrats in disguise.
Brian Bengs of South Dakota, Seth Bodnar of Montana and Dan Osborn of Nebraska made the commitment during a virtual press conference.
Bengs, a Hot Springs resident and military veteran who formerly worked as a professor and park ranger, is running his second U.S. Senate campaign in South Dakota. He ran as a Democrat against Republican Sen. John Thune in 2022 and received 26% of the vote. This time, he is running as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds in the Nov. 3 election. A Democratic nominee dropped out of the race.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Bengs and the other two candidates criticized corporate influence in Washington and said they would support policies from both parties if they benefit the people of their states.
“South Dakotans deserve a senator who answers to them, not to national party leaders in Washington,” Bengs said. 
Meanwhile, the National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a statement dismissing the pledges. 
“The Fake Independent circus is fooling nobody,” said Committee National Press Secretary Bernadette Breslin. “Bengs, Osborn, and Bodnar are Democrats who would caucus with Democrats and fight for the radical left’s agenda if elected to the U.S. Senate.” 
Rounds’ campaign spokesperson Rob Skjonsberg echoed that sentiment in a statement to South Dakota Searchlight.
“Their policies are consistent with Bernie and AOC — they’re not fooling anyone,” Skjonsberg’s statement said, referencing independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who has caucused with Democrats, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York.  
The Republican committee also alleged that senators who do not caucus with either party would lose access to Senate committee positions, limiting their ability to represent constituents.
The candidates acknowledged that remaining independent could complicate efforts to secure committee assignments but argued their votes could carry significant weight in a closely divided Senate, which could allow them to negotiate for committee assignments.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Murphy hits US campaign trail, seeks to boost CT ‘No Kings’ rallies
description: U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy will campaign in five battleground states, spend time with CT candidates and try to boost turnout at 'No Kings' rallies.
text:
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy will fan out across the country in the final weeks before the midterm elections in an effort to boost Democrats’ chances. But he says he’ll spend the bulk of his time in Connecticut — for both campaigning and grassroots organizing.
Fresh off his trip to the Middle East, the Connecticut Democrat will stump for candidates in his home state as well as nearly half a dozen states with marquee Senate races that could affect which party holds the majority. But Murphy said his work won’t be singularly focused on political campaigns.
Murphy, a vocal critic of the Trump administration, is not up for reelection this year so he can spend his time and vast resources elsewhere. This gives him a chance to step further into his role as a campaign surrogate and test the effectiveness of his and the party’s messaging.
“I just want to be a good team player right now. I want to win,” Murphy said in an interview with The Connecticut Mirror. “I think this democracy can survive, but our chances are a lot better if Democrats win both the House and the Senate.”
As Democrats look to build the conditions for a wave election, Murphy will travel to North Carolina, Florida, Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire. Those states have a mix of Senate races with prime pickup opportunities for the party and open-seat races that the party needs to defend because of a retirement.
Some of the candidates running in battleground states are friends like Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who’s running for Minnesota’s open Senate seat. Murphy feels good about her odds.
While the Democratic Party at large is focused on swing states, Murphy will also spend much of the next three weeks in Connecticut.
“I’m not taking anything for granted in Connecticut,” he said. “I’ll be spending most of my time in-state.”
During the 2024 elections, Murphy led Connecticut Democrats in a coordinated campaign the weekend before the election. He easily won a third term that year.
This year, he plans to be a presence on the campaign trail again, whether that’s for Gov. Ned Lamont, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, or a slew of down-ballot candidates running for state House and Senate in the Connecticut General Assembly.
Before running for Senate in 2012, Murphy represented Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District, which remains the state’s most competitive federal race. While he feels good about Hayes’ prospects this cycle, he notes the sprawling western district is “always tough.” She faces Republican retired Navy SEAL Chris Shea this year.
Beyond work on campaigns, Murphy said he wants to focus on boosting turnout for the fourth wave of “No Kings Day” rallies that’ll take place across the country on Oct. 17. The protests have become the main vehicle for pushing back against President Donald Trump’s second term. Saturday’s demonstrations will center on early voting.
In-person early voting in Connecticut runs from Oct. 19 to Nov. 1. Voters can also do absentee voting by mail. The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2. Those ballots must arrive before polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day.
Murphy has gone to past No Kings rallies, and his participation at ones outside of Connecticut hasn’t gone unnoticed. In March, he went to one of the rallies in Los Angeles. Last October, he protested from D.C.
On Saturday, he’ll attend No Kings rallies in Connecticut. He’s working with local Indivisible groups — key players in coordinating the rallies — to increase turnout. Murphy shared with CT Mirror that he donated about $40,000 through his political action committee to Indivisible groups in Connecticut to try and make that happen.
“If that day is bigger, it will help us build momentum into the elections,” he said.
Carol Rizzolo, a voting rights activist and co-lead for the get-out-the-vote action team for CT Shoreline Indivisible, said she appreciated the senator focusing on Connecticut. She noted the “balancing act” he must undergo showing up in the state while also doing his job both around the country and abroad.
“He’s also standing behind a lot of the groups in Connecticut with financial support which we haven’t seen before, but I am just thrilled about it,” Rizzolo said. “I’m delighted to see Chris turn some of his attention back here.”
Rizzolo says the work by activists and others — all the way up to members of Congress — to push back against Trump’s agenda is necessary because despite Connecticut Democrats’ electoral dominance in recent elections, she still doesn’t think of the state as “reliably blue.” 
Joanna Swomley, a co-leader and co-founder of Indivisible Greenwich, said Murphy’s presence at any No Kings rally in Connecticut is welcomed and he has an “open invitation from us” to stop by in the southwest corner of the state.
Swomley said the focus for Saturday is two-fold: early voting and building on the infrastructure that’s already in place for public protests. At past rallies in Greenwich, organizers have seen the numbers range from 800 to 1,000 people. But participation could look a bit different this time in terms of participation and speakers because of the proximity to the elections.
As Democrats eye an ever-expanding Senate map, Murphy, in particular, sees real opportunity in Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, is challenging Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers.
Murphy called El-Sayed a “potentially transformational member of the Senate.” Murphy argued that the Michigan progressive is in the “mainstream” when it comes to issues like the Middle East — that U.S. policy needs to change regarding Israel — and efforts to take on billionaire and corporate power.
El-Sayed has taken some heat, particularly when it comes to his association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, but ultimately prevailed in a contentious and expensive primary this summer. Murphy initially endorsed Mallory McMorrow, one of three Democrats who sought the nomination before dropping out weeks before the primary.
But Murphy and most Senate Democrats have rallied behind El-Sayed, especially after he visited Washington, D.C. The party has mostly unified around his candidacy post-primary, and polling is trending toward him.
El-Sayed won’t be his only focus when Murphy heads to Michigan. The Connecticut senator said he’ll also campaign for some state candidates further down the ballot.
Most of the states Murphy plans to visit have been on national Democrats’ radar. But Florida, a former swing state that’s turned red in recent elections, has emerged as a late target. Angie Nixon, a state representative, prevailed in an upset in the Democratic primary for Florida’s Senate seat after getting significantly outspent.
Murphy wants to give her a boost with fundraising in a state with expensive media markets because he doesn’t want Democrats to completely cede Florida to the GOP. Still, Nixon, who has a loose affiliation as a democratic socialist, faces an uphill battle to flip the seat.
“I think Angie has an appeal that you can’t always read in polls,” Murphy said. “And if this is really going to be a wave year, what a disaster it would be if we didn’t do everything we could to help Angie afford a surfboard. So if I’m going to spend energy raising money for anything other than Connecticut candidates, it will probably be Florida.”
The other Senate candidates Murphy hopes to lend a hand to include U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire and former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina.
Taking back the Senate majority, however, still remains a tough feat for Democrats. Republicans currently control the upper chamber with a narrow 53-47 majority. More races have come into play in recent weeks, but Democrats still need to flip GOP-held seats in deeper-red states, while defending a few of their own vulnerable senators in tougher environments. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win the Senate.
Outside of election years, Murphy has taken steps over the last year to be a bigger player in Democratic circles. He’s spent the last two years traveling around the country with other members of Congress and candidates to push back against the White House.
He launched the American Mobilization Project, a political action committee that’s primarily used its contributions to fund citizen and local grassroots groups that organize around issues, more so than candidates. He also recently contributed money to national and state committees to help with elections. It comes as Republicans have a strong money advantage over Democrats, even with political headwinds against the GOP.
After Democratic losses in the 2024 elections, Murphy has been critical of his party’s outreach and messaging to voters. Since then, he’s described Democrats’ performance as “good but spotty.” He argues Democrats need to elect senators like El-Sayed and Flanagan, whom he believes will take more robust tactics if elected.
“Yes I’m interested in winning the Senate, but I’m also interested in transforming the nature of the Senate, so that there are more people in the Senate Democratic caucus who are willing to more aggressively take on corporate power, are willing to use tougher tactics to defend democracy,” he said.
He believes the issue of corruption is a “universal” message that’ll be a common theme as Murphy travels the country.
Acting as a campaign surrogate could give him an opportunity to expand his own coalition and give him more exposure to voters around the country — especially if he decides to seek higher office, though he has been mum on the 2028 presidential election or any potential future ambitions.
“I think this is the kind of year where you have to spread yourself a little thinner,” Murphy said. “For me, that’s meant putting some of my money into citizen groups, not just campaigns, and when I’m in these states, I’m going to be campaigning for down-ballot candidates as well.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Bernie Sanders, Chris Murphy, and Ro Khanna are coming to Florida to campaign with Angie Nixon
description: Bernie Sanders will take his Fighting Oligarchy Tour to the Sunshine State next weekend, when he will hold four campaign events with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon across Central and North Florida. The Vermont independent senator, one of the leaders of the progressive movement in the United States, endorsed Nixon in her contest against Republic[...]
text:
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent, with advocates at a press conference outside the U.S. Capitol on raising the minimum wage, on May 4, 2023. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)Bernie Sanders will take his Fighting Oligarchy Tour to the Sunshine State next weekend, when he will hold four campaign events with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon across Central and North Florida.
The Vermont independent senator, one of the leaders of the progressive movement in the United States, endorsed Nixon in her contest against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody last month and has donated $250,000 from his political committee to her campaign.
Nixon, a Jacksonville state representative, in August defeated Alex Vindman in the Democratic primary, despite being massively out-fundraised.  She faces similar fundraising challenges against Moody.
The RealClearPolling average of the Florida Senate race shows Moody up by roughly seven points over Nixon, 49%-42%.
Sanders is not the only Washington Democrat making a trip to Florida to campaign with Nixon.
Connecticut U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy and California Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, both of whom are considering runs for the Democratic nomination for president in 2028, also intend to hit the campaign trail with Nixon in Orlando.
Murphy will campaign with Nixon on Oct. 14 and Khanna will campaign with her on Oct. 20.
“I do believe that we’d make a big mistake if we slept on Florida,” Murphy told Politico last week, adding that he intends to push to raise some “serious money” for Nixon’s campaign. “I know it feels like a longer shot, but I just think this year is looking exceptional.”
Sanders’ itinerary in Florida includes stops in Tampa and Melbourne on Saturday, Oct. 17, and Gainesville and Tallahassee on Sunday, Oct. 18. It notably does not include any stops in South Florida, where Sanders’ comments praising Fidel Castro in 2020 received a strong backlash from some South Florida Democrats.
The Tampa Sanders/Nixon event will be held at the Cuban Club, which angered Dan Weldon, a Republican running for the House District 64 in Hillsborough County. He said it was “beyond disgusting that the Cuban Club in Tampa is hosting socialists Bernie Sanders & Angie Nixon.”
“The Cuban Club was founded for the benefit of Cuban-Americans,” he said in a Facebook post. “Tampa has one of the largest Cuban refugee populations in the country — people who lost everything due to socialism. Shame on the Cuban Club for allowing this.”
Punchbowl News reported Monday that Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeen Jeffries “hinted” in an interview that he might head to Florida before Election Day.
Moody will draw some Washington-based support later this week, as well. Senate Majority Leader John Thune will campaign with the Florida Republican sometime this week, Punchbowl News reported. No date or location was listed.

name: Delaware
title: Meyer advances $20 million in solar projects, but how much will Delaware consumers save?
description: Four privately financed installations would expand local electricity generation and offer subscribers lower bills, but questions remain about costs, incentives and broader benefits. By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News DOVER, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer’s administration has announced plans to accelerate four community solar projects representing approximately[...]
text:
Four privately financed installations would expand local electricity generation and offer subscribers lower bills, but questions remain about costs, incentives and broader benefits.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
DOVER, Del. — Gov. Matt Meyer’s administration has announced plans to accelerate four community solar projects representing approximately $20.3 million in proposed private investment, promising additional electricity generation and savings for participating Delaware consumers.
The projects, proposed by King Energy, would add nearly 10 megawatts of solar generating capacity at commercial properties in New Castle and Sussex counties. Construction is expected to begin in spring 2027.
The announcement comes as Delaware residents and businesses continue to face concerns about electricity affordability, generating capacity and the state’s ability to attract private investment.
Although the administration says the projects will expand local energy production and help customers manage electricity costs, its Oct. 9 announcement did not specify how many households would benefit or how much an average subscriber could save annually.
That distinction matters because community solar programs provide financial benefits directly to participating customers but do not necessarily reduce electricity rates for everyone.
Four projects, $20.3 million in investment
The solar installations are among six projects accepted into the governor’s JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator, an initiative designed to shorten government review timelines for housing, energy and infrastructure development.
The six projects represent approximately $165 million in proposed private investment, including two mixed-use housing developments and the four solar installations.
King Energy would develop the solar facilities at commercial properties owned by Harvey Hanna & Associates and Coastal Trade Supply.

According to the administration, the installations would generate more than 12 million kilowatt-hours of electricity annually after completion.
“King Energy is extremely excited to partner with the Delaware JobsFirst program to accelerate the deployment of rooftop solar programs at four commercial properties, owned by Harvey Hanna and Coastal Trade Supply,” King Energy CEO John Witchel said in the announcement.
Witchel said the projects would help address growing electricity demand and costs by expanding in-state generation.
The installations would connect to Delmarva Power’s distribution system. Construction is scheduled to begin in late March 2027, with completion dates varying by location.
How much will customers save?
Unlike traditional rooftop solar, community solar allows eligible residents and businesses to subscribe to a larger solar installation without purchasing or installing panels on their own property.
Electricity generated by the facility enters the utility’s distribution system, and participating customers receive credits on their electric bills based on their subscriptions.
Delaware law establishes minimum savings requirements for newer community solar projects.
For facilities receiving final operating certificates on or after Sept. 3, 2026, residential subscribers must receive savings of at least 10% on the value of their community solar credits. Qualifying low- and moderate-income subscribers must receive savings of at least 20%.
The law also requires at least 15% of a qualifying facility’s electricity output to serve low- and moderate-income customers.
Those savings percentages apply to the value of solar electricity credits after applicable charges, not necessarily to a customer’s entire electric bill.
For example, a residential customer receiving $100 worth of solar credits would save at least $10 under the standard requirement. An income-qualified customer receiving the same credits would save at least $20.
The actual annual savings would depend on electricity consumption, subscription size and billing arrangements.
While those consumer protections are established in state law, the administration has not released expected annual dollar savings for participants in the four newly announced projects.
The number of available subscriptions, eligibility details and enrollment dates also have not been announced.
More generation does not necessarily mean lower statewide rates
The facilities would add locally generated electricity to Delaware’s energy supply, an objective emphasized by the Meyer administration as electricity demand grows.
Solar generation can reduce demand for electricity from other sources during periods when sunlight is available. However, solar panels do not produce electricity at night, and generation varies with weather and seasonal conditions.
The four proposed projects do not include a battery-storage component in the information released by the administration.
As a result, the installations could contribute to Delaware’s electricity supply but would not independently address the need for dependable generation during nighttime hours or other periods when solar production is limited.
The state has not released an analysis quantifying how these four projects would affect wholesale electricity prices, grid reliability or utility rates for customers who do not subscribe.
Those questions are relevant as Delaware considers how to balance renewable energy development with dependable, affordable electricity from a variety of generating sources.
Private investment and public incentives
One notable feature of the announcement is its emphasis on private-sector investment rather than a newly announced state construction appropriation.
King Energy is identified as the developer, with approximately $20.3 million in proposed investment across the four facilities.
However, private financing does not necessarily mean a project operates without public incentives or other financial support.
Depending on eligibility and applicable rules, solar developers may receive tax benefits or generate revenue through renewable energy credit programs.
The governor’s announcement does not identify the specific tax incentives, grants or other public financial assistance, if any, expected to support these installations.
It also does not provide a detailed accounting of utility interconnection expenses or program administration costs.
Those financial arrangements would help establish the projects’ overall economics and clarify whether any associated expenses could affect taxpayers or utility customers who do not subscribe.
Meyer promotes faster permitting
The governor’s JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator is intended to reduce unnecessary delays by coordinating reviews across state agencies.
Established through Executive Order 18, the initiative assigns participating projects a central point of contact and seeks to complete complex permitting reviews within 120 business days.
Existing environmental, public safety and regulatory requirements remain in place, according to the administration.
“The JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator is about cutting unnecessary red tape, moving projects forward faster and making it easier to invest in Delaware,” Meyer said.
“These projects will help lower costs, create opportunities and strengthen the communities Delawareans call home.”
Thomas Harvey, managing director of Harvey Hanna & Associates, said the permitting improvements could help bring needed energy projects online more efficiently.
“We believe projects like these can play an important role in addressing Delaware’s growing need for reliable, affordable energy,” Harvey said.
The approach has implications beyond solar development. More predictable permitting timelines can reduce uncertainty for businesses considering investments in manufacturing, housing and infrastructure.
However, acceptance into the accelerator does not constitute final regulatory approval or guarantee that construction will begin on schedule.
Construction jobs expected
The administration also says the four installations will generate local construction employment.
The announced construction schedules range from approximately five to eight months, depending on the facility.
The state did not specify the number of construction positions, expected wages, how many workers would be Delaware residents or whether the projects would create permanent jobs after construction.
Those details would help evaluate the employment impact of the investments, particularly because the permitting initiative is part of the administration’s JobsFirst economic development program.
Part of a larger solar initiative
The newly announced facilities build on Delaware’s efforts to expand community solar.
In September, the Delaware Public Service Commission highlighted four previously accepted community solar projects in Seaford, Townsend and Clayton.
Those projects represent more than 16 megawatts of proposed generating capacity and over $73 million in investment.
According to the commission, state officials estimated that the earlier projects could provide electricity cost reductions of 10% to 15% for more than 16,000 Delaware households.
Those estimates apply to the earlier projects, not the four King Energy installations announced in October.
The additional facilities would expand the number of proposed solar installations moving through the state’s accelerated permitting process.
Measuring the benefits
The latest announcement represents another step in the administration’s effort to encourage private investment, expand energy generation and reduce regulatory delays.
The projects offer potential benefits, including additional electricity production, savings for participating customers and construction-related economic activity.
Whether those investments also produce broader affordability benefits will depend on actual electricity output, project costs, subscriber participation and how the facilities operate within Delaware’s electricity system.
Several questions remain unanswered in the announcement, including how many Delawareans will subscribe, what average annual savings will be, whether public incentives are involved and how the administration will measure the results of accelerated permitting.
For consumers concerned about rising electricity costs, those figures will help determine how much of the promised benefit ultimately reaches Delaware households and businesses.
The four installations remain proposed developments, with construction planned for 2027. Their economic and energy benefits will become measurable once the facilities are completed and begin operating.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM Medical Center unions approve contracts and avert a strike
description:
A sweeping majority of the more than 2,000 members of the two unions who voted, cast ballots in favor of the agreements, which largely address the unions’ demands surrounding staffing levels.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM Medical Center unions approve contracts and avert a strike.
text:
Vermont Federation of Nurses and Health Professionals President Nicole DiVita, right, and Jacob Berkowitz, president of UVMMC Support Staff United, pictured on Oct. 2. Photo by Olivia Gieger/VTDigger

The two unions representing University of Vermont Medical Center’s support staff and technical professionals have both voted to ratify their contracts, narrowly averting a strike. More than 2,000 of the 3,300 employees in the unions voted, representatives for the unions said, with more than 89% approving the new contracts.
Both unions, which represent employees such as licensed nurse assistants, lab technicians, schedulers and surgical equipment sterilizers, have been jointly negotiating new contracts since April. Discussions have centered around employees’ say in staffing levels, as UVM Health, the hospital’s parent network, has started layoffs in an effort to cut its expenses.
“We did something historic while the healthcare system continues to fall apart around us,” Nicole DiVita, the president of the technical professionals’ union, said in a written statement of the joint effort. “We bargained together, 3,300 strong, we improved patient care through safer staffing measures, and we won community benefits that bring together a broader movement of working class Vermonters in support of a system that serves all of us.”
UVM Medical Center did not respond immediately to requests for comment about the ratification. When the two parties tentatively agreed to contract language last week, Dr. Steven Leffler, the hospital’s president, said that he was grateful for the unions’ commitment to staying at the bargaining table and reaching an agreement.  
The new contracts give the unions many of their requests regarding how decisions on staffing levels are made. The support staff union’s contract gives employees the ability to contribute to staff decisions in each department, which they previously did not have. Technical staff have retained that ability to participate in creating the plans for staffing levels on each floor, and now have a much shorter timeline for when those updated plans will be implemented and enforceable — from 18 months to six.
Relatedly, licensed nursing assistants and mental health technicians pushed for an end to temporary assignments in short-staffed departments in which they had no specialization. The new contract ends that practice. The contracts do not include the unions’ earlier request for incentive pay when working on short-staffed floors. 
The agreements increase wages a combined 7% over two years, which includes a cost of living increase. The hospital had pushed to negotiate wages for the next three years, while the unions had pushed for a shorter timeline to renegotiate raises. 
Union members in short-staffed areas that have relied on traveling staff, such as respiratory therapists and MRI technicians, saw larger wage increases.   
The agreements will remain in place until the support staff and the technical staff contracts expire in April and July 2028, respectively. 
As part of their joint bargaining work, both unions also pushed for the hospital to pledge against lobbying efforts to prevent statewide universal healthcare and for the hospital to source dairy through Migrant Justice’s Milk with Dignity program. Instead, the hospital agreed to penning a joint statement with the unions about the “broken state” of the healthcare system, according to the union, and to continue discussions on joining Milk with Dignity.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM Medical Center unions approve contracts and avert a strike.

name: VTDigger
title: Our schools are being crushed by state mandates
description:
A sharp drop in the state’s excess spending threshold is forcing Hartford to make deep cuts, even as expenses rise.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Our schools are being crushed by state mandates.
text:
This commentary is by Caty Sutton, the superintendent of the Hartford School District; the Hartford School Board; the Hartford School District leadership and the Hartford Education Association leadership.
It is with great disappointment, discouragement and disillusionment that we write to express our profound concerns about what transpired throughout the last legislative session. As we anticipate what will come this year, those decisions will significantly affect and shape our fate as a district.
First, the passage of Act 169 at the end of the last legislative session and the reduction of the excess spending threshold from 118% to 115.5% in one fiscal year are devastating to our district and local community. Our district now faces an almost $5 million reduction in our budget while continuing to absorb the catastrophic, ongoing impact of crushing healthcare insurance costs and crippling inflation.
To put the above into perspective, we are looking at potentially having to reduce our administration, professional staff and support staff by 25% — one in four of our workforce — to present a budget to our community below the excess spending threshold so we can avoid the penalty that the state would impose.
At the same time, we continue to face the Vermont Agency of Education‘s ongoing accountability efforts, requiring districts to engage in significant and unfunded, unsupported initiatives. So, eviscerate our budgets, but expect our staff to take on even more?
All of this comes as the Legislature continues PCB testing in schools while leaving districts already affected in limbo, with little or no funding for mandated quarterly testing and no resources for remediation or abatement. These costs could amount to millions of dollars, leaving local taxpayers to fund a state-mandated response to a serious safety hazard.
We are also being given almost no lead time or transition period to adopt a new Medicaid reimbursement model, which will change how we are reimbursed and involve an entirely new system, requiring hours of training and implementation for staff who must deliver and adopt this approach.

READ MORE

Finally, let’s not forget that Act 170 places us in a Cooperative Educational Service Area (CESA) by statute. Since we were incorrectly placed by the Legislature in the Northeast region, we must also undergo an arduous process laid out in the statute to move from the Northeast into the Vermont Learning Collaborative, with which we have already been collaborating for two years, while simultaneously engaging in district merger committee conversations with regional neighbors who are in a different CESA region and facing the same challenging budget reductions. 
It is beyond challenging to believe that there is not a concerted effort to discredit, disenfranchise and essentially gut public education in Vermont, beginning with this fiscal year and the impossibility of our current budgeting circumstances.
Our community does not deserve this. Our educators have dedicated their careers and their lives to serving our students with integrity and care, and now we are put into the position of radically overhauling our district. For what, exactly? Neither the agency, the Legislature nor the governor has supplied us with any semblance of a realized vision for what this education transformation will give our students as a result of these profoundly damaging changes, and none of these entities has supplied us with the data and evidence that this transformation will lead to cost savings for our taxpayers. 
Our community did not ask for district merger studies, PCBs, changes to Medicaid and additional requirements from the agency. We just want to continue to do what we do best: provide the best possible education and support to our students with the funding our community is willing and able to provide.
Going forward, we expect our local delegation to revisit the abrupt and crushing impact that this reduction to the excess spending threshold will have on our district and to advocate for changes to slow down this process. We also expect them to push for allocation of funding to continue to ensure the law is followed and we do not incur the infinite costs of PCB testing, remediation and abatement. And we expect them to scrutinize the unrealistic timelines and processes related to the formation of CESAs and the district merger committee study groups.
In short, we expect our local delegation to take care of our community, which is struggling to breathe under the weight of the myriad costs of imposed mandates.
Please help us to save our most valuable community resource and advocate for a future with a strong public education system. Center our students, and consider who among us is the most vulnerable and requires the most support. Remember that public education is a fundamental and most vibrant component of Vermont democracy and community life. 
Please give us a lifeline to survive.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Our schools are being crushed by state mandates.
