title: USDA Rural Development invests nearly $13M into Iowa communities
description: Healthcare, manufacturing and community projects in rural Iowa are set to receive millions in loan and grant funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development office.  USDA announced investments of more than $12.9 million in Iowa cooperatives to help support their pass-through and revolving loan funds.  Rural Business Cooperative Service Admi[...]
text:
USDA announced more than $12.9 million in grant and loans going to rural cooperatives to support rural hospitals, community centers, manufacturing and agriculture. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Healthcare, manufacturing and community projects in rural Iowa are set to receive millions in loan and grant funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development office. 
USDA announced investments of more than $12.9 million in Iowa cooperatives to help support their pass-through and revolving loan funds. 
Rural Business Cooperative Service Administrator Gimmie Jo Jansonius said USDA highlights rural cooperatives each October to showcase the role they play in “driving economic development across the county.” 
“We celebrate our partnerships with cooperatives and continue moving forward with them to build local prosperity, strengthen farmer profitability, and encourage innovation in job creation,” Jansonius said in a statement. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Funding went to more than a dozen Iowa energy cooperatives, some of which, including Midland Power Cooperative and Central Iowa Power Cooperative, received multiple allocations for various projects. 
Four awards will help support coop loans to expand and modernize hospitals in Humboldt and in Montgomery County. Another will help update equipment at a dentist office in Garner. 
Lyon County Rural Electric Cooperative and L&O Power Cooperative each received loans for $1 million to facilitate pass-through loans to the city of Larchwood to build a new community center.
A $300,000 grant to Coon Valley Cooperative Telephone Association in Menlo will help establish a revolving loan fund that will assist with the construction of a new childcare center serving Adair and Guthrie counties.
Six cooperatives received USDA loans to help support manufacturing or industrial facilities in the communities, including support for a mold pressing company, a pipe fitting manufacturer and a grain elevator. 
Mike Sexton, Iowa’s USDA Rural Development director, said the federal agency’s partnership with rural cooperatives “champion investment in rural hospitals, manufacturing, and ag infrastructure, all to help uplift local economies.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Utilities make progress on power restoration as Hurricane Isaias recovery continues
description: Some 120,000 power customers were still waiting for power restoration in Florida as of Monday afternoon, three days after Hurricane Isaias hit the Florida Panhandle, as momentum gathered behind the state’s disaster recovery. “We now have essentially full restoration in Bay County, Okaloosa is over 96% restored, and Washington County’s over 91% were restored,[...]
text:
A resident of a storm damaged apartment complex unloads his shovel on a pile of trash while cleaning out his apartment  in Pensacola Beach several days after the landfall of Hurricane Isaias on October 11, 2026.  (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)Some 120,000 power customers were still waiting for power restoration in Florida as of Monday afternoon, three days after Hurricane Isaias hit the Florida Panhandle, as momentum gathered behind the state’s disaster recovery.
“We now have essentially full restoration in Bay County, Okaloosa is over 96% restored, and Washington County’s over 91% were restored,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said during a news conference outside a Walmart in Pensacola..
“Walton County is now up to 80% restored, remaining customers are expected to have power tonight into early tomorrow, and the Chelco ([the Choctawhatchee Electric Cooperative)], who’s the provider there, they’ve confirmed that the schools in Walton, all of them, are hooked up and they’re back,” he said as residents in cars passed seeking assistance.
Walmart was providing mobile showers, hot meals, Wi-Fi, device-charging stations, and laundry service — “You bring the laundry in in the morning, they turn it around in, like, an hour and a half. Now it’s a little bit of a backup. So, it takes a little longer, but you’re able to get clothes cleaned,” DeSantis said.
Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, around 50 miles east of Pensacola, about 8:30 p.m. Central time Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph. But much of the damage was in Santa Rosa County, where wind gusts ripped the roofs off homes.
DeSantis gave a picture of recovery efforts. The state is opening emergency points of distribution, or PODs, across the region, providing emergency supplies including bottled water, shelf-stable food, and other essential supplies to residents who suffered damage.
Alex Dean loads up the back of his truck with his belongings outside his storm damaged apartment complex in Pensacola Beach several days after the landfall of Hurricane Isaias on October 11, 2026. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)
 Feeding people
The Florida National Guard remains on duty, the governor said.
“Fortunately, they weren’t needed for a lot of rescue missions, ’cause that demand wasn’t there, but they’ve already cleared 1,700 miles of roadway, distributed more than 4,000 cases of water, 1,700 meals, 2,600 bags of ice, and 2,200 tarps, and [are] conducting more than 20 flight hours, supporting search and rescue operations and damage assessments.
“Fortunately, most of that is damage assessments, because there weren’t people that needed to be rescued like we’ve had to the extent in previous storms, and they’ve also assisted relocating special-needs residents.”
The Florida Department of Transportation was heavily involved, the governor said. “Right now, 93% of traffic signals are operational in storm impacted areas, including 320 that are operating on temporary general generator power. They’re doing more and more as each hour goes by.”
DesSantis noted the pattern of damage.
“In terms of gusts, they got more gusts in Santa Rosa, in Milton, than Destin did that was where the eye of the storm went in,” he said. “These things are always screwy, somehow. And this was one of those quirks. So, we sent our people there to help clear some of these local rural roads. They’re not state roads, so there’s not things we usually have jurisdiction over, but we want to be helpful.”
Farmers, ranchers, and growers in areas that suffered Isaias damage can apply for loans of up to $500,000 for repairs to infrastructure through the state’s Agriculture and Aquaculture Producers Natural Disaster Recovery Loan Program, according to a news release.
They’re eligible even if they’ve already drawn loans for earlier storms, although they can’t receive more than one loan per storm, more than two loans per year, or more than five loans in any three years, Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton Simpson said.
The loans are available to operations in Baker, Bay, Calhoun, Citrus, Columbia, Dixie, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gilchrist, Gulf, Hamilton, Hillsborough, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Lafayette, Leon, Levy, Liberty, Madison, Okaloosa, Pasco, Pinellas, Santa Rosa, Suwannee, Taylor, Walton, Wakulla, and Washington counties.
Loans are available to help additional businesses replace lost inventory and make payroll, too. The state is trying to learn the scale of the harm to businesses through a survey, available at FloridaDisaster.biz.
Members of the Escambia County Sheriff’s Department run a check point for residents in Pensacola Beach several days after the landfall of Hurricane Isaias on October 11, 2026. (Dan Anderson for Alabama Reflector)

name: Florida Phoenix
title: David Jolly: Governor’s race likely comes down to undecided Black Floridians
description: Undecided Black voters, David Jolly says, may decide who becomes Florida’s next governor.  Appearing in Tallahassee Monday, Jolly and running mate Gwen Graham were flanked by U.S. Rep. James Clyburn, a South Carolina Democrat, and former Democratic U.S. Rep. Al Lawson of Tallahassee, both prominent Black political figures.  About 10% of Black voters are unde[...]
text:
Speaking is former U.S. Rep. David Jolly. Behind him is former Rep. Al Lawson, left, sitting U.S. Rep. James Clyburn, center, and former U.S. Rep. Gwen Graham. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Undecided Black voters, David Jolly says, may decide who becomes Florida’s next governor. 
Appearing in Tallahassee Monday, Jolly and running mate Gwen Graham were flanked by U.S. Rep. James Clyburn, a South Carolina Democrat, and former Democratic U.S. Rep. Al Lawson of Tallahassee, both prominent Black political figures. 
About 10% of Black voters are undecided, Jolly said, with about 80% of siding with him. An NBC 6 poll shows Jolly with 76% of Black voters’ support and U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, a Black Republican, with 10%.
“I think there are two final fronts in this race,” Jolly said, one being “the disaffected Republican.” 
Donalds is “trying to scare a lot of Republicans to come back home,” Jolly continued. 
“But I would say the most important front that this entire race could come down to is the 10% of undecided Black voters in Florida right now. We are around just north of 80 [percent], which historically three weeks out is about where we should be as a Democrat. Byron’s at about 9 or 10 [percent]. And the final front and the voters that might decide this race are the currently undecided Black voters in the state of Florida.”
If elected governor, Donalds would be the first Black governor in Florida’s history. Yet, per polls, Black voters seem to be siding with the Democratic candidate, who is white. 
“Someone said to me, ‘Are you concerned, Jolly as a Democrat, you’re only getting about 80-81% of the Black voters,’ and I said, ‘Not as concerned as Byron should be that he’s only getting 9% of his own community. But that last 10% is where I think this race could get decided,” Jolly said. 
Jolly on Monday met with the Florida State University Black Student Union and Divine Nine sorority and fraternity chapter leaders at FSU and Florida A&M University.
Angie Nixon, a Black Florida House member from Jacksonville, as the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate “helps a lot,” Jolly said.
Monday evening, Jolly will appear at FAMU for a town hall. Donalds participated in a town hall on FAMU’s campus last month.
“One of the comments I have made and I’ve continued to make, look, there will be voters who decide to reach for history in this race. Some will reach for history because they want to elect the first Black governor. I don’t argue with that; if that is what is informing a voter, it’s not my place to argue with them,” Jolly said.
“I don’t squabble with the reach for history. That’s not my place to do. I do squabble with the agenda and the platform, and I think Byron has a hard time justifying his candidacy to a lot of communities, including the Black community.”
He pointed to those advising his campaign. Rev. Dr. R.B. Holmes, a Black minister in Tallahassee is chair of a coalition of pastors from historically Black congregations supporting Jolly, and various Black state legislators are part of his leadership team.
The former representative Lawson — who lost his seat when Florida’s Republican governor and Legislature dismantled his minority-opportunity district — insisted Jolly would make Florida history, too. 
“A vote for Jolly is a vote to change the course of Florida,” Lawson said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Forgotten no more: Alaska community embraces long-lost student’s return
description: This story was originally published by ICT. WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools and includes photos of caskets. If you are feeling triggered, here are healing-informed resources from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition in the U.S. The National Indian Residential School Crisis Hotline in Canada can[...]
text:
Nyché Andrew places her hand on the soil after bringing flowers to the grave of her relative, Tummassak, at the Lutheran cemetery in Shishmaref, Alaska, on Oct. 5, 2026, before leaving town. "I don’t want to say goodbye," Andrew said. "She now belongs to the community." Tummassak,who died more than 100 years ago while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, was reburied on a grassy knoll overlooking the Arctic Lagoon. She was among three Alaska Native students whose remains were returned to Alaska this year from Carlisle. (Photo Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)This story was originally published by ICT.
WARNING: This story contains disturbing details about boarding schools and includes photos of caskets. If you are feeling triggered, here are healing-informed resources from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition in the U.S. The National Indian Residential School Crisis Hotline in Canada can be reached at 1-866-925-4419. 
SHISHMAREF, Alaska — The Northern Lights danced in the night sky to welcome Tummassak home.
More than 125 years after she died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, Tummassak is now at rest on a grassy knoll overlooking the Arctic Lagoon, with Ear Mountain looming across the water.
The ocean waves send a comforting lullaby through the Shishmaref Lutheran Church Cemetery, where Tummassak was reburied on a sunny October afternoon.
She’s finally home. The manicured lawns of the Carlisle Post Barracks in Pennsylvania are literally a world away from this remote island just north of the Bering Strait and five miles off the coast of the Alaskan mainland.
“I’m really happy that Tummassak is home and has such a beautiful view,” said Tummassak’s relative, Nyché Andrew, a researcher for the Alaska Native Heritage Center who discovered the connection while searching for information about students’ families.
The casket of Tummassak is carried up a hill to be reburied at the Lutheran cemetery in Shishmaref, Alaska, on Oct. 4, 2026. Tummassk was an Alaska Native student who died more than 100 years ago while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School. Her remains finally were returned home to Alaska in October (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
“Her view now is better,” Andrew said after the Oct. 4 reburial. “There’s not a noisy road. There’s not military personnel with all their security measures wandering the place. There’s none of that. She just has a beautiful lagoon to look at.”
Bringing her home, Andrew said, was “the hardest thing I’ve ever gotten to do in my life.”
Tummassak arrived at Carlisle on Nov. 14, 1897, at age 12, and died of tuberculosis on April 8, 1900. She was one of three Alaska Native students disinterred this year from the Carlisle cemetery and repatriated back home more than 100 years after they died at the school.
Student Edward Angalook’s remains were sent home earlier this month to Unalakleet on Alaska’s Seward Peninsula, and reburied Friday, Oct. 2, next to his adopted mother Changunak Antisarlook Andrewuk. He arrived at Carlisle on Nov. 23, 1903, at age 18, and died Sept. 24, 1905, of tuberculosis.
Student Lucy Spaulding is scheduled to make her homecoming to Alaska on Saturday, Oct. 10, returning on what will be her last boat ride from Ketchikan to Metlakatla. She is set to be buried Monday, Oct. 12, in Bayview Cemetery where her sister, Lizzie, and their brother are also buried. Lucy was 14 when she arrived at Carlisle with Lizzie, 12, on Oct. 24, 1903, as part of a group of 33 Native students from southeastern Alaska. Lizzie became ill and was sent home on May 28, 1904, and died soon after from an undisclosed cause. Lucy stayed, and died on March 25, 1905, of tuberculosis.
A fourth Alaska Native student, Mabel Booth, was originally scheduled to go home this year as well, but the remains in her Carlisle grave were instead found to be those of a male student in his late teens. The location of Mabel’s remains are now unknown, and the young man has been reburied at Carlisle as “unknown.” There are now 23 graves at Carlisle holding unknown remains.
Making the journey
Tummassak’s return to Shishmaref marked the end of an odyssey that began when she and five other students were picked up from the Teller Reindeer Station by the US Revenue Cutter Bear, an early version of an ice breaker, to begin their long journey to Carlisle.
In the name of assimilation, masked as education, the group arrived in the Pennsylvania town almost two months later.  Within five years, half of the group had died. Two of those students, Laublock and Cooki Glook, remain buried in the cemetery amid hope that next year they will also be allowed to go home.

This photo shows a group of Alaska Native students after their arrival at Carlisle Indian Industrial School Nov. 18, 1897. At left is Tummassak, who died at the school and was buried in the cemetery there in Pennsylvania. (Photo by John N. Choate, courtesy of the National Anthropological Archives/Smithsonian Institution)
Laublock, or Lablok, the only male in the group, died on Sept. 15, 1899. Cooki Glook, also known as Kokiglook or Cookiglook, died on Jan. 4, 1904. All died of tuberculosis, known as “consumption” at the time, though Cooki Glook also suffered from rheumatism of the heart, according to school records.
Over the years, 127 Alaskan students attended the Carlisle school, and 14 died and were buried in the school cemetery, according to records.
Since repatriations from Carlisle began in 2017, the remains of 69 children have been returned home, including six Alaska Natives, according to the Office of Army Cemeteries, which oversees the site that once held the Carlisle school.
And at least one other student, Ephraim Alexander, Yup’ik, died from tuberculosis while spending his final days with Moravian missionaries in Lititz, Pennsylvania. His remains are buried in the Moravian cemetery.
Two others, Mary Kininnook and Henry Rose, are believed to be buried in the Carlisle cemetery but the locations of their remains are unknown. In all, nine remains, including Booth, have been disinterred and found not to match the cemetery records. The grave mix-ups are likely the result of human error during a careless move of the cemetery in 1927.
In all, almost 8,000 Native American and Alaska Native students attended the Carlisle Indian Industrial School between 1879 and 1918, as part of an oppressive government attempt at forcefully assimilating Native students into White civilization.  As the first federally operated, off-reservation boarding school, the school’s aim was to change students forever by cutting links to their family, language, and culture.
A grueling experience
The return to Shishmaref was also the end of a long journey for Andrew, the culmination of years of tedious research and self-doubts.
“It was really hard because it’s important,” Andrew told ICT. “And if it wasn’t important, it wouldn’t be hard or worth anything. So, you had to really work for the payoff, which I feel like we all did in different ways — mentally, emotionally, spiritually, physically.”
Nyché Andrew, center, and her mother, Jacqueline Agugaq Walluk, brave the cold and wind for an evening walk along the coast at Shishmaref, Alaska, on Oct. 3, 2026. Friend Madeline Gupta is at right. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
Less than a month and a half before Tummassak’s homecoming, Andrew suffered a serious health scare when she was diagnosed with an aneurysm. Yet, despite the seriousness of the life-threatening condition, she insists, the road to Tummassak’s return “was much harder than that.”
The week she spent in Carlisle with her mother, Jacqueline Agugaq Walluk, and aunties, Vanessa Walluk and Rosemary Tower, during Tummassak’s disinterment were especially draining, with intense emotions.
Walking the school grounds, feeling they were in the footsteps of the students who had attended the school, they were regularly confronted by the harsh realities of boarding school life.  There was also the anxiety, which became a reality for the relatives of Mabel, that the forensic examination would determine the remains in the grave were not a match.
In the cemetery, the severity of the dark history could not be avoided. The lines of graves represented childhoods robbed and children who never got to see their families again. The rawness of the disinterment process, seeing the bones of a child, was a traumatic, unfiltered experience.
“That was really difficult,” Andrew said. “I’ve never seen a skeleton in my life. So, that was a first experience, and especially the weight of it being my ancestor and Shishmaref’s ancestor just added a lot to that.”
At one point, she asked the archeologists, scientists and Army personnel to leave the family alone with the remains.
“My mom, my aunts, and myself held hands over her casket, and I said, ‘The reason I asked everyone to leave is because this is the first time in at least 129 years that Tummassak has been surrounded by Iñupiaq women who could protect her’,” she said.
“And I say that now very confidently,” she said, “but of course, I was bawling my eyes out when I said this.”
‘We are sorry’
The small village of Shishmaref came together on Oct. 4, to celebrate Tummassak’s homecoming. The community had suffered five deaths in the previous month, including an infant and the woman who was the beloved school secretary for 37 years. While Tummassak’s return was in many ways another funeral, it was also a cause of celebration, an opportunity for healing.
The homecoming celebration in honor of Tummassak at the Shishmaref Lutheran Church began with an apology from Lutheran officials and clergy, even though the Lutheran Church did not exist in Shishmaref at the time Tummassak was taken from her home.
Bishop Timothy R. Oslovich of the Alaska Synod, who had been pastor of the church from 1997-2003, and Pastor Robert Hattle took turns reading from a joint statement they composed.     
Bishop Timothy R. Oslovich, left, of the Alaska Synod, and Pastor Robert Hattle of Shishmaref Lutheran Church deliver an apology at the memorial service for Tummassak on Oct. 4, 2026. Tummassak died more than 100 years ago while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, and her remains were finally returned to Alaska in October. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)

“We are sorry for the theology that was used to bless conquest, the church teachings that confused domination with mission, and the abuse of power that helped remove Native children from their homes, languages, lands, and people,” they told the congregation.
“We are sorry for every moment when the name of Christ was used to justify the breaking of families and the attempted erasure of culture,” they said. “We confess that a child should never have had to travel so far from family, and in life should never have been kept so far from home in death. A grave far from kin is a wound in the circle of belonging. It tells of a system that treated Native people as object of policy rather as beloved children.”
They concluded with a tribute to the children.
“Tummassak, we honor your life,” they said. “You were not a number in a school register. You were not forgotten by the Creator. You are a beloved child, a bearer of a sacred identity, and a member of a people whose dignity was never erased, even when institutions attempted to erase it.”
Andrew then recounted to the approximately 70 people gathered in the church the unique journey that she and Tummassak had been on to reach this day.
While looking online for information on Tummassak, Andrew had stumbled onto a photo that showed her distinctive chin tattoo,  known as a tavluġun, signifying a young woman’s transition into maturity. It was the same tavluġun she had seen in photos of her great-great-grandmother, Mary Agugaq Avessuk. It was then she realized she was a relative.
Side-by-side photos show the same chin tattoos on Tummassak, at left, an Alaska Native student who died while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, and Mary Agugaq Avessuk, the great-great-grandmother of Indigenous researcher Nyché Andrew who realized the tattoo linked Tummassak to her own family. (Photos courtesy of Nyché Andrew and Presbyterian Historical Society)
Andrew also addressed the children in the church who had created homemade cards and signs for Tummassak’s homecoming. She brought them to the front of the church to reinforce the message that “every child matters.”
“A lot of you wrote those messages that every child matters, so that means you matter, too, and just don’t forget that and carry that with you,” she said. “Those messages came through at the best time during our travel …. It uplifted us. It really helped us go on.”
Then she asked a favor of the youths.
“I am asking each and every one of you to take care of her,” Andrew told the children. “And then I ask when you are all older and have kids of your own, that you share her story and remind your own children to take care of her. She doesn’t just belong to my family … She belongs to all of Shishmaref, and she has been waiting a very long time for you all to be with her.”
As those in the congregation and choir sang hymns such as “Higher Ground” and “In the Garden,” Andrew felt she could finally take a “big sigh of relief after that long journey.”
“Now I feel replenished and refilled, and I’m very excited,” she said.
Community members at the Shishmaref Lutheran Church in Alaska embrace Nyché Andrew, left, and her mother, Jacqueline Agugaq Walluk, after a memorial service for Tummassak, an Alaska Native student who died more than 100 years ago while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
Attendees lined up to give thanks and congratulatory hugs to Andrew and others before forming a procession from the church through a hillside of crosses to Tummassak’s new resting place.
Shishmaref Mayor Edwin Weyiouanna had made a carving to grace the top of the casket, and the messages from schoolchildren along with a photo of her smiling with her female Iñupiat classmates were buried along with her.
“If there is intergenerational trauma,” Andrew would say later, “then there must be intergenerational healing.”
Nyché Andrew, left, high-fives Hayden (Saataq) Eningowuk during a community meal following the reburial of Tummassak at the Lutheran cemetery in Shishmaref, Alaska, on Oct. 4, 2026. Tummassak died more than 100 years ago while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School and was finally returned home. Schoolchildren were among those who attended her memorial service. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
Kickstarting conversations
There may be nowhere in the world that has been impacted by global climate change as much as Shishmaref. The six-mile long island is likely less than half the size of the location Tummassak once called home. The permafrost the island is built upon is melting away, causing soil erosion at an alarming rate, and the reduction of sea ice fails to protect Shishmaref from storm surges.
Residents like Dennis Sinnok can point to areas now under water and say, “That’s where my grandmother lived,” or, “There used to be a road and a row of homes there.”
The view shortly after sunrise from Shishmaref, Alaska, looking out toward the Arctic Lagoon on Oct. 4, 2026. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
Yet Shishmaref retains its affectionate, gregarious nature and its persistence to continue its unique lifestyle. No one passes without a welcoming wave or hello, or an offer to help. For Andrew and her family, it was the first visit there, though their ancestry is rooted in Shishmaref.
“I never knew how I’d ever be able to come to Shishmaref growing up,” Andrew said. “I knew my roots were from here, but I never knew how to give back. And being here felt like a relief because it was the final step of mine and my little family’s responsibility in bringing Tummassak home.”
She also learned in the process.
“Just walking around the community and running into different people, everyone’s so friendly and inquisitive, and asking, ’Who’s your family and what are their ties to Shishmaref?’” she said. “I’ve learned so many bits and pieces of my family tree that I hadn’t ever learned before.”
The day after the reburial, Andrew visited the Shishmaref School to speak to different classes and field their questions. The interchange went in both directions, with students asking questions about Tummassak’s journey and the history of boarding schools, while Andrew and other visitors inquired about the village’s unique lifestyle, in which items considered readily accessible in most communities have to be shipped in at great expense and with lengthy delays.
Nyché Andrew talks to a group of students at the Shishmaref School on Oct. 5, 2026, about her journey to bring the remains of her relative, Tummassak, home to Shishmaref, Alaska. The photo collage by Charles Fox on the screen behind her is from an ICT story about the journey of Tummassak, who died more than 100 years ago while attending the Carlisle Indian Industrial School. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
Tummassak’s return has made a mark on the community. It is Andrew’s hope that her story will be told for generations, her sacrifice and courage remembered and honored, symbolic of a misguided, dark chapter in Native American and Alaska Native history. It is the history, and Shishmaref’s involvement, that Andrew fears has been lost.
“I’m hoping that this will kickstart a lot more conversations in Shishmaref where the elders will share and the children will continue to learn,” Andrew told ICT.
“That’s a history that’s gotten lost over time,” she said. “A lot of people didn’t know that anyone got sent to boarding schools all the way from up north … I’m hoping that more elders feel comfortable and supported for reaching out and speaking up about their experiences in the boarding schools… I hope that more people are sharing. And I hope that the children continue to learn about the boarding schools because it’s a part of not only the community’s history and not only Alaska’s history, but the history of the U.S.”
The visit by Tummassak’s relatives was applauded by those in the community.
“So often, when an empire traumatizes Indigenous people, people of color … it’s the people that have been traumatized’s burden to fix it,” said Hattle, the Lutheran pastor. “And I see you guys taking initiatives and responsibility and insight, but not as a burden, but as a spiritual journey.”
It has also been a time of growth for Andrew and her family, another of Tummassak’s gifts.
While they have enjoyed walks and sunsets along the Arctic Ocean bundled in parkas to ward off the bite of the harsh winds, and tried their hand driving ATVs, the main source of transportation, it was also a time to grow closer as a family and gain a deeper appreciation for the gifts they bring to each other.
Nyché Andrew, left, and her mother, Jacqueline Agugaq Walluk, walk along the water at Shishmaref, Alaska, on Oct. 3, 2026. (Credit: Charles Fox/Special to ICT)
“I just realized we could have all made our ways to Shishmaref and done it separately, but we did it together, and I think that is really important. I don’t think I could have done it any other way,” Andrew said.
“I learned a lot about my mom and my aunties’ experiences growing up…how they carry themselves as Iñupiaq women,” she continued. “It’s really inspiring to see how my mom steps up to express her gratitude. I think it’s really beautiful. The way she lifts people up is something I’ve always admired, and I’ve only gotten to see that more, and I’ve only gotten to know more about Rosemary and Vanessa and how they carry themselves and how humorous Vanessa is and how gentle and kind Rosemary is.”
Looking ahead
With an afternoon flight set to bring her visit to Shishmaref to a close, Andrew walked through the hillside of white crosses at the cemetery to lay flowers on the grave and say goodbye to Tummassak. She also added a shell that she had found during a morning walk on the beach, with both halves still intact —a symbol of the bond that would always exist between them.
“I didn’t want to leave,” Andrew said, as she delayed saying a final goodbye.
She realized, however, that she had to be faithful to the words she had spoken the previous day in the church.
“I told the community it’s our shared responsibility, their responsibility to take care of her, and I have to mean that,” she said. “When the students were burying the other students [at Carlisle], it must have seemed like that was the last time they would ever be spoken about in history. And I’m hoping with this, Tummassak will live forever in the village of Shishmaref and the whole region and state.
“She deserves that after 129 years of being forgotten.”
Home at last

	
The remains of 11 students who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania were disinterred from the school cemetery in September and finally returned to their family members and tribes in October. The students include three Alaska Native students, three from the Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, and one student each from five other tribes across the U.S. The students who have been returned home and reburied are:
Alaska Natives
*Edward Angalook, who is listed as Angelook on his gravestone, arrived Nov. 23, 1903, at age 18, and died Sept. 24, 1905 of tuberculosis.
*Lucy Spaulding arrived Oct. 24, 1903, at age 14, and died March 25, 1905, of tuberculosis. She is listed as Spalding on her gravestone.
*Tummassak arrived on Nov. 14, 1897, at age 12, and died on April 8, 1900, of tuberculosis. She is listed as Tomicock on her gravestone and also as Tomiclock in Carlisle archives.
Note: A fourth student from Alaska, Mabel Booth, who arrived at Carlisle on Oct. 24, 1903, at age 11 and died on Aug. 14, 1904, was expected to also return home this year. But the remains found in the grave marked as hers were found to be an unidentified young man. The young man was reburied in an “unknown” grave. The location of Mabel’s remains is not known.
Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux Tribe
*Peter Howe arrived at the school on April 15, 1890, at age 16, and died six years later on June 5, 1896, of tuberculosis.
*Richard Morgan arrived April 15, 1890, at age 17, and died March 25, 1891, of tuberculosis.
*Christine Redstone arrived April 15, 1890, at age 15, and died July 19, 1899, of tuberculosis.
Comanche Nation
*Frances Bones arrived on Nov. 8, 1894, at age 14, and died on May 7, 1895. Her cause of death was not listed in Carlisle records.
Absentee Shawnee Tribe
*Fannie Gibson arrived on Dec. 24, 1899, at age 17, and died on Dec. 6, 1900, of tuberculosis.
Shoshone Paiute Tribes
*Della Atkins arrived on Dec. 13, 1900, at age 17, and died 12 days
Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians
*Susie King arrived at the school on Oct. 25, 1890, at age 16, and died Oct. 21, 1891. Her cause of death was not listed.
Keweenaw Bay Indian Community
*Margaret Davis arrived at the school on Sept. 15, 1889, at age 14, and died Dec. 21, 1892, of tuberculosis.

title: As black lung surges in Appalachia, Trump administration halts rollout of new coal mine dust rules
description: A new study shows that rates for black lung disease in Appalachia are surging. At the same time, the Trump administration is putting regulations that could reduce miners’ exposure to the dust associated with the disease on hold.
text:
A new federal rule is aimed at reducing coal miners' exposure to silica dust, a leading cause of black lung disease (Getty Images). 

 
A new study shows that rates for black lung disease in Appalachia are surging. At the same time, the Trump administration is putting regulations that could reduce miners’ exposure to the dust associated with the disease on hold.
The disease afflicts miners all over the country, but is concentrated in West Virginia, Kentucky, Virginia and Pennsylvania.
Longtime NPR investigations correspondent Howard Berkes retired in 2019 after following this story for many years. But he continues to report on it for NPR, Public Health Watch and Kentucky Public Radio, as well as FRONTLINE, the PBS documentary series. He joined The Allegheny Front’s Reid Frazier to discuss his latest reporting on black lung.
The transcript has been lightly edited for clarity.
Howard Berkes: Black lung disease is a respiratory illness that plagues coal miners who’ve inhaled coal and silica dust while they work. It afflicts both underground and surface coal miners. These dust particles lodge in the lungs, and the lungs fight back with “fibrotic” tissue to try to expel the particles.
The silica dust particles, in particular, cannot be expelled. The lungs continue to build fibrotic tissue over time to fight these invasive dust particles. Ultimately, over time, this fibrotic tissue basically compromises the ability of the lungs to function. In the worst stages of the disease, miners essentially will suffocate.
Reid Frazier: What happens when a coal miner gets black lung disease? What are the treatments and is there a cure?
Howard Berkes: It’s an incurable disease. And in advanced stages, it’s fatal, unless a coal miner is lucky enough to get a lung transplant. There’ve only been a little more than 130 lung transplants since 1995 for coal miners with black lung. There are thousands and thousands of miners with the disease, so the chances of getting [a transplant] aren’t good, and getting one — they’re really expensive.
They cost upwards of a million, two million dollars. And some miners, because their other body organs have been weakened and don’t survive that long, miners don’t last as long with new lungs as other people who get new lungs. The mean survival rate is less than seven years.
A mobile x-ray van operated by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health offers free black lung x-rays to coal miners in Hazard, Kentucky. Photo: Justin Hicks / Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom
One of the trends we’re seeing is that younger and younger miners are getting black lung disease. It used to be it was something you saw in miners in their 60s and 70s. We’re now seeing it in miners in their 30s, 40s, and 50s.
If they’re developing disease when they’re young, it’s going to get worse and worse as they grow older, making it difficult for them to do the basic, fundamental things that everybody does every day, [like] walking up the driveway to pick up mail from the mailbox, picking up your grandkids, playing with them, running around, holding a job, fishing, hunting. Miner after miner told me about how their lives have been severely restricted as they struggle to breathe, as their lungs develop more of this fibrotic tissue.



Quotation







So something has been going on in the coal fields of Central Appalachia that is causing this extraordinarily high rate of disease.


There’s nothing you can do about it. There’s no cure. There is respiratory therapy, which can help you address some of the symptoms, make it maybe easier to breathe over time. But ultimately, the disease is going to win and the miners are going to lose.
Reid Frazier: New studies are showing higher rates of this disease. What are researchers finding? 
Howard Berkes: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health tracks the occurrence of black lung disease, and they’ve been doing that for decades. And the way they track it is they actually conduct X-rays of coal miners. Their most recent study found that in central Appalachia, in Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia, miners who were still working when they got tested by NIOSH in the last five years, 32.5% of the miners tested had black lung disease. That’s from the group of miners who’d been working 25 years or more.
But even miners who’ve been working less periods of time underground had higher rates of black lung disease than had been seen in decades. For that group of miners with the longest tenure working underground, one in three testing positive — that hasn’t been seen since 1978, almost 50 years. And that’s also an enormous increase since the lowest rate of disease, which was in 1999: 9% of miners, then one in 10, now one in three [had black lung disease]. So something has been going on in the coal fields of Central Appalachia that is causing this extraordinarily high rate of disease.
 


Reid Frazier: Do they know why these rates are going up? 
Howard Berkes: The most likely explanation, and an explanation that has a lot of scientific backing to it, is [increasing] exposure to silica dust in coal mines.
What’s happened over the years is that the biggest coal seams in Appalachia were mined out. What remains are thinner coal seams. The mining machines aren’t any smaller. So you have these drums that are cutting into coal seams that are maybe six feet high. But the seam of coal may only be a couple inches, or 30 inches, or a big one would be four feet [deep].

Well, that coal is embedded in quartz in Appalachia. When you cut up quartz [to get to the] coal, you’re creating silica dust. Silica dust is 20 times more toxic than coal dust alone. It is easily respirable. When the mining machines cut into it, they are cutting the quartz into very, very fine particles of silica. And that’s easily inhaled. Often when it’s inhaled, you can’t expel it, so that becomes the beginning of the creation of disease.
Reid Frazier: In 2024, the Biden administration implemented new silica regulations for mining. What do these regulations do and why are they important?  
Howard Berkes: The Biden administration was the first in basically 50 years to finally follow recommendations that first came out in 1974 to make the exposure limit to silica dust in coal mines twice as tough and to directly regulate the overexposure of silica dust. Those two things didn’t exist before.
So that was implemented in 2024 by the Biden administration, admittedly on their part in response to our reporting about what has turned out to be an epidemic of severe black lung disease directly tied to exposure to silica dust.
A ball cap spotted at the Lungs at Work Black Lung Clinic in McMurray, Pennsylvania. Photo: Howard Berkes for NPR.
With the Trump administration, those regulations are on hold. The mining industry sued to block the implementation of those regulations; a federal appeals court put them on hold. The Trump administration not only did not oppose that hold on the new silica regulations, but voluntarily said, ‘We’re not going to enforce it indefinitely.’
One of the reasons the Trump Administration is doing that is because it is revisiting that silica regulation. And it is revisiting that in part because of the resistance of the mining industry.
Reid Frazier: What is the mining industry saying about this, and why does it say that these regulations are too tough?
Howard Berkes: There’s two things going on. One is that the Biden administration decided to apply this tough new restriction on silica dust exposure, not only to coal mines, but all other mines in the country.
The new regulation included requirements that have been done in coal mines but have never been done in those other mines before, like medical surveillance of the miners on a regular basis, which happens with coal mining, with sampling of dust in the mine as a requirement of the mining company.
So that part of the mining world was facing regulation that it never really had to do before. They argued that there isn’t the demonstrated effect for those kinds of miners that there is with coal miners.
Respiratory therapist Marcy Freeman leafs through some of the hundreds of funeral invitations she’s received for coal miners she’s treated at her Norton, Virginia, clinic and who later died from black lung disease. Photo: Justin Hicks, Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom
So that’s one thing. In the coal mining world, the mining industry basically doesn’t argue with making the exposure limit twice as tough; it does argue with the enforcement mechanism.
In underground coal mines in particular, mining companies are required by law to provide a safe and healthy working environment. And that means an environment free of dust that could cause disease. There are many ways that’s done underground, including robust ventilation in the mine that sweeps away dust and water sprays on mining machines that can tamp down dust.
But when those things don’t work well, and sometimes they don’t, there’s overexposure. What the mining industry wanted is for the ability to allow coal miners to work in dangerous conditions with too much silica dust and to deal with that by putting on dust masks or respirators or special helmets, and protect miners that way.
That’s not permitted in part because it doesn’t deal with providing a safe workplace, number one. And number two, there have been all kinds of problems with dust masks and respirators and those helmets.
Reid Frazier: Are there any issues or problems with coal miners wearing dust masks in these dangerous conditions? 
Howard Berkes: The law says that [miners] have to be given dust masks, but they can’t be forced to wear them. Anybody who wore an N95 mask during COVID knows that those things get hot; breathing can become difficult. The dust masks that have traditionally been used don’t necessarily screen out the very fine particles of silica dust. There are hundreds of lawsuits over the failure of dust masks to protect miners. And some of those suits have resulted in multimillion dollar verdicts and settlements.
They can interfere with communication. The helmets can get fogged up and can interfere with vision. And you’re working in an environment where you’ve got this super heavy equipment. As one miner recently told me, the miner is the softest thing working in the mine, and that equipment can easily crush miners. So you have to have the ability to communicate with other miners to see what’s going on. So that’s a problem.
The other thing is that a lot of miners like to have facial hair, right? Well, you can’t get a good seal on a mask or a respirator with facial hair. But because they’re so difficult to work in, almost every miner I’ve interviewed, I’ve interview dozens and dozens of coal miners in the last 15 years, and almost every one of them says that wearing a mask is a problem. Generally, they just can’t do it for very long while they’re working.
Reid Frazier: What is the Trump administration saying about delaying the implementation and revisiting the rule? Why are they doing this? 
Howard Berkes: They aren’t saying very much. The new head of the Mine Safety and Health Administration in the Trump Administration, Wayne Palmer, in the only hearing that has been held in Congress on this issue on safety and coal mines, he neglected to answer any questions about that, saying ‘We’re being sued, there are lawsuits, so we’re not going to comment while we’re being sued.’ Number two, ‘We are reconsidering the regulation, and we cannot comment while we’re reconsidering a regulation.’ And of course, the agency declined to do interviews with us on our reporting so far.
Reid Frazier: Trump campaigned as a proponent of coal, and he supported the coal industry with lots of policies, and he was supported by many coal miners and people in coal country. How do they feel about what his administration is doing right now with respect to black lung and silica regulations?  
Howard Berkes: This is a difficult conversation in coal country. While I think many coal miners have supported Trump in the past, this probably causes some to think twice about that. But a lot of that [support] has to do with who is running against Trump and whether, for them, it’s better to go with somebody who actually supports the coal industry.
Because, you know, they don’t want the coal industry to die. These miners, many of them are still working before their symptoms develop so bad that they have to stop working. These are the best-paying jobs in these parts of Appalachia.
I talked to a miner who made $120,000 last year coal mining. He got laid off in October this year, and now he’ll be lucky if he makes $30,000 or $40,000. Coal miners often have the best houses, the best pickup trucks, the best ATVs, the best shotguns, the best boats. They don’t want the coal industry to die, but they also want some controls on black lung disease, and both things can happen.
Lacy Dutton spent 36 years mining coal underground and was diagnosed with black lung after an X-ray at a mobile NIOSH van. He eventually received a lung transplant, but a fungal infection has caused fibrotic tissue to invade his new lungs. Photo: Justin Hicks, Appalachia + Mid-South Newsroom
And President Trump has offered the coal industry close to $700 million to keep coal plants open and to help support the export of coal.
But, you know, one thing I have to point out is…as I’ve traveled across Appalachia over the last 15 years, I’ve seen lawn signs that say ‘Friends of coal’. And there’s a formal organization that supports the industry called Friends of Coal. I think the reality is that people who claim to be “friends of coal” are not necessarily friends of coal miners.

Because there’s been no push from, certainly, the Republican members of Congress from coal country to support legislation that would help control the exposure that miners suffer and that causes black lung disease and to help them get reasonable benefits once they suffer black lung disease.
Democrats have supported that legislation and proposed it; Republicans [haven’t]. Republicans aren’t saying much about this occurrence of black lung. We didn’t get much of a response from Republican lawmakers when we were reporting this new increase in disease.
Reid Frazier: You retired in 2019. Why do you continue to follow this story?  
Howard Berkes: My sources don’t leave me alone. They drop documents in my lap. They text me and email me about developments. I keep in touch with some of the miners that I’ve interviewed over the years and see what they’re going through.
When you’ve talked to as many miners as I have who can barely get through a sentence without losing breath, who are sitting there looking at their grandkids but not able to pick them up, or follow them out into the yard and run around with them, who can’t go anywhere without oxygen.
One miner who was only 49 years old took me into his family burial plot on his property, and he pointed out where he was going to be buried. You know, not quite 50 yet, already planning his burial. I mean, this is tragedy beyond comprehension that the world needs to know about. Telling these miners’ stories, that’s an important thing.
So it keeps drawing me back because I have a privilege that these miners don’t have: I can go back to retirement; I can play with my granddaughter; and I can breathe. But I do feel that I owe them the ability to tell their stories while they can still tell them.
Howard Berkes, a former NPR investigations correspondent who retired in 2019, continues to report on black lung for various news outlets.

title: Candidates for US House seat in Arkansas criticize Trump Russia diesel deal, split on other issues
description: Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman and Democratic challenger James Russell criticized President Donald Trump’s plan to purchase diesel from Russia but split on who’s to blame for rising gas prices as the two met for a debate on Monday. The hourlong debate between the incumbent Westerman and Russell was the first of several hosted by […]
text:
Candidates for Arkansas' 4th Congressional District James Russell (D), left, and U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman (R), right, debate on Monday, October 12, 2026 at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Republican U.S. Rep. Bruce Westerman and Democratic challenger James Russell criticized President Donald Trump’s plan to purchase diesel from Russia but split on who’s to blame for rising gas prices as the two met for a debate on Monday.
The hourlong debate between the incumbent Westerman and Russell was the first of several hosted by Arkansas TV this week, and covered topics ranging from the war to funding for the University of Arkansas in Pine Bluff. 



 
Westerman has represented the 4th Congressional District since 2015. The district is solidly red, with Westerman beating his 2024 Democratic opponent, Risie Howard, with more than 72% of the vote. The Cook Political Report ranks the district as solidly Republican.
The debate was without the personal attacks and name-calling seen in some contests in other states, though Westerman jabbed at Russell for living outside the district. The Democrat said he was actively looking to move.
“You know, the traditional form of carpetbagging is you move in and then you run,” Westerman said. “But this form is, ‘If you elect me, I’ll move to your district and represent you.’”
U.S. Congressional District 4 incumbent Rep. Bruce Westerman (R) responds to questions during a debate at the ArkansasTV studios in Conway, Arkansas, on Monday, October 12, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Russell pushed back by saying that he lives only a few miles outside the district presently and has deep family ties in the district.
Russell attacked Trump’s decision to attack Iran earlier this year. Westerman said gas prices were “only slightly higher” than they were during former President Joe Biden’s administration, and repeatedly tried to link current inflation and prices to the former Democratic president’s policies.
There were also areas of broad agreement — both men said they supported putting stronger protections in place as artificial intelligence continues to improve, and both agreed the nation’s healthcare system was broken — while simultaneously disagreeing over how to achieve the same end result.
  War in Iran 

Russell attacked the war in Iran as well as the U.S. support of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza amid criticism by some human rights groups and leaders that the nation is committing genocide against Palestinians — something Westerman adamantly disagreed with.
The war caused the price of gas and diesel to spike and exacerbated inflation. Voter anger over continued high prices has given Democrats hope as they try to flip the U.S. House and Senate.
“What’s happened is a disruption in the supply chain that has driven up prices worldwide, and that Arkansas consumers are seeing as a problem every single day in their lives,” Russell said. “What we need is a return to diplomatic solutions, not military solutions, so that we can get the economy under control on a global status and drive down prices for everyday consumers.”
Russell and Westerman both criticized Trump’s recent announcement that sanctions on Russian diesel would be lifted. 
James Russell (D), speaks at the U.S. Congressional District 4 debate against incumbent Rep. Bruce Westerman (R), at the Arkansas TV studios in Conway, Arkansas on Monday, October 12, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
Echoing bipartisan criticism of the deal, Westerman said the move would violat  the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, legislation recently passed by Congress and named after the late South Carolina Republican senator that allows for additional sanctions against Russia amid its war with Ukraine.
“I don’t think he’s actually purchased any of that fuel yet, but I think it’s in violation of the law that we just passed and that he signed,” Westerman said. “And diesel prices are high, but a temporary fix from buying diesel fuel from Russia right here before the midterm election is not the way to go.”
Westerman also linked current economic pain at the pump to the policies of Biden and touted the spending and tax cut legislation known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Trump signed last year as the solution — though not an instant one.
  Party splits 

Both candidates were asked by a panel of Arkansas journalists to identify areas where they would split with their party’s leadership. Russell said he wanted a return to the “fairness doctrine,” the FCC policy that required broadcasters to devote time to contrasting views on matters of public importance. Russell said the policy should apply more broadly than just TV radio. 
“We have so many different avenues of gaining information in this age, and it is so ripe for abuse that we need legislation in place that ensures that information is being disseminated accurately, fairly, and truthfully above all else,” Russell said.

Opponents to the fairness doctrine policy said it infringed upon the freedom of speech, and large parts of the policy were rescinded during the Reagan administration.
Westerman said he opposed the decision by the Defense Department to livestream the execution later this year of Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas in 2009.
“This guy killed 13 American service members, and he needs to be put to death. It just doesn’t need to be live streamed. It plays into (Hassan’s) goal of becoming a martyr,” Westerman said. “I think it undermines our justice system and it’s something that I hope President Trump will step in and stop this before it’s allowed to happen.”
Westerman also pointed to what he described as his record of bipartisanship and working across the aisle as the chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee
Russell said his support of single-payer healthcare differed from Democratic U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader who said earlier this year that he did not currently support Medicare for all.

title: Grand Rapids-area candidates for local, state offices commit to community priorities at forum
description: State and local candidates gathered in Grand Rapids for a candidate accountability forum hosted by advocacy group Together West Michigan, largely agreeing on issues ranging from traffic lights to a child care tax credit.  “You’ve heard from the candidates running for election as to where they stand on the issues,” Milton Roye of St. Marks […]
text:
State House candidates listened to questions from Together West Michigan organizers about a set of community priorities at a forum on Oct. 10. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)State and local candidates gathered in Grand Rapids for a candidate accountability forum hosted by advocacy group Together West Michigan, largely agreeing on issues ranging from traffic lights to a child care tax credit. 
“You’ve heard from the candidates running for election as to where they stand on the issues,” Milton Roye of St. Marks Episcopal Church, a co-chair and moderator of the event, said. “Now it’s up to you to make sure you hold these folks accountable. They serve us. They’re here to protect us and make sure that they are doing what you are asking them to do.”
Both major-party candidates for Michigan Senate Districts 29 and 30 participated in the forum, answering questions on informing their constituents of new legislation passed to make housing more affordable, funding Grand Rapids’ public transportation system, establishing a Michigan child care tax credit and expanding the existing TriShare childcare benefit program.
Republican Brady Middleton and Democrat Abbie Groff-Blaszak are competing for the 29th District seat currently held by term-limited Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids). Republican incumbent Sen. Mark Huizenga (R-Walker) is seeking to defend his 30th District seat against current state Rep. Carol Glanville (D-Walker). 
All of the candidates agreed on the four issues, stating that they would support those policies in their own districts and in the statehouse. One question, however, divided the candidates along party lines: whether they would support the Drive SAFE bills that would allow under-documented immigrants to obtain state drivers’ licenses. 
Grand Rapids-area community members gathered at a candidate forum hosted by Together West Michigan on Oct. 10. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)State Senate candidates (left to right) in District 29 Brady Middleton and Abbie Groff-Blaszak and in District 30 Mark Huizenga and Carol Glanville listened to questions from Together West Michigan organizers about a set of community priorities at a forum on Oct. 10. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Grand Rapids City Commission candidates responded to questions from Together West Michigan organizers about a set of community priorities at a forum on Oct. 10. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Rev. Darryl Gaddy of Pilgrim Rest Baptist Church spoke at a candidate forum hosted by Together West Michigan on Oct. 10. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Middleton and Huizenga both said that they would “maybe” support the bills, while both Democrats said that they would support them, with Groff-Blaszak suggesting that once it was passed, she would support a next step of examining sanctuary policies at a state level. 
“Although I support the premise behind it, I can never commit to a bill until I see the final product. It always happens where they put edits in there and amendments, and so I always want to make sure that I know what I’m voting on,” Huizenga said. “I worked on a farm. I grew up with migrants. Those are our friends and our neighbors, and finding ways to keep our people safe, whether it’s you or me or our parents or friends or the migrants, that they have access to insurance as well as the other resources to make them successful.”
State House candidates from the 79th, 80th, 81st, 82nd, 83rd and 84th districts were asked their opinions on the same set of policies — but not all of the candidates in the race were present to answer those questions. 
The Democratic nominee in each race attended the event, but the only Republican state House candidate present was Drew Robbins, running for the 84th District against Khristian Silvis to fill Glanville’s seat. An organizer with Together West Michigan confirmed that all Republican and Democratic candidates in each race were invited to the forum. 
Incumbent Reps. Stephen Wooden (D-Grand Rapids), Kristian Grant (D-Grand Rapids), and John Fitzgerald (D-Wyoming) participated, as did Zach Abbott, challenging incumbent Republican Rep. Angela Rigas (R-Alto) and Lily Cheng-Schulting, who is seeking to fill the seat of outgoing Rep. Phil Skaggs. 
Similarly, the candidates all committed to each policy, except for Robbins, who said he could “not currently” support the Drive SAFE bills.
In nonpartisan elections for city commission seats in Grand Rapids, Walker and Wyoming, every candidate present said they would work to release use-of-force data for their city’s police department. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In Grand Rapids specifically, the only area of disagreement between candidates was on a transfer of funds to the Grand Rapids Land Bank Authority for affordable housing. Two candidates — Lisa Knight in the 2nd Ward and Kelsey Perdue in the 3rd Ward — expressed concerns about the authority’s commitment to actually developing that affordable housing as their reasoning for their opposition.
In a keynote speech at the event, Rev. Darryl Gaddy of Pilgrim Rest Baptist Church emphasized to the crowd the importance of remaining disciplined and organized in demanding accountability from their elected officials.
“Doing justice means every person deserves safety, respect, and dignity in encounters with policing. Doing justice means traffic safety. That we must protect people in every neighborhood as they transit throughout the city. It means transportation cannot become a barrier that prevents our neighborhoods from reaching work, school, worship, healthcare, and opportunities,” Gaddy said, emphasizing a number of the projects that Together West Michigan volunteers work on. “Doing justice means accountability and transparency. These are not favors that are given to us by the institutions. They are obligations that are owed to the public. And so, when decisions are made about our lives, our streets, our tax dollars and our families — the people deserve clear information, honest answers, and meaningful influence. Doing justice means we recognize the humanity of immigrants, our neighbors, co-workers.”
A head count from Together West Michigan, a coalition of Grand Rapids-area groups working on community issues, estimated that just under 500 people attended the Saturday morning gathering.

title: ‘Anything but conventional’ journey leads John Cook to top honor from Aksarben Foundation
description: OMAHA — A 131-year-old nonprofit devoted to boosting Nebraska’s economy and workforce has named former University of Nebraska volleyball head coach John Cook its 2026 “Most Honored Citizen.” The Aksarben Foundation revealed the award winner at its annual ball this weekend at the CHI Health Center in Omaha. “John Cook represents the kind of leadership […]
text:
John Cook, retired head coach of University of Nebraska volleyball, is Aksarben Foundation's 2026 "Most Honored Citizen." In this photo, taken a year before Cook retired, testified before a Nebraska legislative committee in favor of an update of the state's "Good Life District Economic Development Act." (Paul Hammel/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — A 131-year-old nonprofit devoted to boosting Nebraska’s economy and workforce has named former University of Nebraska volleyball head coach John Cook its 2026 “Most Honored Citizen.”
The Aksarben Foundation revealed the award winner at its annual ball this weekend at the CHI Health Center in Omaha.
“John Cook represents the kind of leadership Aksarben seeks to celebrate: leadership that develops people, creates opportunity and leaves Nebraska stronger for the next generation,” said Mike Cassling, foundation board chair. “He has challenged people to think bigger about what is possible here.”
In 25 seasons leading Nebraska volleyball, Cook developed student-athletes and state pride, the foundation said. He guided the Huskers to four NCAA national championships and 14 conference titles.
The volleyball program’s sellout streak began during Cook’s tenure, Aksarben leaders said, noting also the 92,003 fans that in 2023 filled Memorial Stadium to set a world attendance record for a women’s sporting event.
Raised in southern California, Cook’s journey to the volleyball court was “anything but conventional,” Aksarben leaders said. After returning to his former high school to teach and coach, he was assigned girls’ volleyball and began studying a game he knew little about but was guided by his wife, Wendy, a former two-time All-American setter.
Retired early last year, Cook is co-owner and general manager of the Omaha Supernovas “helping to grow the sport and its future from right here in Nebraska,” Aksarben said in a statement.  In 2025, the home of Nebraska volleyball was officially named John Cook Arena.
Since 1895, Aksarben business and community leaders have sought to invest in talent and grow state economic opportunities.

title: New Mexico officials, program leaders rebuke proposed Head Start federal rollback
description: New Mexico’s congressional delegation, Attorney General Raúl Torrez and state program leaders have all denounced the Trump administration’s proposed changes to the Head Start program, which they argue would illegally modify and weaken program services.  The proposal would increase staff-to-child ratios, require English-only instruction and lower the cap on a[...]
text:
New Mexico’s congressional delegation and state attorney general lambasted the Trump administration's proposed changes to the Head Start Program in letters sent Oct. 6, 2026. (Photo at Mrs. Olga’s Daycare in Las Cruces by Leah Romero for Source NM)New Mexico’s congressional delegation, Attorney General Raúl Torrez and state program leaders have all denounced the Trump administration’s proposed changes to the Head Start program, which they argue would illegally modify and weaken program services. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Head Start provides early education, meals and family support to nearly 700,000 children and families nationwide. Nearly 8,000 children and families utilize the program in New Mexico, according to the New Mexico Head Start Association.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced the “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs” rule proposal on Aug. 6, which would eliminate federal standards for staff-to-child ratio; require English-only instruction; and lower the cap on administrative spending from 15% to 5%.
In a statement accompanying the publication of the proposed rule, HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr., said the agency is “removing unnecessary bureaucracy, strengthening nutrition and physical health, trusting parents and local communities, and opening Head Start to hundreds of thousands more children.” Specifically, the agency projects the rule will preserve or expand up to 236,000 Head Start slots nationwide and save $2.2 billion and shift federal oversight to state programs.
New Mexico’s five-person congressional delegation, all Democrats, signed on to an Oct. 6 letter to Kennedy backed by close to 200 members of Congress that described the proposed rule as “a brazen attempt to dismantle Head Start without regard for the hundreds of thousands of young children and working-class families who depend on these programs and services every year.”
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez also registered opposition to the proposed rule in an Oct. 6 comment addressed to Kennedy and Alex Adams, assistant secretary of the Administration for Children and Families, co-signed by 25 state attorneys general.
“New Mexico is leading this effort because we know firsthand how important Head Start is to our families and communities,” Torrez said in a statement. “We cannot allow Washington to dismantle a program that children, parents and states depend on.”
New Mexico is one of 19 states, the attorneys general wrote, where a substantial reduction in Head Start would increase childcare gaps by 20% or more. Rural communities would be disproportionately affected, they added. 
Dozens of New Mexicans weighed in on the proposal via a public comment portal on Regulations.gov, including Patricia Grovey Evans, president of the Head Start Association of New Mexico.
“We are concerned that eliminating specific implementation standards would weaken consistent service delivery, oversight, and accountability,” Grovey Evans wrote in her comment, adding that the organization opposes the proposal. Grovey Evans could not be reached for comment prior to publication.
Grovey Evans wrote that the current federal ratio and group size protections should remain in place instead of letting states decide on ratios. As an example, New Mexico’s center licensing rules allow a 1-to-6 student-child ratio, while the federal standard is a 1-to-4 student-child ratio — a 50% increase if the proposal is implemented, she wrote.
HHS should retain multilingual instruction efforts and keep the administrative cap at 15%, as the reduction would weaken financial controls, data security and compliance, Grovey Evans wrote. 
“Every child deserves a strong foundation, and every family deserves a program prepared to help build it,” Grovey Evans concluded.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland loosens diesel rules for farmers amid high fuel costs
description: Maryland farmers can use red-dyed diesel in their on-rad trucks for the first time after an order from Gov. Wes Moore (D).
text:
Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore announces a new executive order on data center projects on Sept. 23, 2026. The order establishes a state task force to examine data center proposals. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is allowing farmers and loggers to use tax-exempt diesel fuel in their on-road trucks, amid high fuel prices during the United States’ war with Iran.
In an executive order that took effect on Friday, Moore took an unprecedented step in Maryland, allowing truck drivers hauling products from timber to live poultry to fill their vehicles with “red-dyed” diesel, which is exempt from the state’s motor fuel tax of 47.45 cents per gallon, and the federal excise tax of 24.40 cents per gallon.
“Our agricultural and forestry sectors are the bedrock of our state’s economy, and our administration is dedicated to supporting these vital industries as rising fuel prices put a squeeze on the industry nationwide,” Moore said in a statement issued Friday.
Moore’s order, which declared a state of emergency, will remain in effect for 30 days, but it could be renewed. Unless the governor orders otherwise, the emergency period will not extend beyond Dec. 31. Moore’s order also suspends fees associated with exceptional hauling permits, which allow qualifying vehicles carrying agricultural and forestry products to transport heavier loads on state highways.
Red-dyed diesel is “nearly identical chemically” to regular diesel, according to the order. The red dye is added to signify that the fuel isn’t subject to highway excise taxes, and it’s typically only allowed for use in off-road vehicles and machinery, including tractors and construction equipment.
Maryland’s order came after similar orders in other states, and one from U.S. President Donald Trump. But Maryland officials are still waiting on word about precisely how Trump’s order will be enforced, said Harrison Palmer, chief of staff at the Maryland Department of Agriculture.
As a result, as of Monday morning, officials at the Maryland Department of Agriculture were advising farmers and loggers to avoid using red-dyed diesel in vehicles that plan to cross Maryland’s border, since neighboring states have not allowed the fuel to be used on their highways, Palmer said.
Maryland officials were working on the issue in September, Palmer said. But there were a few kinks to work out between various state agencies, because this was a new step for Maryland.
“We’ve not done something like this before, because we had never been in a situation like this,” Palmer said.
Over the past year, diesel prices have risen about 76.2% in Maryland, according to AAA, reaching $6.467 per gallon on Oct. 5. It comes amid an already difficult year for farmers, Palmer said, as many parts of the state experienced prolonged drought conditions, and a surprise April freeze led to crop losses.
“Everything has sort of been up against you all year, and now — as you’re just trying to get [crops] off the field, you’re getting hit with this enormous fuel bill,” Palmer said.
A high-end estimate indicates that Maryland could lose a maximum of $300,000 per month in tax revenue because of the governor’s move, Palmer said. It’s a price the state is willing to pay, Palmer said.
“We’re making sure that we’re doing right by the folks who are putting food on the table for us every single day,” Palmer said.
The Maryland Farm Bureau had been pushing for state officials to take this step, including in a letter on Sept. 28.
“Diesel is not optional for agriculture,” wrote Maryland Farm Bureau President Jamie Raley. “Feed has to reach animals every day. Livestock have to be moved to market, to processors, and between farms on a schedule set by the animals, not by fuel prices. Timber has to reach mills, and with mill closures in recent years, many of our loggers now drive much farther to find a market.”
Even after Trump’s order, the Farm Bureau continued pushing for Maryland to take action, writing on Facebook: “Dyed diesel fuel is still not legal in our state, and federal action does not automatically waive state fuel taxes or enforcement requirements.”
On Friday evening, the Bureau applauded Moore’s issuance of the executive order.
“We greatly appreciate the state’s action to provide farmers meaningful relief as they face record-high diesel prices at harvest time,” read a statement that the Farm Bureau shared on Facebook.

DOVER — One of 20 educators representing Delaware’s public school districts and charter schools will be named the state’s 2027 Teacher of the Year Tuesday evening.
The Delaware Department of Education will recognize the 20 district and charter Teachers of the Year during an Oct. 13 celebration at the Modern Maturity Center in Dover. The evening will conclude with the announcement of the educator selected to serve as Delaware’s Teacher of the Year.
The nominees were selected by their districts or the Delaware Charter Schools Network during 2026 and recognized for their ability to inspire students, their professional skills and their dedication to teaching.
The honor is intended to recognize an outstanding classroom teacher while also selecting an educator who can represent teachers across the state. Delaware’s winner automatically becomes the state’s nominee for the National Teacher of the Year program.
Twenty educators in the running
This year’s nominees represent elementary, middle and high schools and teach subjects ranging from kindergarten and third grade to science, mathematics, music, social studies, French and special education.

The list illustrates the range of educators considered for the award, from teachers working with some of Delaware’s youngest students to those preparing high school students for college and careers. The Department of Education says the program is designed to recognize educators who can serve as ambassadors for the teaching profession.
A lengthy selection process
Being named a district Teacher of the Year is only the beginning of the statewide selection process.
Each candidate completes an application that includes five essays. Five Department of Education staff members and five former Delaware Teachers of the Year independently review and score the applications.
A former state Teacher of the Year and a department staff member then observe each candidate in the classroom.
An independent panel of judges from outside the Department of Education considers the application scores, classroom observations and a recorded presentation from each candidate before recommending a winner to the secretary of education.
The program seeks educators who are knowledgeable and skilled, inspire students of different backgrounds and abilities, earn the respect of students, parents and colleagues and can represent the profession publicly.
More than a one-night honor
The educator selected Tuesday will become Delaware’s representative in the National Teacher of the Year program, which is administered by the Council of Chief State School Officers.
The state winner also takes on a larger role as an advocate and ambassador for Delaware teachers during the year.
Through action by the Delaware General Assembly, the state Teacher of the Year will receive a $5,000 grant to benefit students and a $3,000 personal grant.
Each of the other 19 district and charter nominees will receive a $2,000 state grant.
The celebration begins with a social hour at 5 p.m., followed by dinner at 6 p.m. The Teacher of the Year announcement is expected after dinner.
For Delawareans who cannot attend, the final portion of the program will be livestreamed, with coverage expected to begin about 7:15 p.m.

description: A former Iowa prison inmate is suing the state’s Department of Corrections over her alleged sexual exploitation by a prison counselor.
