title: Virginia teachers balance AI innovation with student creativity amid rising academic pressure
description: Students face pressure to do well from family expectations, peer competition, college admissions, and a broader achievement-focused culture. Some Virginia education experts say it is leading them to rely on artificial intelligence, at the expense of strengthening their own creative and critical thinking skills. “They want to do well, and so they tend to turn[...]
text:
A laptop is open to ChatGPT during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Students face pressure to do well from family expectations, peer competition, college admissions, and a broader achievement-focused culture. Some Virginia education experts say it is leading them to rely on artificial intelligence, at the expense of strengthening their own creative and critical thinking skills.
“They want to do well, and so they tend to turn to AI as a shortcut to completing assignments or getting assistance,” Alexandria City School Teacher Bernadette Desario said. “While I understand that they want to use that, we still want to see what it is that they know, and we want to see their own creativity and their own thought process.” 
Desario and her colleagues focused on teaching history and social studies attended a recent AI workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus, run by two Virginia Tech professors. 
The event centered on how to use the technology thoughtfully in the classroom, focusing on its capabilities, biases and limitations. 
AI remains one of the most sought-after and heavily criticized technologies available. It has proven useful for processing large amounts of information, making predictions or recommendations, recognizing patterns and automating decisions and actions. 
It also carries risks related to cybersecurity, safety, privacy, fairness, reliability, the workforce and the environment.
Since last summer, Amy Allen and David Hicks, professors in Virginia Tech’s School of Education, have been sharing how generative AI can support critical thinking when educators use it responsibly. 
They pointed out a significant difference in how AI is used in different environments, with digital creators focusing on productivity, while educators key in on discipline.
Allen said many history educators oppose artificial intelligence. But if students use the technology more in the classroom, it’s the job of teachers to equip themselves to utilize it.
Amy Allen, an associate professor in Virginia Tech’s School of Education, is taking questions during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Bernadette Desario, a City of Alexandria history teacher, listens during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)David Hicks, a professor in Virginia Tech’s School of Education, is taking questions during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)Amy Allen, an associate professor in Virginia Tech’s School of Education, is taking questions during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)David Hicks, a professor in Virginia Tech’s School of Education, is taking questions during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)A laptop is open to ChatGPT during an artificial intelligence workshop at the Virginia Tech Innovation Campus in Alexandria. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)
“All of the ideas we have, we hope are a launching point for teachers, and we’re not hoping they go back and do the same things that we’ve shown them, but we are hoping that it broadens their perspective about what can be done,” Allen said. 
Hicks framed the work as helping teachers use AI thoughtfully in history and social studies, not as a shortcut or cure-all.
He also cautioned against AI simulations of historical figures. 
In an example he shared with the Mercury, an Anne Frank-themed chatbot gave antiquated, inappropriate answers to a research prompt, showing how such interactions can whitewash history and downplay difficult experiences.
“(Some people) would argue you could do simulations and think about being advisers and things, but no, that is bordering on the same type of kind of simulations that we’ve seen in the press. … it gets to that same type of trivializing the experience that you’ve got to be wary of,” Hicks said. 
Desario said the session changed her perspective, despite her being an AI novice. She highlighted learning how effective prompting — and drawing on available sources — can generate stronger questions and expand thinking in new directions.
“We are very thankful that we have a group of individuals that are willing to work with teachers and help us using this resource … in a way that makes the most sense and really supports our students,” Desario said.
The Center for Humanities and the Library of Congress’ Teaching with Primary Sources Partner Program made funding for the workshops possible..
Virginia Tech has been studying the use of artificial intelligence, most recently completing a review of CHATGPT Edu, a platform built by OpenAI specifically for higher education institutions to support students, faculty, researchers and campus operations. 
The university is also using AI to study hemorrhagic fever viruses, predict and prevent global pandemics and make transportation safer and more efficient. 
Allen and Hicks, authors of the book “Teaching History with Chatty Geeps,” will continue their workshops in Blacksburg and Abingdon through mid-November.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Trucking industry doubts Trump’s diesel order will dial down fuel prices
description: Road diesel users don’t necessarily have easy access to the tax-free fuel made available to farmers. It’s not typically offered at the truck stops where 18-wheelers and most fleet vehicles fill up their tanks.
text:
A sticker affixed to a gas pump in North Carolina blames President Donald Trump for the high prices. (Photo by Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)In response to record diesel prices, President Donald Trump signed an executive order a week ago to make the tax-free version of the fuel — typically reserved for off-road vehicles, heavy equipment and farm use — available to anyone. But there are doubts within the transportation industry, which by far relies on diesel the most, and among analysts over whether the order will have any impact on their bottom line.
Heading into the weekend, the average U.S. highway-use diesel price was $6.20 per gallon, up nearly $2.50 from a year ago, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The Louisiana average sat at $5.81 per gallon, based on AAA tracking.    
Soon after Trump signed his executive order last Monday during a visit to Nebraska, there were questions about whether truckers and other fleet operators might eventually have to pay taxes on the off-road diesel they buy through the end of the year, when the president’s edict expires. Language in the order directs the U.S. Treasury secretary to “defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations,” stopping well short of waiving the 24.4 cents per gallon it collects.
The Nebraska Trucking Association, representing roughly 900 companies, cautioned members and partners not to fill up with the untaxed, tinted diesel fuel, the Nebraska Examiner reported. 
“We’re being very clear,” president and CEO Kent Grisham said. “Do not put dyed diesel in your tanks — at least not yet.”
Todd Bates, president of the Mississippi Trucking Association, sent an email to its 300 members Wednesday suggesting they set aside 24 cents for every gallon of off-road diesel they buy.
“Treasury has not yet said who owes it, or when, and the order only asks Treasury to look for a way to forgive it,” Bates wrote. “Plan as if you’ll owe it.”  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Henry Hanscom, chief policy and public affairs officer for the American Trucking Association, said in an interview with his group’s news service that he’s awaiting more information about how the order will lower costs for its members.   
“The practical details here matter,” Hanscom said. “The (executive order) directs temporary penalty relief and potential tax deferral, not outright tax forgiveness. We look forward to carefully reviewing the IRS’ implementing guidance once it is available to better understand how this relief will work in practice. Carriers need clear federal and state guidance on eligibility, reporting and any taxes that remain payable.”
Road diesel users don’t necessarily have easy access to the tax-free fuel made available to farmers. It’s not typically offered at the truck stops where 18-wheelers and most fleet vehicles fill up their tanks.
Patrick DeHaan, GasBuddy’s top petroleum analyst, said the president’s order could backfire if there’s a surge in demand for the tax-free diesel that’s dyed red so that law enforcement can detect its unauthorized use by truckers and others.
“The two fuels are the same, and there’s no mystery surge of dyed diesel inventory available, but there is a smaller distribution system, meaning that selling significantly more may negatively impact availability,” DeHaan wrote in his latest Substack entry.
Roughly three-quarters of the diesel fuel available in the United States is used for transportation, according to the U.S Energy Information Administration. That includes 18-wheelers, rail lines, passenger buses, delivery trucks and other fleet vehicles.
The agriculture industry, the primary users of dyed diesel, consumes less than 10%.
In Louisiana, Gov. Jeff Landry issued his own executive order last month that permits dyed diesel use for the road vehicles that farmers and the timber industry use. The president’s order is a more expansive version, with no limitation on who can buy and use it.     
Karl Means owns Razorback Rentals, an aggregate hauling business with 10 trucks based in St. Helena Parish. He said he doesn’t intend to fuel his fleet with dyed diesel because he would eventually have to eat the cost to clean it from his trucks’ tanks.
“Whenever this ends, because it’s not going to be forever, I’ve got dyed fuel now in my fuel tanks that I have to clear out,” Means said. “I have to make sure it’s cleared out so that I don’t get fined down the line whenever this ends.”
Louisiana punishes dyed diesel violations with a fine of $10 for every gallon, based on a truck’s tank size. Louisiana State Police and the state transportation department assist the IRS with dyed diesel enforcement, but none of the agencies could provide data on how many violations they have logged. 
As long as diesel prices remain elevated, the fuel surcharge Means adds to customer bills for each load of material his trucks carry covers less of his costs. The surcharge usually accounts for 90% of his fuel expenses. It’s now down to 75%, forcing him to eat the remaining 25%, he said.
“It’s taking money out of our profits, and then that actually hurts my employees,” Means said. “We’re not able to provide some of the bonuses, the conveniences, the extras we give drivers.”
Means has also noticed higher fuel surcharges on the bills he receives, such as when he needs to have parts shipped to him to maintain his trucks.  
“It’s the price of doing business now,” Means said. “Most customers are accustomed to the fact that there’s a fuel surcharge.”
Trump announced Friday afternoon he had struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market, with Trump suggesting the U.S. could buy some of that supply. Doing so would lift an American ban on Russian petroleum imports that’s been in place since 2022 over Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
The quantity Trump said Russia has pledged is equal to roughly 30 million barrels of fuel. U.S. refineries produce around the same amount of distillate, which includes diesel and heating oil, every six days, based on federal data.
Russia’s ability to export that quantity of diesel is uncertain, as Ukraine has targeted its fuel refineries as a countermeasure for Putin’s continued military incursions.

name: National
title: Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections
description: In the course of a single election cycle, the backlash against data centers has grown from an issue at local planning commission and city council meetings to become a flashpoint in state and federal races across the country. Candidates who once touted data centers as an economic boon have backtracked, and voters in at least three dozen […]
text:
An aerial view shows a data center situated near single-family homes in Northern Virginia. The backlash against data centers has become a flashpoint in state and federal races across the country. (Photo by Nathan Howard/Getty Images)In the course of a single election cycle, the backlash against data centers has grown from an issue at local planning commission and city council meetings to become a flashpoint in state and federal races across the country.
Candidates who once touted data centers as an economic boon have backtracked, and voters in at least three dozen cities, counties and townships will consider ballot measures in November that could ban data centers in their communities. Analysts say the opposition to data centers has come from Republican and Democratic voters alike.
“The people are speaking, and they’re speaking in one voice in opposition to this infrastructure,” said Tatishe Nteta, provost professor of political science at UMass Amherst. “It is not something that people desire in any shape, form or fashion. This potentially could be the issue that gives you the status of a former member of a city council or a former member of Congress.”
Last month, UMass Amherst published a poll, directed by Nteta, showing that only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an artificial intelligence data center in their local community. The poll found that 65% of respondents oppose the construction of such facilities.
Local and national activists have a long list of grievances against data centers, which tech companies are aggressively building to provide the computing power for artificial intelligence platforms. The rapid buildout of data centers is expected to strain the electrical grid and drive up energy costs, some forecasts show.
Opponents are also concerned about the facilities’ pollution, water use, noise and conversion of farmland and other open spaces. Many developers are also building private, “behind-the-meter” natural gas plants to power their data centers, increasing concerns about emissions and public health.
Some activists also object to the artificial intelligence technologies the sites will power, which threaten to disrupt the economy, replace workers, erode critical thinking skills and mental health and even — according to some tech executives — potentially kill all humans.
“For so many years, Ohio rolled out the red carpet to become a tech hub,” said Nick Owens, an attorney with Conserve Ohio, a campaign seeking to block data center development. “Unfortunately, what we’ve become is a tech dump.”
Anger at both parties
Activists across the country have lashed out at elected officials from both parties who have offered state and local tax breaks in order to entice data center developers. They’ve also called out local officials for negotiating deals behind closed doors and signing non-disclosure agreements with large tech companies.
“The politicians are chasing the grassroots, they aren’t leading on the issue,” said Anthony Elmo, public education defender with Good Jobs First, a policy group that tracks government subsidies related to economic development. “(Politicians) who were very pro-data center a year ago are now coming out against them due to political factors.”
As demand for AI rises, so do power thirsty data centers

Tech companies have launched their own political efforts to respond to the backlash. Industry leaders argue that artificial intelligence is key to the nation’s economic competitiveness. They note that the data center boom has created many construction jobs and increased property tax revenue in communities desperate for more money.
Leading the Future, a tech-backed Super PAC, has invested in federal and state campaigns in support of both Republican and Democratic candidates who support artificial intelligence. Josh Vlasto, the group’s co-leader, argued that the narrative around data centers has conflated the industry at large with its worst offenders — speculative projects that disregarded local opposition and failed to meet environmental standards.
“(Voters) want the jobs in their communities, they want the revenue, but they want the risks and downsides mitigated and addressed,” he said. “There is backlash in communities that don’t want them, but if you look to the states that are building and doing it right, these data centers are being welcomed and generating a massive amount of revenue. If this is done correctly, I could see this issue turning drastically in a different direction.”
An investigation earlier this year linked Leading the Future with a news website that used AI bots posing as journalists to solicit quotes for stories that promoted industry talking points. Another investigation found that a dark-money group tied to Leading the Future paid lifestyle influencers to promote artificial intelligence by highlighting the threat of competition from Chinese AI.
The Data Center Coalition, a membership association for tech companies, did not respond to a Stateline interview request. Amazon, Google and OpenAI — industry leaders that have pushed for data center construction — did not respond to Stateline inquiries. Think Big, an associated PAC of Leading the Future that supports Democratic candidates, did not respond to an interview request.
‘People coming together’
Across the United States,  data centers currently use about 49 gigawatts of electricity, according to the website US Data Center Map. New projects planned or under construction total nearly 350 gigawatts — roughly a quarter of the country’s current electrical generation capacity.
While data centers have long powered our online infrastructure, many of the “hyperscale” facilities being built to support artificial intelligence are much larger and use vastly more power.
Ohio has become the political epicenter of the data center backlash. Like many states, Ohio agreed to sales tax exemptions for data centers in the 2010s in order to secure investment from tech companies. In recent years, the state has seen a boom in construction, with 154 operational facilities and 84 more data centers in the works — more than all but three other states.
“Our attraction in Ohio was a very minimal regulatory framework, plentiful farmland and plentiful water,” said Nick Owens, the Conserve Ohio attorney.
Owens, like many data center activists, became engaged on the issue when he learned that a large project was planned in his rural community in Brown County. Owens is a lifelong Republican and was a 2024 delegate for President Donald Trump, who has called data center opponents “backwards and poor.” He said politicians from city councils to the White House have failed to hear residents’ concerns.
“The dysfunction and unresponsiveness of government at all levels is truly sickening and frightening,” he said. “Conversely, it’s one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen, people coming together across communities, putting partisan differences aside and uniting (to oppose data centers).”
Lawmakers fear AI data centers will drive up residents’ power bills

Conserve Ohio has worked with community activists across the state to draft ballot initiatives to ban data centers, change zoning regulations or require voter approval for large facilities. In total, Ohio municipalities will vote on 21 ballot measures related to data centers. Nationwide, 39 measures in eight states will be on the ballot this year, according to Ballotpedia.
In elections earlier this year, four local ballot measures across the country were decided with overwhelming opposition to data centers.
Jen Belt is the leader of Protect Grove City, an Ohio nonprofit backing a ballot measure to block development in that community.
“This is the first issue that I’ve seen Grove City united in such a way,” she said. “It is red, it is blue, it is every age, it is every socioeconomic status. It kind of gives you hope.”
Three communities in Kansas will vote on data center bans in November, including Ottawa, a city in the eastern portion of the state where residents have fought back against a proposed data center. Michael Lewis, with the nonprofit group Ottawa United, which has led the campaign, said locals were outraged when city commissioners announced the planned development.
“Everything was negotiated without public input, it was all done behind closed doors until they brought it out and approved it,” he said.
Lewis serves as vice chair of the Franklin County Democratic Party and is running for state representative. But the data center backlash has been so strong that his allies on the issue include the secretary of the Franklin County Republican Party and GOP state Rep. Rebecca Schmoe, his opponent in the general election.
Issue in statewide races
The issue has been a focal point of statewide races as well. U.S.  Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican, has come under attack for championing tax breaks for data centers during his time as lieutenant governor. His Democratic opponent, former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown, has run ads calling him “the face of data centers.”
Last month, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that data centers are “the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” The Washington Post reported. Husted has drafted a bill that would require state utility regulators to consider making data centers pay to cover the costs of their own electrical infrastructure needs. Senate Democrats blocked the bill last month, calling it “toothless” political messaging.
In Pennsylvania, both gubernatorial candidates have distanced themselves from their previous support for data centers. Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, until recently a staunch data center advocate, issued a moratorium on new data center permits last month, amid attacks from his Democratic opponent.
“Republican candidates know this is a losing issue and one that can do damage to their already questionable electoral positions,” said Nteta, the political science professor. “It’s a unique issue that brings together Americans in ways we don’t usually see.”
Vlasto, with the pro-data center Super PAC, said candidates calling for statewide bans on data centers are overcorrecting.
“Each community is going to make their choice,” he said. “Some communities are just not going to welcome data centers. From a political position, it doesn’t seem like preventing communities that want to build data centers is a palatable position either.”
Elmo, with Good Jobs First, said even longtime data center opponents are surprised at how quickly they have become a top political issue. He said tech companies and politicians who once promoted data centers have now joined calls for “responsible” development.
“This issue puts (politicians) between a rock and a hard place between the grassroots and their wealthy tech donors,” he said. “If the industry you’re trying to regulate immediately agrees with everything you’re suggesting to regulate them, I’d suggest that those regulations are not extremely effective.”
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

Signs on the Newport courthouse square in west central Indiana signal opposition to data centers on Oct. 4, 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)It felt like a gut punch when Jacob Coxon, a researcher with Anthropic focused on expanding artificial intelligence capabilities, publicly resigned to underscore the threat to humanity AI posed and the reckless nature in which the U.S.’s largest tech firms are advancing it. Rather than disputing those claims, executives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft all emphasized the need to pace AI’s development within the bounds of safety. In other words, we need AI to work for us — not against us.
“If the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing,” said Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft.
Despite community pushback, the rapid buildout of AI infrastructure in Indiana is mirroring the reckless advancement of AI capabilities that Bill Gates, Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have raised alarm bells about. According to CNBC, Indiana ranks 4th among states for data center build attractiveness and a recent report by Good Jobs First revealed that Amazon alone benefited from $561 million in Indiana sales tax exemptions in 2025.
Even if the panacea of a safe AI that uplifts humanity and human health is realized, we must also build its infrastructure sustainably to protect the air we breathe, the water that gives life and minimize the climate pollution that magnifies the societal challenges we face. At a time when AI advancement seems to be spinning beyond our control, there are things we can do to affect local outcomes. The framework of pause, plan and protect describes how residents and local officials can shape beneficial investment.
Details on long-expected Meta data center campus unveiled

It is critical to take time or pause to understand the long-term resource demands and environmental impacts of AI data centers. A single AI data center may exceed the energy demands of a city the size of Indianapolis and both their cooling systems and new gas power generation can be significant water users. Without careful study and monitoring of things like river flow and the water table, communities won’t know the impact to local wells, agriculture, aquatic ecosystems and other areas that rely on a plentiful water supply.  Transparent information about water discharge is also critical to make sure harmful substances are removed before returning to the water cycle.
In many instances data centers are extending the life of the costliest and dirtiest form of energy — coal. Coal not only impacts our health and environment, its extended use also increases our electricity bills. Off grid power, such as the reciprocating gas engines proposed for Meta’s data center campus in Boone County, is both noisy and dirtier than grid-connected energy. And massive resources of energy and water will need to be supported by additional infrastructure. What will be the comprehensive costs of that infrastructure and who will pay for it? Communities deserve to know how AI data centers will be powered, the impact to their air, water, and health, and who will pay for the comprehensive infrastructure costs associated with it. If you don’t know the answers to these questions, it’s a good time to pause any approvals until you have answers.
Proactive planning to attract the type of development communities want can attract more sustainable investments. Setting clear expectations through ordinances and public communication, that maximize new clean energy, preserve sensitive natural areas, and require transparency around water use and discharge, lets developers know what is expected. In Minnesota, a new Google data center is supported by 1,600 megawatts of renewables, 300 MW of long-term storage, and a $50 million investment in small local batteries that will help control costs and make the grid more resilient. A plan to attract wanted investment will bring better results than responding to unwanted projects.
Enforceable protection and safeguards are needed to ensure a planned investment delivers on its commitments. In addition to a strong ordinance, communities should build monitoring into their agreements and developer commitments. State requirements through the Indiana Department of Environmental Management lack robust monitoring so monitoring must be done by reputable third parties approved of by the community. Air quality, water discharge, aquifer levels, stream flows, investment commitments and anything else developers commit to need effective monitoring and accountability measures. Monitoring accompanied by incentives for fulfillment, accountability for failure and a legal path for enforcement, provides needed protection in the face of irresponsible or failed developments.
At a time when many feel we are under attack from AI and the data centers that support it, it’s critical that we take time to pause to understand the impacts of new data center development; plan to attract the type of sustainable investment communities want; and protect communities through strong ordinances, monitoring, and enforcement. There is much that we cannot control when it comes to the rollout of AI, but in Indiana, through our local government structure and strong community engagement, we can shape development and investment outcomes.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Audit of Rhode Island’s housing office finds missing records, expired grants and oversight gaps
description: Two years after federal monitors found numerous problems with how grant money was tracked and spent by state housing officials, a new audit echoes many of those same problems.  The 25-page report published Sept. 29 by the state’s Office of Internal Audit and Program Integrity found that the Rhode Island Executive Office of Housing (EOH) […]
text:
A home under construction in Providence's Silver Lake neighborhood in May 2026. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Two years after federal monitors found numerous problems with how grant money was tracked and spent by state housing officials, a new audit echoes many of those same problems. 
The 25-page report published Sept. 29 by the state’s Office of Internal Audit and Program Integrity found that the Rhode Island Executive Office of Housing (EOH) failed to record nearly $2.8 million in federal funds and left more than $200,000 in grant money undrawn after the grants expired. Auditors attributed the problems to a lack of clear procedures for tracking grants and monitoring the organizations that received the money.
“The absence of formalized procedures and standardized templates has resulted in a lack of clarity and uniformity in grant management practices, contributing to inconsistent implementation and incomplete compliance with federal and state requirements,” Andrew Manca, the state’s chief of internal audits, wrote in the report.
Housing officials say they have begun addressing the problems, though some changes were still awaiting formal adoption by the time the audit was completed.
“Several corrective actions have already been implemented, and the remaining items are progressing toward completion,“ Emily Marshall, spokesperson for the Executive Office of Housing, wrote in an email to Rhode Island Current.
Housing officials set an Oct. 31 deadline to address the remaining issues, according to the audit.
The state’s audit examined the Executive Office of Housing’s management of about $54.2 million in federal and state grants from July through December 2025.
As part of the review, auditors looked closely into four federal grants that expired between 2022 and 2025. They found $202,710 in funds were not drawn because organizations receiving the grants did not submit eligible expenses. As of June 2026, the state’s grant management system had not been updated to reflect the status of those funds.
The report notes housing officials said they had asked the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to extend those grants, but could not provide auditors with documentation of the requests.
Marshall said that HUD’s Boston regional office approved extensions for the affected grants on Oct. 1, allowing the projects to continue. 
She added that the office mandated quarterly reviews of all federal grants for fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, 2026. Program and financial staff will review how much has been spent, how much money has been received and how much remains available.
Auditors also found the housing office failed to consistently record federal grant deposits in the state’s accounting system, as is required upon receiving the funds.
Unrecorded funds do not represent money lost by the state, as any federal deposits that remain unrecorded at the end of the fiscal year are transferred to a state escrow account. But Manca wrote the failure to record them increased the risk of inaccurate financial reporting.
Marshall attributed the delays to the state’s transition from its old accounting system to a new enterprise resource planning system. She said housing officials addressed the discrepancies by June 30, 2026, with remaining amounts recorded in July.
The state audit comes after HUD in 2024 flagged weaknesses in Rhode Island’s oversight of federal housing grants. That analysis found Rhode Island housing officials failed to keep adequate records of how some COVID-era grant money was spent, track who benefited from the funds and ensure the money wasn’t duplicating other assistance.
The HUD review covered funds received between 2021 and 2023, mostly before the housing office became a standalone agency.
“After this came out in 2024, our office reviewed the findings and concerns and were in communication with HUD about how we understood the work to have been in compliance or have addressed and resolved them,” Marshall said.
Rep. June Speakman, a Warren Democrat who chairs the House Commission on Housing Affordability, said she was concerned about the housing office’s tracking of grant money but couldn’t tell from the state’s audit whether the accounting problems stemmed from agency shortcomings or the transition to a new state financial system.
Speakman also pointed to leadership turnover and staffing challenges at the housing office, which became a standalone agency in 2023 after bouncing from the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation to the Department of Administration. 
“I would not be surprised if it took it a minute to get some systems in place to make sure that they were complying with all the federal rights and all the auditor’s requirements,” Speakman said.
The agency, originally established as the Department of Housing, was renamed the Executive Office of Housing in 2025 under Secretary Deborah Goddard as part of an effort to consolidate state housing oversight.
Speakman said Goddard has brought more staff on board than the office had under its two previous leaders. The housing office had 17 employees in early 2023 and 26 by May 2024. Marshall confirmed that the agency now has 31 employees.
Still, Speakman cautioned that she could not independently assess the agency’s performance. Based on the office’s responses to the audit, she said, it appeared officials were addressing the concerns.
“It seems to me that they’re on it,” she said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Why older lawmakers may wait too long to step aside
description: This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article. U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century. His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, shown at a Senate Judiciary Committee meeting on Thursday, July 23, 2026, is 93. He hasn’t said whether he’s going to run again in 2028. (Screenshot from committee webcast)
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century. His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the Sept. 1, 2026, primary anyway by nearly 30 percentage points.
He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections. The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican.
It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9.
My colleagues and I study succession in family-run businesses and other occupations where leadership, identity and longevity can become deeply intertwined. Whether someone is in charge of a company or is a lawmaker, their work does not only keep them busy. It provides status, an identity and a sense of mission. Letting go means giving up more than a job.
When business leaders or politicians linger for too long, it can be costly for their companies or constituents because potential successors may become frustrated by waiting and decide to move on.
When any kind of leader remains in their role for decades, underlying reasons can range from a genuine love for what they do to not knowing what they will do – or who they will be – once they leave. However, waiting too long can mean they’ll have to hand off their responsibilities in crisis mode.
In family businesses, my research team found, the people closest to their leaders – including relatives, employees and longtime supporters – may go quiet rather than press the issue.
This dynamic is not limited to the business world. It also applies to many of the older members of Congress.
A closer look at the large numbers of legislators who continue to serve during their golden years reflects two trends.
First, many are elected for the first time when they’re middle-aged. New House members were about 50 years old and new senators around 55 in 2025.
Second, although the median age of House lawmakers is now about 60, and 66 in the Senate, there’s a small group of long-serving members who remain in office into and past their 80s and keep running for reelection.
 Seeing the advantages of ‘not yet’

Every lawmaker can have a reason to say “not yet.” So can their staff members, who may be loyal to them and their missions and professionally invested in the work they have built together.
Political parties value the electoral advantages of incumbents, while constituents may value the seniority, relationships and influence that come with having spent decades serving in Congress. And incumbents can sincerely believe important work remains unfinished.
However, unusually prolonged service in any position increases the possibility that illness, cognitive decline or death will lead to an unplanned and probably rocky transition.
What’s more, when politicians serve into their late 70s, 80s or beyond, they are breaking with ordinary employment patterns.
The typical American retires in their early 60s, with two-thirds of U.S. workers exiting the labor force before their 65th birthday.

 Setting good and bad examples

There are examples of long-serving politicians choosing to plan their exit closer to standard retirement age.
One is Barbara Boxer. After more than three decades in Congress, the 74-year-old California Democrat announced in January 2015 that she would not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate the following year. “There is a time when you want the next generation to step in and step up,” she said.
Boxer’s early decision gave prospective successors nearly two years to organize and voters the opportunity to choose among them. Kamala Harris won the seat but stepped away to serve as President Joe Biden’s vice president.
This departure offers a striking contrast with that of Boxer’s longtime colleague, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who remained in the Senate through a lengthy health-related absence in 2023. Feinstein, also a California Democrat, died in office that September. She was 90 years old.
She served on the influential Senate Judiciary Committee, which considers federal judicial nominations, including Supreme Court nominees. During her nearly three-month absence, the committee was deadlocked on dozens of Biden nominations after Republicans refused to let the Democrats appoint a temporary replacement for her and she refused to step down.
The tragic way Feinstein’s storied political career ended illustrated what can go wrong when lawmakers keep saying “not yet” until it’s too late.
That turned out to be the case with Biden, who reluctantly ended his presidential reelection campaign in July 2024. However, several books published since then include details about how his inner circle initially advised him to run again.
A rushed attempt at succession followed Biden’s abrupt withdrawal from the race. Harris became the Democratic nominee without participating in any of the 2024 primaries.
When change finally came, it arrived under duress rather than by design. And Harris lost the election to Donald Trump.
Kentucky Republican U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, 84, a former Senate majority and minority leader, is shown with his wife, former Secretary of Labor and Secretary of Transportation Elaine Chao, in July. He was in a rehabilitation center recovering from a fall that required hospitalization a month earlier. He plans to step down when his current term ends in January 2027. (Photo provided by U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell’s office)
 Fearing what might follow

U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, announced in 2023 that she would not seek reelection the following year. It soon became clear that severe health problems were preventing her from serving her constituents.
The former House Appropriations Committee chair didn’t cast a vote in her final six months in office for a good reason: She had dementia and was staying in a Texas assisted-living facility that provided memory care services to some residents. Granger died in August 2026 at 83.
U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, a former Senate majority and minority leader, has announced that he will step down when his current term – the Kentucky Republican’s seventh – ends in January 2027. But a fall, hospitalization and subsequent stint in a rehabilitation center in mid-2026 prompted renewed public scrutiny of the 84-year-old’s health and ability to complete his term.
U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, who turned 93 on Sept. 17, 2026, and appears to be in good health, has not yet said whether he’s running for a ninth six-year term in 2028. But the Republican, who is the oldest person serving in Congress, has urged his constituents to vote for a Republican for governor.
“I don’t plan on dying in office, but if I did, I don’t want a Democratic governor choosing my successor,” Grassley said at a political event in Des Moines in late September 2026.
 Learning from palliative care

My colleagues and I found an unlikely way to think differently about leadership transitions: considering lessons about letting go from palliative care.
Leaving political office or another leadership role, of course, is not the same as dying. But, as is true before someone develops a terminal medical condition, advance planning is most useful while people can still articulate what matters to them and exercise meaningful choices about what comes next.
I’ve learned that it’s a mistake to treat succession as something to discuss only when a leader must move on for health or other reasons. So, in addition to my work as a management professor, and to inform my research, as well as the workshops I hold for aging business owners and members of their inner circles, I have been trained as an end-of-life doula. I decided to do this because I lacked the vocabulary and tools that facilitated difficult conversations and decisions about their legacy and what is important to the leader as they let go.
Palliative care supports the act of letting go long before death – the same challenge confronting business leaders and the companies they run.
When voters consider whether to vote for an aging incumbent, they may wonder whether that lawmaker is already too old for their demanding job or soon will be. But that may be the wrong question. It might be better to ask whether the legislators who represent you, no matter their age, have a plan for letting go.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Democrats hope Beau Bayh leads them from political wilderness
description: Beau Bayh professes unconcern about any weight upon him for lifting Indiana Democrats from the political woes they’ve suffered for more than a decade.
text:
Democratic secretary of state candidate Beau Bayh speaks with a supporter during a Democratic Party volunteer rally in Fishers, Indiana, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Tom Davies/Indiana Capital Chronicle)This is the first of four profiles in Indiana’s secretary of state race.
Beau Bayh professes no anxiety about expectations that he lift Indiana Democrats from the political woes they’ve suffered for more than a decade.
That expectation comes for the secretary of state candidate as the son and grandson of the state’s most prominent Democratic figures stretching back some 60 years.
“I don’t feel pressure to win for my political party,” Bayh said while sitting on a bench outside a recent Democratic volunteer rally at a Fishers community center.


About Beau Bayh
Age: 30
Residence: Indianapolis
Education: Bachelor’s and law degrees from Harvard University
Occupation: Attorney with Indianapolis law firm MacGill PC since fall 2025
Previous: Served in the Marine Corps, honorably discharged in 2024 with rank of captain. Worked as a law clerk for a Bloomington-based federal appeals court judge in 2024-25


“I feel pressure every time I talk to a mom, a young mom, throughout our state, who has had to travel across county lines or across state lines even to give birth in a hospital because of Medicaid cuts paid for by tax cuts for the rich,” he said. “I feel pressure when I talk to kids in the public schools that are not getting the support that they need. … That is the pressure I feel, and that’s a good type of pressure because that’s why I’m doing this, to help people like that.”
Online critics have derided the 30-year-old Bayh as a “nepo baby” and Republican nominee Max Engling labeled him “a prep school kid with a familiar name” for growing up in the Washington area after his father, Evan Bayh, was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1998.
Others, however, have goodwill for the Bayh family that includes Beau’s grandfather, the late Birch Bayh who served in the U.S. Senate during 1963-81, and Beau’s mother Susan Bayh, who was 61 when she died of brain cancer in 2021.
“I was lucky enough to meet Beau’s mother many years ago, so I’m really hoping for him to be able to win,” said June Levey, a retired medical billing worker who was among about 100 people at a recent Democratic rally in Fishers.
“I’ve had a lot of opportunities”
Evan Bayh was in his seventh year as Indiana governor when Beau — full name Birch Evans Bayh IV — and his twin brother Nick were born the day after Election Day 1995 at an Indianapolis hospital.
From the time Beau Bayh first announced his candidacy last October at Holliday Park in Indianapolis (which has an outdoor classroom named in his mother’s memory), he’s faced questions about benefiting from his political legacy.
“Who would I be if I didn’t make the most of the advantages I’ve been given in my life?” he said at the time. “Look, I’ve had a lot of opportunities given to me and to people who are to receive a lot of blessings, much is expected.” 
Bayh grew up in the Washington area after the family moved there when he was three years old following his father’s U.S. Senate election in 1998. 
The family remained in the D.C. area after Evan Bayh’s Senate retirement in 2011, with Beau and Nick graduating from the private St. Albans School in 2014.
Beau Bayh, left, sits next to his father, former governor and U.S. Sen. Evan Bayh, and his brother, Nick, while awaiting voting results during the Indiana Democratic Convention on June 6, 2026, in Indianapolis. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Both brothers then went on to Harvard, where Beau majored in government and got sporadic playing time with the varsity lacrosse team.
His next step after 2018 Harvard graduation was to join the Marine Corps, completing officer training before enrolling in Harvard Law School in 2020. He took a leave from law school in 2021-22 for Marine Corps active duty and was honorably discharged from the reserves as a captain in November 2023.
Throughout his Harvard and Marine Corps years, Bayh voted in Indiana elections — mostly by mail — using an Indianapolis condominium owned by his father as his registration address. 
Bayh moved full-time to Indiana after his 2024 Harvard Law School graduation. He gained an Indiana law license and worked as a law clerk for federal appeals court Judge David Hamilton (who previously was the top governor’s office lawyer under Evan Bayh) in Bloomington for a year until August 2025.
He now owns a condominium near downtown Indianapolis and works for the five-attorney law firm MacGill PC.
Bayh’s rise comes with criticism
Republicans dole out criticism of Bayh over his East Coast upbringing and his reliance on big-dollar campaign contributions from donors tied to his father.
Engling also argues Bayh’s resume is thin when compared to his own that’s highlighted by a dozen years in Washington as a GOP congressional staffer.
That was followed by time as a top aide to U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, whose endorsement in May helped propel him to defeating current Secretary of State Diego Morales for the Republican nomination.
“I don’t hold it against Beau for his parents taking him away to Washington. That’s how life works,” Engling told the Capital Chronicle. “But I would say, maybe, come back to Indiana, understand what it means to be a Hoosier, live life here for a little bit. … I think he should take more time to experience that and learn that before he decides to jump into his first real professional job, which would be secretary of state if he gets across the finish line.”
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates and tools you need to cast your vote.]
Bayh bristled at such criticism when asked about it during an interview at a bakery near his Indianapolis home.
“I hope Max Engling is not denigrating the service of the Americans that have served in our United States military,” he said. “I was in command of a few hundred Marines. I don’t think Max Engling has ever had that responsibility placed on his shoulders. Being a staffer in Washington, D.C., and a part of the gridlock of our Congress, I don’t think makes you qualified to run for a statewide elected position. Much less so than someone who’s been in command of men and women who raise their right hand to serve our country.”
Bayh also spurns the presumption that he plans to use the  secretary of state’s office as a stepping stone to a higher position — possibly following his father’s career path of winning election in 1986 at age 30 as secretary of state and then successfully running for governor two years later.
Bayh said the office’s role in overseeing statewide election policy gives it a vital role in “our country’s most precious resource, our democratic process.”
“This is too important of a job to be thinking about anything else other than doing it,” he said. “So I’m running for this office to do a good job in this office and that’s that. That’s what Hoosiers deserve.”
Bayh’s TV ads knock Republicans for tolerating what he calls corrupt spending by Morales in the secretary of state’s office and he pushes issues such as seeking to end straight-ticket voting and establish citizen-led ballot initiatives.
 But the spots also have him touting topics such as data center regulation and support for tax cuts that are outside the office’s responsibilities.
Candidacy gives Democrats “whole different momentum”
Many Democrats see him as their party’s best hope in years to break a streak that has seen Republicans go 23-0 in statewide elections since 2014 — a streak that includes Evan Bayh’s failed 2016 Senate comeback bid.
Beau Bayh meets with the media at Holliday Park in Indianapolis on Oct. 6, 2025. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Bayh won the party’s nomination in June despite some convention delegates wanting a more progressive candidate they argued would better energize voters. He’s also faced Republican jeers for sometimes not identifying himself as a Democrat in his advertising.
On the day Bayh formally announced his candidacy last October, longtime Democratic Hammond Mayor Tom McDermott said Bayh could revive the party’s prospects in the state where campaigns such as his own for the U.S. Senate in 2022 failed to gain traction.
“He’s got everything going for him — last name, he’s going to be well financed. He’s smart as hell. He’s a veteran,” McDermott said. “If he can’t do well, that is going to be demoralizing for the party.”
Hamilton County Democratic Chair Josh Lowry said after the rally in Fishers that having Bayh heading up the party’s statewide ticket gives “a whole different momentum” for Democrats.
“You have a guy come in that’s a Marine who’s just focused relentlessly on ‘we’re going to crack this corruption up,’ and then you have his name,” Lowry said. “It just feels like he’s the right candidate for the right moment. He’s got the energy, the motivation. I just feel like if you drew a candidate up for this specific year in this cycle, he’s the right guy.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Public school districts reminded to accept EFA recipients for free
description: Beginning this school year, education freedom account recipients will be allowed to take classes, join sports teams, and participate in clubs and extracurriculars at their resident public school district — without paying extra.  The change, brought about with the passage of House Bill 1817, was hailed by school choice supporters as a way to empower […]
text:
"The department’s advisory makes clear that public school districts must now provide EFA recipients with access to classes and programs, unless it determines they are at capacity." (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)Beginning this school year, education freedom account recipients will be allowed to take classes, join sports teams, and participate in clubs and extracurriculars at their resident public school district — without paying extra. 
The change, brought about with the passage of House Bill 1817, was hailed by school choice supporters as a way to empower EFA students and denounced by public school advocates as a mechanism that would force schools to provide services without reimbursement. 
It is now up to school districts to comply. 
On Sept. 25, the state Department of Education issued an advisory to schools stating that “each school district should review its enrollment, participation and fee policies” in accordance with the new law.
Launched in 2021, the education freedom account program allows New Hampshire families to receive around $5,000 of state education funding per year to help pay for private school or home education expenses. 
Previously, EFA students required special permission to use public school resources, and some public schools imposed tuition for that access. The department’s advisory makes clear that public school districts must now provide EFA recipients with access to classes and programs, unless it determines they are at capacity.
That list includes curricular courses and co-curricular programs, such as clubs, sports teams, performing groups and career technical education programs.
It also includes standardized tests, such as the statewide assessments given to public school students in middle school and high school, and the preliminary scholastic aptitude test (PSAT).
“This change, which will take effect starting in the 2026-2027 school year, is likely to increase the number of EFA students who elect to participate in activities in their resident district public school,” the department noted in its guidance.
But the law contains a key caveat: If EFA participants, or other nonpublic school students, are enrolled in 50% or more of the instructional time offered by the public school, they will be considered full-time public school students. 
And when it comes to determining what activity breaches that 50% mark, the state is giving school boards flexibility. 
“Local districts should ensure that their own district policies define instructional time and what 50% enrollment means for each district school or grade level,” the department’s advisory notes.
That means districts could choose a time-based approach, where the number of hours of instructional time a non-enrolled student takes part in cannot exceed 50%; a course-load approach, where the number of courses can’t exceed 50% of all courses available; or a credit-based approach, where the number of credits cannot exceed 50% of those possible.
The law applies only to EFA recipients who live in the school district; public schools are still allowed to charge tuition to out-of-district students for courses or programs. 
Additionally, the guidance notes, school districts are not required to accept non-enrolled students into classes that are “at or near capacity” with enrolled students. That should be determined by whether it would take additional resources or staff to accept non-enrolled students, the guidance notes.
And the law does not require schools to accept non-enrolled students into every program; EFA students must still meet the entry requirements for honors classes or advanced sports teams, for instance. 
However, if there is space, the districts are not allowed to treat EFA students differently when they choose whom to accept.
The new law gives EFA recipients rights that non-EFA-receiving homeschooled students have had for years. Public schools have long been required to accept those students as long as the students did not exceed the 50% instructional time limit.
But the extension to EFA students contains one substantial difference. When home-schooled students enroll in public school programs, New Hampshire’s school funding formula allows those schools to request the state reimburse them on a pro-rated, per-credit basis. For every one credit a homeschooled student receives, the school receives 15% of the amount the state would send a full-time student. 
Public schools will not receive that reimbursement for EFA students under the expansion this year. 
Addressing lawmakers in the spring over HB 1817, Department of Education Bureau of School Finance Administrator Mark Manganiello noted that providing that 15% reimbursement for EFA recipients would require the state to pay twice — once for the value of that student’s EFA account and again for the courses offered by the public school district. Lawmakers did not add in a reimbursement mechanism to the law. 
The lack of reimbursement has raised concerns from opponents, including the New Hampshire School Boards Association, that the law will shortchange public school districts by allowing students who don’t count toward the district’s per-student reimbursement to use the district’s services.
“Currently, families can access school district programs for their students now by using their ‘Education Freedom Account’ voucher to pay for those resources,” the National Education Association of New Hampshire, the state’s largest teachers union, wrote in a statement opposing the bill. 
Meanwhile, even if the lack of reimbursement means the state is not double-paying, the taxpayers in the school district are, the NEA argued. 
“… Local taxpayers will pay twice — once for a voucher and again for classes provided by the local public school.” 
To supporters of the move, though, the change addresses a different unfairness: the inability for EFA-recipient families living and paying school property taxes in a school district to access that district’s programs for free.
“New Hampshire has long valued responsibility, local connection, and parental commitment,” reads a post on the Children’s Scholarship Fund, the nonprofit organization that contracts with the state to run the EFA program. “Families who choose flexible educational models continue contributing to the public education system through local property taxes while often assuming additional financial responsibility to create the learning environment that works best for their children.”
In an opinion piece in the New Hampshire Journal, Kate Baker Demers, executive director of that organization, deployed an analogy. 
“Imagine paying dues to a local recreation center for years,” she wrote. “Your money maintains the basketball courts, the fields, and the after-school programs. Then, one day, your child tries to sign up for the youth league and gets turned away because your family does not use the facility full-time. Most people would call that unfair.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Court blocks SNAP penalties, clarifies eligibility, but advocates still worried
description: A recent court ruling may have saved states from "potentially ruinous financial penalties" related to changes in SNAP rules, but advocates worry that thousands of Maryland families may still lose coverage as they try to navigate the changes.
text:
Thousands of immigrant families have already lost access to federal food assistance due to shifting eligibility restrictions based on documentation status. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)A recent court ruling may have saved states from “potentially ruinous financial penalties” related to changes in SNAP rules, but advocates worry that thousands of Maryland families may still lose coverage as they try to navigate the changes.
Those changes stem from provisions in H.R. 1 — the One, Big Beautiful Bill Act — that affect individuals’ eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and states’ management of the program. At stake for immigrant families is the availability of food assistance; for the states, potentially hundreds of millions of penalties if they fall short of the new rules.
Both groups got a break when U.S. District Judge Mustafa T. Kasubhai in Oregon on Sept. 17 sided with 22 states and the District of Columbia, which argued new restrictions on SNAP eligibility ran afoul of federal regulations and arbitrarily barred some non-citizens from receiving food assistance.
And while Kasubhai’s ruling may provide clarity over which immigrants are barred from SNAP and which ones qualify, advocates for immigrants and food assistance programs say the uncertainty and the fear stoked in immigrant communities is driving some people away from federal programs, even the ones they qualify for.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture, which manages SNAP, “tried to read the SNAP law in a way that shut out refugees, asylees, humanitarian immigrants out of SNAP even after they became lawful permanent residents,” said Ray Serrano, national director of research and policy at the League of United Latin American Citizens. “The court said, ‘No, they have a green card. They qualify for SNAP.’
“This ruling clarifies who can get SNAP … but I think the fear and the chilling effect from it is still going to be there,” Serrano said.
Mixed-status immigrant households expected to lose benefits under new public charge rule

Prior to H.R. 1, certain categories of noncitizen immigrants were allowed to receive SNAP benefits, such as those who entered the country as refugees or had been granted asylum, as well as some who were granted humanitarian parole.
H.R. 1, which was signed into law on July 4, 2025, limited SNAP eligibility to immigrants lawfully admitted for permanent residence, Cuban and Haitian entrants, and individuals lawfully residing in the United States in accordance with a Compact of Free Association. The USDA issued clarifying guidance to states in the months that followed.
In a complaint filed against the administration in November, Maryland and the other states claimed the USDA issued a memorandum in October that “misleadingly” provides that some noncitizen populations were not eligible for SNAP unless they obtained lawful permanent resident (LPR) status, commonly known as “green card holders.”
States argued that H.R. 1 and follow-up guidance from the administration arbitrarily excluded immigrants in “humanitarian immigrant groups” from receiving benefits. Groups identified as ineligible for SNAP, unless they have a green card, included Certain American Indians Born Abroad, Conditional Entrants, Battered Aliens, and Victims of Severe Trafficking and Certain Family Members.
But the guidance also suggests that immigrants who are refugees, individuals granted asylum, parolees and other humanitarian immigrant groups are categorically not eligible, without an acknowledgement that those immigrants could also receive SNAP if they receive green card status.
“Irrespective of someone’s immigration status before becoming an LPR, once they obtain their Green Card, they are eligible for SNAP if they meet other statutory requirements,” the states argued in their November complaint.
Kasubhai agreed that the October 2025 guidance from the administration was “arbitrary and capricious” and ran contrary to the law, affirming that humanitarian immigrant groups can receive SNAP benefits if they become get green cards, just as other noncitizen categories.
“The Non-Citizen Guidance itself provides no explanation as to why Humanitarian Immigrant Groups are omitted from the list of non-citizen groups that are … eligible for SNAP if they are an LPR,” Kasubhai wrote. “The Court’s judgment will reflect that LPRs are eligible for SNAP regardless of prior status.”

It’s not clear how many Maryland households the court decision could apply to, but provisions in H.R.1 have already disrupted SNAP benefits for more than 4,500 households that no longer have access to meal assistance due to citizenship status under the legislation, according to data from the Maryland Department of Human Services.
The states’ filing against the H.R. 1 rules reported that Maryland agencies “experienced a twenty-five percent increase in calls from residents affected by the Non-Citizen Guidance.”
“Families are depending on SNAP … It’s our nation’s and our state’s first line of defense against hunger,” said LaMonika Jones, director of Maryland Hunger Solutions. “When a household … becomes eligible, and ineligible, and they lose access, that increases a household’s economic instability, their financial instability, their food insecurity.”
Jones says that Maryland families are struggling to keep up with the shifting eligibility requirements to qualify for SNAP, which can have devastating impacts.
“Since H.R. 1 passed in July of 2025, we’ve had close to 40,000 (Maryland) households lose access to SNAP … that includes households with children,” Jones said. “They’re going to have to use whatever additional money they have to now cover the cost of food, which means that something else in their household budget will have to get cut.”
Kasubhai’s decision also prohibits administrative errors issued under the USDA’s October noncitizen guidance from being calculated in a state’s “payment error rate,” which will determine how much states have to pay. The Trump administration failed to give states adequate time to adhere to the guidance as required by federal regulation, the judge wrote.
“Defendants have placed Plaintiffs in an impossible situation to timely implement H.R. 1’s changes to SNAP though contradictory, absent, and misleading messaging,” Kasubhai said in the decision. “Defendants now seek to penalize Plaintiffs’ inability to overcome that impossibility by retroactively setting an exclusionary period that gives rise to potentially ruinous financial penalties.”
Maryland may be steeply penalized after reducing SNAP payment error rates

USDA regulations allow states a 120-day grace period to implement new rules under SNAP so states can incorporate those changes without fear that administrative errors during the adjustment period will contribute to the payment error rate. Under H.R. 1, states with high error rates face steep financial penalties based on the payment error rates in the current fiscal year.
The guidance, issued on October 31, 2025, declared that the 120-exclusionary period started on July 4, 2025, when H.R. 1 took effect — meaning the grace period would be over Nov. 1, one day after the guidance came out.
“The exclusionary period is also arbitrary and capricious for failing to provide fair notice to Plaintiffs,” Kasubhai wrote. “Defendants did not release their interpretation until well after the enactment of H.R. 1.”
The stakes are high for states. The federal government currently covers the full costs of SNAP benefits, but starting next year, the feds will only cover the full cost of benefits for those state with error rates below 6.00 in this year or last. States with error rates of 6.00 or higher will have to pay the cost of benefits — 5%, 10% or 15% depending on how high the error rate is, with certain exceptions.
Maryland’s payment error rate for federal fiscal 2025 was 13.08, leaving the state on the hook to pay more than $240 million in SNAP benefits starting in 2027 unless the error rate improves this year.
“When a state is undergoing an evaluation … this type of issue is counted as an error against a state agency,” Jones said. “That means it potentially will increase the state’s payment error rate, which means there’s more state costs that will have to be covered to continue to administer SNAP.
“This administration … is not giving state agencies the proper time they need to implement it to make sure the program is running efficiently and effectively, so that we can reduce payment error rates,” she said. “If we truly want to do that, then we have to make sure we’re giving states the applicable time to implement the guidance.”
But Jones and Serrano believe that instability in trying to qualify for SNAP under new federal policies will have a greater immediate impact to Maryland’s immigrant families.
“Restrictions on refugees, asylees, any humanitarian immigrant on SNAP benefits, I think it’s one of the cruelest things you could do. It’s families, it’s children that are being cut out,” Serrano said. “The implications is that families just don’t have food. They don’t have food assistance so they either go to food banks or they don’t eat.”
